The real cost of a permanent chain is that it needs rules it did not have: a cycle must be impossible at the merge (a merge is refused when the chosen survivor resolves to the person being absorbed — checked on the way in, never by a read-side hop limit, because a step limit's only achievement is choosing which wrong answer to return), and chain length becomes a signal — resolution has no bound, but a chain over three hops is reported, because four merges on one line of people is a statement about the matcher's queue and not about the row. 01-identity §10 treated "survivor itself tombstoned" as a breach; with chains decided, that is normal, and only the length means anything.

The asymmetry worth remembering. A merge can be undone; the merged period cannot be. The four reversal steps in domain/03 §6 lift the tombstone and return rows created before the merge, but rows created inside the window — above all the access_grant rows, which are flagged rather than guessed — stay one row's history, because the grants exercised there really were exercised by somebody the record can no longer separate. Unmerging needs no new permission code: undoing an identity correction is the same act as making one, so it is person.merge.

docs.title: B-3 ✅ Closed — the accounting skeleton is permanent, the audit trail is short
docs.text:
Answered: the skeleton stays, the trail ages out (D-088).

The two clocks, which are deliberately opposite. membership, fee_obligation, payment and the anonymised person row: no clock, because that is the organization's own history and the shape this item had already settled ("redact the person, keep the skeleton") is now justified rather than merely unopposed; redaction_log.retained_reason has a real value to hold. audit_log: payloads for 24 months, rows forever — after the window a row is reduced, old_values/new_values emptied, everything else standing, so the trail answers "who changed this, when, and were they allowed to" for the life of the system and stops answering "and to what" after two years.

What this pays for, and it is not free. D-086 accepts that audit.view exposes whatever the payloads hold; a bounded window is the cheapest control that organization will ever get for that, and it is the strongest thing AT-4 will hear. What it costs is the history that D-085 was justified by. Values live in one overwritten row, the copy of them depends on a write path remembering to log, and the copy now expires — so "what did we believe about this child in 2019" is unanswerable twice over, and the honest description of the trade is no long history, not merely no temporal columns. If a case ever needs the long version the fix is temporal values (D-085 reversed), not a longer trail, since stretching the trail stretches exactly what D-086 graded and D-083 refuses to duplicate.

Also: the legal review this item asked for is narrower now, not gone. Indefinite retention of named membership and fee rows is a claim that needs a basis, and a decision log cannot grant one; what exists to review is now a concrete policy instead of a blank, and it is recorded as an assumption with a name attached rather than as settled law.

Residual, non-technical. Confirm the accounting retention period with whoever is liable for the books, and confirm the same 24-month window for access_log (F-8, proposed at the same value).

docs.title: B-4 ✅ Closed — one live account; a colliding sign-up files a claim
docs.text:
Answered: refuse, and queue a claim (D-089).

The rule that enforces it, and it is not a new table. One live account per person stands (01-identity §4); joined to it, an account may not reach active while an unresolved identity_hypothesis names its person. The identity review queue already existed, already records its signals and already has a role for it, so the collision case is a gate on activation plus a hypothesis raised at sign-up — no fourth queue, no new permission (person.merge, already held by identity_reviewer).

Where the danger actually sat, and the threshold is the whole answer. The tempting version — link automatically once the e-mail verifies — is D-004 under another name, and its failure mode is one human's descriptive data becoming another human's record. The version you chose has its own failure mode, which is a brand-new person blocked by a false positive, so the trigger is a strong match only (exact legacy number, or exact birth date with a normalized name) and the soft scoring band must not raise a hypothesis at all. Two obligations come with it and both are checks rather than intentions: an age check on a hypothesis that is blocking an account, alerting rather than logging, because a stalled identity queue is now a specific child who cannot sign up for a camp; and a refusal that confirms nothing, since a sign-up form that answers "yes, that person exists" is an existence oracle over a roster of children.

The everyday case is not this case. "I have a new e-mail" was never a second account — account_credential holds many credentials for one account, so it is an addition to the login a person already has. The collision case is a person arriving through a door the system did not know they had.

docs.title: C. Organization — closed
docs.text: Six questions, closed in two rounds. C-2 was resolved long ago and never appeared here: a unit may not be reparented at all, so a unit that moves is a new unit (D-036).

docs.title: C-1 ✅ Closed — the root may not read into its sub-units
docs.text:
Answered in round 3, closed here for tidiness: no — scope_exposure is the only crossing, and no reporting channel is built (D-049).

What was not obvious until it was answered. The question existed on the assumption that the root needed a way around the no-inheritance rule in order to report nationally. It does not, because the root owns the membership registry and the fees — so "how many members in 2019?", "who is currently a member?" and "what fees are outstanding?" are all answered from the root's own tables, with no exposure at all. Only the sub-units' own material — their events, their rosters, their local leadership — requires one.

The consequence that will be misread as a bug: registrar holds unit_participation.view at organization scope and cannot read a pack roster. Scope is an exact match; it reads the root participation rows, which mirror membership (D-041). See domain/06 §2.1. D-094 gave this the same shape in the other direction: imported events belong to the root, so a unit-scoped "our events" report sees historical camps it did not run — a date filter, not a unit filter, is what makes either list mean what it looks like it means.

docs.title: C-3 ✅ Closed — a reused unit number is a new unit
docs.text:
Answered: a new unit, unless somebody records the continuity (D-096).

The question came back as a question, and that was the answer. Asked whether a number appearing twice across decades is one unit or two, the reply was "what is a unit number?" — which is the right thing to ask, because a code turns out to be a short human label somebody types (T12, 4. oddíl), not an identity, not a name (names are temporal rows in org_unit_name), and not unique: uniqueness is per parent among live rows, which is precisely why a closed unit's number is free again (data-model/02 §3). A label that gets retyped is not a continuity.

What was decided, and what was refused. One org_unit per unit that existed; continuity is an assertion, written as org_unit_relationship with successor_of, never a match on the label. The opposite default is what "match on code" does if nobody says, and it invents a thirty-year lifespan. What this lost is almost nothing, and the reason is C-5: the corpus names no units at all, so there is no import-time collision to get wrong. This question outlived its urgency by exactly one round, which is worth knowing when reading it.

See: domain/04 §3, §6

docs.title: C-4 ✅ Closed — a group is filled by a rule and a list, and appointing creates nothing
docs.text:
Answered: filling rules on groups, and the two things the model refused to do (D-091).

The question was about a convenience workflow and the answer was about the group model, which is why it is the largest decision of the round. Asked whether appointing someone to a position should create the matching role assignment, the answer described filling rules: each permission group states who is placed in it on top of the manually added people — "everyone with membership", "a leader role", "anyone", "members of permission group ABC" — with worked examples from a system where a group's population derives from enrolment in a course.

Three of those four rules already existed (everyone, all_members, unit_leaders), which is the quiet part of the answer: an appointment creates no role assignment, because the derivation belongs on the group's rule rather than copied per appointment, where it would have to be found again and revoked. (Positions are deleted, D-100 — see the round-10 note at the end of this entry.) Two parts were forbidden and are now decided:

  • A group is a rule and a list. audience.kind's builtin-XOR-group split is gone; membership is the union of a rule arm, a manual arm and an inclusion arm.
  • A group may include another group. The one-line ban — "They do not nest" — is withdrawn, and its reason (cycles, unpredictable answers) is answered the way D-087 answered the same reason for merge chains: the cycle is refused when the edge is saved, not defended against in the read path.

What was deliberately not taken from the answer. In the system described, permissions sit on the group; here a role is still held by one named person, because role_assignment is the office record that answers "who was treasurer in 2023" and a derived holder list cannot. That extension is F-12, not a silent schema change.

What it costs, and where to look for the bill. A grant's reach is no longer visible in the row that grants it, so the editor must show the expanded set; and "who could read this in 2023" now depends on a recomputation of sets that were never stored, on state that has moved, with the audit payload that also held the answer expired by D-088. ~~F-7 is the route back and is no longer only a performance question.~~ — this sentence stood until round 13 and was the last live claim in this entry pointing at a question that no longer exists. Two things happened to it, and the second is the one that matters. The rebuild arrived (D-111) and F-7 was dissolved rather than answered, because a nightly rebuild of cached answers and a materialized effective-permission table turned out to be one job with two names — and round 14 deleted the rebuild (D-114), which changes nothing here: this paragraph's conclusion rests on the second event, not the first. Then the bill this paragraph was pointing at was cancelled rather than paid: D-110 ruled that the audit record of whom a grant reached is the expression, with the preview logged only as a rendering on a date — so "who could read this in 2023" is a question the system no longer owes anybody an answer to. Recomputing it stays possible and is never promised; the control that stands in place of the lost answer is procedural, the editor printing the resolved set before a shared expression saves.

Round 10 redrew the line this answer drew, and it still holds — in a different place. D-091's "a group is a rule and a list and other groups, unioned" is no longer how a set is built: an audience is now an expression tree over named sets with + - * and brackets (D-101), and a group is the opposite of a rule — a person_group states its members and nothing derives them (D-098). So the union that D-091 built into one table became an operator in a language, and the hand-kept list that D-091 insisted on survived twice over: as LIST inside an audience, and as the whole content of a group. That was round 10; round 11 deleted one of the two — LIST and audience_member are gone (D-105), so the hand-kept set survives as a group's roster, or inside an expression as PERSON(a) + PERSON(b), which is the second of those two and not a third thing. The two halves of D-091's answer that were refusals — an appointment writes no assignment, a cycle is refused when the edge is saved — both stand, the first confirmed by D-100 and the second widened to references across audiences by D-103. What is now dead wording here is audience.kind, the unit_leaders rule, "level", and the link to §4 of domain/04, which was about positions.

See: data-model/05 §8, domain/04 — its §4 held the positions this round deleted

docs.title: C-5 ✅ Closed — the corpus names no units, and none are assigned
docs.text:
Asked, and answered by correcting the premise: the corpus is people and events, and it says nothing about sub-units (D-092, D-093, D-094).

This question was not in the register. It appeared when B-1 was read against the unit model: the import matches roster rows to org_unit rows, org_unit.unit_type_id is required, no sub-unit type is seeded (D-054), and the pipeline's only documented behaviour for an unknown unit is a warning that does not block. Something had to create those units, and nothing said what.

The answer removed the question. The rows are mainly "person with names, birthdate and when they were members of the root unit", "events with attendance". Not much more — do not solve assignment to org units. So:

  • People arrive as a person plus a bounded membership — D-090's absolute ban on imported memberships is narrowed to what it was protecting, never open-ended and never inferred from attendance — and ~~each membership brings its root participation row with it, as 03-membership §5.1 requires~~. That obligation is gone (D-097); what survives of the sentence is the part that was load-bearing for the import: an imported membership is bounded at both ends, always. No fee_obligation is created: the corpus has no money, and an obligation per historical year would arrive as debt.
  • Events arrive ~~owned by the root, which satisfies D-058's exactly-one-unit with a rule instead of a judgement~~ — withdrawn by D-102, which deleted event.org_unit_id and with it the question of who an imported event belongs to; the import writes an event row and registrations, and owes one answer-view grant per event row instead (F-10 shape 1). Attendance becomes registrations — with not_attending written for nobody, because an export lists who came and silence is not a refusal (D-059).
  • Units are not imported, not created, and not matched. The parser keeps its parsed_unit_code for the day an export surprises someone; nothing reads it.

The consequence to keep in sight: the historical record contains no sub-units. "Who was in pack X in 2011?" has no answer on day one — not a wrong one, none — and the first answer it has will be typed in by hand. Nothing in the model is missing; the source cannot say it. This is also the round to note that B-1's closure now rests on a different description of the corpus than the one recorded in it, which is why B-1 carries a pointer rather than an edit to its own wording.

See: domain/03 §7, data-model/06 §3.1

docs.title: C-6 ✅ Closed — units carry no restrictions; joining one is somebody else's act
docs.text:
Answered: no restrictions on units, and no self-assignment anywhere (D-095).

Asked whether a unit type marked allows_minors = false should refuse a minor's position as it refuses their participation, the answer refused the premise from both sides: a unit does not have any restrictions — however, persons can't assign themselves; they will be assigned to the unit by the counselors — and on entry, into the root unit there is a fee; into the sub-units there is no fee, it is entirely managed by the organization, including adding more members.

Two entry paths, one gate each. The root: you pay, and the membership flow is the only self-service entry in the system. A sub-unit: somebody else writes the row, through unit_participation.manage held at that unit, with no self-scoped variant and none to be added; the same for position assignment. No fee anywhere below the root, and no model wants one.

What was deleted, and what that leaves. org_unit_type.allows_minors goes, with the check it drove and the seed's allows_minors = false on the root type — a flag documented as a safeguard and enforced on one of two write paths is a receipt, not a safeguard. D-081's requirement is answered with a change of kind: the rule "do not place a child where nobody supervises them" is now enforced by who may write the row — an audited write by a named adult — rather than by a boolean on a type. It is a stronger control for the wrong-person case and it is silent on the which-units-are-for-children question, which the system can no longer answer at all; with D-043 recording no background checks either, that is the whole of the organization module's safeguarding story, stated where it can be argued with.

See: domain/04 §1, §4, data-model/02 §1

docs.title: D. Membership
D-6 ✅ Closed — the gate was deleted, so there is nothing left to waive
docs.text:
Withdrawn by D-100, which deleted the membership gate outright: role.requires_membership, the person-level permission system.gate_exempt, and the row that recorded an exemption for a named person. There is no clause in the resolver left to waive, and no flag a configuration screen could weaken. What carries the control now is the expression — a grant that should stop with membership says MEMBERS * ROLE(x) and one that should not says ROLE(x) — so the exemption this entry recorded became a different operand rather than a permission. The posture reversal, and the three things standing in for the deleted guard, are in D-100 and in domain/06 §6.1.

Answered, and kept because the reason still applies to its replacement (D-051): the gate was waived by a person-level permission in addition to the role-level flag, because otherwise the 1 January sweep locks the administrator out of the system on the day it needs repair. That argument did not go away; it moved. It is now the argument for why the seeded grants name MEMBERS explicitly rather than assuming it, and it is the first thing to re-check if a MEMBERS term is ever added back to a grant nobody thought about.

"Which other roles carried it" was never answered here, and there is nothing left to answer. Roles are runtime data (data-model/05 §3); the exemption was a configuration act, not a specification fact. ~~An access_grant cannot lift the membership gate, because system.gate_exempt sits in the system namespace and so can only arrive through a role~~ — the guarantee was real and its subject is gone; its descendant is the one D-100 records instead, that a role confers nothing, so nothing arrives through an office at all until a grant says so.

The report survived, renamed. What was check 7b is now the standing report D-100 lists among its controls — §11 of data-model/05 was renumbered for round 10 and no longer has a gate to report on.

docs.title: D-7 ✅ Closed — the root participation row is deleted
docs.text:
The subject of this question was deleted by D-097, which took unit_participation with it, root row included: there is one unit, it is the organization, and it is a scope rather than a row, so there is no row to extend at renewal. The answer below stands as the answer that was given, and the reasoning behind it is not dead — data-model/03 §9 keeps it visible because the argument about backdated periods is what the renewal rule in §3 still rests on, and §5 is the tombstone. The accepted cost below — a lapse erased from the roster view — has no carrier any more, which is one of the losses D-097 records rather than replaces.

Answered: it is extended, not closed and reopened (D-050).

The yearly sweep moves the root row's valid_to forward to the expiry date rather than closing it, and a renewal inside the window stretches that one row over the new period. The join between the two is person and date (new_m.valid_from = up.valid_to), not a membership FK — the participation table has none, deliberately.

The accepted cost, recorded rather than hidden. This erases the visual evidence of the lapse: a person who lapsed and renewed looks, in unit_participation, exactly like a person who never lapsed. Accepted because membership remains the authority on payment and the lapse is fully visible there, while the participation table answers a roster question — and for "who was in this pack when" a child who was present across the period has one answer, not two.

See: data-model/03 §5 (the §5.1 this used to cite was the root-row subsection; it is gone, and §5 is kept deliberately as the tombstone)

docs.title: D-8 ✅ Closed — retired with the table it asked about
docs.text:
Retired by D-097, which deleted unit_participation, so there is no table left to add a nullable membership_id to. This is not the refusal of the argument but the removal of its subject, and the refusal still matters: data-model/03 §9 records the retirement and keeps the reasoning, because the same argument recurs one table later — participation had to survive without a membership, which is exactly why person_group_member is keyed on a person and not on a membership (data-model/02 §2). Read the answer there rather than re-arguing it here.

Question, as asked. A nullable membership_id on unit_participation would give referential integrity between "paid up" and "takes part", at the cost of being unenforceable for imported historical rows, where no membership exists to point at.

Impact, as assessed. Integrity vs. import coverage. The current design chose person-based linkage for exactly that reason — and round 10 left that reason intact while deleting the table that had it.

See: data-model/03 §5, data-model/03 §9

docs.title: D-9 ✅ Closed — household is removed entirely
docs.text:
Answered: drop it (D-057). household, household_member, fee_obligation.household_id, its CHECK arm, ix_obligation_household and integrity check 7 are all gone.

Why removal rather than a derived view. D-037 had already taken the load-bearing half — the fee is flat and per person, so there is no family price. The two survivors were both served by tables that must exist anyway: a billing address is a person_contact row where contact_type = 'postal' AND purpose = 'billing', and "who lived at this address in 2003?" is a query over that table's own valid_from/valid_to history. The household table was duplicating the address under a second key, and the copy had already gone stale — its postal_address was documented as denormalised from the contact row, with nothing keeping it true.

The safeguarding property is untouched, and this is the point to check first. Shared address never granted access: a child's records are reachable only through a guardianship row, whatever the household arrangement beside it. Removing a table that granted nothing cannot grant anything. D-019 stays in the log, marked superseded, because "why does living together not imply access?" will be asked again.

The one thing genuinely lost. A household was a group with a name and its own lifetime; two people at one address are now related by a query, not a row. There is nowhere to hang "the Novák family" as a first-class thing. Accepted because nothing used it. If family-level communication or a family discount is ever wanted, the grouping comes back as a group with a period — not a fake person.

One knock-on worth knowing. Finance question 2 (family/sibling discounts) is now more open, not less: a per-family discount needs the grouping designed again before it can be priced. A per-person discount is unaffected.

See: data-model/04 §3

docs.title: E. Guardianship
E-2 ✅ Closed — the system takes no position on majority
docs.text:
Answered: nothing at all. No job, no review queue, no computed candidate date (D-069, reversing D-024). A guardianship is ended by a person ending it.

What was wrong with the review queue the docs had recommended: it was still automatic, and it computed a date the system has no authority to assert. Deferring a decision is not the same as declining to make one.

This closes E-2 and immediately opens E-5 below. With no automatic end and no queue, the only exit is guardianship.end — and the adult who is the subject of the row holds no permission over it.

docs.title: E-5 ✅ Closed — the parties administer their own row
docs.text:
Answered: the guardian and the subject both act on the row themselves; there is no management-team route (D-073).

All three of the shapes above were wrong in the same direction. Support request, ownership channel, and request object each assumed the answer had to come from somewhere other than the people in the relationship. It does not. A guardianship is a relationship between two people, both of them are principals on the row, and either may end it. A guardian may add another guardian. No staff approval, and no workflow invented for the purpose.

It is not the ownership channel, which is why option (2) was the right answer for the wrong reason. Ownership is your own record; a guardianship row belongs to neither party alone. The guardianship channel simply gained a direction — from "may guardian G act on D's records?" to also "may a party act on this row?" — and the resolver still has four channels.

The gap this closes was real, and it is now closed at the only place it could be. D-069 removed both the automatic end and the queue, leaving guardianship.end as the sole exit and the subject unable to reach it. That was a door with no handle on the inside.

Two things this opens, both below.

docs.title: E-6 🟡 A guardian may appoint a guardian
docs.text:
Raised by closing E-5. D-073 lets a guardian add another guardian, so anyone with authority over a child can hand that same authority to a second person with no approval from the organization. The ordinary case is a mother adding the father. The design does not prevent the non-ordinary case; it attributes it — who added whom, when, from which account, audited, with the other party notified.

The open question is whether attribution is enough, and specifically whether adding a guardian over a minor should also notify somebody at the organization beyond the audit log. A child gaining a second legal stranger with write over their records is not the same kind of event as an adult adding a co-parent.

Recommendation. Notify a safeguarding contact on guardianship.assign where the subject is a minor, and nothing else. Notification is visibility, not approval, so the parties still do not need the organization's permission — which is the whole point of D-073.

Impact. One notification rule. No schema change.

docs.title: E-7 ✅ Closed — one level cannot separate the medical record from the profile, and nobody wanted to
docs.text:
Raised by D-074, which deleted the eighteen dependent.* codes that existed for this case.

What could not be said. "This guardian may register the child for events but may not read the medical record." "Read-only, except not the health data." "The grandmother may see the roster and nothing else." A guardian either sees everything about the child or nothing. The case the old namespace was built around — a court order restricting one parent's medical access while their other access continues — was inexpressible.

Why it was accepted anyway. Three values a volunteer treasurer can hold in their head, versus eighteen whose differences nobody outside a court uses. And the alternative had a failure mode of its own: a granular list that administrators ticked without reading is not more protective than a coarse one, it only looks more precise.

Answered (round 7), and the answer was not the one the question expected. The question assumed a medical record worth separating. Asked directly, you answered: "ignore 'court order', guardian has all rights on a child if it's permissions say so. Medical data is not different in any way." Recorded as D-083.

So this closes as a dissolved question, not an answered one. "Everything except the medical record" is not a sentence the organization wants to say, which means the missing granularity was never a gap — it was the absence of a feature nobody asked for. There is now no inside and outside to the person record, because there is no separate record: everything the system knows about a person other than name, gender and age is one class of data, reached by person.view and governed by the guardian right level whole.

What the closure trades away, in one sentence and on purpose: a system that cannot express "everything except the diagnoses" cannot express an arrangement a court might order, and will express it instead as a guardian who either has the record or does not. If the case arrives in reality, the route back is one new grant scope over a defined set of data, argued once as a decision entry — not a namespace of eighteen codes, which is what was deleted and why this question existed.

Impact. None left open. One value, three choices, over the whole record.

See: D-083, data-model/09-attributes.md, glossary — Descriptive data.

docs.title: E-3 🟢 Guardian acting for an adult child
docs.text:
Question. Can a parent register their adult child for an event, with the child's consent?

Recommendation. An explicit consent-based delegation, not a guardianship — the legal basis differs and access_grant.is_delegated already supports it.

Note. Now that grants can target audiences (D-042), the event-wide version of this question — "register everyone in this group" — is answered without touching guardianship at all. What remains is the individual case.

docs.title: E-4 🟢 Guardianship lifetime, now that the gate it was exempt from is gone
docs.text:
Question, restated — and it is sharper than it was. Guardianship used to be exempt from the membership gate (D-039), so a lapsed parent kept their guardian's right over their child's records. The gate is now deleted (D-100), and that does not resolve this — it removes the thing that used to make the exemption visible. The membership test moved into grant expressions, and a guardianship is not a grant: it is one of the three channels, reached through guardianship_permission, and there is no expression in it to write MEMBERS in. So a lapsed parent keeps their right exactly as before, and there is now no mechanism anywhere that could condition it short of a new rule in the resolver. Confirm that is intended rather than inherited: an unpaid parent and a paid one are indistinguishable inside the guardianship channel, and they have become indistinguishable everywhere else too. ~~unless somebody writes MEMBERS * GUARDIANS(p) into a grant — which grants the permission, not the relationship, and is therefore not the same lever.~~ — and that last lever has now been removed, which converts this entry from "confirm it is intended" to "there is nothing left to confirm". GUARDIANS is not a selector in either arity (D-113): no expression can name a ward's guardians, so a grant cannot condition on guardianship either, and this entry's conclusion — that membership and access deliberately do not meet inside the guardianship channel — is now a structural fact rather than an oversight with an escape hatch. D-113 also sharpens what the channel is, in a way this entry should not be read without: a check reads guardianship.right_level ∈ none | view | write off a live guardianship row, and guardianship_permission is that value's history — no grantee, no permission code, no audience, no expression column — so there was never anywhere in it for a selector to be seeded, and a guardian's authority is a level over a child, not a list of codes.

Impact. None structurally, and that is the answer being asked for in writing. It is the one place where membership and access deliberately do not meet, and "why can this person still see that?" should have a written answer rather than a retired gate to blame.

docs.title: F. Authorization
F-1 ✅ Closed — the catalog stays comprehensive and granular
docs.text:
Answered: keep the catalog large and granular; more permissions arrive with the unbuilt modules (D-055).

It is a menu, not a checklist. Administrators assign people only the permissions they actually need, and that is only possible if the capabilities exist as separate rows to assign. The parts of the question that remain — the exact contents — are tracked in appendix/permission-catalog.md §12 and will move as events, documents, communication and reporting land.

Note the asymmetry with roles, because it looks like an inconsistency and is not. Roles are runtime data the organization invents (D-052); permissions are capabilities the code implements. You cannot assign a power that is not expressible in the schema, so a comprehensive catalog costs only rows. A comprehensive role list, by contrast, would be a specification pretending to be data.

The sharp edge. Granularity only buys least-privilege if the grants are narrow, and D-007 means any new permission in a namespace is retroactively held by everyone with that namespace's .admin, with no assignment written. That is intended — and it is the reason role.edit is marked 🔒🔒.

docs.title: F-3 ✅ Closed — nothing forces an assignment to end
docs.text:
Answered: nothing — rely on the gate, and on the report. No NOT NULL, no application-layer requirement, no per-role policy (D-071). The docs had recommended yes, at the application layer; that recommendation is withdrawn. Half of the answer's title has since lost its subject — the gate is deleted, D-100 — and the report half is what the decision now rests on entirely, which is argued immediately below rather than papered over here.

Why the recommendation was wrong, as argued at the time. It claimed the membership gate makes an open-ended assignment more dangerous. It makes it less: the gate already expires authority for exactly the population an expiry date would target, and ties expiry to a fact the organization maintains on purpose rather than to a date somebody typed. That argument is withdrawn along with the mechanism; the conclusion did not need it, and the paragraph after this one is the one to read.

The residue, restated — the answer survives its own reasoning. This decision leaned on the membership gate, and D-100 deleted the gate, so the sentence "unit_leader and assistant_leader have requires_membership = false" names a column that no longer exists. The residue it described is bigger now, not smaller: the case used to be a handful of roles flagged as exempt, and it is now any grant written without a MEMBERS term, which is the default way to write one. So the conclusion is unchanged and the emphasis is: a periodic human review over open-ended rows is not a nice-to-have, it is the entire defence. D-053 put the weight on role_assignment.valid_to; that table is role_holder, the column is the same, and D-100 declined to add a guard rail there too. Read the two decisions, and D-100's three controls, as one set.

See: data-model/05 §4, §4's own conclusion

docs.title: F-4 ✅ Closed — the question was answered by deleting the premise
docs.text:
Answered obliquely and decisively. Asked whether person.admin should subsume person.merge/person.redact, the answer was "Only the system should have admin permissions, not the individual items" — which removed the subsumer rather than choosing between the two options offered (D-068, reversing D-007).

The question moved rather than dissolved — and then moved again. A role bundling all person.* codes still reaches person.merge and person.redact. What changed at the time was where that is decided: it used to be a resolver rule, invisible in every role editor and true for every resource whether or not anyone wanted it. It became the contents of a role somebody wrote — and the answer given in round 6 named a table: ~~visible in role_permission, dated, alarmable, and audited on change~~. D-100 deleted role_permission, because an office confers nothing, so the bundle is now the live grant rows naming ROLE(x), one row per code, each dated and each auditable in its own right. The guidance is the same sentence with a different carrier, and it got more visible rather than less: there is no longer a role editor where the bundling could hide, because there is no such editor — you have to look at the grants.

What carries the guidance now is the seed table and the grant rows beside it, not the schema: no seeded role is meant to have person.merge/person.redact bundled with routine person.edit, and identity_reviewer is the one that deliberately holds person.merge. A role that does gather a resource including its irreversible codes should be named for it.

See: appendix/permission-catalog.md §11

docs.title: F-4a ✅ Closed — the catalog is the only list now
docs.text:
Surfaced by D-068, not created by it. When the two were reconciled during that work, 22 documented permissions had no INSERT row — including unit_participation.view, which five of the catalog's own seed roles assign, and person.redact, one of the two codes D-068 exists to protect. A further 12 were the event.* set, catalogued when events were designed and never seeded. All 34 are now fixed; both sides list 91 codes and the diff is empty.

Why nobody noticed, which is the part worth keeping. D-068 made a harmless inconsistency into a live one. Under the prefix-match wildcard, a role holding unit_participation.admin reached unit_participation.view whether or not a permission row existed — the catalog could advertise a capability the database could not name, and nothing noticed, because the wildcard papered over the gap and only the permission editor showed it. The cushion was itself the bug's hiding place.

What is open is the discipline, not the data. There is no SQL check for this — one side is a Markdown file. Integrity check 18 reads the table, so it can find a permission no role grants; it cannot find a permission the catalog promises and the seed never contained. The reconciliation is scripted in data-model/05 §12, and it is a review rule, not a test.

The actual question: should the catalog be generated from permission rather than maintained beside it? That is the only change that makes the two incapable of disagreeing. Against it: the catalog's value is its prose — the sensitivity marks, the rationale notes, the §5a and §8a argumentation — none of which belongs in a table. A middle path is to keep the prose in Markdown and generate the code tables from the database, so only the commentary can drift.

Impact. If left manual, this recurs on every module added, and D-055's decision to keep growing the catalog guarantees modules get added.

✅ Closed — answered by deleting one of the two lists. Asked whether to generate the catalog from the seed, the answer was "delete the schema, I will use ORM anyway" (D-072), which removed the seed blocks, the DDL and the 19 integrity checks from the documentation altogether.

The generation question dissolved rather than being settled, and the difference matters for what is still true. Nothing is generated, because there is no longer a table to generate from. The catalog is now the only list that exists — which answers the drift problem completely and removes, at the same time, the executable form of every rule the DDL had been carrying. That trade is D-072's to make and its entry records what it costs: integrity check 18, the orphaned-permission check that was the safety net for the deleted wildcard, is now a prose instruction rather than a query. A check nobody runs is a convention.

What remains genuinely open is the thing the check was guarding. With no seed and no wildcard, a capability in the catalog that no role bundles is unusable and silent. It is now caught by review of the catalog, and there is no automated backstop at all.

docs.title: F-5 ✅ Closed — nothing is missing from the registry, and the last gap was a selector that should not have been in it
docs.text:
Answered by D-113, and the answer came from the wrong direction, which is the part worth keeping. This entry spent three rounds asking which primitive facts the language still cannot state, and its final open bullet turned out not to be a missing fact at all: GUARDIANS is not a selector, in either arity, the registry drops to thirteen, and the thing the word was pointing at is the guardianship channel — a right_level of view or write over a child, which is a relationship carrying its own authority and not a set anything resolves. A guardian at write may already perform any action whose subject is their ward, so an operand aimed at a ward's guardians would have offered a subset of what those people already hold, one code at a time. The count of open bullets in this entry is zero: round 12 closed the age bullet with OLDER/YOUNGER, round 13 closed this one by deletion rather than by addition, and the SCHOOL question was refused as D-108.

What it cost, since the cost is real and D-113 records it rather than smoothing it. Deleting the operand removes no capability — but it does confirm absent a thing nobody ever wrote down wanting: nothing in this language can now denote "whatever guardians the person this item is about has". D-113's own first draft thought that was a loss and minted an open question for it, then the user's ruling dissolved the premise ten minutes later, because the worry presumed view/write is a ceiling on codes when it is a ceiling on acts about that child. So there is no F-24. The residual case — guardians of this child should get at something that is not about the child — is not a permissions question: it is a list of people, and lists are groups, which is why the substitute is a named GROUP(x) with kept members and not a new operand. A derived guardian list is a feature this system does not have, checked rather than assumed, and saying so in the entry that closes this one is the honest place to leave it: a missing feature is a decision entry, never an operand nobody checked for.

One seam the two rulings left between them, recorded here because neither of them owns it. D-109 ruled that nothing a stored expression may name is ever deleted while a rule may name it — you give it a state instead. D-113 then deleted a row outright, and the argument that carries the deletion is about authority (write already reaches any act about the child), not about what is already sitting in audience_operand. The bound form could never be saved; the explicit one plausibly could. GUARDIANS shipped with takes_argument optional and argument_type person; the item-type match is a check the binding rule reads, and the events module says out loud that the explicit form stays legal at the unit (data-model/08) — so GUARDIANS(p) on a unit-scope grant is not obviously refused by any save rule I can point at. If such a leaf exists anywhere, deleting its row turns it into a failing leaf, which is the state D-109 retired deletion in order to prevent and the state D-109 said only a redacted person could still produce. What is needed is one sentence, in D-113 or at the resolver: either no GUARDIANS(p) was ever savable — name the check that refused it and the seam closes — or existing leaves are found and repointed, the way a person merge repoints leaves. This is deliberately not a new F-entry: it leaves no design choice open, only a migration statement missing, and "run one query over the leaves and fix the rows" is not a question to put in front of anybody. It is here, in the entry that closed the operand, so that the row deletion does not read as cost-free.

Two rules this closure leaves behind, both belonging to F-10's list rather than to this entry. First: every selector name that appears in a document must be a selector_type row, and a check should be able to say so — a lint of documents against a seed list, which is a strange thing to want until the fourteenth selector turns out to be a prose idiom. Second, D-113's verdict on the method this file trusts: a count is a good alarm and a bad oracle. Fourteen disagreed with six pages using a fifteenth name, and that alarm correctly said something is wrong twice and correctly said which side was wrong neither time — the first pass blamed the prose, the ruling blamed the registry.

Round 10 answered the question that was asked and left a different one standing. C-4's four filling rules — "anyone", "everyone with membership", "a leader role", "members of a named group" (D-091) — all exist now, and none of them is an audience: they are the operands EVERYONE, MEMBERS, ROLE(x) and GROUP(x) (data-model/05 §8, D-101). The seeded audiences went the other way — down to two (everyone, all_members), because a built-in audience turned out to be a sentence someone else composes rather than a row the code ships. So this entry is no longer "how many built-ins"; it is which primitive facts the language still cannot state, one bullet per missing fact. No count appears in this heading, because the count changed while this entry was being written — see the first answer below.

Answered while this entry stood open, and answered against its own assumption: PERSON(x) is a seeded row, not shorthand, and the registry was one row short when this entry said so in bold. PERSON arrived as the thirteenth row — takes_argument true, argument_type person, binds_to_item false — added by the amendment paragraph at the end of D-101's grammar (D-101). The table is twelve rows now: the round after this one deleted LIST and the table behind it (D-105). That is the honest sequence rather than the tidy one, and it is written out because this entry has now printed a count that stopped being true twice — which is exactly the argument for why the heading carries no number. What this entry got right was the need: a grant does not need the operand, because the grantee pair already names one person, but an audience does, because a saved expression aimed at several things cannot carry a grantee — so the "except Honza" in MEMBERS * ROLE(x) + PERSON(y), the control that replaced the membership gate's exemption, had nowhere to live. The registry was written from the evaluator's arm list instead of from the grammar, and an arm list copied from an implementation loses the arm nobody has implemented yet. As a selector_type.code it also joins the reserved namespace, which is the reservation this entry's Impact used to ask for. The wrong repair was already circulating: the pages that noticed the gap read PERSON(y) as LIST, and that is not a wider spelling of the same thing — LIST is one set of several people belonging to one audience, so subtracting it removes everybody on it. The defect class is F-19, which this round also closed. That particular repair is now unwritable: one spelling is left, so there is nothing to substitute — the only way in which D-105 ended a bug this entry described without anybody deciding to end it. The class it was an instance of is untouched, and PERSON(x) is now the operand that would be misread, since it went from a curiosity to the only way to name a set of people by hand.

Round 11 found the same defect again, this time in prose. domain/06a keeps its own copy of this table for readers who never open the data model, and that copy had never grown a PERSON row or an AUDIENCE row while still carrying the LIST row D-105 deleted — so the page that teaches this language to everybody who is not implementing it taught a language in which two of the twelve operands could not be written, and taught one that no longer exists. Third instance of one defect, one round apart: a decision entry adds an operand, the seeded table gets the row because somebody is holding it, and every prose copy is updated by whoever happens to read it. F-19 counted four instances of this defect in ten rounds, every one of them a table disagreeing with prose; this one is prose disagreeing with prose, which is why no diff over rows would have caught it either. The remedy is the one F-19 adopted and D-104 argued for, aimed at documents instead of codes: a token written in three files is not one fact stored three times, and nothing in §11 can see any of the three.

Retired by the round, listed so nobody re-raises them.

  • "everyone who registered for this event" — shipped four times over as ATTENDED, PLACED, CONFIRMED, ON_WAITLIST, plus ORGANIZERS, all bindable to the event a grant is scoped to (D-102). The joining-instructions rule this bullet used to ask for is ATTENDED, and it is more precise than what was asked: the old rule could not distinguish someone the capacity refused.
  • "everyone in this section and everything under it" — there is no hierarchy to walk (D-097), so the D-031 argument this bullet carried is not answered but unaskable. unit_ancestors() is deleted.
  • "are parameterised groups seeded per instance or created on demand?" — moot. There were never any per-instance audiences to parameterize once there was one unit, and the three parameterized seeded audiences are gone with the names they carried (§12 of data-model/05).

The bullets this entry carried, and where each one stands now.

  • ✅ ~~A bound GUARDIANS cannot be written on any legal grant.~~ — closed by D-113, and the finding is kept visible in full because it is the evidence that the registry and the prose had drifted apart. The registry gives GUARDIANS binds_to_item = true with argument_type = person, and §8 says the binding check compares that column against the grant's item type. But grant_scope_type is seeded with unit, event, person_group, role and document — there is no person item, because authority over a person arrives through the guardianship channel, not through a grant. So the bound form passes the arity check and is then refused by the binding check on every scope that exists, and §12's claim that GUARDIANS may be "bound as GUARDIANS on a grant about that person" describes a grant that cannot be saved. The two options this entry offered were "person joins grant_scope_type" and "binds_to_item is false for GUARDIANS", and D-113 took neither: it removed the row. Was the contradiction real? Yes, on both sides of it — which is why the bullet stays verbatim rather than being summarised. The registry had a row that should not have been in the registry at all, so the contradiction this entry read as "the model cannot host this operand" was in fact "the model never had this operand", and the six pages that used the argument-less form were describing a channel with a selector's syntax. A defect report that is accurate about the symptoms and wrong about the cause is still the most useful kind of defect report, and this is the one that found it: the registry row, the §8 binding check, the §12 claim of a grant that could not be saved, and the absence of any person item type were all correctly observed and all correctly refused to add up. D-113 also clears the word out of the prose that used it live, and the site that mattered most is domain/06 §6.2's operand table, whose row promised "guardians of the person this item is about" — a selector no grant could write — and now stands struck with the channel spelled out in its place. No guardian-shaped operand is bound to anything, because there is no guardian-shaped operand, so binds_to_item keeps its meaning and loses its exhibit: what justifies the column now is the five event operands (ATTENDED, PLACED, CONFIRMED, ON_WAITLIST, ORGANIZERS), which is a large and ordinary reason instead of one strange case that was never real.

  • ~~Age is now unsayable in the model, and one of these questions will want it.~~ — closed by D-107: age was a set all along. The bullet argued that age has no table to point at — argument_type names a table, an age band is a range and not a row — and offered two exits: seed a band table for the sake of two or three rows, or write down that age never enters the selector language. Both exits were wrong in the same direction, and the direction is the interesting part. argument_type has gained a scalar: OLDER(n) takes a whole number of years, which points at no table and needs none. And the premise under the whole bullet — that an operand has to be a stored set — is the sentence D-107 deleted, along with "an attribute is not a set of people … age is not". OLDER(n) and YOUNGER(n) are seeded rows now, read against the birth date on the date being checked, so event.register_self granted to MEMBERS * YOUNGER(15) states a ceiling in this language. EV-1's escape hatch is therefore open rather than closed, which changes the reason that entry is closed and not its answer. What the bullet got right is still true and is why it is written up as a closure instead of deleted: age arrived exactly the way the rules for new facts require — a decision entry and a seed row, never a row typed into a screen — and "leaving it unstated is the one option that gets worse quietly" was the correct call, because this bullet was three rounds from being quoted as a design principle.

  • ~~A prose expression names an operand that does not exist: all_in_school.~~ — retracted; that defect is not in this corpus, and writing it here is the real finding. The paragraph this bullet replaced cited domain/07-events.md §1 as opening its age-gating story with an audience named all_in_school, and argued from there that the prose was advertising a registry row nobody had minted. The token appears nowhere in this repository — not on the line cited, not in that file, not in any file: a grep for SCHOOL and in_school across docs/ returns this bullet and nothing else. It arrived from a subagent's report of a defect it said it had found and deliberately not touched, it was plausible — the registry genuinely has no SCHOOL, and the sentence it described is the kind of sentence that page does write — and it entered the register without the one grep that would have killed it, which is the same operation this entry's entire finding consists of. D-104 named the class: prose contradicting a registry is a fiction. This is the fourth page of that class and the only one that was about the registry, filed in the file whose job is to hold verified open questions — which is what makes it the expensive kind. A wrong entry in a domain page describes something wrong; a wrong entry here directs work, and nothing checks this file: no CI, no schema, no resolver, and no reader who would notice, because every sentence in it is written as a question and a question cannot be falsified by reading it. The control this suggests is not "trust reports less", it is the same control as everywhere else in this module: grep before you write, including — especially — when the sentence being written is an accusation against somebody else's page.

  • SCHOOL — asked directly, and refused: it is not an important selector, at least not for now. The question above was worth answering even though its premise was invented, because the underlying question is real: could a SCHOOL(x) operand be added, and should it? It could be, and it is not, and D-108 is where that is decided — with the reason, the shape to use instead (a person_group per school, which is expressible today), and the one thing that would reopen it. "For now" is honoured by naming the trigger rather than a date.

What rounds 11, 12 and 13 changed here, and what this entry still does not own. No bullet is open — round 12 closed the age one with OLDER/YOUNGER, and round 13 closed the GUARDIANS one by deleting the selector rather than hosting it (D-113), which is the fourth way this file has closed a question about a missing operand: build it, refuse it, discover it was already expressible, or discover it was never about the language. PERSON(x) did not close either of them, and deleting LIST did not open a third, because the language can state exactly the same facts about people as it could with thirteen operands — a claim that was true of round 11 and is narrower than round 12, which is the difference between deleting an operand that added nothing and adding one that adds a kind of fact. The one thing that went with LIST is the dates on individual names, and that is not a missing operand: no row could restore it, and D-105 ruled that a windowed exception is a second grant with its own period instead. Two adjacent questions are deliberately not this entry's, and are named so they are not folded in: WHITELISTED is a refused candidate, not a missing fact, and it is F-20's to answer — and it has now answered, refused, with the need served by a person_group per whitelist — with EV-6 carrying its events half; counting it here would be counting a refusal as a gap. And the legibility of a hand-typed set of forty names is F-22, also now closed: D-105 pointed it at this entry's neighbourhood, but it was never a question about a missing fact — the language states it fine, and reading it back is the problem, which is an editor question.

Impact. The GUARDIANS bullet is the cheap one — either one row in grant_scope_type, or one corrected registry row and one corrected sentence in §8 and §12. The age bullet is the expensive one in kind rather than in size: it is a new kind of fact in a language whose rules for new facts are now written down — an operand is a decision entry plus a seed row, never a row typed into a screen (D-101), which is what keeps this 🟢, since the cost is not code, it is the argument. The one bullet this round settled cost exactly what this paragraph predicted a missing operand would cost — one seed row, one reserved word, one namespace reservation — which is the only way in which it was a cheap question: it was cheap to fix and took a whole round to notice. Round 12 paid the age bill and it came to precisely this invoice, plus one deleted sentence: two seed rows, two reserved words, D-107, and the correction of a claim this corpus repeated for four rounds because it sounded like a type system. The bill was never the expensive part; not noticing which claim you were leaning on was. Round 13 then presented the only invoice in this entry with a negative line: closing the last bullet cost one deleted registry row and no seed row at all — no reserved word gained, no namespace reservation, no decision about whether a person is an item, and the orphan check left untouched, because person never joined grant_scope_type after all. What it did cost is everywhere the word was: 31 occurrences outside the decision log, across eight pages, counted with grep rather than remembered — and the cheap-looking half of that bill is the part this entry's whole existence argues for, because a notation that parses reads as a decision somebody made, and thirteen pages of prose had silently made one.

docs.title: F-6 ✅ Closed — the permission cache is rebuilt nightly, on any ruleset write, and on request
docs.text:
*Retitled twice. Round 10 moved the weight of this question: it used to be "how long may an answer be reused", with the invalidation list settled underneath it, and the list became the hard half while the TTL became a number nobody could pick until the list was. Round 13 refused both halves, and the reason the entry could be closed at all is that the thing underneath both was removed rather than answered.

Amended by D-114 in round 14, and the amendment is a deletion rather than a correction: there is no permission cache, so this entry's subject no longer exists. The heading is kept exactly as it stands, and on purpose — this is D-081's shape applied to a title: the name outlived the mechanism, and the entry's job now is to say what closed it rather than to look current. So read this heading as the name of the round-13 closure, not as a description of the current design; anyone who takes the title for the design has been warned by the first line beneath it. It is also infrastructure — three files link to this slug, ten links — and a question that died by having its premise removed earns a stale heading far more cheaply than this corpus earns a broken link. What round 13 left standing, item by item. The key dies: (person_id, permission_code, scope_type, scope_id, at_bucket) left with the table that held it, so part (a) and part (b) are not answered but unaddressable — there is no entry to put a lifetime on and no entry to invalidate. The version integer survives, narrowed: it now keys a compiled expression rather than an answer, and its bump set is audience_operand and selector_type — two tables where D-111 named eight kinds of write: six tables, the D-109 flag and a merge. And one finding out lives its own key, which is the part this entry must keep visible: D-102 made a grant's reached set a function of the item, and that is a property of an expression, not of storage. A form computed while checking one item may never be served for another — but note where the binding now sits, because D-114 is precise about it and this entry should not be sloppier than the decision it amends: a compilation holds "no person and no item", both arriving as parameters, so the item binds at resolution, not at compilation. Anything that caches a resolution — a named roster, an expansion keyed per (audience, item) — is keyed by the item or it is wrong on the 401st event. Why the object was deleted rather than repaired belongs here too, since this entry is where the reasoning lives: the boundary round 13 made load-bearing, "the line between those two lists is the entire safety property", omitted membership — while membership.terminate ⛔ is the most safeguarding-shaped write in the catalog — and the list could not be fixed by adding a row, because a correct invalidation set is the read path and not a policy boundary anybody can keep true by hand. Everything below is kept as printed, including the invalidation table and the two lists, which now describe a mechanism that does not exist. They are still the best four rounds of reasoning in this file about which answers move, a question that has outlived every answer it was ever given.

~~Question, in two parts. (a) What TTL is acceptable on a resolved (person, permission, item) answer? (b) What events invalidate a cached answer, and how wide is each one's fan-out?~~

Answered by D-111: one policy, three triggers. Every cached authorization answer is rebuilt (a) nightly, in full; (b) immediately on any write to the ruleset; (c) on explicit request — an administrative action, which sits on the same permissions page as the tab F-21 now has. No TTL per entry, no asymmetric TTL, and no partial invalidation list to get right. The user's answer, verbatim: "All cache is represhed at night every day OR on manual request and ruleset change."

All three of those triggers are retired by D-114: (a) and (c) went with the cache they served, (b) went with the boundary it was defending. What follows in this entry is therefore what round 13 decided and why, not what the system does — kept because the reasoning is the entry's real content and because the invalidation table below is still the clearest statement anywhere in these documents of which answers move.

What that refused, said plainly, because this entry spent four rounds building the thing that was refused. Part (a) is refused outright: there is no per-entry lifetime to configure, so there is no number to argue about and no asymmetry between an allow and a deny. Part (b) is refused by removing its premise — the fan-out question was only hard because per-entry invalidation was assumed. What replaces the whole table below is a rebuild plus one rule about what counts as a ruleset change, and that is a smaller thing to be right about: one boundary to state, versus a row per write type whose width had to be computed correctly every time, including by the next person who adds a table and does not know this one exists.

The whole design now hangs on one boundary, so it is quoted rather than summarised. The ruleset is: a write to access_grant, audience_operand, guardianship_permission or permission; to role_holder and person_group_member; to the deprecated | hidden | disabled flag of anything in D-109's table; and a person merge or unmerge. That flag must itself be a ruleset write, and D-111 says so in these terms: if it is not, "turn off this naming" waits until midnight, which is exactly the failure the flag exists to prevent. A control whose effect arrives the next morning is not the control anybody agreed to. Read that list as the defect, not the design. It is quoted here in full because round 13 called this boundary the whole safety property — and it omits membership, while membership.terminate ⛔ is held by safeguarding_officer and is the most safeguarding-shaped write the catalog carries. Under D-114 the flag is not a version bump at all: it is read live at check time, which is why "disabling takes effect now" no longer depends on anybody remembering to put a table on a list.

What "immediately" means, because the hardest writes are the ones that name nobody — the mechanism D-111 added the same round, since the ruling was incomplete without it. ~~The cache key is (person_id, permission_code, scope_type, scope_id, at_bucket), and an audience appears in it nowhere.~~ Ending one role_holder row names its person; ending one person_group_member row names its person; an edit to a shared audience_operand tree names nobody at all — ~~the people it stops reaching are whatever the expression happens to resolve to, and finding them means evaluating the expression for everyone, which is the rebuild itself and not a way around it.~~ That is the exact reason this entry's fan-out table looked intractable for four rounds: per-entry invalidation has no answer for a write whose subject set is a computation. D-114 dissolves the hard half from the other side, and it is worth naming how: a compilation is keyed by an expression's root, not by the people it reaches, so the unanswerable question "whom did this edit stop reaching?" is simply never asked — and because a compilation is finite and enumerable over the audience tree, "an edit to a shared audience invalidates everything" becomes "it invalidates the compilations that embed it", which is a bounded walk: the same reachability walk the save path already performs for cycles (D-103). The fan-out that made this entry hard was only hard because it fanned out to people. The answer is one integer — a ruleset version, bumped by any write in the set above, ~~carried in every cache entry, and an entry is valid only while its version matches~~. "Rebuild immediately on a ruleset change" then means bump the version: one write to one row, which never needs to know whom a rule reaches. ~~The nightly full rebuild stays as the correctness backstop for what the version cannot cover — the calendar cases — and the manual request becomes bump it and warm it.~~ What D-114 kept of this mechanism is the integer and nothing else: it is now carried by a compilation rather than an answer, and its bump set is audience_operand and selector_type — the two things a compilation actually depends on, an expression's shape and the seeded vocabulary it is written in. access_grant dropped out because grants are not compiled at all: the expression lives on the audience and its operand rows are already inside the surviving set, while a check reads the person's grant rows live — so inserting, editing or revoking a grant changes what that read returns and leaves no compilation behind to drop. role_holder, person_group_member and a person merge dropped out for the adjacent reason: they move rosters, which are the other thing still cached across requests — keyed by the name the write touches, holding dated rows, invalidated locally rather than folded into a version. Concretely: adding a child to a group, which used to drop the entire cache, now drops nothing. What it does not buy: it is not a version per audience and not a version per grant, and a system large enough to want either is the system D-112 says this one is not — which is the trigger that reopens this entry alongside the size numbers. The check worth writing, in D-111's words, survives its mechanism: ~~if the deprecated | hidden | disabled flag ever stops bumping the version~~, the failure to watch for is now a flag that has been compiled into a cached form — D-109's "deprecating or hiding must not change the answer" would still hold while "disabling takes effect now" silently stopped being true, and under D-114 that can only happen if somebody stops reading the flag live.

Why the key changed shape. The answer used to be a function of a person and a permission, with a scope that was either the organization or a unit somewhere in a tree. D-102 made the reached set depend on the item itself — a bound operand like PLACED or ORGANIZERS means the same grant says something different about every event it is written on — so ~~the item must be in the key, not merely the scope type~~. Two consequences worth stating before anyone builds this: ~~an item-scope grant can no longer be answered by one cached row per person, and a per-item preview is a per-item cache entry~~ (F-15). Both were statements about a table that no longer exists, and neither was a statement about the wrong thing. The dependency D-102 discovered is in the expression, not in the storage: a bound operand is evaluated against the item under check, so nothing computed while checking one item may be served for another. Under D-114 the item is a parameter of a compilation rather than a component of a key — which is stronger than what this paragraph asked for, not weaker: a compilation is reusable across items exactly because nothing in it has been resolved to one yet.

Why the invalidation list grew a transitive edge. D-103 lets an audience name another, so ~~a cached answer now depends on~~ a compiled expression depends on every audience its expression references, transitively — not only the ones a grant names directly. Editing volunteers must invalidate anything whose closure reaches volunteers, three levels up if something is three levels up. The walk that computes that closure is the same reachability walk the save path already performs to refuse cycles, which is the convenient reading; whether it is cheap enough to run on every edit is exactly what F-16 asks, and nothing has measured it. ~~An invalidation that is too slow to run is not a slow feature, it is a stale allow.~~ The sentence's failure mode went with the answer cache (D-114): a compilation drop that is slow to run delays an edit, it does not widen anyone's access, because a stale compilation can only be wrong about the words it holds and never about who is in a set. But the transitive edge itself is not history — it is now the reachability walk that finds the compilations to drop, so F-16's question returns, in a bounded form rather than a fan-out-to-people form.

The invalidation table, kept visible and replaced. ~~What invalidates what, as of round 11.~~ Every row below is superseded — first by D-111's rebuild, then by D-114 deleting the thing the rebuild rebuilt — none of it is what an implementation does now. It stays because it is four rounds of reasoning about which answers move, and that question survives even though its answer no longer does: ~~read the column "Invalidates" as "what the nightly rebuild would have to notice anyway", which is exactly what a full rebuild does notice, for free, without a single one of these rules being implemented correctly by hand~~ — read it now as the read path, which is the only honest reading left: every row is a table some operand can reach, and D-114's finding is that a correct invalidation list is exactly that set, which is why it could not be maintained as a policy boundary. Two rows are worth reading against what replaced them rather than struck through, and one of them is the reason there was anything to replace: membership open and close has a row in this table, dated round 11, and it is missing from the single boundary D-111 substituted for the whole table two rounds later. That is the hole, recorded in this file the entire time it was open: the narrowing that made the list smaller is what made it wrong.

Write Invalidates (what D-111 rebuilt instead, and what D-114 made moot — no row here is a rule any more) access_grant insert, update, revoke that grantee × that permission × that scope (and the unit, for the dead-weight-deny report's sake) audience_operand — the tree, not just the rows every answer whose expression reaches this audience, transitively (D-103). Since D-105 this is also the row that covers "somebody added a name": adding a person edits the expression, so the widest cache-busting write in the module got one step more common and one step less visible, and two clerks editing one audience at once can now lose one of the two additions unless the editor carries a concurrency check ~~audience_member (the LIST leaf)~~ retired — the table is deleted (D-105), and the write that replaced it is the row above role_holder everyone holding that office × each permission granted to ROLE(x) person_group_member everyone in that group × each permission granted to GROUP(x) — and anything naming an audience that references the group membership open/close, and the 1 January sweep by person, not by scope, and only where an expression contains MEMBERS — the sweep is no longer the universal invalidator it was while the gate existed event_registration insert, waitlist move, is_confirmed every cached answer on that event for the four attendance tiers, which are computed rather than stored person merge or unmerge both directions, by person id, since sets are keyed on person — and since D-105 invalidating is not enough: every audience_operand leaf whose selector_arg_id names the absorbed person has to be repointed, because a leaf that resolves to nobody is the empty set, which is silent on the allow side and widens a deny on the - side (F-10) no write at all — somebody turns sixteen every cached answer about that person whose expression contains OLDER(16) or YOUNGER(16), at midnight, entirely predictable and announced by nothing. This is the list's first entry with no causing write, and D-107 accepts it by ruling, not by oversight: "I know, that the time will change, how the rules resolve and IT IS FINE." The row is here so that nobody implements it as a bug — the cache is already keyed to a date, a check for a past date has to answer for that past date, and there is no row to expire because nothing was ever stored. No new mechanism, and one more reason the TTL below is the actual question ~~a unit's parent changing~~, ~~a scope_exposure write~~ retired — the hierarchy and scope_exposure are deleted (D-097), and with them the two widest fan-outs the list used to have

The residual window, and why it is not the thing this entry was afraid of. ~~D-111 allows exactly one kind of answer to be up to a night stale: an answer that moved without a write — a birthday crossing OLDER(n)/YOUNGER(n), the 1 January membership sweep, a role or group period ending on its own date, attendance writes behind the event tiers.~~ There is no window, and the sentence above is the one D-114 deleted rather than defended. A birthday, a sweep, a period reaching its own valid_to and a registration write all move the answer at the instant they happen, because the answer is computed when it is asked for. The fear this entry carried for four rounds was the opposite case: a stale allow is a permission the organization has already withdrawn, with the safeguarding story behind the withdrawal. That case is impossible, and not for the reason this entry gave — ~~because every withdrawal a person performs is a write — revoke, add a deny, close a grant's period, end a guardianship, end a role assignment, set the disabled flag. Each one is a ruleset write, so each one rebuilds immediately.~~ That argument was load-bearing and it had a hole in it: the boundary it leaned on did not list membership, so membership.terminate ⛔ rebuilt nothing. What actually delivers the asymmetry now is that nothing is stored — a withdrawal cannot be stale because there is no copy of the answer left to go stale. The safeguarding case and the calendar case are now immediate for the same reason. The asymmetric TTL this entry kept proposing as "the obvious answer nobody wrote down" is not needed at all: the asymmetry it wanted to buy no longer has a mechanism to be bought for, which beats both a clock and a boundary.

This is D-107's ruling ~~with its mechanism attached~~ with its mechanism removed. "I know, that the time will change, how the rules resolve and IT IS FINE" described a behaviour when it was written and described a policy under D-111: the acceptance had a number in it (one refresh) and the refresh had a cause (the nightly rebuild). ~~That is the difference between a known-and-accepted gap and a gap nobody has decided to accept, which is the distinction this file keeps insisting on.~~ D-114 keeps the ruling and retires the need for it: under live resolution the calendar moves the answer when it moves, so what D-107 waived has stopped being a gap in the first place. A ruling that turns out to be unnecessary is a better outcome than a ruling that had to be defended — and this file's discipline of writing the acceptance down anyway is what let it be recognised as discharged rather than quietly forgotten.

What it cost. The transitive-audience invalidation problem this entry called the hard half dissolved rather than solved — ~~a full rebuild reaches the closure by definition, so "can it be invalidated incrementally at all?" has no answer required.~~ The price is honest and D-112 pays it: ~~a nightly full rebuild is affordable specifically at the stated size (a few hundred people × 66 codes × a small number of items), and D-111 says in the same breath that this would be a different decision at ten thousand people. The second price is that an answer can be a night stale on the calendar cases, and the corpus has now said that out loud rather than inheriting it from OLDER(n)~~ — D-114 retires both prices, and with the second one goes the only staleness this file ever accepted on purpose. The remaining cost is on the other side of the ledger: the key's space at that size was a few hundred people × 66 codes, order tens of thousands of entries, so the rebuild was cheap too — but role_holder and person_group_member were two of the eight kinds of write D-111 named — six tables, the D-109 flag and a merge — and they are the two most ordinary writes in this organization, so every Thursday group edit dropped the whole cache and the effective hit rate was time since the last group edit. A cache whose invalidation is free and total is one step from no cache.

What reopens it. The same trigger as F-15: the population reaching a few thousand people, or a thousand registrants on one event (D-112). ~~There the rebuild is the last of that round's list to hurt and the last to need redesigning~~ — which is why this entry closes at the size rather than in principle. What returns at that trigger is now named instead of vague (D-114): materialize effective_permission per person, call it that, and carry three things this entry's cache lacked — a per-person invalidation handle beside the global one, a stated list of the tables it watches, and that list derived from the operand registry rather than from a list of ideas.

Impact. ~~No schema. What changes is a job that has to exist, a definition of the ruleset the write path has to obey~~ — round 14 inverts this line: the schema change is a deletion, permission_cache goes (D-114), the job disappears, and the definition the write path had to obey goes with it. What is left to build is a request-scoped memo and two batch entry points, neither of which is a table.
