The D-103 incremental-invalidation question stays closed, now for the second time: first because a rebuild reached the closure anyway, now because the only thing invalidated through the closure is a compilation and that walk is bounded and already exists. The per-person effect of the sweep is no longer an invalidation question at all (data-model/05 §10) — it is a fact about what MEMBERS evaluates to on the checked date, which is a description of what moves, and nothing more.

docs.title: F-7 ✅ Dissolved — a nightly rebuild of cached answers and a materialized effective-permission table are one job
docs.text:
Dissolved by D-111, which is a different event from being answered, and is written as such on purpose. This entry asked the system to pick one of two designs. What happened is that the design got chosen for another reason altogether — a rebuild cadence, decided in F-6 — and a nightly full rebuild of cached answers and a nightly materialized effective_permission table turned out to be the same job with two names. There is now one job. Nothing weighed A against B, no trade-off was adjudicated, and a dissolved question is the kind that comes back if nobody writes down that it dissolved, so this heading is the writing-down — and like F-6's, the heading is kept as the name of what round 13 did, not as a description of what exists (D-081): five files link this slug, thirteen links, and the two designs it names are now one deleted and one unbuilt. domain/06 §8 carries the longer argument; this entry is the pointer, not a second copy of it.

Re-amended by D-114, because one of the two things this entry dissolved between has just been deleted. Read the paragraph above as history or it becomes a false statement: there is no longer "one job", because the nightly rebuild of cached answers is gone and a materialized effective_permission table was never built. So the dissolution has to be restated in the terms that survive it, and these are the honest ones. The two designs did converge in 2026 — a nightly full rebuild is a materialization with a worse name, and D-111 saw that — but they converged into an object that round 14 removed. What F-7 actually established is the part that does not depend on which of them was built: there was never a third thing to choose, no design in which you cache answers per person in one place and materialize them per person in another. That finding stands, and it stands more cleanly now that only one of the two arms is even on the table. What is therefore not settled, and never was: whether this system should ever hold effective_permission rows at all. At D-112's trigger that table returns on its own merits — not as the surviving half of a dissolved choice, but as a decision entered under its own name, with a per-person invalidation handle and a stated staleness window, which is what D-114 says the deleted cache should have carried if it was going to exist at all (D-112).

~~Recommendation. Start with cache-only. Materializing is a denormalization requiring transactional maintenance, and a silent refresh failure is an access bug nothing detects.~~ ~~That recommendation was right and is now unaddressable, because there is no longer a choice to make: the rebuild exists, and whether its output is called a cache or a table is a naming decision about one job.~~ It is unaddressable still, and for a starker reason than the one above gave: neither arm exists now. Note what the reasoning was for — the fear of a refresh that fails silently and changes who has access. ~~is a real property of the surviving design, and it survives as a duty on the nightly job rather than as a reason to prefer the other arm~~ — that fear was the best argument in this entry, and D-114 answers it the way it answers everything else: there is no refresh to fail. ~~a duty on the nightly job~~ is gone, and with it the failure mode F-7 was weighing when it said cache-only. If effective_permission is ever materialized at D-112's trigger, this is the paragraph that obligation comes back to, and it comes back as a monitoring duty on a real table rather than as a tiebreak between two designs nobody is choosing between.

~~Impact. Performance only; revisit if measurement demands it. The membership gate makes materializing harder, not easier — every membership transition would have to rewrite rows.~~ The membership gate half of that sentence was already dead when it was written — the gate is deleted by D-100 — and it is kept here struck because it is the clearest illustration in this file of an entry reasoning from a mechanism nobody had noticed removing.

The one constraint that is not dissolved, because it points the other way — and it is now the whole surviving content of this entry. ~~The rebuild may evaluate expressions per person — that is what warming a cache is, and at~~ at D-112's size ~~it is cheap~~ a per-person evaluation would have been cheap; there is no longer a job that does it. What stays forbidden is the way to get this wrong that domain/06 §8 names: inside a check, an expression is compiled to a predicate on the person being asked and never materialized as a set. Otherwise ~~the nightly job is correct and~~ every request still costs three thousand rows. A reader who takes from this entry that "materializing was accepted" has taken the wrong thing in both rounds it has been written: the job was adopted and then deleted, and the read path was never adopted at all. ~~the job was adopted, the read path was not~~ What is left standing is a prohibition with no permission next to it — which is the correct shape for a system that stores no answers, and the reason invariant 19's structural half is that the schema now has nowhere to put a per-person answer even if somebody wants one.

What reopens it. ~~Nothing reopens the choice, because there is nothing left to choose between.~~ Round 14 reopened the choice by deleting one side of it, which is the one way this heading could become false — so the honest line is that the entry stays dissolved as a choice and stays closed as a plan. What can move it is the D-112 trigger — a few thousand people, or a thousand registrants on one event — at which point ~~the question is no longer cache-versus-table but whether a full rebuild is the right shape at all,~~ the question is exactly one question: does this system materialize effective_permission per person, under that name, with a per-person invalidation handle and a stated staleness window. It is a genuine question and, per D-114, it must arrive as a decision entry of its own — not as this one quietly reopened, and not as a cache reintroduced in a migration.

docs.title: F-8 🟢 Retention policy for access_log
docs.text:
Question. How long do the login and authorization-decision rows live?

This entry used to answer itself, in the wrong direction. It said: partition monthly, archive to cold storage, never deletion. That is right about the rows and wrong about everything else, and the mistake is the same one D-088 made salient for audit_log: a retention policy stated as one number silently decides what the row contains, which is the part with the person data in it.

Proposed — and it is a proposal awaiting you, not a position these documents hold: access_log takes the same window as audit_log's payloads, 24 months, with rows kept and their contents emptied on the same schedule, because a trail of who was allowed to see what that outlives the trail of what was actually changed answers the interesting half of an incident and not the other half. Monthly partitioning survives as the mechanism; it is how the window gets applied cheaply, and it was recommended long before anybody decided on a window.

Why the question is structurally weaker here than it is for audit_log. 05-authorization §9 keeps the contents of a read out of this table to begin with — it records that a permission was exercised, not what was on the screen — so there is no payload-expiry argument and no long-history loss to weigh. What remains is the ordinary tension: a security review wants the login trail back to the start of the system, and a privacy review wants a record of somebody's late-night browsing to stop existing eventually. Inverting the arithmetic is worth noticing: the original "never deletion" made this table outlive the person record it describes; the proposal makes it shorter-lived than the business rows, which is a different objection and a defensible one.

Needed. Your confirmation of the 24 months, and the same legal review assumption 49 registers — which now has both clocks in front of it rather than one.

Impact if unanswered. Neither table can be shrunk afterwards without a migration over the two largest tables in the system, and the first time anybody wants to answer "how long have people been able to read this?" the honest answer is that nobody wrote down when the logging started.

See: data-model/05 §9, D-088.

docs.title: F-9 🟢 Should membership_type stay a table with one row?
docs.text:
Question. D-037 kept membership_type as a table with a single seeded member row, on the principle that vocabularies are rows and not enums — at the cost of an FK that always holds one value.

Impact. A deliberate trade, not an oversight. Worth confirming it is the trade you want, since it is the one place the design pays a structural cost for a hypothetical future.

See: data-model/03 §1

docs.title: F-10 🟡 Which invariants the ORM cannot express, and who writes those
docs.text:
Question. D-072 moved the schema to an ORM. Most of what the deleted DDL asserted an ORM will generate from a model definition. Four shapes it generally cannot, and each appears dozens of times in these documents.

The four are not equally bad, and round 10 moved them in opposite directions, which is the reason this entry changed colour. Shapes 1, 2 and 3 gained instances — the round that deleted the hierarchy spent itself inventing new temporal tables and a new expression language. Shape 4 lost its only instance, and shape 4 was the entire reason this question was red.

  1. No two open rows overlap — the temporal invariant under memberships, guardianships, grants, and — new — person_group_member (D-098) and role_holder (D-100). On PostgreSQL this needs an exclusion constraint over a range built from two columns. The two new ones are stricter than the idiom is usually generated: both state "may not overlap, counted over all rows and not only the open ones", which is the opposite of the partial-index habit this shape normally pairs with. An ORM that generates the familiar "one open row per key" version silently permits the overlapping closed row that a group member's history is full of, and the imported corpus guarantees one.
  2. Unique, but only among rows satisfying a condition — "one open request per person and type", "one primary contact among open rows", and new: audience.code unique where set (D-103), because naming an audience is optional and most audiences are a grant's private addressee list. These need a partial unique index; a plain unique constraint over the same columns is a different and wrong rule, forbidding the second NULL that history requires — and here it would forbid every unnamed audience, which is most of them. Gone: "one live exposure per unit and assignment", with scope_exposure (D-097).
  3. Anything whose answer comes from another table or from the resolver — this is where round 10 worked, and it had five instances where it had three; round 11 added a sixth, and it is the first one whose subject is a column that deliberately has no key to follow:
  4. Gone: the holder limit (max_holders, deleted with positions, D-100), the nesting rules and the exposure direction (both D-097). Naming them keeps the count honest.
  5. Kept: per-scheme identifier uniqueness (D-080 item 1 is this class), and one current value per (person, definition), whose condition lives in attribute_definition.allow_multiple — a uniqueness rule some definitions want and others forbid (data-model/09-attributes.md §3). It stays the cleanest example in the list: the same two columns are unique for one definition and repeatable for the next, so no partial index can be written without knowing which definitions exist at runtime.
  6. New — requiredness conditioned on another table: an audience_operand leaf must carry selector_arg_id exactly when its selector's takes_argument is true, and must leave it null exactly when the operand binds to the item (D-102). The condition is a value in selector_type, three tables away from the row it constrains, so NOT NULL cannot state it and the arity check has to.
  7. New — a check that reads another table: an AUDIENCE(...) leaf may not point at an audience whose code is null (D-103; §11 check 12 of data-model/05). Nothing about the operand row tells you this; only the row it references does. The same class carries the name namespace, now spanning role, person_group and audience.code with every selector_type.code reserved against it — no single constraint spans three tables and a fourth table's values, so the write path carries it and check 12 only asserts that the write path exists.
  8. New, and the mirror image of the rest: two rows that must coexist. Creating an event obliges an instantiated event.answer.view grant aimed at ORGANIZERS (D-102) — one row in one table requiring a row in another, in one transaction, with nothing in either schema stating the debt. A constraint can forbid a missing child or an orphan parent; it cannot make an INSERT in event write a row in access_grant. The backstop is the events with no answer-view grant report, and an organizer whose event arrived without its grant is a person with a title and no permissions — which reads as a bug report, not a constraint violation. The legacy import owes one per event row, so the first occurrence of this is expected in bulk, not at the margins.
  9. New in round 11, and the first whose subject is a column with no key on purpose: a person merge or a redaction must repoint every audience_operand leaf whose selector_arg_id names the absorbed or erased person (D-105). The column carries no foreign key by design (D-011's accepted trade-off), so there is no cascade to inherit and no key for an ORM to walk: the merge reassignment table gains the row, the erasure path gains the scan, and both have to reach all five argument kinds — person, role, person_group, event, audience. Nothing in the schema notices a missed leaf. The nightly orphan check becomes the backstop rather than the only mechanism, and the failure is this module's quietest one: a subtraction that stops subtracting, because a leaf resolving to nobody is the empty set and an empty set behind a - makes the result wider. Until this round the hand-named people lived in a table that did have a key, which is the only reason the instance is new rather than long overdue.
  10. A column that may not change once it is set — its only named instance is gone: org_unit.parent_unit_id (D-036) was deleted by D-097, so this shape is currently empty. That is a fact about the corpus, not a proof, and the two candidates left are worth naming because they were previously hiding behind the dead one: permission.code — the catalog's own words are "adding one is free, renaming one is a migration", and nothing in a schema enforces a migration — and audience.code once something names it, since AUDIENCE(code) resolves through that column and a rename rewrites every expression that reached it, which is exactly what rule 5 of the name namespace promises does not happen for names.

What made this shape different from 1–3 was that there is no report, and that is the half worth re-examining rather than inheriting. A reparent left no offending row: every row stayed individually valid while the meaning of a subtree's history moved under it, and the path the damage would show up in was itself derived and would simply be recomputed to match. audience.code has a report — which grants name this audience, and at what depth — and D-103 requires the editor to show it before saving an edit. So shape 4 is no longer the shape with no evidence, provided that listing is cheap: see F-16. permission.code needs the same query over a different table and nobody has written either. This entry is 🟡 rather than 🔴 on exactly that condition, and 🟡 is a bet, not a measurement.

Why this is a question and not a task. The fallback an ORM offers for all four is validation in the model layer, and data-model/00 §6a explains why that is not the same guarantee: an import, a data fix, and a second client all bypass it. The legacy import is the specific case that makes this urgent rather than theoretical — the corpus arrives through exactly the path that model-layer validation does not cover, and an overlapping membership written by the importer is nearly impossible to diagnose afterwards, because the two rows look like two memberships and only one of them was ever real. Round 10 gave the import two more of these: consecutive dated periods for the same person in whatever table ends up holding them (shape 1), and one answer-view grant per event row it creates (shape 3) — a debt the importer owes in bulk, whose first failures will therefore also arrive in bulk. Add the third new graph rule to shape 3's list while the section is open: a cycle across audiences is refused at save by a reachability walk over the reference closure (D-103), which is a rule about a graph spanning two tables and is the least constraint-shaped thing in the model.

Needed. A decision per shape — hand-written migration, database check, or application check plus report — before the first migration is generated, not discovered during one. The recommendation in data-model/00 §6a is that shapes 1 and 2 are hand-written migrations, and that this is the condition on which using an ORM is safe rather than an argument against using one. Shape 3 needs one more thing than a decision: its checks are the only enforcement the selector language has, so the arity and null-argument checks have to be written before the first expression is saved, and the §11 list in data-model/05 — renumbered for round 10, several checks having lost their subjects — is a review instruction rather than a test.

Impact if unanswered. Not a crash. A system whose constraints are quietly absent, whose integrity checks (every "Invariants to verify" section) then start reporting rows, and whose first report is read as a data-quality problem rather than as the missing guarantee arriving on schedule.

See: data-model/00 §6a, appendix/erd.md's inventory, which marks every temporal entity.

docs.title: F-11 🟢 Does the identity reviewer need to read the person record to settle a claim?
docs.text:
Question. D-089 routes a colliding sign-up to identity_reviewer and resolves it with person.merge. The seed role holds person.merge, import.view and import.apply — and not person.view. So a reviewer decides "is this the same child?" from match signals, names and dates, without opening either record.

Why this is a question now and was not one before. Merging already needed a human, but the alternative to merging was doing nothing: a wrong call left two rows side by side, visible in the nightly duplicate report, correctable next quarter. The activation gate changed the stakes. A reviewer who rejects a hypothesis lets an account go live; one who confirms it joins two lives, including a login, into one row. Both directions now have a person waiting on the far side of the answer, which is a different job from tidying a queue, and a job the permission set does not obviously cover.

Positions. - Leave it — the signals are the decision, and a reviewer who needs to read both records is a reviewer who is about to merge on a hunch anyway. Cheapest, and consistent with "identity is what the match says, adjudicated by a person". - Grant person.view to identity_reviewer — settles it, and quietly makes an identity role one of the roles that can read a child's whole record, which is a bigger thing than the role's name suggests and is exactly what the catalog's top tier is reserved for. - A narrower read the catalog does not have yet — the resolver code that would expose only the two candidate rows and their signals, which would be a new code and therefore a decision entry, not an edit to this file. It is not proposed here, and would need arguing.

Recommendation. Leave it, and watch the queue rather than the design. If reviewers start resolving hypotheses at a suspiciously high confirmation rate without asking for context, that is the sign the signals are not enough — and the honest response is a person.view grant discussed as a top-tier membership, not a new code invented at a desk.

Needed. Nothing before implementation. Revisit when the first real import has produced a real queue.

docs.title: F-12 ✅ Closed — may a role be held by a rule, as an audience is?
docs.text:
Answered: no, and the split is the design (D-100). The first of the three options below is the decision. A role is an office held by a named person for a period and it confers nothing; a group is company, a dated set of people with no authority of its own; and what reaches a set of people with a permission is a grant, which has had a grantee pair since D-042. Round 10 did not defend that boundary so much as make it cleaner than the question assumed: it renamed role_assignment to role_holder, deleted role_permission, deleted positions, and deleted the membership gate — so "everyone with a current membership holds role X" is now not a missing feature of the office table but a sentence about who the grants reach, written MEMBERS * ROLE(x) where it is wanted.

Why the answer is no, in the decision's own terms. role_holder is the office record: it is what a report reads to answer "who was treasurer in 2023", and a holder list derived from live state cannot answer that, because there is nothing to date. D-100 keeps the two tables specifically because they answer different questions and because merging them would put 🔒🔒 role.assign in one table with ⚠ person_group.member.manage in another — the same objection this entry raised, accepted, and then sharpened. The office record stays the one human-readable answer in the permission model, which is also the resolution of assumption 51.

What closed the other two options. Both began by putting a grantee pair on the office table. With role_permission gone there is nothing left for a rule-held office to carry, so the second arm's materialization sweep would be recording membership in a thing that grants nothing — at which point it is a group, which already exists, is already dated, and does not pretend to be an office. The third arm's cost was never worth having: it deletes the office record's guarantee to buy a row the group table already gives you. ~~F-7 stays open~~ and stays the right place for the materializing question; it is no longer coupled to this one. (This sentence was written before round 13 and got one clause wrong from the day it was published: F-7 is dissolved, not open. Round 14 makes the pointer worth keeping and corrects the clause — F-7 is where the materializing question lives, amended rather than reopened by D-114, and the table it speaks of would now arrive on its own merits at D-112's trigger.)

What the question was, kept because the reasoning recurs. Raised by D-091, which refused to decide it: the answer that produced D-091 described permission groups — a set of people with filling rules, carrying permissions — and that was expressible here for anything an access_grant could target, but not for a role, which named one person, one role, one scope, one period with no grantee pair like the one D-042 put on access_grant. ~~"everyone with a current membership holds role X" cannot be written~~ was true of the old table and is false of the language: what cannot be written, still, is a rule-held office — which is the thing that was asked for and refused.

Left open by the answer, deliberately. Whether an office should record elected versus appointed, and what an election writes, was a property of the deleted position tables and is F-18. Whether a grant naming ROLE(x) should carry a MEMBERS term is F-13.

docs.title: F-13 ✅ Closed — a rule that resolves correctly but looks odd is listed as unusual, never as broken
docs.text:
Answered: a listing, not a lint — and no decision entry was needed, because the surface it needed was already being built for another reason. D-109 built a tab on the permissions page, and it refused every save-time refusal. A grant naming ROLE(x) with no MEMBERS term resolves perfectly and looks odd, which is this entry's entire population. So the second and third positions below ("warning at save", "require an explicit choice") are refused by the same move that refused every refusal in this module: the save always succeeds.

The tab has two sections, and the split is this entry's contribution — recorded here because it arrived as a collision, not as a design. D-109 defines Broken: a live rule whose expression names a deprecated, hidden or disabled thing, or fails to resolve at all. A grant that omits MEMBERS is none of those — it resolves, its set is exactly what the writer asked for, and calling it broken would be the same category error F-21 refuses, where an expression that is merely surprising gets reported as though it were wrong. So the tab is split: "Broken" holds only what D-109 defines, and "Unusual" holds rules that resolve correctly and look odd — this entry's population, and nothing else. The two sections are kept apart because they carry different claims about the writer: Broken says something has happened to your rule behind your back; Unusual says your rule means what you wrote and somebody else finds it hard to read. Collapsing them would make the safeguarding signal depend on how tidy the reader's taste runs, which is a fast route to ignoring the half that matters. Each section belongs to the entry that defines it: Broken is D-109's and is carried by F-21; Unusual is this entry's, and its answer therefore stays here rather than moving into F-21.

The premise that closed it, which is D-107's and not this entry's. The whole reason this was a question rather than a one-line rule was that the test fires on the intended case as often as on the mistake — ROLE(counselors) without MEMBERS is how an appointed counselor keeps serving through a lapsed year, and that is the point of D-100, not an accident of it. A warning that cries wolf dies, and a refusal that cries wolf is worse: it teaches the writer to route around it. Against that, this corpus now has an explicit premise to lean on, stated when D-107 opened the grammar to attribute operands and refused to add lint to match: the people writing these rules know what they are writing. They are organizers naming their own groups and their own offices, not anonymous input. Given that premise, a save-time prompt is not protection, it is a doubt expressed on somebody's Tuesday, and the listing — where a writer who is already in the permissions page can see what they wrote next to what everything else they wrote does — is the honest amount of doubt to encode.

What it cost: one section of a page, and the finding is in how small that is. No column, no refusal, no new page — the tab already exists for D-109's purposes and it gained a heading. The cost is carried by the weaker answer instead: the failure this entry described (a person with an office and no powers, discovered by the person least able to diagnose it) is still not prevented by anything. It is listed, in a section that says the rule works. That is D-081's shape again — a convention, not a guard — and this entry now joins F-21 and F-19 as the third instance of the module choosing to show rather than to stop, with the same weakness and, since D-109, the same single place to look. The one thing the split buys is honest labelling: a reader who has decided the tab's Broken section is full of false alarms can still tell that its Unusual section says something different, which is the difference between a signal and noise.

What would reopen it. Not another odd-looking rule. The trigger is a count: if the Unusual section's MEMBERS-less office grants turn out to be mostly mistakes rather than mostly deliberate, the premise above is falsified for this case, and a save-time prompt on is_system roles only — the narrow arm of the recommendation below — becomes worth its false positives again. That would be a decision entry, and it would be the first refusal this module has made about the content of an expression rather than its arithmetic.

Question. D-100 moved the membership test out of the resolver and into the expression, and reversed the posture while doing it: the gate used to be default-on with named carve-outs, and now every sentence about membership is written by hand. Three controls were accepted in place of the deleted mechanism — a standing report, the promise that seeded grants carry MEMBERS, and an import-time counselor count. None of the three inspects a hand-written grant at the moment it is saved. So: when somebody writes ROLE(treasurer) where they meant MEMBERS * ROLE(treasurer), should the editor warn at save, or is the standing report the whole control?

Why it is a question and not a lint rule. The two forms are both legal and one is not always wrong — that is the entire point of the decision, since ROLE(counselors) without MEMBERS is how an appointed counselor keeps serving through a lapsed year. A warning therefore fires on the intended case as often as on the mistake, which is the classic way a warning dies. Against that: the mistake is invisible in the row (a grant with a missing operand looks exactly like a grant that was finished) and its symptom is a person with an office and no powers, discovered by the person least able to diagnose it.

Positions. - Report only — what D-100 says today. Cheapest, no false positives, and the failure is at least aggregate-visible: a report listing role grants whose expression contains no MEMBERS term is a list somebody can read down once a period. - Warning at save, not a refusal — the editor already parses the expression to store the tree, so the test is one node lookup, and the save still succeeds. The cost is a prompt on the legitimate case, which D-100's own example shows is not rare. - Require an explicit choice — the editor asks "must this holder be a current member?" and writes the MEMBERS term or a comment field. Honest, and it is designing a new column out of a question nobody asked yet.

~~Recommendation. The report, plus one narrow save-time warning: fire only when the expression names ROLE(x) for a role whose is_system is true and contains no MEMBERS term~~ — the report half is the answer; the warning half is refused. It is kept struck rather than deleted because it is the best-designed version of the refused option in this file, and because is_system really is the only signal in the schema distinguishing "the organization's own vocabulary" from "a role somebody invented this afternoon" — which is why the narrow arm survives above as the thing that would reopen this entry. A convention, not a guard, in D-081's wording, is now the whole answer rather than the residue of one: nothing stops a client from writing the grant anyway, and nothing warns the writer while they write it. One section of one tab notices afterwards, and says unusual rather than wrong.

Schema impact. None for the report or the warning — both read access_grant joined to the audience_operand subtree. The third arm is a column. No seeded row changes.

Needed. Before the grant editor ships, because "we warn on nothing" and "we warn on this" are different products and the second is cheaper to add first.

docs.title: F-14 ✅ Closed — nothing computes semantic equality of two expressions, and nothing will
docs.text:
Answered: refused, on three grounds, none of them cost.

  1. The stored canonical string is the only identity an expression has. D-105 ruled that the tree is stored exactly as the writer wrote it, and this round's F-22 closes the last route around that: display is free, storage is not, because the write-path checks — the cycle walk, the reserved-name rule, the listing of what names an audience — all reason over the stored form. A fingerprint is a second identity, and a second identity is a second answer to "is this the same audience?", which is precisely the question D-101 gave up in order to keep storage honest.
  2. It is not decidable anyway, and this entry already knew that. With AUDIENCE(code) references, two expressions can fingerprint differently and reach identically because the difference is inside a referenced audience — so the honest design was always "a warning over the expression as written, references treated as opaque atoms". A check that must advertise how much it cannot see is not a control, and D-105's deletion of selector_depth_limit removed even the bounded resolver run that would have made the strong version possible on a deadline.
  3. Nobody is deduplicating audiences, at this system's size. D-112 fixes the population at a few hundred people; the near-duplicate this entry feared "accumulates slowly" is a problem at a scale this corpus will not reach, and the third arm's syntactic fix — storing + children sorted — is now explicitly refused by ground 1. That answers the sentence this entry flagged as unwritten ("whether sorting the children of a commutative operator falls inside what D-105 refused is a sentence nobody has written"): it does not fall inside; it is outside, and it is refused. The stored form is what was typed, including the order.

What this concedes, since a refusal read as a resolution is the usual damage. Two audiences meaning one thing are still two audiences, and the failure this entry described is untouched: an organization names the stale copy, a grant points at it, and the fix looks like a permission change because it is one. The mitigation is not a fingerprint, it is the listing — which grants name this audience — which D-103 already requires and F-16 now prices; plus the D-109 flag, which lets a redundant audience be hidden rather than reconciled with the copy nobody uses. Two ways to live with the duplicate, and no way to detect it, which is the trade D-101 chose and this entry confirms rather than relitigates.

What would reopen it. A real organisation reporting that two audiences diverged and a grant followed the wrong one — not two audiences existing. The trigger is an incident, not untidiness, and the entry stays findable under assumption 59, which already says nothing will compute equality.

Question. D-101 gave up semantic equality to keep storage honest: two audiences are equal when their trees are equal, so MEMBERS + ROLE(x) and ROLE(x) + MEMBERS are two different stored expressions with one meaning, and the canonical fully-bracketed rendering does not fix it because it canonicalizes brackets, not order. Should the system compute a derived fingerprint — canonicalize operands into a sorted multiset per operator, normalize */- where the algebra allows — and warn when a second audience fingerprints the same as a first?

Why it is 🟢 and why it is still here. Nothing depends on it. Two identical sets cost one extra row and one extra evaluation, and the confusion is cosmetic until someone edits one copy. But D-101 explicitly registered this as a question rather than a promise, and the failure mode it prevents is a slow one: an organization accumulates near-duplicate audiences, a grant names the stale one, and the fix is indistinguishable from a permission change — which is audited, alarmed, and requires explaining to somebody.

The part that should not be oversold. The fingerprint is not decidable in general once AUDIENCE(code) references exist (D-103): two expressions can fingerprint differently and reach identically because the difference is inside a referenced audience, and expanding the closure to compare them is a resolver run, not a save-time check. So the honest design is a warning over the expression as written, with references treated as opaque atoms — which catches operand reordering and misses everything nested, and must say so in the UI rather than implying an equivalence proof.

What round 11 did to it, and it was in both directions at once. PERSON(a) + PERSON(b) is now the ordinary way to write a set of people (D-105), so the near-duplicate this entry assumed would accumulate slowly now arrives the first time two people type the same twelve names in a different order. The duplicate is no longer entropy, it is the normal output of hand-typing — and "the confusion is cosmetic until someone edits one copy" describes the common case rather than the rare one. The option that made the duplicate syntactically equal, storing + children sorted, is meanwhile in tension with the same round's ruling that the tree is stored exactly as the writer wrote it, with no rebalancing: sorting the children of a commutative operator is not rebalancing, but it is the same temptation in a milder uniform, and whether it falls inside what D-105 refused is a sentence nobody has written — which is now a thing that has to be said before it can be done. And the fallback already called the honest one, expanding the reference closure to compare two expressions, lost its bound with selector_depth_limit, so a warning that wanted one resolver run now wants a walk of no promised length. The colour stays 🟢: nothing depends on the answer, and a duplicate still costs one extra row and one extra evaluation. What changed is how often it is paid, not what it costs.

Positions. Warn on equal fingerprints (catches the common case, false-positives on deliberately identical sets like two events' ORGANIZERS); compute nothing and let the which grants name this audience listing (F-16) do the work of showing redundancy; or normalize at write so + children are always stored sorted, which makes the common duplicate syntactically equal and needs no new machinery — at the cost of storing an order the language says does not matter.

Schema impact. One derived column on audience, or nothing, and it must never be a unique constraint: a warning that became a constraint would refuse two audiences that legitimately reach the same people, and D-101's reason for giving up equality is precisely that the two are not the same question.

Needed. Not before implementation. Revisit when the first organization has enough audiences that someone asks why two of them behave the same.

docs.title: F-15 ✅ Closed — the per-item preview is cheap at the stated size, and this is what reopens it
docs.text:
Answered by D-112, which supplied the missing number rather than a missing optimisation. The size is written down now, in the decision's own words: a few hundred people in the organization, a few dozen registrants on a typical event, a big camp on the order of two hundred. At that size a preview that resolves an audience for one item is "evaluating a couple of hundred predicates — nobody will feel it". So the preview stays exactly as it was: per-item and lazy (assumption 60), no cap, no background job, no cache of its own.

Why this closes an entry that had asked for a measurement for three rounds. The measurement was never the missing thing; the population was. "At what size does that stop being an interaction and start being a job?" is unanswerable without a size, which is why it stayed 🟡 through three rounds of increasingly precise reasoning about a cost nobody had bounded. D-112 names the failure mode directly — "a cost argument without a number is not an argument, it is a mood" — and notes the number is not a target but this corpus's own scale: the legacy export is a few hundred people and their events.

What it costs, and what is now explicitly not done. The second and third positions below are both declined, and the third deserves the note because it was the entry's own favourite: the preview does not decline to list above a threshold. That arm was attractive precisely because it cost the model nothing, and it is still true that a threshold on a listing is legitimate where a threshold on a check is refused — but a threshold nobody needs is not a cheap feature, it is an untestable screen state and a number nobody can justify. It comes back only with the trigger below. The cost that is paid is honest and stated: nothing bounds what a preview can evaluate, and that is now accepted at a stated size rather than merely unmeasured, which is a different epistemic state and the only one this entry was ever going to reach.

What reopens it — the trigger, because a stated assumption without a trigger is a guess with more confidence. If the population reaches a few thousand people, or a thousand registrants on one event, reopen this entry first: D-112's ordering is that the preview is "the first thing a user will feel and ~~the nightly rebuild the last~~" — and D-112's own copy of that sentence now carries the same correction: the nightly rebuild was last in that list and is now deleted; what sits in its place is nothing, so the order is unchanged and one shorter. Reopening does not mean the design was wrong; it means the two rules that must survive any growth — a check compiles its expression to a predicate and never materializes the set, and a listing is paginated — start earning their keep here before anywhere else.

A dependency recorded by D-114, which changes what this entry's cheapness is paid for. The preview is still cheap, and nothing about the size argument above moves. What changed is who pays. A nightly job used to pre-pay this work off the interaction — not by design, just as a side effect of a cache that had to be warmed anyway — and with the answer cache deleted the preview now computes on open, every time, with no fallback behind it. The batch entry point exists for exactly this: a screen of affordances is one can_many(person, codes[], item?), not a loop of single checks, so the N+1 that made a cache look necessary is removed at the place that actually caused it. Recorded as a dependency and not as a risk: the preview's stated affordability now rests on the memo and on can_many existing, which is an implementation duty these documents can name but cannot enforce — assumption 60 is amended to say so.

Question. Before D-102 the question "whom does this grant reach?" had one answer per grant. Now a bound operand makes the reached set a function of the item, so an editor that wants to show whom this reaches must compute it per item: for a camp, the audience's tree evaluated against that camp's registrations, waitlist, confirmations and organizer roster. At what size does that stop being an interaction and start being a job?

Why this arrived with round 10 and not before. The preview used to be one expansion of a rule against a set of people. D-102 made ATTENDED, PLACED, CONFIRMED, ON_WAITLIST and ORGANIZERS read the item's own tables, and D-103 made each AUDIENCE(code) node a nested evaluation rather than a row fetch — so one preview can now touch four registrations tables and re-evaluate a tree per referenced audience, and the number of people it expands to is the size of an event roster. F-7 asked whether answers should be materialized for enforcement; this is the same cost centre for preview, where staleness is a UI lie rather than an access bug — which is the softer failure and the more tempting one to ship.

What is assumed and not measured. That expanding a few hundred people at a screen is fine, and that the tree walk is cheap because it is small. Neither has been measured against a corpus of thousands of roster rows (B-1) and an event with a real registration list, and the case that hurts is the nested audience three levels deep, evaluated once per item in a list of items.

What round 11 took away. The second of those assumptions used to have a backstop it never mentioned: the depth bound made "the tree walk is cheap because it is small" true by construction rather than by habit, and D-105 deleted it, so the size of a preview is now bounded by the same nothing a check is bounded by — acyclicity, and whatever the writer typed. The hand-typed set is the new thing in the walk as well: forty names are forty leaves, expanded per item, where they used to be one LIST leaf over a table with an index. And the save-time cost moved too: the closure whose size a preview walks is discovered by walking it, so the first preview of a wide audience and the save that accepted it pay for the same traversal. What this does not change is which answer is honest. Of the three positions below, the third — refuse to list above a threshold, show a count — is now the only local bound on offer, and unlike a cap on the enforcement path it costs the model nothing, because a preview that declines to list changes what a screen shows and not whom a grant reaches. That distinction is the whole reason a threshold is acceptable here and refused in F-21. Still 🟡: this was already a measurement the editor owes before shipping, and the round made the measurement more urgent without changing who takes it.

Positions. Preview lazily, per item, on demand, and never for a list of items (the honest default: a count, not a name list, until somebody opens one). Cache the expansion per (audience, item) with the key shape F-6 settles. Or refuse previews above a threshold and show "too many to list; export instead", which is cheap, honest, and the kind of answer a spec is allowed to give before it has a number.

Schema impact. None for the lazy form. ~~A cache is not a table, but the key must include the item (D-102) and the dependency set must include every referenced audience transitively (D-103), so F-6 and this are one decision about keys taken twice if they are not decided together.~~ (Round 14 makes this paragraph a report on a decision about keys that no longer has any keys to decide — D-114 deletes the answer cache, so the item is a parameter of a compilation rather than a component of a key. Both findings inside it outlive that wording: whatever is served for an item was resolved for that item, and anything reached through AUDIENCE(x) is reached transitively — which is now the walk that drops the compilations embedding an edited audience, exactly as § F-16 has it.) Still none, and now for a stronger reason: there is no cache left to key.

Needed. A measurement before the editor ships, because "show the set" is a promise the resolver has to keep on a UI thread. Assumption in the meantime: previews are per-item and lazy, and no screen expands a set for more than one item at a time.

docs.title: F-16 ✅ Closed — listing the grants that name an audience is a scan over a small table, at the stated size
docs.text:
Answered by D-112: D-103's assumption is true, now on stated grounds rather than on hope. Listing the grants that name an audience is "a scan over a small table with a handful of referencing rows each", at a few hundred people and a few dozen registrants per event, a big camp on the order of two hundred. Pagination is a UI nicety, not a requirement. So both D-103 protections that hang off this query — refusing to end a referenced audience a live grant reaches, and showing which grants name it, and at what depth before such an edit saves — stand as written, and the fallback this entry kept polished (weaken the D-103 rule, in the open, as a decision entry) is not needed.

What it cost, and one caller that quietly disappeared. No schema, no decision entry, and — worth recording, because this entry's whole argument was that the walk had gained callers — F-6 has just removed one of them. Round 12's worry was that cache invalidation across the reference closure might be too expensive to run on every edit ("an invalidation that is too slow to run is not a slow feature, it is a stale allow"). ~~D-111 deletes that caller: a nightly full rebuild does the walk itself, in batch, and the incremental version is never implemented.~~ Round 14 removes the rebuild too, and hands the caller back in a smaller shape (D-114): the only thing now invalidated through the closure is a compilation, and because a compilation is finite and enumerable over the audience tree, "an edit to a shared audience invalidates everything" is "it invalidates the compilations that embed it" — a bounded walk, over the same closure, using the walk the save path already performs. So the caller count is two, not one: the cycle check on save, which is mandatory and was always mandatory, and compilation invalidation, which is optional in the sense that a compilation can simply be dropped and re-made. What changed about being fast is the consequence of being slow, and it got much smaller: a slow walk now delays an edit instead of leaving a stale allow standing, because nothing an expression reaches is cached as an answer any more. At this size both are cheap, and only one of them has to be correct.

The reasoning stays, because it is the part that transfers. Everything below about the reverse-edge walk — that the index serving "what is in this tree" does not serve "what points here", and that the plausible answer "a selector_arg_id index" is the kind of answer that stops being true the first time an OR over selector_kind and selector_arg_id walks past it — is still how the query has to be thought about, and still unwritten. D-112 makes it affordable; it does not make it correct. These documents still contain no SQL (D-072), so what is settled is the cost, not the plan, and a future implementation that reads this entry as "already solved" will write the slow version of a query that is only fast because the table is small.

What reopens it. The D-112 trigger — a few thousand people, or a thousand registrants on one event — with this entry second in that list, after the preview. Note what reopening costs here and nowhere else: the fallback is not a slower screen but a weaker D-103 rule, which is a decision entry, because the property being traded is the one that keeps a retired set from widening access.

Question. D-103 makes two safety rules depend on one query: an audience may not be ended or deleted while a live grant — or a live audience reachable from one — names it, and saving an edit to a referenced audience must show which grants name it, and at what depth. The decision entry states its premise as an assumption: that finding the referrers is cheap. Nothing has measured it, and the whole of D-103's protection is built on it.

Why the answer is not obviously yes. audience_operand denormalizes audience_id so that "what nodes are in this audience's tree" is indexed — that is the cheap direction. The protection needs the opposite direction: which other audiences contain a leaf pointing here, then transitively upward, then the grants aimed at each of those. That is a reverse-edge walk over a tree table, and the index that makes the forward walk fast does not serve it. A selector_arg_id index probably answers it — one lookup per level — which is exactly the kind of answer that looks certain until the first OR over selector_kind and selector_arg_id stops using it.

Why it matters more than a UI query. Because under - an empty operand makes the result wider, not narrower: an audience that stops resolving does not quietly stop granting, it can start granting. That is why the listing is not a nicety on top of the deletion rule but the only way an editor can tell a person what they are about to widen. A protection you cannot see is a protection you will route around — and the route is right there, because naming an audience is optional, so an editor that blocks the safe action teaches people to inline the subexpression instead, which removes the reference the safety rule needed.

Positions. Add the reverse index and state it as an invariant to verify (cheap, and it is a row in §11 of data-model/05 rather than a design change); ~~cap the listing by depth so the walk is bounded by selector_depth_limit, which D-101 already enforces and which makes the worst case finite by construction~~ — this position is void, and it was the cheapest of the three: the parameter and the save-time bound behind it are both deleted (D-105), so there is no number for a listing to inherit, and the walk is finite only because the closure is acyclic and is discovered by walking it; or drop the "and at what depth" half of the requirement, which removes the transitive walk and keeps the single-hop refusal.

What round 11 did to it: this measurement gained callers rather than changing shape. Adding a name to an audience used to be an insert into audience_member; it is now a save of the whole expression (D-105), so every hand-typed exception added to an audience that references another one runs the editor's referrer walk — the listing is priced per name added, which is a different traffic pattern from once, when somebody edits a rule, and it arrives next to the two-writers problem D-105 names in the same breath. The same walk also became, in the same round, the only structural guard the save path has at all: the cycle check across audiences is a reachability walk over the closure, and with the depth bound gone it is the only thing standing between a saved expression and one that never terminates. One measurement therefore now answers two questions — is D-103's protection cheap enough to be obeyed, and does saving a wide audience cost anything an editor can feel — and the second is a question nobody had to ask last round. Still 🟡, for its original reason: the fallback is already written down as a decision entry (weaken the D-103 rule, in the open), so the exposure is a guard people route around rather than a design with no answer.

Needed. Before an editor offers to name an audience. If the answer is "not cheap", the fallback is not a slower screen but a weaker D-103 rule, which is a decision entry, not an implementation detail — and it should be taken in the open, because the property being traded is the one that keeps a deleted set from widening access.

Impact. If the walk is slow at real sizes, either the guard is skipped under time pressure or the feature people use is the one that bypasses it. Both are worse than the measurement.

docs.title: F-17 ✅ Closed — the expression is the record, so a nested audience's past is recomputed and never promised
docs.text:
Answered by D-110, which removed the premise rather than filling the gap. "Whom did this grant reach in May?" is answered, if at all, by evaluating the words against the data of May, and these documents do not promise the answer. The audit record of a grant's reach is the expression; the preview is logged as a rendering on a date, not as a statement of members. None of the three positions below is adopted — not acceptance-by-declaration, not materialized dated expansions, and notably not the audience_revision row this entry recommended, because D-110 refuses exactly what made it attractive: the audit trail records the edit, not the meaning that existed before it, so a history of inner expressions is not being kept and a table for it would be a promise these documents have just declined to make.

Why the question lost its force rather than its argument. Two things changed the ground under it. First D-109: if nothing a rule names is deleted, the words stay evaluable long after their reason is gone — a retired office still resolves, a deprecated group still resolves, a name stays reserved — so a past-date recomputation is usually computable rather than usually impossible. Second D-110's own refusal of the roster: the tempting fix was always "keep the list", and the list is the table this corpus has deleted twice. What is left is honestly bounded, which is the most any answer here was ever going to be.

The part that is conceded rather than solved, written down so nobody finds it sideways. Editing a shared audience changes what every grant that names it has meant all along, because those grants hold a word and not a copy — an edit to a shared audience is therefore a retrospective edit to every rule that names it — and a re-evaluation for a past date uses today's inner expression. This is why a past-date answer can be wrong rather than merely missing, which is worse and is the reason the entry was 🟡. What D-103 already provides is the control, and it is the only one there will be: the editor prints the resolved set before an edit to a shared expression saves, so the person editing sees, at least once, the thing they are changing backwards in time. What is not kept is a history of inner expressions. D-103 accepted this as the price of reuse; D-110 makes it an explicit consequence for the audit question instead of an implication.

The one asymmetry that survives, and it is the real residue. A group still answers "was she in it on 1 June 2024?" from dated rows, and an audience still does not. D-110 settles what an audience records, not what it can reconstruct, and the guidance this entry already gave stays the guidance: a set you must be able to reconstruct across time is a group, not an audience — which is now advice backed by a ruling about the record rather than by a gap in the storage.

What reopens it. An incident, not a gap. Specifically: a question asked during an actual safeguarding or dispute review that a recomputation could not answer, because that is the moment the promise these documents just declined starts costing something, and D-110's honest boundary ("possible, never promised") is the sentence that will be quoted at somebody. A second trigger is the D-112 size trigger, since a recomputation over years of data is cheap at a few hundred people and may not be at a few thousand.

Question. "Whom did this grant reach on 1 June 2024?" is answerable for a group — its roster rows are dated — and unanswerable for an audience, whose expression is evaluated live. D-103 makes that sharper: with AUDIENCE(code) a rule can now contain another rule, so the set reached in 2024 depended on the shape of an expression that nothing has stored a copy of, edited ever since. The one place the old shape existed is the audit trail, and its payloads expire after 24 months (D-088). So past a two-year window, a nested audience's past reach is not reconstructable at all — not imprecise, unavailable. Is that acceptable, or is this the case that finally justifies F-7's materialized table?

Why this is the strongest version of F-7's argument, and why it is stated separately. ~~F-7 is framed as performance and answered "start with cache-only"~~, which is right on its own terms. (Two corrections from later rounds, both against this sentence rather than this entry: F-7 was dissolved in round 13 and never answered, and D-114 has since deleted the cache-only arm the recommendation preferred — so there is no longer a first arm to start with, and a materialized table would arrive on its own merits at D-112's trigger. The question raised below is untouched by that, and is the harder one.) This question is not about speed: it is that the audit trail's short half and the question's long half do not overlap. A safeguarding question ("who could see this child's record while X was treasurer?") is asked years later, of a system whose expressions are recomputed from state that has moved, over a set — referenced audiences — that nobody versioned. D-103's own note that the listing matters "more than it looks" is the same observation one hop away.

The uncomfortable symmetry, which round 11 made sharper. D-098 kept person_group_member and audience_member as two dated sets of people on purpose, and refused to unify them, because a group states its members and an audience computes them — and that refusal is exactly what made one of them answerable across time and the other not. D-105 deleted the second of those two tables, so the pair these documents have to live with is now a group's dated roster against a PERSON(x) leaf that carries no date at all. The hand-written set, which used to be the half of an audience that could answer "was she in it in 2024?", moved to the unanswerable side along with the rest of the expression: same asymmetry, one table narrower, and worse in one specific way — a set somebody keeps by hand was the cheap instance of the reconstructable answer, and there is no hand-kept set left inside an audience that can give it. Any answer here still pushes toward making an audience a dated snapshot series, which is what D-101 refused to store and D-098 refused to merge; what changed is that the pressure now arrives from the plainest audiences in the system rather than from the nested ones this entry was written about.

Positions. Accept it, and write it down — these documents state plainly that an audience has no reconstructable reach beyond the audit window, and that a set you need to be able to reconstruct is a group (cheap, honest, and consistent with D-098's "a group states its members; a selector picks them"; this is the default these documents currently assume). Materialize dated expansions for audiences a live grant names — F-7's option, arriving with a sweep that must not fail silently, since a silent refresh failure is an access bug nothing detects. Version the expression instead of the result — an audience_revision row per edit, small because it is a tree of ids, which answers "what did the rule say" but not "whom did it reach", and is a much cheaper promise to keep.

What round 11 did to it: it widened the hole and raised the value of one answer. D-105 did not dodge the history question — with audience_member deleted, "who was on this audience in 2026?" joins the questions that are a recomputation over audit payloads, the payloads expire after 24 months (D-088), and so the question stops being answerable in 2028: the same hole, one table wider, accepted rather than papered over. What moved is the worth of the third position. audience_revision used to answer "what did the rule say?" and to stop there, because the hand-typed people lived outside the rule in a table of their own. A name somebody typed is now part of the rule, so versioning the expression versions the names with it: for a hand-written set — and for exactly that part of any audience — a revision row now answers the reached-set question outright, dated by edit rather than by validity, which is the as-of/audit-time distinction the glossary insists on rather than a new one. It still answers nothing for GROUP(x), ROLE(x) or a referenced audience, all of which move under an expression without being written in it. A narrower promise than the entry implied, and a real one. The colour stays 🟡: this is the same question with more evidence behind one option, and still no question implementation waits on.

Recommendation. The third, plus the first. Storing the expression per edit is nearly free, it is the question a reviewer actually asks, and it keeps the answer honest about what it is; the reached set stays a group's job and these documents should say so out loud rather than leaving a reader to discover the gap during an incident. The second only if a real question demands it, and then decided together with F-7 rather than as a history feature, because a maintenance sweep that can fail silently is the same liability either way.

Schema impact. One append-only table (audience_revision, or a dated copy of audience_operand); or materialized expansion rows and the sweep that keeps them true; or nothing, and a sentence in domain/06 and the glossary fixing what an audience does not promise. Note the tension with D-101's design note that an audience's history is not stored — whichever way this goes, that note has to be checked against it.

Needed. Before someone asks the question during an incident, which is when the answer gets written as an emergency migration.

docs.title: F-18 🟢 Does a role record elected versus appointed, and what does an election write?
docs.text:
Raised as a loss by D-100, not as a feature request. position carried is_leadership, min_age, max_holders and a position_assignment row, and the corpus's organization keeps an elected committee. Those columns are deleted, so the model now has one kind of office and cannot distinguish "elected for a two-year term by a vote" from "appointed by whoever holds role.assign". role_holder has valid_from, valid_to, granted_by and note, which is nearly enough to describe an election — and granted_by names the person who wrote the row, which for an election is a secretary, not a mandate.

Question. Does a role say elected or appointed; and if so, what does an election write — one role_holder row whose note says who voted, a document attached to the row, or a row in a table that does not exist yet?

Why it might be nothing. An election is an event in the world that the system records, not a process it runs: there is no ballot, no candidate table and no quorum rule anywhere in these documents, and D-043 settled that this system does not hold background checks either — it is not the registry of everything true about a volunteer. note, valid_from, valid_to plus a document answer "we voted and here is the minutes", and is_system keeps the seeded offices distinct from the organization's invented ones. A convention, not a guard: nothing will ever refuse to appoint someone to an office the bylaws reserve for an election.

Why it might be something. Two things the deleted tables answered by construction now have no answer at all: the vacancy question (max_holders made "two chairpersons is one too many" a check) and the term-limit question (role.max_term_months is a per-role cap, not an electoral rule — a two-year term renewable once is a different claim from "may hold for at most 24 months"). Both recur in a Scout-like body with annual meetings, and both will arrive as one-off questions.

Positions. Nothing — note and a document (cheapest, defensible, and consistent with the round's direction); a boolean on role that says only how the office is filled, which answers the bylaws question and writes nothing new; or an election/appointment record, which is a new module and therefore a decision entry with an actual argument in it, not a column added here.

Schema impact. Either zero, one boolean on role, or a table plus its permission codes plus its audit behaviour. The boolean is not free either: it invites a check ("may a non-elected holder be written for an elected office?") which D-100's posture — opt-in, review by report — would refuse to enforce, and a column nobody enforces is a column that lies after the first exception.

Needed. Not before implementation. Before the first AGM, which is when somebody asks whether the system can show that the current chair was elected.

docs.title: F-19 ✅ Closed — A permission code is a row, prose names codes, and nothing checks the two
docs.text:
Answered: the class is real, the naming grammar is now rules, and the check is a hand-run report (D-104). The question is kept whole below rather than summarised, because the answer turns on what the fourth instance turned out to be, and that is only visible against the three that came first. One of the four was resolved by deleting the thing, not by deciding its name — which is the part of this entry worth reading twice.

Question. A permission is a seeded row whose code is a stable identifier; the catalog is prose about rows; and the rest of these documents are prose about the prose. Two hops, and no reference back. This is the fourth time the gap has produced a defect, and the four are different defects, which is why one entry covers them instead of four:

Instance What disagreed How it was fixed What that fix cannot do dependent.medical.view a code vs a rule over codes — the code was correct, the namespace/prefix reading made it reach further than anyone granted the subsumer was deleted: no per-resource admin, no prefix match (D-068) it removed one way prose could be wrong about a code; it did not make the catalog and the rows incapable of disagreeing event.answer.view / event.answers.view a code vs its own spelling — D-102 wrote the plural while its entry was new, and §12 of data-model/05 did too reconciled. Declared: the catalog's spelling is the registered one, one code, not two (data-model/08 §8). The plural is now gone corpus-wide — grep reports zero, so this row is fixed rather than disputed it relied on the catalog being the arbiter, and that assumption is what the third case breaks the event QR capability a code vs the catalog's own naming grammar — it was being registered as event.qr while prose elsewhere called the same capability event.qr.rotate, against patterns the catalog stated as descriptions of the codes it already had closed: neither spelling was chosen — the capability never existed. Neither string survives anywhere in the corpus. It entered the round as prose, was half-designed in the course of arguing about its name, and left as prose, with no decision entry involved at either end it proves the registry refuses nothing. A capability that never had a row never had a check, so the argument could run for a whole round in two files that both looked like they were describing something real PERSON( two decisions vs a second registry — D-100 and D-101 both wrote PERSON(x) from the start, while the seeded selector_type registry — copied from the evaluator's arm list rather than from D-101's grammar — carried twelve rows without it, for the whole round the registry grew its thirteenth row (D-101's amendment; see F-5). The control this round wrote for itself, MEMBERS * ROLE(x) + PERSON(y), did not parse — and the pages that noticed the gap "fixed" it by reading PERSON(y) as LIST, the wrong reading, since LIST is one set belonging to one audience and subtracting it removes everybody on it this is the instance that argues for the report, and it was found by reading, in a file nobody had been asked to check — one round, two registries, same defect

What the third case actually was, because this entry guessed wrong about it. It asked whether qr was an object with actions hanging off it — rotate, print, preview — or the whole action, and answered itself that "the answer is which shape the seeded row has". There is no seeded row, and D-104 says the question was the wrong one to ask. Grepping the closed round finds neither string anywhere: not in the catalog, not in the events module, not in the ERD, not in the decision log. What survives of the event door code is this entry's own description of a dispute about it. Presence is left where D-067 and EV-5 put it: somebody holding event.presence.mark records who came, with a clipboard if necessary. So the honest answer to "did we decide against check-in codes?" is no — and that is the finding, not a typo and not a morphological disagreement: a thing was possible in prose, argued over as though it were in the model, and removed without ever having been in the model. There is no QR capability in this system, seeded or deferred, in the events module or anywhere else; if door scanning is ever wanted it arrives as an open question, then as a decision entry naming the permission, the artifact that gets rotated and who may reprint it — not as a code appearing beside a paragraph about a door. The only QR code in these documents belongs to a payment, and D-075 already rules that a QR code is a rendering, not data.

Why the earlier fixes could not have caught it, stated once. answers versus answer was settled by naming an arbiter, and that worked only because the catalog was self-consistent; the QR case was the first where it was not, because both readings of event.qr fit the catalog's two stated shapes — resource+action, or resource+subresource+action. A description of how existing names happen to look cannot arbitrate a new name. And the fourth instance was not a code at all but a selector, in a different registry, in the same round — which is why the fix below is a diff over every registry rather than a rule about permissions. Underneath all four is one sentence from D-104: a convention that is followed and not stated fails exactly once, on the first thing nobody thought to compare. It applied the rules below to the registry as it stands and found nothing to correct — of the sixty-six live codes in the catalog, sixty-five satisfy both tests and the sixty-sixth is the named exception. The corpus was already right, the rule was nowhere written, and the capability arrived anyway.

The naming grammar, promoted from a description to three rules (D-104 §2, written up as rules where the patterns live, in permission-catalog §1). Three, for a code being added — the only moment they cost nothing:

Rule What it refuses The last segment names the action. Read the code alone and ask what does this let me do? event.grant_access answers it, event.qr does not. A noun-final code states an object, and since D-099 a grant states exactly one thing: a grant of an object would need a second sentence to say what it permits, and a second sentence is where a permission's real scope always hides. A middle segment names something the schema stores. answer is event_answer, presence is a column of event_registration; contact, credential, member, participant, request are rows. qr is nothing — D-075 is explicit that it is a rendering of a symbol, an amount and a recipient. A permission may not be built out of an artifact the database does not keep, because a grant has to be checkable against stored state and there is none. This is the substantive test the QR case needed, and it settles the case without appealing to morphology at all. No grade words, and no prefix. admin, all, everything, and any code whose meaning is "every sibling under this prefix" — D-068 deleted sixteen of them and computed the wrong answer for dependent.admin. Restated as a rule about codes that have not been written yet, which is the only form of that decision that can still prevent anything.

system.admin is the single named exception, and a rule with an unnamed exception is a rumour. Its last segment is not an action and it stays, because its meaning is defined by the resolver — checked outright, applies_to = unit, never reachable through an item grant — rather than read off its name, and because D-068 exempted it in so many words rather than by omission. It is the only code in this system allowed to be a noun, and the exemption is not a precedent: <resource>.admin is exactly what the third rule refuses and exactly what was deleted.

Adopted: the diff report, stated honestly. Before a round closes, every dotted token in prose is diffed against every seeded registry these documents keep by hand — permission.code, selector_type.code, grant_scope_type.code, reason_code.code, the seeded audiences — in both directions, so the report says which tokens name no row and which rows no prose names. This entry's own recommendation, taken: it is the only option that would have caught all four instances, including the two the catalog wrote itself and the one nobody had noticed.

  • It is a report run by hand. This repository has no build step and no CI to hang a check on, so D-081's wording applies exactly: a convention, not a guard. Saying that is part of adopting it, not a caveat appended afterwards — nothing in the system will ever notice a code drifting from its row, including after this entry, because the enforcement adopted here is a person remembering to run a script.
  • It runs on the documents, because there is no schema to check against (D-072) — and that is the condition that makes the whole class possible: the prose is the specification, so prose is free to contradict the registry, and there is no compiler to notice.
  • The cost is the allow-list and it is not small: illustrative codes, and deleted codes shown struck on purpose, both match no live row. The report is worth running only if that list is re-read rather than frozen — the same discipline the struck-text rule already imposes on the decision log.

The half of this that was time-critical, and still is. A code is the only identifier in this system explicitly not renameable: the catalog's own words are that adding one is free and renaming one is a migration over every grant row naming it. Today the cost of a naming mistake is a grep; the day the first grant row exists it becomes a migration — and that asymmetry, not the typo, is why D-104 was written as a decision rather than fixed quietly. Related, and still unfixed, because D-104 reaches codes and not attributes: permission.applies_to and permission.right_kind are seeded columns prose gets to contradict the same way, and a code named in prose with the wrong applies_to is a subtler version of all four instances above — a capability described as grantable somewhere it cannot be. The report diffs tokens, so it will not catch this one either.

The two options not adopted, and why.

  • Declare the catalog the registry and link every prose mention — a code appearing in prose is a link to its catalog row. Correct in principle, unenforceable here: a link nobody is required to write is a review convention, in D-081's exact wording, a convention, not a guard. It is also what the report makes easy afterwards rather than a substitute for it, since a wrong code linked to the wrong row is still a wrong code.
  • Ban codes from prose — no. The codes are the specification's vocabulary; a document that cannot name event.presence.mark cannot say what it grants.

(The third option, the diff script, is the adopted one above. Its own wording before closure was the honest part of it: it said the check "generalises for free to the other registries these documents keep by hand", and the fourth instance landed in exactly one of those — selector_type, against §8's table — one round later, having been found by nobody who had been asked to look there.)

Schema impact. No rows change. The grammar renames nothing today; system.admin's exemption already existed and is only now written down; and the QR capability is absent, not renamed — the seeded permission row this entry was braced for is a row that never ships. The report is zero-schema (D-072), and what it will diff against is data-model/05 §8 with its thirteen rows — twelve for the whole of round 10, thirteen when this entry was written, twelve again for the one round after LIST went (D-105), fourteen with the two age operands, and thirteen since D-113 deleted a row that was never a selector — the catalog's sixty-six codes, grant_scope_type, reason_code and the two seeded audiences. The count moving under the report is the point of adopting it: a row appearing or vanishing is exactly what the diff exists to notice, and the round that deleted LIST is the round that would have caught a page still naming it, had anyone run the script. The registry has now changed size in four consecutive rounds, which is the strongest argument this file has for a diff over a sentence — and note what a diff would not have caught: GUARDIANS was in the table, in the prose and in the count, and agreed with itself everywhere (F-5).

What stays open after this. The failure mode is the only one it has, and D-104 says so plainly: a report that cannot be violated, only forgotten. The entry becomes obsolete when there is an implementation with a seed directory and a test that loads it; until then the registry and the prose are two copies of one thing (F-10's general shape, in its cheapest instance) and the report is the check that they still agree. The applies_to / right_kind half above is the same class, explicitly unfixed, and four instances in ten rounds is not bad luck — every module added (D-055) multiplies the surface it would have to catch.
