docs.title: F-20 ✅ Closed — WHITELISTED stays unseeded because there is no state to evaluate, and the feature arrives anyway
docs.text:
Answered: refused, and the refusal is not the loss it has been reading like since it was filed. The operand stays out of the registry for its own stated ground — there is no state to evaluate — and it is confirmed rather than re-argued by D-113, which deleted a selector for exactly this class of error: a name in the language with no selector_type row behind it, or a selector naming a mechanism the model implements somewhere else. WHITELISTED is the same shape one step earlier — the row would be minted to describe a flag no table carries — and D-108's SCHOOL refusal is the third instance of the same refusal. Three refusals, one rule: an operand names a fact the model stores, or it is not an operand.

The part of this entry that was always about a feature, now answered as one. What people reach for the word WHITELISTED to get is "these particular adults, and only these, may do this" — and that need is served today, by a person_group per whitelist, aimed at the grant, dated by the grant's own period, revocable, deny-able. D-109 is what makes that answer newly good rather than merely adequate: retiring such a group is now a deprecated or hidden flag, not a delete, so a per-event whitelist can be retired without the repoint every expression naming it would once have needed, and without the empty-operand-widens-a-deny hazard that made retiring a set dangerous in the first place. So the thing people actually wanted from the operand — a named set you can point grants at, and put away when you are done — exists, as grants over groups. What the operand would still add is a derived set, and this system derives no such thing: it stores a guardianship row and no query over it as an audience (D-113 checked this rather than assuming it), exactly as it stores no is_whitelisted column.

What it cost. One sentence in the tiers-and-refusals list, which is all this entry ever asked for, and the continued obligation that the two halves stay decided together: if EV-6's "invited, has not answered, we made room" ever gets a column, WHITELISTED arrives as its operand automatically, and at that moment it stops being a refusal and becomes a seed row with a fact underneath it. That is the reopen, stated as a condition rather than a date: WHITELISTED is unseeded because there is nothing to evaluate, so it becomes seedable the day there is — and the day there is, this entry's answer flips without needing a new argument.

This is one question asked in two modules, and it is carried twice on purpose. The events half — whether a person's standing on one event ("invited, has not answered, we made room") deserves stored state — is EV-6, where the tier algebra lives. This entry is the language half, which is smaller and gets answered first.

Question. D-102 shipped four attendance tiers and refused PRESENT on a stated, representable ground: nothing is stored until a person marks it. WHITELISTED is the second name people reach for, and it must be refused on its own ground rather than by inheriting that one — because unlike PRESENT there is something that could be stored, and the refusal is therefore a decision rather than an observation.

The answer these documents already imply, stated once so it stops being re-derived. "Let these people register" is an allow grant on the event naming event.register_self, aimed at an audience whose expression is either the hand-typed PERSON(a) + PERSON(b) or a GROUP(x) — revocable, deny-able, aimed at a set rather than a flag, and dated by the grant's own valid_to now that the per-name dates of audience_member are deleted (D-105): "these three until August" is that grant carrying a period, and a different set for August is a second grant, which is the shape this refusal now has to keep paying for. Which of the two spellings the sentence wants is something these documents do not settle, and it is written out rather than picked: the handful of names a leader ticks for one event is the sum, the standing camp-staff list is the group, and D-105 kept both on purpose — a set that outlives the event belongs in a roster somebody maintains, while a set that exists only to widen one grant must not become one, because editing a roster moves every grant that reads it (D-098, and D-105 restates that reason as unchanged). A WHITELISTED operand would reimplement grants with fewer powers, and it would do it in the one place where the model has just spent a round deleting hard-coded sentences from the resolver and replacing them with grant rows (D-102's whole move). So: refuse it, and say why beside the PRESENT refusal. What is not answered here is the narrower sentence EV-6 carries, and if that one ever gets a column, WHITELISTED arrives as its operand automatically — which is the reason this entry exists as a pointer rather than being folded into EV-6: the two halves have to be decided together, and the language half is the one that gets decided first, by whoever adds the column.

Needed. A paragraph where the tiers and the refusals are listed. Nothing else, and nothing before implementation.

docs.title: F-21 ✅ Closed — no report; a tab on the permissions page; and unbounded cost is accepted at the stated size
docs.text:
Answered in two pieces, by two decisions, and the second is the one that made the first affordable.

1. There is no report. There is a tab. D-109 retires the standing reports about rules with one tab on the permissions page, and this entry is the third of the three its Supersedes line names — D-106's failing-leaf report, D-105's merge-repoint duty, and part of this entry. Precision matters here, because "every report" would be false: reports outside the expression language survive it — the dead-deny hygiene line in Deny (a live deny matching no live allow is dead weight), and D-071's report of role assignments nobody forced to end. What the tab replaces is a standing report about what an expression names and what it costs, which is exactly what this entry was. Its Broken section lists every live rule whose expression names a deprecated, hidden or disabled thing, or fails to resolve at all — which is D-106's failing-leaf column, arriving on the page instead of on a report. It does not list wide audiences, because nothing produces that list any more, and the reason is the elegant part of D-109: the leaf broke because the thing it named was deleted, and here nothing is deleted. A deprecated group still resolves; a hidden office still resolves; a disabled one resolves to the empty set knowingly, with the flag write printing the rules it touches. The reader question this entry spent a round on — "who reads it?" — resolves to nobody, because there is nothing to read, and that is a better answer than naming a person and a cadence would have been. What replaces it is better than a report for the ordinary reason D-109 gives: a report has to be remembered and a tab is where the person already is.

The tab has two sections, and this entry owns only one of them. Broken is D-109's definition and this entry's population: something has happened to your rule behind your back. "Unusual" — rules that resolve correctly and merely look odd — is F-13's, and its answer stays there. The two are not one list, and neither entry may claim the other's population: a grant that omits MEMBERS is not broken, and putting it in Broken would train readers that the safeguarding section is a matter of taste.

2. Nothing bounds what a check costs, and that is now accepted at a stated size rather than merely unaddressed. D-112 put a number under the refusal: a few hundred people, a few dozen registrants on a typical event, a big camp on the order of two hundred. At that size "nothing bounds what an expression can cost" is accepted, which is a different claim from "nothing bounds it and nobody has looked". The refusal of a cap is untouched and gets stronger: a budget the resolver stops at is an operand resolving to nobody, an empty set behind a -, and the cap becomes the thing that decides who a grant reaches. D-112 states the same boundary from the other side — "nothing in the design depends on the number, on purpose", with the two rules that must survive any growth being a check compiles to a predicate and never materializes the set and a listing is paginated, so the system gets slow before it gets wrong.

What it cost. Three reports retired, one tab built, no schema, and the last standing report of this shape gone — which retires the meta-filing below rather than confirming it, and is worth reading against the paragraph underneath this one. The residual hazard is unchanged and now honestly labelled: the wide audience nobody looked at, on a check path that has no reason to complain. It is survivable because of a number, so the reopen is that number.

What reopens it. D-112's trigger — a few thousand people, or a thousand registrants on one event — which reopens F-15, F-16, F-7 and this entry, in that order. ~~This entry last, deliberately: the nightly rebuild is the cheapest of the four to redesign and the expensive ones are the ones a user feels first.~~ Round 14 re-arranges that ordering rather than confirming it, because the thing ranked last has been deleted (D-114): the rebuild was the cheap one to redesign precisely because it was affordable, and what it quietly paid for — pre-resolving the expensive screens off the user's thread — is now paid for on open. The ordering is unchanged and one shorter, matching what D-112 now says in its own copy of that list: what used to be buffered by a nightly job is buffered by nothing.

A dependency recorded by D-114, and this entry is where it belongs because this entry owns the tab. D-109 ruled that the permissions tab is computed when opened rather than kept as a standing report — a ruling that was comfortable while a nightly job was resolving expressions anyway, and which now has no fallback: an opening tab walks the live grant and expression rows, resolves each expression, and does it in front of the person who clicked. That is affordable at the stated size and the ruling stands; what changed is that it is now the only thing standing under it. The tab is written against which_of(people[], code, item) and can_many(person, codes[], item?) rather than a loop of single checks, so the cost is one pass and not N — and "unbounded per-check cost accepted at a stated size" now means unbounded cost paid at open, which is the same number with a different name on it. Recorded as a dependency, not as a risk, and the reopen is the same number as ever.

Three findings, and the answer that ended them. ~~Three things are missing from it and all three are this entry: no role is named as its reader, no cadence is set, and no number says where wide becomes too wide.~~ That diagnosis was correct and the fix it argued for — name a person, name a cadence — is not what happened. The user's answer was to stop building reports and put one tab where the writer already is, which retires the reader-and-cadence-and-threshold problem by removing the thing that needed a reader. The finding that named this pattern is kept verbatim at the end of this entry, because it is the discovery and D-109 is the answer to it.

Question. For ten rounds a permission check cost a bounded amount, and the bound came from one place: selector_depth_limit, applied at save over the expanded tree. D-105 deleted the parameter and the save-time check with it, and ruled that the tree is stored exactly as its author wrote it — one row per node, left to right, no rebalancing, because a rebalanced tree is a different expression than the one a person wrote. What survives as a structural guard is the two cycle walks: one inside the expression, one across audiences through every AUDIENCE(x) leaf. They refuse an expansion that never terminates and they say nothing whatsoever about one that merely costs a lot. A check's cost is now bounded by acyclicity alone — no bound on height, and none was ever asserted on breadth — and the expensive shapes are not exotic: EVERYONE is one leaf that reaches everyone the resolver can see, and a hand-typed set of forty names is forty leaves where the last round kept one leaf and an indexed table.

What replaced the invariant, and what kind of thing it is. This is D-081's pattern executed exactly: the rule's name outlives its mechanism. "Depth must be refused at save, over the expanded tree" retires as an invariant and survives as a standing report of the widest and deepest audiences with their per-check cost, beside the operand cache. D-105 states the weak half itself rather than letting it be discovered: a report, with no CI behind it — a convention, not a guard, and the third control of this shape the authorization module now depends on, after F-13 and F-19. Three things are missing from it and all three are this entry: no role is named as its reader, no cadence is set, and no number says where wide becomes too wide.

The half that is refused on purpose, and has to stay refused. Whoever reads this entry will reach for a cap on the read path — a depth the resolver declines to walk, a budget it stops at — and the design refuses that for a reason that got stronger, not weaker, when the bound went: the cap becomes the thing that decides who a grant reaches, because a walk that stops early is an operand resolving to nobody, and an empty set behind a - makes the answer wider. Until last round that refusal was the back-up position behind a guard that existed at save time; now it is the entire design, and the only sentence left to say about cost is a number on a report somebody has to choose to open. The line worth keeping is the one F-15 already walks: a limit on what a preview lists changes what a person sees and is allowed; a limit on what a check walks changes who has access and is not.

Positions. Name a reader and a cadence — the cheapest answer in this file, one sentence, and it changes no data; the report exists and nobody owns it. Print a warning threshold — honest only while it stays advice in the report's own text, because the moment somebody is forced to obey a threshold it has become the cap the paragraph above refuses, and a guard that pretends to be a report is worse than either. Or accept unbounded per-check cost as a property of the system and lean on the operand cache and the assumption behind it (assumption 61) — which is what an implementation would do by default anyway, and the reason this entry exists: to stop that being an accident. (Of the three arms, this one aged best and then strangely: both caches behind it were deleted. D-114 takes the answer cache and the operand cache together, and the operand cache deserves the sharper blame: it was keyed (person, selector_kind, selector_arg_id[, item]), so it named a person in the key exactly like its neighbour did — which is why no narrowing of a bump set could have saved either of them. What survives is a roster, and a roster is a different object: keyed by a name, holding dated rows, with no person and no item in the key. MEMBERS is not a roster and cannot be cached as one; it is evaluated on the checked date. The per-request memo is the nearest surviving relative of an operand cache, and it is not an answer cache because it dies with the request. assumption 61 is struck, so this arm's backing row is a history row.)

Schema impact. None, and that is the trap. There is no column to hold a limit, deliberately: a limit in a column is a limit in the check, which is the refused thing, and D-072 means these documents will not write the query either — what exists is a walk over audience_operand that someone has to run.

Needed. Before an implementation ships a resolver and no report. 🟡 and not 🔴 because nothing blocks the schema and the likeliest answer is one sentence naming a person; but the failure this entry describes is not a slow system, it is the wide audience nobody looked at, on a check path that has no reason left to complain, and unlike F-16 there is no measurement that makes it go away — only a reader.

Round 12 gave this report a second column, and it should not become a second page. D-106 refused every refusal that would have made a broken operand stop a save, and what it bought instead is a list: the audiences with a leaf that resolves to nobody. That is the same page, the same audience owner, the same "somebody has to open it" weakness — one report, two columns: the widest expansions, and the failing leaves — and F-23 would have added a third ("whom does this reach today, against whom it reached when it was saved"). Three findings from three rounds, each of which concluded that the answer is a report nobody is obliged to read, is itself a finding: this module now has a page it cannot do without and no decision that anyone looks at it. Whoever answers this entry is answering all three, and the honest version of the answer names a person and a cadence rather than a feature.

How all three were actually answered, recorded against the prediction above. Not by naming a person, and not by a feature either — by removing two of the three lists and putting the third where the writer already stands. The widest-expansions column is gone because nothing produces it (D-109 deletes the cause of the broken leaf, and D-112 accepts the cost of the wide one). The failing-leaves column survives as the tab's Broken section, which is this entry's population and D-109's definition. F-23's third column was refused outright by D-110 — the words are the record, so there is no then-and-now comparison to display, and the page stays two things deep rather than three. The weakness the paragraph above found was real, and it was cured by subtraction, which is the pattern round 13 keeps landing on.

docs.title: F-22 ✅ Closed — the editor may fold and flatten for display; the stored canonical string never changes
docs.text:
Answered, as an editor decision with one hard limit on it. The first position below is the answer. The editor may fold a sum of same-kind leaves onto one line and render PERSON(a) + PERSON(b) + PERSON(c) as a list rather than as thirty-nine pairs of brackets; it may do the same for any sum of like operands. What it may not do is change the stored canonical string. The rendering is a rendering, and these documents now say so in one place: display is free, storage is not.

Why the limit is load-bearing and not aesthetic. D-105's ruling that the tree is stored exactly as its author wrote it is not a nostalgia rule, and this round's F-14 is the reason it cannot be bent for comfort: the stored form is the only identity an expression has, and the write-path checks — the cycle walk over the reference closure, the reserved-name rule, the listing of which grants name an audience — all reason over that. An editor that stored its own tidier spelling would be rewriting the expression it was handed, which is the one thing D-105 named as making a stored grant mean something nobody wrote. So the flattening happens on the way to the screen and never on the way to the row, and a reviewer who needs the exact stored text — during an incident, or a diff, or an audit export — can still be shown it, because nothing overwrote it. This is the same ruling F-14 reached from the other side: sorting + children so duplicates collapse is refused for being a storage change, and this entry refuses the identical temptation for being legible instead of being tidy, which is the more persuasive version of the same error.

What is not decided, and stays open inside a closed entry. Nothing here sets a size at which a writer is told to reach for a person_group, and the second position — refuse above a size — stays refused for the reason this entry already gave: an editor that blocks the safe action teaches the unsafe one, and here the unsafe one is inventing a group that other grants will read, which is the exact widening D-105 spent its entry arguing against. D-105 named the destination (a set big enough to be unreadable is a person_group) and no round has set a trigger, and none needs to: the flattened rendering removes the pressure that would have made a trigger necessary, and the judgement is left where it was always going to be left, with the writer.

What it cost. No schema — not one column, as this entry predicted — and one rule an editor has to obey: the renderer is allowed to lie about shape and forbidden to lie about content. The cost that is real shows up in F-21's world rather than here, and the paragraph below about the widest-audiences report is now superseded by D-109 and D-112, which deleted the report: a hand-typed set no longer competes for a page nobody is building.

Question. D-105 left D-101's canonical form standing: the stored rendering prints every bracket, always, and a sum is a binary tree, so a hand-typed set of n people is n−1 nested pairs. Forty names is thirty-nine pairs before a single - or * appears. D-105 saw this coming and said the honest thing — storage and display both say what was written, and if that turns out unreadable then a set of people big enough to be unreadable is a person_group — and then pointed this judgement at F-5's neighbourhood. F-5 has already declined it, in its own entry: that one asks which facts about people the language cannot state, and the language states this one perfectly. What is left is a question about reading, and it belongs to whoever opens the editor.

What D-105 did not decide, and what would be decided here. It named the destination and not the trigger. Nothing in the corpus says at what point a writer is told to reach for a group, or whether anyone is told at all; nothing says whether the fully-bracketed form is what a reviewer is shown, or merely what is stored — D-101's ruling is about the stored rendering, and it already has the editor rewriting what is typed into that form before saving, so the two are separable and nobody has said whether they are. And nothing says whether an unreadable-but-exact expression is an acceptable thing for a second person to audit a year later, which is the actual question: the model is fine with the forty-name tree either way, and only the editor cares.

Positions. Say the canonical form is storage, not display — show a flattened PERSON(a, b, c) on screen, keep the nested tree in the rows, and write down that the screen is a rendering; cheapest, and it keeps D-105's "we store what was written" untouched. Or refuse above a size — the editor will not save a sum of more than n names and says "make this a group". That is a cap, and the honest difference from the cap F-21 refuses is that it governs what an author may write and not whom a stored grant reaches — but it carries the same hazard F-16 names for the deletion guard: an editor that blocks the safe action teaches people the unsafe one, and here the unsafe one is inventing a group other grants will read, which is the exact thing D-105 kept its whole argument about. Or do nothing and let the widest-and-deepest report be the feedback — which is dumber than it sounds only because of the next paragraph.

The link to F-21 that made this entry worth more than a style preference (kept as filed; its premise is gone — the report below was retired by D-109 and its cost question answered by D-112, so this paragraph is now evidence about how the two entries got coupled, not a live argument). With no depth bound, a hand-typed set is the deepest thing most organizations will have, and a forty-name list will top the deepest-audiences report while costing less than a two-level nested audience. So the report F-21 has to find a reader for will spend its top rows on typing rather than on structure — the signal is about who typed a lot, not about who composed something expensive. A threshold here, or a flattened display there, is what keeps that report legible as a cost report. Say which of the two it is, before the report is the only control left.

Why this is 🟢, and what would move it. The corpus gives no hand-typed set bigger than a handful — every worked example in these documents names one to three people, and the thousands-of-rows legacy import arrives as memberships and participations, never as an audience expression (D-090). So the forty-name audience is a shape the editor must not make painful, not a shape that has happened. It becomes 🟡 the first time a reviewer quotes back an expression they could not read, or the first time somebody types twenty names because making a group felt like more paperwork than they were owed — and that second one is a story about the editor, which is the whole point of keeping this entry separate from the model.

Schema impact. None. Not one column: a size rule lives in the editor, a flattened display lives in the editor, and the storage stays what D-105 ruled it is. Needed: when the audience editor is designed, which is also the moment someone decides what a grant looks like on a screen.

docs.title: F-23 ✅ Closed — words only: the expression is the record, and the preview is a rendering on a date
docs.text:
Answered by D-110, in four words: "Words only — the expression is the record." The first row of the table below is the answer, the third is refused, and the middle row — the reach query — is not adopted either, which is the part a reader who only skims this entry will get wrong. The audit record of a grant's reach is the expression. The preview still prints a resolved set before a save, and that printing is logged as a rendering on a date, not as a statement of who was in it. "Whom did this grant reach in May?" is answered, if at all, by evaluating the words against the data of May, and these documents do not promise the answer.

Why the refused row is refused, in the two terms that settled it. Storing the resolved set beside the audit row is the roster table this corpus has deleted twice — audience_member in D-105, and the assumption row recording every prior attempt at it — and it would hold, indefinitely and against D-088's window, a per-person record of people who were never granted anything: everyone a rule happened to cover, kept after the rule was withdrawn. Storing that to make a historical question comfortable is the trade this corpus has refused every single time it has been offered, and this is the fourth offering. The tell this entry already named is the right one and survives the closure: the middle row answers a question a person asks, while the third stores an answer to a question nobody asked, about people who did nothing, indefinitely.

What the answer concedes, since "words only" is not a free answer. A row now says this person wrote these words on this date about this item — which is a fact that cannot go stale — instead of this grant reached these 214 people, which starts decaying the night somebody's birthday falls. The audit trail gets smaller and more honest, and what it gives up is any claim to know whom a grant reached. That trade was only payable because of D-109: refuse to delete the nouns, and keeping only the words is not an amputation — a retired office still resolves, a deprecated group still resolves, so the words stay evaluable long after their reason is gone. Without D-109 this ruling would have meant "the past is usually unanswerable"; with it, the past is usually computable and what is left is honestly bounded. F-17 carries the half about a shared audience being edited backwards in time.

What reopens it. Not the calendar, and not a stale snapshot — both were ruled on in D-107 and D-111 and are settled, and D-114 settled them further by deleting the snapshot: there is no cached answer that could be stale, so the only thing left to be stale is a record that was never a snapshot in the first place. The reopen is an incident: a real review in which a recomputation over the data of the date could not answer, and the missing list was the thing that would have. If that day comes, the temptation returns in its fifth costume, and this entry — with its table and its tell — is where the answer is argued against.

(arrived with round 12, from D-107.)

The question. A grant's reach is printed by the editor before the grant is saved, and that printing is what the audit trail keeps as "whom this grant was made to mean". Until round 12 every operand in the language moved only when somebody wrote something, so the snapshot and the set could only diverge for as long as a cache was warm. OLDER(n) and YOUNGER(n) are the first operands whose set moves on its own, at midnight, with no row changing and no event to subscribe to — so the record of a decision made in March is now a snapshot of a set that has, by November, quietly changed members. What exactly is the record of: the words, or the people the words reached on the day they were saved?

What this is not, stated so it is not raised again. It is not a performance question, not a cache correctness question, and not a request to make the language static. Those three were put and answered (F-6 carries the ruling: "I know, that the time will change, how the rules resolve and IT IS FINE"), and a check for a past date already answers for that past date. What survived the ruling is the record, not the resolution — the difference being that resolution has an answer for every date, while the audit trail has an answer only for the date it was written.

Options, none of them free.

Options, none of them free — verdict added by D-110, the reasoning left exactly as filed. Row one adopted; row two not adopted (a query nobody is obliged to run is what row one already is, and D-109 deleted the page it would have lived on); row three refused.

Option What it buys What it costs Nothing — the words are the record ✅ adopted The design stays exactly as decided; an audit row records an expression and a person's act, which is arguably all a document about a rule can honestly hold The people-list printed in March stops being reproducible, so "who could read this in May" has no answer in the audit trail and must be re-derived from birth dates on demand Re-derive on demand: a "whom does this reach today, and on any date" query A real answer for any date, computed from data the model already keeps, with no new stored set It is a report nobody is obliged to read, i.e. a convention, not a guard, and it is the same page F-21 and D-106 already put on one page — which argues for building them together, once Store the resolved set with each preview ❌ refused — it is the roster table this corpus has deleted twice, and it holds data about people who were never granted anything The March snapshot stays readable forever A per-person history of an audience is exactly the roster table this corpus deleted twice (D-105 and the assumption row behind it), and it would hold personal data about people who were never granted anything — which collides with the redaction window

~~How to answer it. Pick the middle row and say plainly that the third is refused~~ — row one was picked instead, and the entry was wrong about its own middle row in a way worth keeping. The reasoning for refusing the third row was exactly right and survives verbatim: the temptation to keep the list is the oldest reflex in this module and it has now been declined in four costumes, not three. What the entry got wrong was thinking a query someone might not run was better than no query at all — D-109's finding, that a report has to be remembered and a tab is where the person already is, applies to a reach query just as flatly as it applied to the widest-audience report. The tell that this is the right shape still reads true and is what makes the first row survivable: the middle row answers a question a person asks, while the third row stores an answer to a question nobody asked, about people who did nothing, indefinitely — and D-110 added the third possibility this file had not considered, which is that the words themselves answer the question, given that nothing a rule names is ever deleted.

Needed. One sentence in the audit module about what a preview snapshot is — a rendering of the words on a date, not a statement of fact about people — and a decision about whether the reach query is one page with F-21's two columns or a third page nobody will open.

docs.title: G. Events — designed, with three things left open
docs.text: The module is written: domain/07-events.md and data-model/08-events.md. Fifteen questions have been answered (D-058 … D-067, plus EV-1 and EV-5 in a later round); what remains below is what those answers did not settle. None of it blocks implementation.

docs.title: EV-1 ✅ Closed — there is no age ceiling; the grant is the rule
docs.text:
Answered: leave it. No min_age/max_age on event, and no age test anywhere in the path that places a registration (D-070).

The residual risk is accepted, not eliminated, and it is worth restating so nobody "closes" it later without knowing: an event opened to all_members can be registered for by a nine-year-old and nothing objects. What makes it survivable is attribution (source = 'staff'), a roster query one join away from birth dates, and the fact that the age-bounded case is already handled by opening an event to the right unit.

If it ever needs closing, the shape is a built-in audience, not a column on the row — all_members is a rule the resolver evaluates, so members_aged_13_plus can be one too. That keeps every answer to "who may register" inside access_grant, which is the property D-060 bought and D-070 defended.

Round 12: this entry stays closed, and its reason changed. The escape hatch above assumed an age test would have to be built in — a named audience, a row somebody ships. D-107 seeded the test instead: event.register_self granted to MEMBERS * YOUNGER(15) is the ceiling, written by an organizer on the day they want it, previewed, and attributed. So the ceiling is now statable and this entry is still answered "leave it", which makes it a choice the organization makes per event rather than a consequence of the model being unable to say otherwise. That is a strictly better place for a closed question to sit, and it is worth marking as such — because the previous reason was a limitation dressed as a decision, and a limitation quietly stops being one the day the vocabulary grows. Nothing else in this entry moves: the nine-year-old, the tick box nobody ticked, source = 'staff', and the roster query one join from birth dates are all still exactly as accepted.

docs.title: EV-2 🟡 Retention of event_answer
docs.text:
The question, restated once so it stays answerable. It used to read "a dietary answer citing a medical condition is health data, and health data has a retention obligation" — and D-083 removed the second half of that sentence's subject: there is no class of health data with its own obligation, only personal data, of which a dietary answer is one instance. The question survives, and it is now the ordinary version of a question this system has not answered anywhere: event answers end with the event, "end" is not a defined policy, and a fact recorded on a form is the same kind of fact as the same sentence recorded as a person_attribute (data-model/09-attributes.md), which raises the sharper form of the question — should an answer about a child be deleted on a schedule at all, when the same information held as an attribute is kept until someone retires it? The paragraph at the end of this item is where that doubling is worked out; what changed here is only that the question can no longer be filed under a category of data that no longer exists.

Why it is not trivial. D-061 made an event form the route by which a camp leader learns a child has a nut allergy. That is a deliberate widening, and it puts health-adjacent data in a table whose protections are weaker than the health record's — and in round 6 that gap widened twice over: there is no longer a dependent.medical.* code marking which data is the sensitive kind (E-7), and the audience entitled to read an answer is whoever runs that event, a set sized by whoever creates it. The retention policy is the remaining half of that trade.

Needed. Legal input, of the same kind B-3's indefinite retention still needs. The technical question — where does it live, who may read it — is answered; whether it must be deleted, kept, or archived is not.

Changed in round 7, in a way that strengthens the case rather than settling it. D-083 made every fact about a person one class of data held on the person, so an event answer naming an allergy is now the same kind of fact stored in two places by two different rules — one on the person, where it is audited, curable and erased with the person; one in an event's table, readable by whoever runs that event, with no retention policy. The retention question and AT-1 are the same question from two directions: an answer worth keeping is an attribute that was collected at the wrong address, and an answer not worth keeping should be deleted on a schedule rather than surviving because nobody wrote a policy. Until one of the two is decided, the weakest-protected copy of a health fact is the one that is freshest.

docs.title: EV-3 ✅ Closed — cancelling voids the request, and paid money queues
docs.text:
Answered by D-076, in the finance module rather than here. The recommendation was right and the mechanism arrived before the policy did:

  • Cancelling an event voids its outstanding payment requests, recording why (finance model §2b).
  • Money already received becomes a queue item for a person to refund or carry forward. Not auto-refunded — that needs an outbound bank integration and would return a grandparent's mistaken camp fee.

Why the recommendation held. It said neither, automatically, because an automatic release would be a second automatic transition in a module with exactly one (D-066). That argument was strong enough to survive contact with the payment design unchanged. Voiding an outstanding request is not that second transition — a request nobody has paid against has no state to preserve and nobody is disadvantaged by its withdrawal, which is exactly the property the waitlist release had and this does not.

What actually moved. The question assumed cancellation was the interesting case and payment an afterthought parked in finance. It is the reverse: cancellation is where most of the unmatched queue's volume comes from, because a cancelled event keeps its registrations (D-064) and therefore its money obligations, unless something explicitly voids them.

Impact. Answered; the queue itself lives in the finance module.

docs.title: EV-4 🟢 was_present as a safeguarding record
docs.text:
The question. Presence is the record of who was actually in the organization's care (D-067). Does it need its own retention, or its own permission?

Why it might. It is the record that answers "was this child at camp on the day of the incident" — the question insurance and any safeguarding review will ask. That is a heavier thing than "who said they were coming", and it currently shares both a table and a permission with the registration.

Why it might not. It is meaningless without the registration it belongs to, and splitting it would put two rows in two places describing one fact.

Impact. Splitting it is a table; keeping it is nothing. The argument for splitting is permissions — a volunteer who takes the register at camp is not the same trust as one who may alter the roster. See EV-5, which is the same tension.

docs.title: EV-5 ✅ Closed — it split, and the new permission sits a level lower
docs.text:
Resolved in favour of the split: event.presence.mark, at contribute.

The reasoning recommended the split and the recommendation stood. Marking the register at a camp door is not the same trust as deleting a child from the roster, and one permission forced organizations to hand the clipboard-holder both. Note where the new permission landed: contribute, not manage — so the volunteer taking the register is somebody who could already register themselves, which is the right bar for the job and plainly the wrong bar for altering who is coming. Same shape as membership.lapse versus membership.terminate (D-022): one routine, one consequential.

Thirteen event.* codes now exist; event.admin is not one of them (D-068).

Round 10 note, because the answer's wording no longer exists. The split stands; the level it was placed at does not — D-099 deleted access_level, permission_level and the rank integer, so "at contribute, not manage" is now carried by nothing but the two codes themselves. Read it as: event.presence.mark is a separate code precisely so it can be granted without event.manage_participants, and the gradation the level expressed is now expressed by which code a grant names. The comparison to membership.lapse versus membership.terminate (D-022) is the part that still says what it meant.

See: appendix/permission-catalog.md §8a

docs.title: EV-6 🟡 WHITELISTED — the word people reach for, with no stored state to name
docs.text:
Question. D-102 named four attendance tiers a grant may bind to and refused a fifth (PRESENT, refused because was_present is NULL until somebody marks it). WHITELISTED keeps coming up in the same sentence and there is nowhere in the model for it to read from: no flag on event_registration, no roster on event besides organizers, no column anywhere that says this person was let in. Should the language refuse the word, or should the model give it state?

The half that is already answered, and should be said before anything is built. "These named people may register for this event" needs no new anything: it is an allow grant on the event naming event.register_self, aimed at an audience whose expression is the hand-typed PERSON(a) + PERSON(b) or names a GROUP — one row per sentence, revocable, audited, and dated by the grant rather than by the names, since the dated rows those names used to live in are deleted (D-099, D-102, and D-105 for the deletion; F-20 settles which of the two spellings a given sentence wants, and this entry does not). That is the D-102 answer to the sentence, and it is better than a flag because a flag cannot be aimed at a group, cannot expire, and cannot be refused by a deny. Anyone adding is_whitelisted is reimplementing grants badly.

The half that is not answered. There is a different sentence that sounds identical and is not about permission: "she was invited, ahead of the public opening, and she has not answered yet." That is a fact about a person's standing on one event, and the model cannot state it. Worse, the tiers actively misreport it: PLACED is the capacity set, so an invited person who registers onto a full event is ON_WAITLIST — the model says waiting where the organizer's head says has a place, we made room — and D-065 records an organizer exceeding capacity by report, not by state. So the overrun is real, visible in a report, and invisible to any selector, which means a grant aimed at "the people we actually have room for" and a grant aimed at "the people we invited" are the same four tiers stretched over two different questions.

Positions. - Refuse the word — say plainly, where the tiers are listed, that there is no WHITELISTED and that the sentence it wants is a grant. Consistent with D-102's refusal of PRESENT, costs nothing, and leaves the invited-but-unanswered person described the way unanswered already is: by the absence of a row (D-059). This is the default these documents hold today. - Give it state — a boolean or small status on event_registration, which makes it a fifth tier and forces the tier algebra to be restated: is an invited person PLACED by right, or only once capacity lets them through? Whatever is chosen, PLACED's definition — the set the capacity let through, the one the index already serves — stops being one predicate, and that is the cost, not the new column. - Make it a group — the invitation list is a person_group (D-098), named, dated, and separately answerable across time. This is cheap and it is almost right: it says who was invited, which is the fact people actually ask for later, and it is answerable on 1 June 2024 in a way an audience never is. It is wrong for the per-event case, because it makes an invitation a thing with its own lifetime.

Needed. Not before implementation, and not before someone asks — but the word should be refused in writing now, in the same paragraph that refuses PRESENT, because "no WHITELISTED" is a sentence that has to exist somewhere before the first person implements it as a column. The PRESENT refusal is the precedent to copy: it was refused for a representable reason (nothing is stored until a person marks it), and this one needs its reason stated rather than inherited.

Impact. Refusing costs a paragraph. The column costs a restated PLACED, a re-derived index, and a report that now has two ways to be full.

docs.title: Ga. Personal attributes — designed, with four things left open
docs.text: The module exists: domain/08-person-data.md and data-model/09-attributes.md, decided by D-083, D-084 and D-085. It arrived instead of the health-records module, because the question "what is a health record here" answered itself a size larger: everything about a person except name, gender and age is one class of data, defined by the organization at runtime, with no privileged subset.

docs.title: AT-1 🟡 Should an event question bind to an attribute code?
docs.text:
Raised by D-085, which made the event form the fallback rather than the ceiling.

The situation. A returning camper types their allergy into every event form, every season, and the answer lives in event_answer.value for that event only. Meanwhile the organization may already hold the same fact as an attribute on the person, with a name, a value_type, and a recorded author. Nothing connects them.

Why this is a question and not an obvious improvement. Prefilling an answer from the record makes the record the thing a leader relies on, and the record is: whatever was typed, by whoever, possibly two years ago, with no obligation on anyone to update it. Today's arrangement is worse data and better epistemics — the form asks now, about this event, and the answer is dated today. Bind the two and an out-of-date attribute becomes a wrong answer that looks authoritative, which is the one failure mode a health fact has that makes it dangerous.

Recommendation. Prefill as a suggestion the registrant confirms or corrects on the way in, and write the confirmed value back to the attribute with today's date and this person as its author. Then the form stays the authority for the event, the record gets refreshed by the act of using it, and nobody ever relies on a two-year-old entry without a human having just looked at it. The variant to reject is reading the attribute directly into the organizer's view without the registrant's confirmation pass — that is the same convenience with the safety removed.

Impact. One binding on the question definition, one write-back rule, and a rule about which is authoritative when they disagree. No new permission.

See: D-061 (as amended), data-model/08 §7.

docs.title: AT-2 🟡 Who curates the vocabulary, and how long may a proposal sit?
docs.text:
Raised by D-084, which made attribute.define a permission instead of a release.

An open vocabulary is only as good as somebody tending it, and "somebody" is currently nobody in particular. Two halves:

  • Who holds attribute.define. The starting role set (permission-catalog §11) is the place this gets answered, and the honest answer is that a volunteer organization has one or two people who will do this and not a committee. Too narrow and the proposal queue is a bottleneck that teaches people to file facts into notes instead; too wide and it is not a curation.
  • How long a proposal may sit before it is promoted, merged or discarded. The check exists (09-attributes §8 checks 1 and 2) and the number does not. A quarter is a defensible default: long enough that a seasonal field is not judged off a single use, short enough that a proposal is answered inside the season that produced it.

Recommendation. One named role, a stated age limit on proposals, and a standing decision that an expired proposal's values stay — the curation is about the name, never about deleting what was recorded.

Impact. Configuration and one role, no schema change. The thing it prevents is the slow failure: a vocabulary nobody curates stops being queryable and the layer keeps storing everything, which looks like success for years.

docs.title: AT-3 🟢 Do attribute labels need translation?
docs.text: Inherited from the multi-language row in §H, and sharper here than anywhere else because the vocabulary is runtime data: if a code's label is Czech-only, a Slovak-speaking volunteer cannot pick the field at all. Whether the answer is a translation column on attribute_definition, a separate label-per-language table, or "the organization is single-language, stop asking" is unrecorded. The cost of not answering is asymmetric — a label table added later is a migration; a body of codes accumulated with one label each is a data-cleaning project.

docs.title: AT-4 🟡 Is one permission enough to guard a trail that holds person data?
docs.text:
Raised by the reversal recorded in D-083, which decided the audit trail does hold a person's descriptive values — because D-085 made that trail the only history such values have, and stripping them would have made the history empty while quietly grading health-shaped fields above a change of address. What protects the copy is then one thing: audit.view, graded ⚠⚠ beside person.view (permission-catalog §8). Three positions exist and none is recorded as taken:

  • The guard is enough (current documents). One permission, marked honestly, and a rule that whoever holds it is reading person data. Simple, and it makes the auditor role — which has audit.view and not person.view — a reader of the entire person record (permission-catalog §11 note 3).
  • Per-entry filtering in the history view: show an audit row's values only where the reader could also see the live field. Consistent with everything §9 of data-model/05-authorization.md says about channels, and it was considered and left unimplemented, because it means running the resolver per audit row against rows that may no longer exist — a grant withdrawn last year is exactly the case a history is read for.
  • Split the permission: the trail's shape (who changed which table, when) apart from its payloads. Honest about what an auditor usually needs, and it is the option that reintroduces a sensitive subset through the back of the catalog — which is why the documents do not recommend it.

The cost of not answering is asymmetric in the uncomfortable direction: the first position is already implemented by default, so leaving the question open is choosing it, and the choice is made invisible — nobody signs off on "volunteers with audit.view can read children's medical history" because there is no moment at which anybody has to say it.

docs.title: H. Not yet designed
docs.text:
Each of these is referenced by the schema and has hooks left for it — except health records, which has no hooks because it has no design at all, and whose missing design is load-bearing in two other documents. Read H-0 below before the table.

Area Hooks already in place Notes Events ✅ Designed — domain/07, data-model/08 Fifteen questions answered; three left in § G above. Fees and payments data-model/07-finance.md — architecture settled, policy open Nine open questions, of which one is new. Round 6 closed the architectural ones: money arrives by bank API, is requested by variable symbol + QR code, there is no card gateway, and unmatched money queues (D-075, D-076). What remains needs somebody in the organization asked: proration, discounts, insurance, waivers, invoices. Documents access_grant.scope_type = 'document'; the evidence-reference hook belonged to the removed requirement tables Needs: storage, versions, retention, consent-driven access. Consents No dependent.consent.* any more — a guardian at write may give and manage consents (D-074) Needs: template, per-activity consent, expiry, revocation, who may consent. No longer connected to a membership requirement (D-044). is_legal_decision_maker on the guardianship row is the existing hook for "who may sign" — and it is now the only place that distinction lives, since the right level cannot express it. Health records ✅ Designed — as domain/08 and data-model/09 Highest-sensitivity data in the system, and the exposure grew in round 6. D-074 deleted the codes that used to gate medical visibility, so "read everything except the health file" is no longer sayable — see E-7. This raises the case for designing the module before the coarse default is relied on, rather than after: separate retention, separate access, likely separate storage, and its own legal review. Communication message.send_direct, message.broadcast (scoped) — shape decided, detail undesigned Shape decided by D-077: internal first, external channels are delivery; everyone may send direct; broadcast is one scoped permission; the recipient picks the channel. Needs: templates, opt-out granularity, retention, moderation. The rule against contacting minors directly was declined as a sender restriction — see MSG-1 below. Reporting report.* permissions sketched The historical queries in domain/05 are the starting set. Query 10 (members per year since 1985) is the acceptance test. API and UI — Not started. The resolver's p_at parameter exists partly for this. Notifications — Expiring roles, members inside the renewal window, unpaid fees. Note the renewal window makes this dated rather than status-driven — a nightly job over in_renewal_window(). Payment gateway — Answered, so this row is now narrower than it was. The organization collects via bank API, not a card gateway (D-075): no webhooks, no disputes, no processor reconciliation. What remains undesigned is the statement import itself — file formats, the idempotency key, and what happens to an account the bank revises. Multi-language — Unit names and permission display names are all in the database. Whether they need translation columns is unanswered.

docs.title: H-0 ✅ Closed — the medical record was cited everywhere and defined nowhere, and it turns out there was nothing to define
docs.text:
Found while starting the health-records module, and it changes what that module is. Sentences across five files discuss who may read the medical record as though it were a table:

Where What it says §H, this file, Health records row "a view guardian already sees them" E-7 "a guardian either sees everything about the child or nothing" permission-catalog §9 a view guardian "reaches the fee history and the health record" data-model/08 §7 "the medical file, which no event permission reaches" data-model/04 §2 the case the old codes existed for is "access to medical information"

No document defines one. There is no health or medical entity in any data-model file and no box in the ERD. The only thing that ever had a medical shape in this model was a medical_form requirement code, and D-044 deleted that table. So the referent is a habit of speech inherited from the old dependent.medical.* permission codes, which named a sub-resource of a table that was itself removed with D-074.

What this does to the arguments built on it — most of them survive, one does not.

  • E-7 stands, and is sharper than it looked. "One right level cannot separate the medical record from the profile" is still true about a record that does not exist: it says the guardian model has no granularity to offer whenever something sensitive is later attached to a person. That is a real finding about the model, not about a table.
  • "No event permission reaches the medical record" is true but empty. Nothing reaches it, because nothing is there. The paragraph in 08-events that leans on this to reassure is right about permissions and wrong about the risk: the only health data the system actually holds today is in event_answer.value — free text typed into a form, read by whoever runs the event, with no retention policy (EV-2). The sensitive data is in the weakest place, not the strongest.
  • "A view guardian already sees them" is simply false, and was written as a reason not to design the module early. It is replaced by the question below.

The question, before any field is designed. What is a health record in this system? Not "which fields" — the shape. Three coherent answers, and they imply different systems:

  1. Structured entries (allergy, medication, condition, instruction) — queryable, so "who in this unit has a nut allergy" is answerable, and the price is that the organization is now a custodian of diagnosable data with everything that implies.
  2. Documents only — a scanned form filed against the person, using the document scope that already exists in the catalog. Cheap, legally simple, and useless in an emergency, because nobody reads a PDF at 23:00 in a tent.
  3. Hybrid — a small set of structured, actionable entries plus documents behind them for anything a form can hold. This is what organizations actually do on paper, and the option the rest of the corpus seems to assume.

Why this is H-0 and not a row in the table. Every other open question about health — who may read it, whether the guardian default changes, what event organizers get, how long answers survive, whether E-7 needs its exception — takes a different answer depending on this one. It is also the only module whose absence is already load-bearing: two documents cite the medical record's protections in order to argue that something else is safe.

Answered (round 7), by rejecting the framing. You answered the three-way question with a fourth answer: "I consider everything apart from name, gender and age a 'medical record'. It is fields in the database, not files." So the referent was not missing — the category was missing, and the phrase in those five files was groping at a distinction nobody makes: there is no medical record inside the person record, because the person record is the thing, and it is fields. Recorded as D-083, with the shape of the layer in D-084 and the boundary in D-085. The three options above are recorded nowhere else, which is right: they were the shape of the question, not the shape of the answer.

See: section Ga, data-model/09-attributes.md.

docs.title: MSG-1 ✅ Closed — a direct message to a minor is mirrored to their guardians
docs.text:
Raised by D-077, which declined the restriction rather than forgetting it.

The situation. Messaging has two sender tiers — direct, which everyone may do, and broadcast, which is a permission. Neither tier mentions age. So any person with an account may send a private message to any child with an account, and nothing in the model prevents it, records it as unusual, or tells anyone. This is not a gap created by oversight: the question asked whether staff may address a child or only their guardians, and the answer replaced it with a model in which age is not a sender concept at all. The rule the communication section had promised — "a rule against contacting minors directly" — is therefore not implemented, and it is worth being blunt that this is the most consequential unanswered question in the file.

Why restricting senders is the wrong fix here. An age branch in the resolver is what D-070 refused for events, on the grounds that a condition evaluated at check time which the capability model does not know about becomes the first rule in a rule engine nobody wants. It would also be the kind of restriction that gets loosened the first time it inconveniences a leader, and a permission that is routinely bypassed on a messaging system is worse than none, because it makes the bypass normal.

Recommendation — restrict visibility, not permission. Mirror direct messages reaching a minor to that minor's guardians, and make the mirroring visible to the sender. Then:

  • nothing is blocked, so the resolver still has no age branch;
  • nothing is secretly unread, which is the actual safeguarding property;
  • it is built on the guardianship rows the organization already maintains, so it needs no new authority concept;
  • and it degrades honestly — a child with no guardian on record gets no mirroring, which is the same safeguarding gap check 4 in data-model/04 §6 already alerts on, arriving through a second channel.

The variant to reject. "Only guardians and unit leaders may message a child." That is the restriction wearing the visibility recommendation's clothes: it is a sender rule, it needs the age branch, and it silently tells a child that the adult messaging them has been vetted — which the model does not establish, and the organization records no background checks (D-043).

Answered (round 6): the recommendation is adopted, as D-082 — mirror to guardians, tell the sender, block nothing. Three details were settled with it, because "mirror it to the guardians" does not by itself say who the guardians are to this message:

  • Which guardians. Those whose right level is view or write. A guardian at none receives nothing: none is the organization having already decided that this party sees nothing about the child, and a safeguarding rule is not a licence to undo a recorded decision by side effect. A minor whose guardians are all none is therefore reported with the minors who have no guardian at all — otherwise the exclusion would be a way to make a child silently unwatched.
  • Which set, as of when. The guardianships open at the moment the message is sent, frozen into the delivery. A guardianship closed afterwards does not lose its mirror, and a guardian added later does not acquire old threads — same discipline as 06-audit §2, which keeps the trail answering "what was true then".
  • Broadcast is not mirrored. A scoped broadcast is already addressed to a set, recorded, and attributable; mirroring exists for the private case, which is the one that can be invisible.

What mirroring is not. Not approval, not a gate, and not evidence anyone read it. It buys the one property the safeguarding argument actually needs — no private conversation about a child is secretly unread — without putting an age into the resolver.

See: D-082, permission-catalog's message row, glossary — Mirroring.

docs.title: R. Resolved — moved to the decision log
docs.text:
Kept here so a reader of this file knows the question was asked and where the answer lives, rather than finding it silently deleted.

Was Question Settled by In one line A-1 The organizational structure D-035 One root; all sub-units nest arbitrarily beneath it. A-1 The unit type vocabulary D-054 Not seeded — org_unit_type is runtime data; only the root type ships. B-1 How much legacy data, in what shape? D-056 Large, with legacy member numbers — exact matches, so review is a work queue. Fully answered in round 8: thousands of roster rows, no payment data at all, so every historical row is a participation (D-090). D-9 Is household load-bearing at all? D-057 No — removed entirely. Addresses are temporal person_contact rows. F-1 Which permissions and roles does the organization need? D-055 The catalog stays large and granular; it is a menu, not a checklist. — Eligibility for an event — a separate rule engine? D-060 No — eligibility is capability. event.register_self at contribute, via audiences. — Is unanswered a stored attendance value? D-059 No — absence of a row. Two stored values: attending, not_attending. — Is a weekly meeting an event? D-058 No — it is unit_participation. No recurrence, no series table. — One owning unit per event, or several? D-058 Exactly one. A joint camp is one unit's event another unit participates in. — Are organizers a grant or a roster? D-062 A roster on the event — labelled and ordered. Grants stay separate. — Do unit roles reach the unit's own events? D-063 Yes — an event is an artifact of its unit, not a child. Not inheritance (D-031 stands). — Does an event have a status (draft, published)? D-064 No status column. Visibility is the permission model; cancellation is a fact. — What happens when a full event gets another registration? D-065 Waitlisted for self-service; admitted for organizers; the overrun reported. — Does paying confirm a place? D-066 Yes when the event has a fee; most events are free and confirm immediately. — Do organizers record who actually came? D-067 Yes — was_present, three-valued. It is the "who was in our care" record. — May an event form collect medical detail? D-061 Effectively yes: answers are read by that event's organizers, and no event permission reaches the health record, so the form is the only route for a camp leader to learn an allergy at all. A recorded widening, restated after D-074 removed the namespace the original wording relied on. A-2 Permissions conditioned on membership status D-039 Yes, enforced by the resolver, with guardianship and ownership carved out. A-3 Activate on payment or on approval? D-040 On payment; the fee expires yearly and a dated renewal window replaces a grace status. A-4 Background checks D-043 None are recorded in this system. A-4 The expiry date D-047 1 January; the organizational year runs with the calendar. A-4 The renewal window length D-048 60 days, stored as a parameter rather than compiled in. C-1 May the root read into its sub-units? D-049 No. scope_exposure is the only crossing; no reporting channel is built. Formally closed in round 9, and D-094 gave it a mirror: imported events belong to the root, so a unit's own event list contains history it did not run. C-3 Is a reused unit number the same unit? D-096 A new unit, unless someone records continuity as successor_of. A code is a typed label, not an identity. C-4 Does appointing someone create a role assignment? D-091, restated by D-098, D-100, D-101 No. Round 10 redrew the line the answer drew: the union-of-three-arms became an expression language (+ - *), a group became a hand-stated dated roster, and an audience became the rule. Appointing still creates nothing, and there are no positions left to appoint. Rule-filled roles went to F-12, which round 10 closed no. C-5 What creates the units the import's rows point at? D-092, D-093, D-094 Nothing, because the rows name no units. People arrive as bounded memberships, events as root-owned events with registrations. The historical record has no sub-units in it. C-6 Should allows_minors refuse a minor's position as it refuses their participation? D-095 Neither: units carry no restrictions and the flag is removed. The control is that nobody joins a unit or takes a position themself — a counselor writes the row. D-6 How may the membership gate be waived? D-051 A person-level system.gate_exempt permission, in addition to the role flag. D-7 The root participation row at renewal D-050 Extended across the renewed period; one row, no gap. B-3 (part) Erasure: what shape? your answer, round 5 Redact the person, keep the financial and membership skeleton. Retention decided in round 8 — the skeleton is kept indefinitely, audit payloads expire (D-088); what is left is the legal review of the indefinite half, not the design. C-1 (largely) Organization-wide operational roles without downward inheritance D-035 The problem dissolves: the root owns the registry and the fees. What remains is a reporting question — see C-1. C-2 May units be reparented retroactively? D-036 Not at all — a unit that moves is a new unit. D-1 Fee per person or per household? D-037 Per person, flat, yearly. D-2 One open membership, or several of different types? D-037, D-041 One type, so one open membership, enforced person-wide. D-3 Age-out timing D-038 Retired — there is no age-out. D-4 Child → adult transition D-038 Retired — there are no membership categories to transition between. D-5 Membership type vocabulary D-037 One type, member; counselor is a position, not a type. E-1 Default rights when a guardianship is created D-046 write for a self-registered child's guardian; view for staff-created and imported rows; chosen at creation when recorded manually. D-074 turned the answer from a code bundle into one level, which is why the decision still stands on its original wording. F-2 Polymorphic scope_id vs a grantable_item supertable your answer, round 6 Polymorphic — scope_type plus scope_id, as currently designed. — The bulk scope-exposure tool D-045 Removed once audiences existed to cover the case it was for. — What a membership request must contain D-044 Identity and the fee. The whole requirement mechanism is gone. — Whether grants may target groups D-042 Yes — built-in rule-evaluated audiences plus admin-managed named groups. E-2 What happens to guardianship at majority? D-069 Nothing — no job, no queue, no computed date. A person ends the row. (Reverses D-024.) F-3 Must a high-authority role assignment have an end date? D-071 No. The membership gate plus a human review report; the earlier "yes" recommendation is withdrawn. F-4 Should person.admin subsume merge and redact? D-068 Moot — there are no per-resource admin permissions. The choice moved into reviewable role contents. (Reverses D-007.) — Should every resource expose an admin permission? D-068 No. Sixteen codes and the resolver's prefix match are gone; roles are the bundle. EV-1 Does an event need an age ceiling? D-070 No. The grant is the rule; a future ceiling would be a built-in audience, not a column. EV-5 Should event.manage_participants split? this round Yes — event.presence.mark at contribute, one level below the roster. Round 10 note: the split stands; the level does not (D-099). D-8 Should unit_participation reference the membership? D-097 Retired with the table. The refusal is still live reasoning: participation had to survive without a membership, which is why person_group_member is keyed on a person. See data-model/03 §9. F-12 May a role be held by a rule, as an audience is? D-100 No. An office is held by a named person and confers nothing; a group is company; a grant is what reaches a set. The office record stays the one dated, human-readable answer. — Is there more than one unit, and does anything belong to it? D-097 No. org_unit and friends, unit_participation, scope_exposure and the traversal functions are deleted; the unit is a scope, not a row. Two-way door: no. — What is a group? D-098 person_group: named, dated, states its members, has a lifetime, grants nothing by itself. A group is company; a selector picks people; a grant is what reaches them. — What does a grant do, and how much? D-099 Allows or denies one permission at one scope, for a period. Allowed iff some live allow applies and no live deny applies. No levels, no rank integer, no locality. — Is a role a bundle of permissions, and is membership a precondition? D-100 Neither. role_assignment → role_holder; role_permission, positions and the membership gate are deleted; the test moved into the expression (MEMBERS * ROLE(x)). Posture: default-on → opt-in. — How is an audience stored? D-101 As an expression tree over named sets — + - *, brackets, fully-bracketed canonical form, cycles refused at save, the language seeded as selector_type. Semantic equality given up (see F-14). — Who owns an event, and whom does a grant about it reach? D-102 Nobody owns it. event.org_unit_id, can_event() and the artifact rule are deleted; four attendance tiers and ORGANIZERS bind to the item, and the answer-view grant is a seeded template instantiated per event. — May a rule be reused by name? D-103 Yes: AUDIENCE(code), referenced by code, one namespace with roles and groups, cycles refused across audiences at save, and an audience named by a live grant may not be ended. Its past reach is not reconstructable (see F-17). Amended in the same round: the same refusal now extends to a group named by a live grant — see assumption 63. F-19 A permission code is a row, prose names codes, and nothing checks the two D-104 The class is real — four instances in ten rounds, in two different registries. The naming grammar is now three rules (action-final; a middle segment names stored state; no grade words, no prefix) with system.admin the single named exception. The event QR capability never existed: invented in prose, deleted in prose, no decision entry at either end. The check adopted is a hand-run diff report — a convention, not a guard.

docs.title: I. Assumption index
docs.text:
Every Assumption: in the documentation, so they can be reviewed as a group. Once you confirm one, it should be promoted to a numbered decision and struck from § R.

Rows marked † are now backed by a decision rather than a bare assumption — kept here because the docs still cite them and because the decision is worth seeing in this list.

# Assumption Where 1 PostgreSQL 14+ with btree_gist data-model/00 2 No automatic merging (D-004) † domain/03 3 Minors need guardian consent for an account domain/02 4 A self-registered child's parent gets a write right over the child (D-046, as amended by D-074) † data-model/04 5 ~~Locality orders allows only~~; deny is absolute (D-032) † — half of this row is deleted: locality went with the levels (D-099), and the surviving half is now the whole decision rule: allowed iff some live allow applies and no live deny applies domain/06 6 Membership activates on payment (D-040) † domain/05 7 The fee is per person and yearly (D-037) † domain/05 8 Renewal opens a new row, not an extended valid_to (D-016) † domain/05 ~~9~~ ~~Guardianship reviewed at majority, not auto-expired~~ — superseded: neither, the system takes no position (D-069) data-model/04 10 Display name uses preferred_name if set data-model/01 11 Merge chains are allowed, because reversing a merge has to stay possible (D-087) † data-model/01 12 Only confirmed payments count toward a balance data-model/07 ~~13~~ ~~No sub-unit types are seeded; nesting is permissive by default~~ (D-054) — deleted, not reversed: org_unit_type and org_unit_type_rule went with the hierarchy (D-097), so there is nothing left to seed and no nesting to be permissive about. A-1's closure is the decision of record data-model/02 14 membership_type is seeded with exactly one row (D-037) † data-model/03 15 person.gender is needed for reporting data-model/01 16 Imported rosters end at the organizational year end (D-028) † data-model/06 17 All business tables are audited data-model/06 18 Currency is EUR data-model/07 19 access_log is not human-annotatable data-model/05 ~~20~~ ~~Each permission has an admin sibling~~ — superseded: no per-resource wildcard codes (D-068) throughout 21 No downward inheritance; ~~exposures are written by the unit~~ (D-031) † — deprived of its subject, not weakened (D-097): the rule was always about a hierarchy that no longer exists, and what survives is the ordinary reading of a scope — a grant reaches its scope and nothing beside it domain/06 §2 22 The person record holds no deceased flag (D-034) † data-model/01 ~~23~~ ~~Positions are multi-holder unless max_holders says otherwise~~ (D-033) — deleted by D-100 with position, position_assignment, is_leadership and max_holders. The vacancy question it answered is now unanswered by construction; see F-18 domain/04 24 Membership is ageless — no category, no min_age, no max_age (D-038) † data-model/03 25 A grant targets a person or an audience, never both (D-042) † data-model/05 26 ~~Built-in audiences are rules evaluated by the resolver, not stored lists~~ (D-042) † — reversed twice, and the second reversal is the one to keep. Round 10 found both halves wrong in opposite directions: no built-in audiences (two seeded rows remain, and the rules are the selector_type operands), and an audience does contain a stored list — its LIST leaf (D-101, D-103). Round 11 deleted that leaf (D-105), so an audience stores an expression and nothing else: a hand-written set is PERSON(x) leaves inside the expression — rows of the tree, not rows of a roster, with no dates of their own. D-042's original half is therefore true of an audience again, and true for a new reason: the words are what is stored, and the words can happen to name people. (The count this row quoted was stale the moment assumption 58 recorded a thirteenth row arriving, and is twelve again now that LIST is gone — right by subtraction, not by the same fact.) data-model/05 ~~27~~ ~~Belonging to a sub-unit is participation, not membership~~ (D-041) † — deleted with the sub-units (D-097). The distinction it drew is now drawn between a group (company) and a grant (authority), by D-098 data-model/02 ~~28~~ ~~Roles require a current membership unless requires_membership = false~~ (D-039) † — the gate is deleted (D-100); membership is now a term a writer puts in a grant expression, and the posture is opt-in data-model/05 ~~29~~ ~~There is no bulk exposure tool and no bulk: reason marker~~ (D-045) † — moot twice over: scope_exposure itself is deleted (D-097), so there is no tool to build and nothing to mark data-model/05 30 No background checks are recorded anywhere (D-043) † throughout 31 access_grant.scope_id is polymorphic, with no foreign key (F-2) † data-model/05 32 The organizational calendar is 1 January plus a 60-day window (D-047, D-048) † data-model/03 ~~33~~ ~~The root reads into a sub-unit only through scope_exposure~~ (D-049) † — there is no sub-unit and no exposure (D-097). C-1's closure is the record; the safeguarding property it protected ("a child's records are reachable only through a guardianship row") was never carried by this mechanism and is untouched domain/06 ~~34~~ ~~A renewal extends the root participation row rather than closing it~~ (D-050) † — the row is deleted (D-097). The reasoning survives where the row did not: data-model/03 §9 keeps it, because the renewal rule in §3 still rests on it. See D-7 data-model/03 ~~35~~ ~~The membership gate is waived by a person-level permission, not only a role flag~~ (D-051) † — the gate and system.gate_exempt are both deleted (D-100). What survives is the reason: a sweep must not lock out the one person who can repair it, which is now an argument about the seeded grants carrying MEMBERS. See D-6 data-model/05 36 The permission catalog is deliberately comprehensive and granular (D-055) † appendix/permission-catalog.md 37 The legacy corpus is large and carries legacy member numbers (D-056) † domain/03 38 There is no household table; addresses are temporal person_contact rows (D-057) † data-model/04 39 ~~An event belongs to exactly one unit~~; a weekly meeting is not an event (D-058) † — first half deleted by D-102 (event.org_unit_id is gone; nothing owns an event), second half intact but no longer named "participation": a Thursday group is a group now (D-097, D-098), and no row says who attended a given evening data-model/08 40 "Unanswered" is the absence of a registration row (D-059) † data-model/08 41 Eligibility is capability — there is no rule engine (D-060) † domain/07 42 Event answers are read by that event's organizers (D-061) † — still true, and no longer a resolver clause: it is one seeded grant row (event.answer.view, scoped to the event, aimed at ORGANIZERS) instantiated per event, which D-102 calls out as the deliberate move from prose to data. An event created without its grant has organizers who can read nothing data-model/08 43 Organizers are a roster on the event, not grants (D-062) † data-model/08 ~~44~~ ~~An event is an artifact of its unit, so unit roles reach it~~ (D-063) † — deleted by D-102, along with can_event().
