Nothing reaches an event from a unit any more; authority arrives through a grant scoped to the event itself, and the sentence "an event is an artifact, not a child" is withdrawn rather than restated domain/07 45 There is no event status; visibility is the permission model (D-064) † data-model/08 46 Capacity is a waitlist threshold organizers may exceed (D-065) † data-model/08 47 Payment confirms a place; free events confirm immediately (D-066) † data-model/08 48 Presence is a three-valued fact, not a boolean (D-067) † data-model/08 49 Keeping named membership and fee rows indefinitely after an erasure request has a legal basis (D-088) — unverified, and commissioning the review is the organization's job data-model/00 50 access_log needs the same window as audit payloads, neither longer nor shorter (proposed, F-8) data-model/05 51 Audience membership is recomputed at check time and never stored, so "who could read this in 2023" may be unanswerable once the audit payloads expire (D-091, restated for D-098/D-101) † — the half of this that used to be true of roles is no longer at risk: an office is a dated role_holder row and a group is a dated roster, both stored, and F-12 closed on exactly that ground. What remains exposed is the expression, and it is now a question with a number: F-17 data-model/05 52 The historical record contains no sub-unit participation, because the corpus names no units (D-092) † — now true for a second, stronger reason: even if the corpus had named them there would be nowhere to put the answer (D-097). The finding about the source is what matters and is unchanged data-model/06 53 An imported membership carries no fee obligation, and its outstanding_balance is NULL rather than zero (D-093) † data-model/07 54 A bare name in an expression resolves to a role or a group only, never to an audience — and the one-namespace rule across role, person_group and audience.code, with every selector_type.code reserved, is carried by the write path with no constraint spanning three tables (D-101, D-103) † data-model/05 55 Delegation is a set-membership test, and role.is_delegatable does not exist — the model has no column that says an office may delegate (no decision; domain/06 carries it as an assumption) domain/06 56 Finding which grants name an audience, and at what depth, is cheap enough to show before saving an edit to a referenced audience (D-103) — stated as an assumption in the decision itself and measured by nobody F-16 57 A grant's scope is the unit or exactly one item, so the seeded answer-view grant is a template instantiated per event rather than one row for every event (D-102) † data-model/08 58 ~~The PERSON(x) appearing in D-100's and D-101's worked expressions is shorthand for a second grant row, not a missing seeded operand~~ (D-101's registry amendment, class in D-104) † — the opposite: it was seeded — as the thirteenth row to arrive (takes_argument true, argument_type person, binds_to_item false), and today as one of the twelve that remain, because D-105 deleted LIST in the round after. The ordinal belongs to round 10 and the count to round 11: the registry has never held thirteen rows at the same time as it held twelve, and neither number says anything about how many it holds now. The registry was the side that was wrong. It was written by two decision entries while the seeded table — copied from the evaluator's arm list rather than from D-101's grammar — carried twelve rows without it, so MEMBERS * ROLE(x) + PERSON(y) did not parse for a whole round and the wrong repair (PERSON(y) read as LIST, which subtracts everybody on the list) was already circulating — a repair that is now impossible to write, the only fix this one got without a decision. The assumption this row recorded was the wrong answer, and saying so is the point: the registry was checked against nothing D-101, F-5 59 Two expressions with one meaning are two audiences: nothing computes semantic equality, and nothing will (D-101) † F-14 60 An audience preview is per-item and lazy, and no screen expands a set for more than one item at a time (consequence of D-102's per-item reached set) — unmeasured at real event sizes; round 14 amended this row without changing the assumption: it adds a dependency. Nothing pre-pays a preview any more — the nightly job used to warm what a preview reads, and with the answer cache deleted the preview computes on open (D-114). Its affordability now rests on the request memo and on can_many existing, which these documents can name and cannot enforce F-15 61 ~~A cache key is (person, permission, item), and a stale allow is the failure that matters because deny is absolute (D-102, D-099) — the asymmetric-TTL answer is proposed in F-6 and decided by nobody — round 12 made the key short by one component: OLDER(n) puts the date being checked inside the answer with no write behind it, so a key of (person, permission, item) can hold an answer from before a birthday unless the cache cannot outlive the day.~~ — round 14 deleted this row's subject rather than settling it: there is no cache, so there is no key, no TTL and no stale allow (D-114; see also D-111, whose answer this is). Two halves of the row outlive the object they were written about, and both turn out to be about meaning rather than storage: (i) the item belongs to whatever a permission predicate is bound to — a compilation carries the item as a parameter and holds no item, so nothing resolved while checking one item may be served for another: D-102's finding, surviving the key it was first written into; (ii) the checked date belongs inside the answer, which is why a cached roster must hold dated rows or validity ranges and never "today's set". D-107's acceptance is discharged, not amended — under live resolution a birthday moves the answer at the instant it happens, so F-6 no longer carries a consequence D-114, data-model/05 §10 62 A person_group_member row lies inside its group's own period — assumed in §2 of data-model/02, reported by integrity check 2 as "a list to read rather than a breach", and ruled nowhere. Raised by the page's own author as an assumption these documents are standing on data-model/02 §8 63 ~~A group may be ended while a live grant or a live expression names it~~ (D-103, amended in the round after the audience row) † — refused at save, in both directions: ending a group while a live grant, or a live audience reachable from one, names it, and writing a new grant onto an already-ended group. The reason is the - asymmetry, not the allow side — a live grant on an ended group is safe on the allow side and widens a deny on the - side, so an ended operand is a way to silently empty a set that was narrowing something. Checked over audience_operand rows whose selector_kind = 'GROUP', the same query as the audience rule. ROLE(x) needs no such rule, and the difference is the finding: an office has no role.retire, no status, and deletion is already refused while holder rows exist, so an office cannot be emptied quietly while a group can be emptied in one click. The hazard is a property of the shape, not of the idea D-103, data-model/02 §8 64 An operand's set moves when somebody writes — twelve rounds of invalidation lists were built on this and none of them said it out loud † — falsified by design by D-107: OLDER(n) and YOUNGER(n) move at midnight, for one person, with no row to change and no event to subscribe to. ~~Accepted, not fixed — "I know, that the time will change, how the rules resolve and IT IS FINE" — and the residue that survived the ruling is not resolution but the record, which is F-23~~ — round 14 closed the gap this row accepted, and in doing so found the one in the opposite direction (D-114). The calendar case is discharged: with resolution live and no answer stored, a birthday moves the answer at the instant it happens, so the acceptance has nothing left to accept and its "IT IS FINE" stands with no mechanism owed. The write case was never safe: the lists assumed a write is what moves a set and then could not say which writes — and the boundary D-111 finally drew left out membership, whose membership.terminate ⛔ is the corpus's most safeguarding-shaped write. So the corrected form of this row is not "sets move on writes" but "sets move whenever anything they can read changes", which is the read path, not a list F-6, D-114

docs.title: How to answer
docs.text:
The blocking set is still empty, and round 10 is the reason nobody should find that reassuring. Ten rounds in, nothing here has to be answered before implementation could start — but round 10 was not a round that closed questions about the model, it was a round that redesigned the model: the unit hierarchy, the permission levels, positions and the membership gate are gone, and in their place are a group table, an office table, a grant that allows or denies one thing, and an expression language stored as a tree. That is D-097 through D-103, and it is the largest change since the documents began. The blocking set stayed empty because the round's cost went into questions that were not open before it, and eight of them are new in this file.

What remains is genuinely deferrable, and the most useful next ones are — a list that round 13 had to cut roughly in half, which is worth saying before the list itself is trusted again:

  1. F-10 — which invariants the ORM cannot express. Round 10 put three new instances into shape 3 and emptied shape 4, so the shape list is now the shortest path to everything the write path has to carry: an event row that obliges a grant row, requiredness conditioned on a value in selector_type, a check that reads a referenced row, a name namespace across three tables, and exclusion constraints over all rows rather than open ones. Round 13 handed it a fifth shape it has never had: an invariant over the documents rather than over the data — every selector name that appears in a document must be a selector_type row, and a check should be able to say so (D-113's rule, minted when the fourteenth selector turned out to be a prose idiom). It is a lint of prose against a seed list, which belongs to F-19's machinery rather than to the write path, and it is now the only check that would have caught it.
  2. F-18 — does a role record elected versus appointed, and what does an election write? This is the sole survivor of what used to be items 2 through 5 of this list, and it is here on its own merits, not by inheritance: it is a property of the deleted position tables that a real elected committee still needs a place for.

What round 13 removed from this list, so the removal is auditable rather than silent. Four of the nine items below were closed by D-109 through D-113, and their reasoning lives on in the entries rather than here: old item 2 was F-17 with F-18 and the which-grants-name-this-audience measurement — F-17 is closed by D-110 (the words are the record), the listing is closed by D-112 (cheap at the stated size), and the third protection named there, cache invalidation across the reference closure, is the one D-111 deleted outright — and round 14 deleted the rebuild that deleted it, which hands that walk back as a bounded job over compilations (D-114, § F-16); old item 3 was F-6, closed by D-111, and the open half it was ranked on — a stale allow is a permission already withdrawn — turned out to be impossible rather than managed, ~~because every withdrawal is a write~~ because nothing stores the answer — the first reason was the one the corpus wrote, and it had membership missing from it; the second is D-114's correction and does not depend on anybody having listed the right tables; old item 4 was F-21 with F-22, closed by D-109 (no report, a tab) and by an editor ruling (display free, storage fixed); old item 5 was F-5, closed by D-113 deleting the last operand it thought was missing. Note what the pattern is: four of these did not receive the answer the entry was built to receive. They were closed by removing a mechanism — a report, a per-entry TTL, a history question, a registry row — which is the move this round made repeatedly and the one a register of open questions is structurally bad at predicting. 3. AT-2 / AT-4 — who curates the attribute vocabulary day to day, and whether one permission is trusted to guard a trail that holds person data. These are one question seen from two ends: the data that lands in the trail arrives through the vocabulary. 4. EV-2 — how long an event answer is kept once the event it answered is gone, which is a sharper question now that the audit payloads which also held those values have a clock on them (B-3). 5. F-19 — the one thing in this file that could be settled this afternoon: four times in ten rounds prose and a seeded registry disagreed — three about a permission code and the fourth about a selector in a different registry — and the fix is a script that extracts the code-shaped words from these documents and diffs them against the registries in both directions. It costs no schema and would have caught all four, including the two the catalog itself wrote. Round 11 found the same defect in prose rather than in a table — domain/06's own selector list, which had silently kept LIST and never gained PERSON or AUDIENCE (F-5 carries the instance) — which is the sharper argument of the two: a diff of tokens against rows catches four of them and misses the copy that is only ever read by a human. Round 13 made it five, and the fifth is the one that argues for the script hardest: GUARDIANS was a name in six pages of prose with a row in the registry behind it that should not have been there, so both sides of the diff were wrong at once — and unlike the first four, this one was not hand-typed into a screen anywhere, it was a prose idiom that parsed. D-113's rule (every selector name in a document must be a selector_type row, and a check should be able to say so) is this item, extended from permission codes to selectors, in the round that proved the check was needed in the registry's own direction too. 6. The legal review, which is not a question this register can answer and now has a concrete policy in front of it: named membership and fee rows kept indefinitely, audit payloads kept 24 months. Assumption 49 is that review's subject — and since D-093 the indefinitely-kept population includes thousands of imported people who never used the system, which is the same judgement at a scale the review has not yet been shown.

Everything else can be answered as we go. The schema is built so that most answers change data rather than structure — which is why the ones above are worth a moment and the rest are not.

Answered in round 10: the organization's shape, in the other direction. F-12 closed no (D-100) — an office is held by a named person and confers nothing. And five questions' subjects were deleted rather than answered, which is recorded here rather than quietly erased: the membership gate that D-6 and E-4 were argued against, the root participation row of D-7 and D-8, the unit types of A-1 and C-1, scope_exposure, positions, and the level ladder that EV-5's answer and A-1's framing both leaned on. The pattern worth noticing is not the deletions, it is what happened to the questions: a question about a mechanism outlives the mechanism, and the honest options are restate it against whatever replaced the mechanism (E-4, F-3, F-6) or say that the premise is gone and keep the reasoning (D-6, D-7, D-8, C-5, C-4). Both were done here, and neither touches the reasoning that a later round may need. Eight new questions came in, and they are all consequences of the new machinery rather than new wishes: the listing D-103's protections lean on is unmeasured (F-17), a preview is now per-item (F-16), a cache key gained the item and a transitive dependency (F-6), an audience has no past (F-17's neighbour F-18 is the materializing case), and three operands the language wants do not exist (F-5). One habit from the round is worth carrying: the entries that survived did it by naming what enforces a rule now — D-081's discipline, applied to sections that had been written as if the hierarchy were permanent. (One of those four consequences has since lost its subject: the cache key F-6 gained in this round was deleted whole by D-114 in round 14, and the item survived it — not as a key component but as what a resolved predicate is bound to. That is the pattern above working as intended: the mechanism went, the question about the mechanism stayed, and the entry is where the difference is written down.)

Answered in round 9: the organization, in whole — groups and their filling rules (C-4, D-091), the shape of the corpus (C-5, D-092/093/094), who may join a unit and the deletion of allows_minors (C-6, D-095), and what a reused unit number means (C-3, D-096). Two things came out of the round that are worth more than the questions that were asked. A rule that lives only as prose in one section is still a rule: "audiences do not nest" sat in data-model/05 §8 for three rounds and quietly cost two grants for one intention, until an answer asked for the forbidden thing. And a decision recorded from a description of the data is only as durable as the description — D-090's absolute import rule lasted one round because nobody had read the file, which is why D-092 exists and why the corpus questions are now asked in the present tense about a real export.

Answered in round 8: identity and history, in whole — merge chains and unmerge (B-2, D-087), the two retention clocks (B-3, D-088), the second account (B-4, D-089), and the shape of the legacy corpus (B-1, D-090). None of the four changed a table, which is why they were worth holding to the end: they were questions about the organization rather than about the model, and three of the four turned out to be answerable simply by looking at what the organization already has — a roster with no money in it settled a rule that had been written as a default, and a wanted feature settled a trade that had been written as an assumption.

Answered in round 4: the unit type vocabulary (A-1 — not seeded, D-054); the permission catalog (F-1 — comprehensive and granular on purpose, D-055); the legacy corpus (B-1 — large, with member numbers, D-056); and household (D-9 — removed entirely, D-057). All four are in § R with links to the decisions that settled them.

Answered in round 3, for reference: the organizational calendar (A-4 — 1 January, 60 days); the root's read access into sub-units (C-1 — scope_exposure only); the membership gate's waiver (D-6 — a person-level permission, in addition to the role flag); and the root participation row at renewal (D-7 — extended).

docs.title: Appendix — Entity Relationship Diagrams
docs.text:
This appendix describes relationships — what points at what, how many, and whether the link is temporal. Field-level definitions live in the data-model documents, each in the one that owns the entity, and are deliberately not repeated here.

Diagrams of the schema in ../data-model/00-conventions.md. Split by subject area so each stays readable; the areas connect through person, which appears in all of them.

Notation: → is a foreign key pointing at the referenced table. ⇒ is a polymorphic reference (no database-level foreign key). Temporal tables are marked [T].

docs.text:

docs.title: 1a. Personal attributes — everything that is not a name, a gender or an age
docs.text:
erDiagram

    PERSON_ATTRIBUTE }o--o| ATTRIBUTE_OPTION : selects

Key point: these three tables are the whole of what the system knows about a person beyond name, gender and age. There is no health table beside them and no privileged corner inside them: D-083 removed the category and D-084 put an organization-maintained vocabulary in its place. Reading is person.view, writing is person.edit, and only the vocabulary needs a code of its own (attribute.define). Fields and rules: ../data-model/09-attributes.md.

None of the three is [T], and the no beside them in §7 is a decision, not an omission. A person_attribute row is the current belief, overwritten in place, and audit_log holds the sequence of beliefs, values included for as long as the payload window lasts — 24 months, after which the row is reduced and the values are gone (D-088) — which is why the trail is guarded as person data is (the permission catalog §8). This corpus gives periods to things that are true over an interval — a membership, an address, an office held, a guardian's authority — and a descriptive value is not one of those: it is a statement made now about whatever it is about, with a timestamp on the assertion. A valid_from here would ask a volunteer when an allergy began, which is a question the organization is not competent to record and has no rule that could use (D-085). The cost is named rather than left out: the history of a value lives in the one control D-081 calls the corpus's weakest, and §7 lists it as the accepted risk. It is also a deliberate departure from guardianship two sections below, which keeps its current value and its history in business tables — because authority is asked "what was it on that date?" as a routine part of answering whether an act was permitted, and an allergy list is not.

The two vocabulary tables are non-temporal for a smaller reason of their own: a code leaves service by status, not by a period, so a value recorded against a retired option keeps meaning what it meant on the day it was chosen. Retiring therefore never touches a fact — only redacting a person erases one (../domain/08-person-data.md).

docs.title: 2. Organization
docs.text:
There is no organization-structure diagram, because there is no organization structure. There is one unit, it is the organization, and it is a scope and not a row: grant_scope_type carries a code unit with is_item_scoped = false, and a grant written at it has no scope_id (D-097). What this section drew until round 10 was a hierarchy of bodies with a vocabulary of types, rename history, lineage edges, rosters and offices. Every one of those tables is deleted, not moved; the ledger of what each took with it is ../data-model/02-organization.md §5. What is left for this section to draw is the group — a set of people, not a body.

erDiagram
    PERSON_GROUP {
        uuid id PK
        uuid public_id
        string name
        string description
        date valid_from
        date valid_to
    }
    PERSON_GROUP_MEMBER {
        uuid group_id FK
        uuid person_id FK
        date valid_from
        date valid_to
        uuid added_by FK
        string note
    }
    PERSON ||--o{ PERSON_GROUP_MEMBER : "is in"
    PERSON_GROUP ||--o{ PERSON_GROUP_MEMBER : has

Key point: a group is a named set of people with a lifetime, and that is the whole of it — no parent, no type, no code, no path, no nesting rule, no rename history, no split or merger edge, no leadership, no roles, no fee (D-098). The member row is dated, so the roster answers "who was in schuzka2026-1 on 14 March 2026" from its own rows rather than from the audit trail, whose payloads expire after 24 months (D-088). No two rows for one person and one group overlap, counted over all rows and half-open, so a person who left in 2020 and came back in 2024 is two rows and never one row edited in place.

Membership of a group confers nothing. A set is not a grant; a group member is reached only because some grant's expression says GROUP(x) (D-005). The group is an item in grant_scope_type, so a grant may be written on one — that edge is in §5a, not here, because access_grant owns it and not this module. The box is deliberately alone beside its roster: name is unique across role and person_group together, but no constraint spans two tables, so that is a write-path rule and not a drawn edge (D-101).

Gone from this diagram, one line each, so that a reader hunting for a box finds the decision:

  • ~~org_unit~~, ~~org_unit_type~~, ~~org_unit_type_rule~~, ~~org_unit_name~~, ~~org_unit_relationship~~ — all deleted by D-097, with path, depth, the unit vocabulary, the nesting checks, the rename history and the lineage edges. There is no unit table anywhere in this appendix. The unit appears once, as the unit row of grant_scope_type (§5a) — a lookup row naming a scope, not a body.
  • ~~unit_participation~~ — deleted by D-097. person_group_member is the roster that outlived it and membership (§3) is membership of the unit; the import owes participation rows to nothing.
  • ~~position~~, ~~position_assignment~~ — deleted by D-100: with one unit there is no body to be a leader of. is_leadership and max_holders went with them; the office survives as role + role_holder (§5a).
  • ~~org_unit_type.allows_minors~~ — the flag was deleted by D-095 and the table that carried it by D-097. Do not place a child where nobody is responsible is now person_group.member.manage held by a named adult, and the system can no longer say which groups are for children — that loss is D-095's, restated in D-098.
  • ~~scope_exposure~~ — deleted by D-097 with the direction-of-authority check and the nightly alert that was its only detector. §5 says what was lost with it.

See ../data-model/02-organization.md and ../domain/04-organization-structure.md; the scope itself is ../domain/06-authorization-model.md §2.

erDiagram

    }

    PERSON ||--o{ MEMBERSHIP_REQUEST : submits
    MEMBERSHIP_REQUEST }o--o| MEMBERSHIP : produces
    MEMBERSHIP ||--o{ MEMBERSHIP_REQUEST : precedes

Four points that matter:

  • membership_request has two person references: person_id (the child, who would become a member) and submitted_by_person_id (the parent, who applied). Collapsing them makes the audit trail false.
  • A request asks for membership of the unit and names nothing else. requested_unit_id is deleted with the units (D-097, D-098), and there is therefore no edge from this diagram to any body: which group a new member lands in is a write on the group — one person_group_member row, §2 — and not a preference on the request. The ~~unit this request was aimed at~~ is withdrawn, not moved; the want behind the column is served by the free-text notes the row already carries.
  • Belonging lives in two shapes now, and neither is a membership. person_group_member (§2) is a group's dated roster and is keyed on person, never on membership — the argument unit_participation made and D-098 carried over: an imported roster or a 1998 camper has no membership row to point at, and inferring an open-ended one would sweep that person into MEMBERS today. The table that held it, ~~unit_participation~~, is deleted by D-097, along with the root participation row every membership used to owe. Field rules: ../data-model/03-membership.md.
  • membership_type exists with exactly one row, and category, min_age, max_age and requires_background_check are all gone. Membership is ageless (D-038); age is read from person.birth_date where it matters, which is guardianship — positions carried the last stored eligibility rule and D-100 deleted it, so age is nobody's check and membership never was one.

Key point: guardianship is a general graph — one guardian → many dependents, many guardians → one dependent, and a person may be both. Authority is per guardianship row, and since D-074 that row carries one value — none, view or write — so a parent may write one child's records and only read another's. See ../data-model/04-relationships.md.

   five argument tables, one integer, and the operators are still `+ - *`.         │

   on a check-in screen would revoke a leader's access to their own camp when      │

   ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

       item of every type; a personal deny beats an audience allow, because this step has
       already returned (D-013 — whose `revoked` LEVEL is now an EFFECT on a grant row).
    1  a live ALLOW at the unit ── reaches every item of every type: after D-097 there is
       no tier between the unit and an item, and after D-102 no owner to ask.
    2  a live ALLOW on this exact item ── exact scope type and id. Nothing precedes it:
       `can_event()` and the unit-authority rule are deleted (D-102).
    3  OWNERSHIP ── the checked person is the actor. Their own row, their own data.

   the audit names, never what the answer is. **Locality is deleted** — it only ever ordered
   allows against each other, and a boolean has nothing to order (D-099, deleting the second
   half of D-032; the first half is step 0 and is now its entire content).

Key points:

  • One table grants. access_grant is the only place authority is written, plus the one table over a single person, guardianship_permission (§4, step 4 above). role_holder, person_group_member and every operand of an audience decide only whom a grant reaches — being in a set is worth exactly what the grant aimed at that set says (D-005, restated for roles by D-100). ~~role_assignment and access_grant are the same idea at two granularities, sharing scope_type, the level model and the resolver~~ — withdrawn by D-100 and D-099: role_holder has no scope columns, no level and no resolver channel, and what the two now share is only the temporal shape every dated row has.
  • There is no wildcard permission. A check for X.y needs an exact grant of X.y, or system.admin. The old <resource>.admin prefix match was removed with its sixteen codes (D-068, reversing D-007); "can do everything about events" is a role some grants name, each grant naming one of the thirteen event.* codes. ~~Note access_level.admin (rank 40) is a grant level and survives — same word, different mechanism~~ — there is no grant level now (D-099), so the collision the sentence existed to warn about cannot occur: admin is only ever the code system.admin.
  • Deny is absolute, and this round quietly upgraded it. D-013 said revoked beats deny, which left an escape hatch — a stale denial could be outranked by a newer act, and revoking it was a decision somebody could take late. Deleting the ranking deleted the hatch: a live deny now beats every live allow with no tie-break, and the only thing that removes one is a person ending its period. That is why valid_to earns its keep on a deny row and why a live deny matching no live allow is a reported shape rather than a harmless row — a deny that denies nothing is how a stale restriction outlives its reason (D-099).
  • The membership gate is deleted, and the posture reversed from default-on to opt-in. ~~The gate sits on the role tier and nowhere else (D-039): no current membership → the role grants nothing, unless the role opts out~~, and ~~system.gate_exempt waives it for one named person (D-051)~~. Withdrawn by D-100: MEMBERS is an operand evaluated live on the checked date, so MEMBERS * ROLE(x) gates and ROLE(x) alone does not, and the "except Honza" case is written inside the same expression. The new failure mode is a grant written ROLE(x) with no MEMBERS, authorizing a lapsed member silently and forever, failing closed-looking so nobody notices — the control is the Unusual section of the tab on the permissions page, which lists exactly that shape and refuses nothing, plus seeded grants that always carry MEMBERS (D-109, F-13). Ownership and guardianship were never gated and are untouched.
  • The guardianship channel is entered by shape, not by permission name (D-079): the check is about someone other than the actor, and the channel answers with allows only. A sufficient right_level returns true; no row, none, or too low a level returns nothing at all and the actor's own grants are tried. A prohibition is therefore a deny grant, never a low level. What the channel compares a permission against is now permission.right_kind — a column D-099 added and names as having exactly one customer, this channel.
  • There is no downward crossing, because there is no down. ~~Authority never inherits downward; a sub-unit's authority reaches outward only through a scope_exposure row, written by the sub-unit granting coverage over itself~~ — deleted by D-097, taking the direction-of-authority check, the scope.expose code and the nightly alert that was that check's only detector. D-031 was not weakened, it was deprived of its subject: with one unit there is no "outside it" to be stopped from. What is genuinely lost and reproduced nowhere is the safeguarding property — access to a body's children had to be granted by that body, by people who recruited the leader and can be asked. What remains is a permission held by a named adult, an audit trail whose payloads expire after two years, and a report of who holds the write, minus the part where the adult was somebody the body chose. A grant at the unit therefore reaches every item of every type, and system.admin with it.
  • A grantee may be an audience. access_grant.person_id and audience_id are mutually exclusive — never both, never neither. An audience is now an expression over named sets (D-101), so the old sentence "built-in audiences are rules evaluated at check time; named groups are stored lists carrying the stale-group problem knowingly" no longer describes three arms: every operand is evaluated live and nothing is stored as a roster — D-105 deleted LIST and its table, so a hand-written set is PERSON(a) + PERSON(b) in the expression — and the composition D-091 wanted is an operand instead of an edge. Author in sets, evaluate per person — a check compiles to a predicate and never materializes a set, and an operand that does not resolve is the empty set. That has not moved; what moved in round 12 is the wording around it (D-106). The compile-don't-materialize half is now load-bearing rather than tidy: it is one of the two rules the stated scale names as the ones that must survive any growth — the other is that a listing is paginated — which is why the system gets slow before it gets wrong (D-112). ~~Fail closed in every direction~~ names a volume where there is a direction: a failed operand on + or * narrows the set, a failed operand on - widens it, so EVERYONE - PERSON(x) with a dead x is fail-closed and lockout-everybody in one step rather than a safe state. The failure stays fail-closed and stops being silent — an audience carrying a leaf that resolves to nothing is listed on the tab on the permissions page (D-109), and no save is refused for it. One thing can still produce such a leaf: a redacted person. Nothing else a rule names is deleted any more, and the empty set a disabled operand yields is somebody's deliberate act, not a failure. A person with no birth date is not such a failure either: that operand resolves perfectly well, and they are simply not in the set.
  • Nothing owns an event (D-102). event.org_unit_id is deleted, so the people connected to an event are named by operands that bind to it — ORGANIZERS, PLACED, CONFIRMED, ATTENDED, ON_WAITLIST — each a set the item itself defines. An operand is a set, not a grant, which is why D-062 ("an event_organizer row grants nothing") stands untouched while the resolver stopped special-casing it. The consequence worth remembering: a bound operand is illegal at the unit, so "every event's answers go to its organizers" is a template the event-creation path instantiates beside the event row, one per event, in one transaction — and an event whose creation died between the two rows has nobody who can read its answers, which is what the events with no answer-view grant report is for.
  • scope_id is polymorphic (no FK) so a new grantable item type is a config row, not a migration. Accepted cost, with mandatory mitigations. D-101 extended the same trade-off, and the same four mitigations, to audience_operand.selector_arg_id.

See ../data-model/05-authorization.md and ../domain/06-authorization-model.md.

    PERSON ||--o{ ACCESS_GRANT : "is granted to"
    PERSON ||--o{ ACCESS_GRANT : "delegated by"
    AUDIENCE ||--o{ ACCESS_GRANT : "is granted to"
    PERMISSION ||--o{ ACCESS_GRANT : "is its one code"
    GRANT_SCOPE_TYPE ||--o{ ACCESS_GRANT : "types the scope"

Key point: access_grant is a pentagon of references and grants exactly one thing — a grantee (person or audience), a scope, one permission, an effect, a period (D-099). Uniqueness follows the shape: at most one live allow per grantee, scope and permission, with denies deliberately outside the rule so a deny can sit beside an allow on the same item — that pair is the only way to say "this person has the unit's events, except this one".

No line leaves scope_id, and that is the diagram telling the truth. The edge that exists runs to grant_scope_type, the seeded registry (unit — the only row with is_item_scoped = false, event, person_group, role, document deferred) which is what states which table the unresolved id belongs to. The id itself is ⇒ polymorphic: no foreign key, validated by the registry plus a nightly orphan scan per type (D-011, §8). A unit grant carries no scope_id at all, which is the entire schema-level content of "the unit is a scope, not a row".

A role is not a permission bundle. role_permission is deleted by D-100: the codes an office carries are the live grant rows whose audience names ROLE(x), so "what may a treasurer do?" is a query over rows a screen can show. role_holder is a dated holder row — person, role, period, who granted it, note — and names one person, never a rule (F-12 is closed with the answer no, because an office that cannot answer "who was treasurer in 2023" is not an office record). role itself has no period: it is a definition, valid always, and the period lives on the holder row (D-053). The second arrow into person is granted_by, and it is drawn to a person because the column records who appointed — a fact carried on the appointment, readable five years later by whoever has to ask. The act of appointing is what audit_log holds, with its actor taken from the request context rather than from the row (../data-model/06-audit-and-import.md §2); the two are not one column's job, and every other actor column here (access_grant.granted_by, person_group_member.added_by) points the same way for the same reason — the third of the three, audience_member.added_by, is gone with its table, and what it used to answer per name is answered now only by who last saved the expression and by audit_log (D-105).

Names are one namespace. role.code, person_group.name and a set audience.code are unique together, case- and separator-folded, and every selector_type.code is reserved — so a group called MEMBERS is refused at the save rather than discovered later as an expression whose meaning moved. No constraint spans three tables, so the write path carries the rule and an integrity check asserts the write path still does (D-101, D-103, D-081). What is stored is always kind + id, so a rename never rewrites a grant.

docs.title: 5b. The audience expression
docs.text:
The rows of one audience's expression tree. The audience is the tree; audience_operand holds its nodes and leaves, one row each.

erDiagram
    AUDIENCE {
        integer id PK
        string code
        string name
        boolean is_system
        date valid_from
        date valid_to
    }
    AUDIENCE_OPERAND {
        integer id PK
        integer audience_id FK
        integer parent_id FK
        string operator
        integer left_id FK
        integer right_id FK
        string selector_kind FK
        integer selector_arg_id
    }
    SELECTOR_TYPE {
        string code PK
        string name
        boolean takes_argument
        boolean binds_to_item
        string argument_type
        boolean is_system
    }
    ROLE {
        integer id PK
        string code
    }
    PERSON_GROUP {
        uuid id PK
        string name
    }
    PERSON {
        uuid id PK
    }
    EVENT {
        uuid id PK
        string title
    }
    AUDIENCE ||--o{ AUDIENCE_OPERAND : "has its tree"
    AUDIENCE_OPERAND ||--o{ AUDIENCE_OPERAND : "has a child"
    SELECTOR_TYPE ||--o{ AUDIENCE_OPERAND : "types the leaf"
    AUDIENCE_OPERAND }o--o| ROLE : "ROLE(x) - no FK"
    AUDIENCE_OPERAND }o--o| PERSON_GROUP : "GROUP(x) - no FK"
    AUDIENCE_OPERAND }o--o| AUDIENCE : "AUDIENCE(code) - no FK"
    AUDIENCE_OPERAND }o--o| PERSON : "PERSON(x) - no FK"
    AUDIENCE_OPERAND }o--o| EVENT : "ORGANIZERS(x) - no FK"

Five of these lines are ⇒ in the notation above, and not one of them is a foreign key. A leaf's selector_arg_id is one integer column pointing at role, person_group, audience, person or event depending on selector_kind — the same polymorphism, the same four mandatory mitigations and the same nightly orphan scan that access_grant.scope_id already accepted (D-011, carried over by D-101). Drawing it as five real edges would be the lie; drawing it as no edges at all would hide the fan. The registry is what resolves the ambiguity, and it is a real edge: selector_type says whether the code takes an argument, whether the argument-less form binds to the item being checked, and what type the argument is — the parser reads its reserved words from that table, the editor builds its dropdown from it, and the save path checks arity against it (D-101). It is seeded, every row is_system, and organization-read-only: "the language becomes data" has never meant the language is extensible at runtime, and a seeded code with no shipped evaluator arm is a deployment bug that surfaces as an empty set — which is why the registry holds no row waiting to be implemented.

argument_type has six values and five of them are tables. OLDER and YOUNGER (D-107) take an integer — a whole number of years — so selector_arg_id holds 18 for OLDER(18), and this is the first operand argument in the registry that names no row. The five drawn edges are still exactly five, and the count this appendix keeps is unchanged for the right reason rather than by luck: a scalar sitting in selector_arg_id is not a reference, so there is nothing to repoint when a person is merged, nothing for a cascade to find, nothing for the orphan scan to walk, and the binding check that compares argument_type against a grant's item type simply does not apply to an operand that binds to no item. There are still exactly two reference-less polymorphic keys — access_grant.scope_id and audience_operand.selector_arg_id — and 18 is not one of them, because the check is about references (§8). The two operands read person.birth_date as of the date being checked, which is why they are a registry row and nothing more: they are ordinary named operands, composed by + - * like every other, and the set they name changes with no write at all.

No leaf resolves to anything but people, and that is why there is no GRANTS(…). An operand resolves to a set of people, because a set of people is what a grantee is; a set of grants is a filter over the grant list, and "these twenty rows, now also for that office" is something an editor does while finding the rows to act on, not something a stored grantee could ever be evaluated against. The bulk operation stays an affordance over the list, and the registry refuses the kind rather than leaving it unimplemented (D-101).

One row is one node or one leaf, never both. A node carries operator (+ union, * intersection, - difference) with left_id and right_id, which are not interchangeable because - is not commutative; a leaf carries selector_kind and, where the registry says so, selector_arg_id. parent_id lives on the child, so a node belongs to exactly one expression and a sharing table is refused — editing a shared node would silently widen every grant using it. audience_id is denormalized onto every row so the read path fetches one audience's rows in one indexed read and assembles the tree in memory; it never walks a parent chain (D-101). Round 12 changed nothing in this paragraph. OLDER and YOUNGER arrived as two seeded rows of the registry and not as anything here: the operator enum is still + - *, no node kind was added, no column was added, and (MEMBERS * OLDER(18)) - YOUNGER(6) is stored as the same node and leaf shapes that already existed — a * node with a MEMBERS leaf and an OLDER leaf, under a - node whose right operand is a YOUNGER leaf (D-107).

AUDIENCE(code) is the leaf that points back into this diagram (D-103): it names another saved audience by its code, which is why code exists and is optional, and why an unnamed audience is simply not composable. The AUDIENCE leaves are the reference edges — there is no audience_include table, so "does this cycle", "how deep", "which grants name this audience" and "may I end it" are all one indexed query over selector_kind = 'AUDIENCE' rows. One sentence of D-101 is false and stays struck: ~~a tree cannot cycle, so the only acyclicity guard left is the cheap parent-chain one~~ — true of one tree, false of a forest of trees pointing at each other, so the save-time reachability walk is back — inside the tree, and across audiences through every AUDIENCE(x) leaf — and D-105 deleted selector_depth_limit and left those two cycle walks as the only structural guard there is. It walks for cycles and nothing else: the tree is stored exactly as the writer wrote it, with no depth bound and no rebalancing, and nothing bounds what an expression may cost — which is now an accepted property rather than an unaddressed one, because it is affordable at the stated size of a few hundred people and a few dozen registrants per event, with a named trigger to reopen it (D-112). There is no report of the widest and deepest audiences: the report round 12 added was withdrawn with the standing reports in round 13, and what remains is the tab on the permissions page, which lists the rules that name something deprecated, hidden or disabled or fail to resolve, and says nothing about how wide a set any of them is (D-109). Still a convention, not a guard (D-081). The protection that keeps the dangerous case out is that an audience named by a live grant may not be ended or deleted while that grant lives: under -, an emptied operand makes the answer wider.

audience_member is deleted, and LIST with it (D-105). A hand-written set of people is now written where every other set is written — in the expression, as PERSON(a) + PERSON(b) — and what the table carried that the tree does not is written as lost, not as managed: no per-person dates (a person is in the audience or not; a June-to-August exception is a second grant with its own period, which is what D-099's shape is for), and no who added this person beyond who last saved the tree. The reason it was never merged into GROUP(x) survives the table unchanged: a group's members are the organization's record and are true with no grant pointing at them, while a name written into an expression is meaningless outside the expression it completes (D-098). Naming people inside a grant must not make them group members: (GROUP(kitchen) + LIST) - PERSON(a) becomes (GROUP(kitchen) + PERSON(honza)) - PERSON(a) — same meaning, one fewer kind of thing — and merging the two would still make the permission table the system's roster.

PERSON(x) is drawn as the person argument edge, and it was the thirteenth seeded selector_type row added — with LIST deleted it was one of the twelve that remained, it was one of the fourteen seeded for round 12 alone, and it is one of the thirteen seeded today, OLDER and YOUNGER having arrived in that same round 12 and GUARDIANS having left it in round 13 (D-107, D-113). It got there late and by an odd route: D-101's grammar and D-100's exemption table both wrote PERSON(y) from the start, the registry was written from the evaluator's arm list instead, and the two disagreed for a whole round without any check noticing (D-104). The edge has exactly one occupant, and it always did. Its label used to read PERSON(x) or GUARDIANS(x), and the second name was never a selector in either form (D-113): "True, GUARDIANS should not be selectable in the audience, guardians can perform ANY action (their read/write perms grant) on behalf of the child." A guardian's authority is a level over a child — none, view or write read off the guardianship row (D-074) — and not a set the expression language resolves, so an operand aimed at guardians would offer, one code at a time, a subset of what those people already hold. The storage fact the old label leaned on was never the disputed part either way: selector_arg_id may hold a person id per D-011 — which is why this appendix drew the edge while the language was still being argued about. What the row adds over that storage fact is one fact of meaning: an expression may name a single human who is on nobody's roster — and since a hand-written set is a sum of these (D-105), the edge is load-bearing: every hand-named person in the system is now a selector_arg_id with deliberately no foreign key. PERSON is the one argument kind the repoint duty still reaches (D-109): retiring an office, a group or an audience is now one write to that row and no expression is edited, because nothing a rule names is deleted any more — it goes deprecated, hidden or disabled, and only disabled changes the answer. A person is not in that protected set, because D-088 lets a redaction require the row to actually go and erasure wins. So a merge repoints the PERSON leaves naming the absorbed person, a redaction leaves the rest resolving to the empty set, and a redacted person is the corpus's only remaining way to produce a broken leaf — shown on the permissions tab rather than in a report nobody opens, with the nightly orphan scan as backstop rather than mechanism. PERSON, ROLE, GROUP and AUDIENCE are the four codes whose argument names a person, an office, a group or another audience. The fifth drawn edge, to event, belongs to the item-bound codes — ORGANIZERS, PLACED, CONFIRMED, ATTENDED, ON_WAITLIST — whose argument is optional exactly because the item being checked usually supplies it (D-102).

See ../data-model/05-authorization.md §8 and ../domain/06-authorization-model.md §6.

docs.title: 6. Temporal pattern, illustrated
docs.text:
Every [T] table above uses the same shape. The returning-member case shows why:

flowchart TB
    P["person 100 — Jan Novák"]
    M1["membership #1 · member<br/>1990-09-01 → 2010-06-30 · terminated"]
    GAP["14-year gap<br/>no rows; visible as data, not inferred"]
    M2["membership #2 · member<br/>2024-10-01 → open"]
    G1["person_group_member · oddílová rada<br/>1996-09-01 → 2004-06-30"]
    G2["person_group_member · registre 2025<br/>2024-10-01 → 2025-12-31"]
    RH["role_holder · treasurers<br/>2025-01-01 → open"]
    AU["audience · MEMBERS * ROLE(treasurers)<br/>an expression, evaluated live"]
    AG["access_grant · payment.record<br/>allow, at the unit<br/>2025-01-01 → open"]
    GA["guardianship → child A<br/>2015-03-01 → open<br/>right_level: write"]
    GB["guardianship → child B<br/>2018-07-01 → open<br/>right_level: view"]
    P --> M1
    M1 --> GAP --> M2
    P --> G1
    P --> G2
    P --> RH
    P --> GA
    P --> GB
    RH -.->|"named by code inside"| AU
    AU -.->|"aimed at by"| AG
    RH ==>|"the office reaches him only<br/>through that grant"| AG

Note the two membership rows have the same type. They differ only in period and end reason — this person was a member twice, and was a child and then an adult throughout. The old diagram called them child and adult; that was the framing the ageless decision replaced (D-038).

Where the first row came from is not drawn, and the answer moved twice this round. A 1990s roster row states a period of membership, and since D-093 one reviewed batch may turn that stated period into membership #1 itself: both ends dated, data_confidence low, the batch id on it, no fee_obligation and a balance that stays absent rather than zero, because the corpus carries no money in it (D-090). Two shapes remain forbidden, and they are the two the ban was ever really about: an open-ended imported membership, and one inferred from an attendance row. A closed period gates nothing in the present; an open one hands authority to whoever signs up under that name tomorrow. What the pipeline no longer produces at all is the second row of this diagram's previous version: the participation rows it owed beside every membership went with the unit hierarchy (D-097), so a people batch writes the membership and nothing else, and the group rows are written by somebody who knows the group exists (../domain/03-identity-and-legacy.md §7).

Questions this shape supports, all of which fail against a design with person.is_member:

  • Was this person a member on 1998-06-01?
  • How many years of membership, excluding the gap?
  • Which groups was he in during 2003? — person_group_member answers it, because those rows are dated rather than derived from a rule that could change its mind.
  • Who held the office of treasurers in 2023? — the same shape of answer, one role_holder row, which is the reason F-12 was closed with the answer no.
  • Would that grant have reached him on that date? — holder row, expression and grant are all evaluated as of the same at, and none of the three may be stored as a materialized list (D-101).
  • How old were they when they joined the second time? — answered from person.birth_date, which the membership rows never copy.
  • Who are the returning members — more than one membership with a gap between?

Every one of them is answered as of a date, and an as-of date must be applied to every join in the answer, not only to the first one — a period joined without it leaks the present into the past. That is what the [T] marking on the tables above exists to make visible.

docs.title: 7. Table inventory
docs.text:
One entry per entity: what it is, what it references, how many may exist, and whether it is temporal. ⇒ marks a polymorphic reference with no foreign key. Entries that exist only to join two other entities say so. An entity that no longer exists keeps its row, struck, in the block a reader would have looked for it in, with the decision that deleted it — and its Points at and How many cells are empty, because there is nothing left to point at and no rule left to count.

Read the [T] column as a decision, not a default. A no is normally a lookup table, a definition, or an append-only trail — the kinds of thing that have no period to carry. Exactly one no in this inventory is a choice about a person's data rather than a lack of one: person_attribute, and the reason is written out under its own block below and in §1a.

Identity

Entity What it is Points at How many [T] person The human being. Holds identity only — no status, no role, no membership Nothing, except itself: merged_into_person_id ⇒ self One per human, effectively; a merged row survives as a tombstone and is never deleted. The pointer is never rewritten forward when the survivor is itself absorbed, so chains persist and resolve_person() walks them (D-087) no person_name One name a person has had, and when person Many per person; one current row per name_type yes account The ability to log in. Optional, and independent of membership person Zero or many per person over a lifetime; at most one live row no account_credential One authentication method's secret or external handle account — deliberately not person Many per account; one current row per external issuer and reference pair yes person_contact An email, phone or postal address, as a dated row rather than a column person Many per person; one current primary per type and purpose yes person_identifier An identifier issued outside the system person; identifier_scheme for its scheme Many per person; (scheme, value) unique among current rows yes identifier_scheme The vocabulary of identifier schemes Nothing Lookup table, one row per scheme no identity_hypothesis A proposal that two person rows are the same human person twice; the reviewer is a person At most one live hypothesis per pair; a rejected pair may be re-proposed no person_merge The record that one row was absorbed into another, and how to undo it person twice; identity_hypothesis, optional One per merge performed; a reversal is recorded on the same row no field_conflict One value a merge could not decide between two candidates — raised for either half of the record, an identity field or a descriptive value (§1a) person_merge; ⇒ (entity_table, entity_id) — polymorphic by nature Many per merge no

Personal attributes — everything known about a person other than name, gender and age (§1a)

Entity What it is Points at How many [T] attribute_definition One thing the organization collects about people: the code, its label, its type, and whether several values may be current at once Nothing One code per normalized spelling — Allergy and allergy are one row; statuses proposed, live, retired, and retiring keeps the row and its values no attribute_option One allowed value of a one_of definition attribute_definition One row per code per definition; a retired option is never re-meaning, because values stored against it are historical facts no person_attribute The value one person currently has for one code person, attribute_definition, and attribute_option when the type is one_of One current row per person and code; more only where the definition sets allow_multiple, which no constraint can check (it reads another table) no — deliberately

That last no is the decision, and it is the reason this row spells it out. Values are overwritten in place and audit_log — carrying the values themselves, for 24 months — is the only history. This is the one place in the schema where "what did we believe in 2019?" would be answered from the trail rather than from business data, and since round 8 the answer is that it is answered for two years and not beyond (D-088): the honest description of this trade is no long history, not merely no temporal columns, and if a case ever needs the long version the fix is temporal values — D-085 reversed — not a longer trail. On top of that expiry sits the older caveat: D-081 records the trail as discipline rather than guarantee. The trade was made with that in view and is reversible in one entry (D-085, ../data-model/09-attributes.md §3). The two vocabulary tables carry status instead of periods, which is what lets a code be retired without touching a fact; only redacting a person erases values, and a redacted person still holding attribute rows, or still having their values readable in the trail, means the redaction did not happen (../data-model/09-attributes.md §8).

Groups and offices — what the organization module holds now (§2), plus the two office tables it shares with authorization, drawn in §5a and specified in ../data-model/05-authorization.md §3 and §4

Entity What it is Points at How many [T] person_group A named set of people with a lifetime — a crew, a registration team, everyone who ever ran the camp. Confers nothing: authority arrives only through a grant aimed at the group Nothing. Its name is unique together with role.code and a set audience's code, which no constraint can express, so the write path carries the rule and an integrity check asserts the write path still does One row per name. Ended by valid_to, never deleted while member rows exist, and ending it is refused while a live grant — or a live audience reachable from one — names it, because EVERYONE - GROUP(x) with an emptied group denies everybody yes person_group_member Join entity: this person was in this group for that period. Written by a person, never derived from a rule person_group; person — person, not membership, so a 1998 roster row does not have to invent a membership in order to be true; and person as the one who added them Many per group at once; no overlapping periods for one person in one group, over all rows including ended ones, which the write path enforces (../data-model/02-organization.md §2) yes role An office — treasurers, registrar, counselors. A definition, valid always; the period lives on the holder row. It carries no permissions and confers nothing: the codes an office holds are the live grants whose audience names ROLE(x) Nothing. Its code joins the same one namespace as group names, and every reserved selector_type.code is refused against it One row per code; deleting one is refused while holder rows exist, so an office cannot be emptied in one save no role_holder Who holds an office for what period — one named person, never a rule: F-12 was closed by D-100 with the answer no, because an office record that cannot answer "who held this in 2023" is not one role; person twice — the holder, and the person who appointed them At most one open row per person and role; no overlap over all rows; nothing forces a row to end, and the standing report is the control (D-071) yes ~~org_unit~~ ~~A unit — the root, or anything nested beneath it to any depth.~~ Deleted by D-097: there are no sub-units, and the unit is one row of grant_scope_type rather than a row of its own table — — — ~~org_unit_type~~, ~~org_unit_type_rule~~ ~~The organization's vocabulary of kinds of unit, and which kind may sit under which.~~ Deleted by the same decision; the shape of the organization is now nobody's data, and no group table replaces it — — — ~~org_unit_name~~ ~~One name or code a unit carried, with the period it was carried in.~~ Deleted by D-097, and nothing replaces it: a group is named by one column, so a rename loses the old name — the recorded cost in ../data-model/02-organization.md §5 — — — ~~org_unit_relationship~~ ~~A typed lineage between two units — split_from, merged_into, successor_of.~~ Deleted by D-097; D-098 refuses group-to-group edges outright, so continuity is prose on a group's row — — — ~~position~~, ~~position_assignment~~ ~~A defined slot in a kind of unit, and a person filling it.~~ Deleted by D-100: an office that had to be filled before it meant anything was a second way to hold authority, and role_holder is the one way now — — —

Membership

Entity What it is Points at How many [T] membership_type The fee and renewal parameters. One row, member, kept as a table so the vocabulary can grow Nothing Exactly one row today (D-037) yes membership One period of membership, with its own ending person, membership_type; itself via renewed_from_membership_id Many per person over a lifetime; one open at a time, ever yes membership_request An application. Two person references on purpose: the subject and the submitter person twice, membership_type, and membership twice (what it produced, what it renews). No unit: requested_unit_id is deleted by D-098 — a request asks for membership of the unit and names nothing else, because which group a new member joins is somebody's act afterwards, not a term of the application At most one open request per person no ~~unit_participation~~ ~~Belonging to one unit — the root's mirror of a membership, or a sub-unit's roster.~~ Deleted by D-097, which also removed the obligation to open a root row beside every membership. It had itself been renamed from unit_membership by D-041; person_group_member is the dated roster that outlived it — — —

Relationships

Entity What it is Points at How many [T] guardianship One adult's responsibility for one dependent, carrying one right_level person twice — never the same person twice One current row per pair; unlimited past rows; a dependent may have any number of guardians at once yes guardianship_permission The temporal history of that row's right level — not a capability list since D-074 guardianship Exactly one open row per guardianship; its value is what guardianship.right_level copies yes

Authorization — the tables are drawn in §5a and the expression in §5b

Entity What it is Points at How many [T] permission One coded capability — the only thing a check asks for, and a grant names exactly one Nothing One row per code; the code never changes. applies_to says whether the code may be granted at the unit or also on an item, checked when the grant is saved; right_kind exists for exactly one customer, the guardianship channel (D-099) no grant_scope_type The registry of things a grant may be written on, and the table its id lives in. unit is its only non-item row — which is where the unit now lives Nothing One row per scope kind: unit, event, person_group, role, and document deferred. Adding a grantable thing is a row here rather than a migration no access_grant The only table that grants. A grantee, a scope, one permission, an effect, a period person or audience, never both; grant_scope_type and ⇒ scope_id, absent exactly at unit; permission; person as grantor, delegator and revoker At most one live allow per grantee, scope and permission — denies sit outside the rule on purpose, because allow-beside-deny is the only way to say "the unit's events, except this one"; a delegation must carry an end date yes audience A set of people a grant may name — an expression over named sets, stored as a tree (D-101), not a rule XOR a list XOR an inclusion Its own operand rows; code is optional and is the only thing another audience may name (D-103); resolver_key, scope_parameter, include_depth_limit and selector_depth_limit are deleted, the last of them by D-105 One row per audience; the tree is stored exactly as the writer wrote it and its height is bounded by nothing — the save-time cycle walks are the only structural guard, and nothing bounds what resolving one costs, which D-112 accepts at the stated size rather than leaves unaddressed (D-081); an audience a live grant names is never deleted — it is flagged deprecated, hidden or disabled, the first two changing no answer and the third resolving to the empty set on purpose, as an audited write that prints the rules it touches (D-109) — not a ruleset_version bump any more: a flag is a state and not part of a compilation, so resolution reads it live, once per request, which is what makes disabled still mean now (D-114); an ended audience reaches nobody, so ending one is refused while a live grant names it yes audience_operand Join entity: one row of one audience's expression tree — a node (operator, left_id, right_id) or a leaf (selector_kind, ⇒ selector_arg_id), never both audience, denormalized onto every row so one audience's tree is one indexed fetch; itself, parent_id on the child; selector_type; and ⇒ a role, person_group, audience, person or event with no foreign key — D-011's accepted trade-off, extended by D-101 One row per node or leaf; a node never belongs to another audience than its parent's; the forest is acyclic, checked on save no selector_type The registry of operands the language has: the reserved word, whether it takes an argument, whether its argument-less form binds to the item being checked, and what type the argument names Nothing Thirteen seeded rows — fourteen for round 12 alone, until D-113 removed a row that should never have been in the registry — built from eleven in the evaluator's arm list, PERSON as the thirteenth to arrive, LIST gone in between (D-105), and OLDER and YOUNGER added in round 12 (D-107) — the first two whose argument_type is a whole number of years and not a table, and the first two whose membership changes with no write, because they read person.birth_date on the checked date. Six argument_type values, five of them tables; the operators stay + - *. Every row is_system and organization-read-only, and every row both seeded and shipped — a code with no evaluator arm is a deployment bug, not a held feature (D-104) no ~~audience_member~~ ~~The LIST leaf: this audience's own hand-typed list of people — the only operand that was not a rule about anybody.~~ Deleted by D-105, LIST and its seed row with it: a hand-written set is now PERSON(a) + PERSON(b) in the expression, with no per-person dates — a time-windowed exception is a second grant with its own period. The refusal to merge names into a group survives the table: a PERSON(x) leaf is not a GROUP(x) because merging them would make the permission table the system's roster — — — access_log The audit trail — who did what, by what authority, with what result person as actor and as subject; ⇒ authorization_ref_id naming access_grant or guardianship_permission — role and system are gone from the channel enum, so an old row reading role is unreadable by this model on purpose (D-100); ⇒ entity_id Append-only today; proposed to take the same 24-month window as the audit payload, which would make this cell wrong as written — F-8, unconfirmed (D-088) no ~~permission_cache~~ ~~A computed answer kept so checks are cheap.~~ Deleted by D-114, and the deletion is the invariant: no row, table or field may map a person — or a person and a code, or a person and an item — to a permission answer (invariant 19, TIME-BOMB), and after this deletion the schema has nowhere to put one. The key (person_id, permission_code, scope_type, scope_id, at_bucket), the nightly full rebuild and both lists of which writes bumped a version went with it. What answers a check instead: a compiled expression, cached across people because it holds no person and no item (keyed by the expression's root plus ruleset_version); one indexed read of the checked person's live grant rows per request, with every code, item and date in that request evaluated against them in memory; and the batch reads can_many(person, codes[], item?) and which_of(people[], code, item). The one thing still cached across requests is a named roster — ROLE(x) over role_holder, GROUP(x) over person_group_member — keyed by the name the write touches, holding its dated rows so the checked date is applied at check time. ruleset_version survives with its bump set cut to audience_operand and selector_type, and it now invalidates compilations rather than answers (domain/06 §8) — — — ~~role_permission~~ ~~Join entity: this role carries this permission, and nothing else.~~ Deleted by D-100: the codes an office holds are the live grants naming ROLE(x), so the bundle is a query a screen can show rather than a table — — — ~~role_assignment~~ ~~Authority held for a period over a scope.~~ Deleted by D-100 and replaced by role_holder, which keeps the person and the period and drops the scope columns, the level and the resolver channel — — — ~~scope_exposure~~ ~~A unit granting one named assignment coverage over itself — the only downward crossing.~~ Deleted by D-097 together with the direction-of-authority check it existed to serve, which had no detector but this table's own alert — — — ~~access_level~~ ~~The ordered ladder revoked, view, contribute, manage, admin, compared by rank.~~ Deleted by D-099: the answer is one boolean, revoked survives as effect = 'deny' on a grant row, and admin survives only as the permission code system.admin — — — ~~permission_level~~ ~~Join entity: this permission needs this level on this kind of scope.~~ Deleted by D-099. The one question it still answered — may this code be granted on an item at all — is permission.applies_to now — — — ~~audience_include~~ ~~Join entity: this group includes that group, to a depth limit.~~ Deleted by D-101; an AUDIENCE(code) leaf is the edge now, which is also what put the cycle check back on the save path (D-103) — — —

role and role_holder are inventoried under Groups and offices above, where the module keeps them; both are drawn in the authorization diagram, because that is where a reader meets what they do — which is nothing at all, on their own.

Audit and import

Entity What it is Points at How many [T] audit_log The row-level trail of changes to business tables, before and after values included until the payload window passes ⇒ (table_name, record_id) — polymorphic; person as actor, and on whose behalf One row per change; the row is never deleted, but a scheduled payload reduction empties the values 24 months after writing (D-088) no redaction_log That a redaction happened to a person, by whom, and to what person; the person who requested and the person who performed it One per redaction performed no import_batch One arrival of historical data, where it stands, which half of the corpus it carries (people or events), and the raw-column→code map a person read before it applied person as creator, applier and reverting party One per batch; the map lives here as one object rather than per staged row, because it is one artefact a human reads top to bottom and the codes it names arrive live (D-090, D-092); staging rows may be truncated once applied no staging_import A raw source row, verbatim, with its file and line import_batch One per source row per batch no staging_import_row That row parsed, plus what the parse could not decide, and what it eventually created staging_import; person as resolver; and what it created — person and, on a people batch, the membership whose both ends the source stated (D-093: a stated period may be imported, an open-ended one may not and one inferred from attendance may not), and on an events batch the event and the event_registration. No participation id any more — D-097 deleted both halves of that pair One per staged row no

Finance (provisional)

Entity What it is Points at How many [T] fee_schedule What may be charged, for what kind of period membership_type, optional — absent means it applies to any type. Not a unit: org_unit_id went with the unit (D-097), so a schedule is now organization-wide by construction As the organization defines yes fee_obligation What one person owes for exactly one thing person (who it is for), fee_schedule, and exactly one of membership, membership_request, event_registration Many per person; the target is never two and never none. An imported membership creates none, and its outstanding_balance is NULL rather than zero, because zero would be a claim the export does not support (D-093) no payment Money that arrived person as payer — deliberately not the person the fee is for One per recorded receipt no payment_allocation Join entity: this payment counted towards this obligation, by how much payment, fee_obligation A given payment is allocated to a given obligation at most once no payment_request The ask, carrying the variable symbol that ties a bank transfer back to it fee_obligation — the amount is copied, never recomputed Several per obligation over time; at most one live; the symbol is unique over every symbol ever issued no bank_transaction One incoming transfer as the bank reported it payment_request when matched — absent means it is in the queue; import_batch Unique per bank reference within an account; immutable once imported no

Events

Entity What it is Points at How many [T] event A dated occasion people register for. Owned by nobody fee_schedule, optional, when it costs money. No unit: org_unit_id is deleted by D-102, which also deleted can_event() and the unit-authority rule that read it — the people connected to an event are named by selectors that bind to it (ORGANIZERS, PLACED, CONFIRMED, ATTENDED, ON_WAITLIST). created_by is attribution, not ownership, as D-005 always said One row per occasion; no recurrence, no series no event_organizer Who is running an event, with a label and an order — an appointment, not a grant (D-062) event, person Many per event; the list is the domain answer to "who runs this", and it is the one cascade delete in this design (§8) no event_registration One person's answer about one event, plus whether they turned up event, person — person, never membership, so a 1998 camp roster does not smuggle its people into MEMBERS today One per person per event; unanswered is the absence of a row (D-059); was_present is three-valued and is deliberately the basis of no selector no event_question One thing this event asks, of attendees, organizers or both event As many as the event asks; defined per event, never shared yes event_answer What one person said to one question, stored as a row and not as JSON event_question; person — who answered, for a child the child, not the registration row and not whoever submitted on their behalf One row per question per answerer no ~~event_medical_note~~ ~~Medical facts about one person at one event, reachable only by a medical permission.~~ Deleted by D-083 — no file, no privileged reach: personal data is one class of data, so what the organization needs recorded is an ordinary person_attribute under §1a, read with person.view and protected by the same grants as everything else — — —

Reference vocabularies — reason_code, grant_scope_type, selector_type, identifier_scheme, permission. Each is named by a value held elsewhere rather than pointing at anything, and each exists so that a vocabulary is data the organization can see rather than a list inside the application. Two of this list's former members are gone: access_level (D-099) and org_unit_type (D-097), and selector_type arrived in the same round, which is the whole of the change here. attribute_definition is the same kind of thing in spirit and a different shape in fact — it has a curation lifecycle, a child table, and rows pointing back at it — so it is inventoried above rather than here.

event carries no [T] — it has no valid_from / valid_to, because an event is a dated occasion rather than a period-tracked record. Its lifecycle is starts_at / ends_at / cancelled_at, and it has no status column at all (D-064). event_registration likewise stores no period: a person is attending, or they are not, and "unanswered" is the absence of a row (D-059).

Removed since the first draft, listed so the inventory stays honest: requirement_code and membership_request_requirement (nothing gates a request — D-044); unit_membership (renamed unit_participation by D-041 — and deleted with it by D-097, so the rename was itself undone); every background-check structure (D-043); every medical structure, event_medical_note included, because personal data is one class of data and no table of it is (D-083); the whole unit and position family, with scope_exposure (D-097, D-100); the level ladder and its per-scope requirements (D-099); the role's permission bundle and its assignment table (D-100); the group-inclusion edge (D-101); and audience_member with the LIST operand and its seed row (D-105), the only row the selector registry has ever lost, in its one round of existence. Recorded here too, because it is the kind of entry this list exists for: event.qr, a check-in capability that never had a row in this appendix or anywhere else — it entered a round as prose, was argued about by name, and left as prose (D-104).

[T] = temporal, carries valid_from / valid_to. A no says it does not; where the reason for not is a decision about someone's data rather than the nature of the table, the row says so — which in this inventory is person_attribute, and nowhere else.

docs.title: 8. Foreign key summary
docs.text:
Columns with no FK, and why:

Column Why no FK access_grant.scope_id Polymorphic by design. Validated by grant_scope_type + orphan checks. It is absent exactly when the scope type is unit, and that absence is the schema-level form of "the unit is a scope, not a row" (D-097). audience_operand.selector_arg_id The second one, and newer: one integer pointing at a role, a person_group, an audience, a person or an event depending on selector_kind, resolved by selector_type.argument_type and caught by the same nightly orphan scan. D-101 carried D-011's trade-off across deliberately, mitigations included — the registry is the only thing that says which table an id belongs to, so an unmapped kind is the empty set, not an error.
