It also sometimes holds no reference at all: OLDER(n) and YOUNGER(n) store a whole number of years here (D-107), and that does not make a third key — 18 points at nothing, so the orphan scan has nothing to walk, a merge has nothing to repoint, and this row is still describing one column that sometimes carries a reference and sometimes carries a scalar. access_log.scope_id Same shape as the grant's; absent for a check at the unit. access_log.authorization_ref_id Points at one of two tables, access_grant or guardianship_permission. It named role_assignment as a third until D-100 deleted that table; a historical row whose channel reads role keeps the word and loses the reference, which is the honest state of a value whose table is gone. access_log.entity_id Polymorphic target of the audited action. field_conflict.entity_id Polymorphic; recorded alongside entity_table. audit_log.record_id Polymorphic; recorded alongside table_name.

access_grant.scope_id is no longer the only reference-less key, and this appendix said it was for nine rounds. That sentence is worth keeping where it can be found, because the class is what matters and not the count: an id with no constraint behind it needs a registry that says which table it belongs to, a save-path check against that registry, an orphan scan the scheduler owns, and an explicit rule that failure resolves to the empty set. Two columns now carry that debt and both carry the same four mitigations. ../data-model/00-conventions.md §9 still calls access_grant.scope_id "the one reference-less key"; the events module is where the newer row is written, and that page has not caught up. The count is still two after round 12, and it is worth saying why, because it could have looked like three: OLDER and YOUNGER put an integer in audience_operand.selector_arg_id, and a scalar is not an id with no constraint behind it — there is no table it should have named, so there is no registry lookup to miss, no orphan for the scan to find and nothing for a merge to repoint. The count is about references, and 18 is not one (D-107).

access_grant has no grantee column — that is the one mutual-exclusion case rather than a missing-FK case: exactly one of person_id / audience_id is set, never both, never neither. Both columns are nullable, so nothing but the rule says whom a grant means; a grant naming neither is meaningless and one naming both is ambiguous about whom in the audience it speaks for. audience_operand carries the same shape of rule one table down — operator with left_id/right_id, or selector_kind with selector_arg_id where the registry says the code takes an argument — and for the same reason: a row satisfying neither is a node in no tree, and an expression containing one resolves to nobody.

Every other column ending in _id has a real foreign key with ON DELETE RESTRICT, with one exception: event_organizer.event_id is the single ON DELETE CASCADE in the design — an appointment is nothing once the occasion it appointed somebody to is gone, and the guards in ../data-model/08-events.md §8 are what make that delete safe to allow at all. Round 12 changed the count of nothing here: two operands whose argument is an integer add no key and no cascade, because there is no row for either to be a child of — still one cascading column, still event_organizer.event_id. Everything else that merely looks like a child restricts: a registration, an answer, a member row, a holder row, a grant. The general rule is still ../data-model/00-conventions.md §9 — nothing cascades in front of a 40-year trail — and this row is the exception that page does not yet list.

docs.title: Appendix — Permission Catalog
docs.text:
Every permission code, its namespace, and the grant that carries it.

This is the proposed catalog, seeded in ../data-model/05-authorization.md.

Round 10 rewrote this page. D-097 deleted the unit hierarchy, D-099 the level ladder, D-100 positions, role_permission and the membership gate, D-101 the audience's rule/list/inclusion arms, and D-102 event ownership. Thirteen codes here lost their subject, and five arrived for the two new tables. What changed shape is not only the list: a code is no longer paired with a level, so a row in this catalog is a capability and nothing more. Whoever grants it says how far it reaches, for how long, and to whom — in one row, whose grantee is an expression (§1). And §1's two naming shapes are rules now, not descriptions of the rows below: the last segment names the action, a middle segment names something the schema stores, no grade words and no prefix — with system.admin named as the single exception (D-104).

Deliberately comprehensive and granular, and staying that way (D-055). This is a menu, not a checklist. Administrators assign people only the permissions they actually need; that is only possible if the capabilities exist as separate rows to assign. Further permissions arrive with the modules not yet specified — documents and communication. Events were on that list and are no longer: §8a carries their thirteen codes (§10).

This is the opposite disposition from roles, and the asymmetry is deliberate. Roles are runtime data the organization invents (D-052); permissions are capabilities the code implements. You cannot assign a power the data model cannot express, so a comprehensive permission catalog costs only rows — while a comprehensive role list would be a specification pretending to be data.

Codes are still stable identifiers: adding one is free, renaming one is a migration (§1). What is not yet settled is the exact contents — tracked in §12.

docs.title: 1. Conventions
Code shape
docs.text:
<resource>.<action>               e.g.  person.edit
<resource>.<subresource>.<action> e.g.  event.answer.view

resource is always the first segment and matches permission.resource. Codes are stable identifiers — the display_name may change, the code may not. Renaming a code is a breaking change requiring a migration that rewrites every access_grant row naming it. Before D-100 the same migration also rewrote role_permission rows; that table is deleted, and a grant is now the only place a code is written down — which makes the rule smaller, not weaker.

Those two shapes are rules for adding a code, and since D-104 they are written here as rules rather than as a description of what is already in the tables below. As a description they arbitrated nothing: both readings of one disputed name fitted them exactly, and that dispute ended with the capability deleted rather than either spelling chosen (§12). Three rules, and the moment they cost nothing is the moment a code is added:

  1. The last segment names the action. Read the code on its own and ask what does this let me do? event.grant_access answers it; a noun-final code states an object instead. Since D-099 a grant permits exactly one thing, so a grant of an object would need a second sentence to say what it permits — and a second sentence is where a permission's real scope always hides.
  2. A middle segment names something the schema stores. answer is event_answer, presence is a column of event_registration, and contact, credential, member, participant and request are rows. A permission may not be built out of an artifact the database does not keep, because a grant has to be checkable against stored state and there is none to check against: the payment's QR code is exactly that artifact, and D-075 already ruled it a rendering of three stored facts rather than data. No code in this catalog spells qr, and none may (§12).
  3. No grade words, and no prefix. Not admin, all or everything, and not any code whose meaning is "every sibling under this prefix" — D-068 deleted sixteen of them and computed the wrong answer for the one it chose to exempt, dependent.admin — which D-074 then deleted too, for having no set left to stand for (the table further below). D-104 restates that decision as a rule about codes that have not been written yet, which is the only form of it that can still prevent anything.

One exception, named because a rule with an unnamed exception is a rumour: system.admin. Its last segment is not an action, and it stays. It survives because its meaning is defined by the resolver — checked outright, applies_to = unit, never reachable through an item grant (§7) — rather than read off its name, and because D-068 exempted it in so many words rather than by omission. It is the only code in this system allowed to be a noun, and the exemption sets no precedent: <resource>.admin is precisely what rule 3 refuses and precisely what was deleted.

The three rules were run against the sixty-six live codes in the tables below and corrected nothing — sixty-five satisfy both tests, and the sixty-sixth is system.admin. That null result is the reason this section changed voice rather than its contents: a convention that is followed and not stated fails exactly once, on the first thing nobody thought to compare, and the thing this round failed on had never existed anywhere but in prose (§12). Nothing in the schema will ever notice a code drifting from its row — the check D-104 adopts is a person remembering to run a report over the seeded registries in both directions, which this repository can only ever do by hand (F-19).

docs.title: What a grant is, and what it used to carry
docs.text:
A grant is five things: a grantee (a person or an audience expression) + a scope (the unit, or exactly one item) + one permission code + effect ∈ allow, deny + a period. The answer it feeds:

allowed when some live allow applies and no live deny applies. (D-099)

That is the whole of the precedence rule, and this catalog carries no column beside a code because of it. What the level column used to promise, and what covers it now:

~~access_level used to~~ Now ~~bundle several codes under one word — "manage on this event"~~ One grant row per code. A bundle is a role or an audience, which is what D-068 already said: roles are the bundle ~~grade one act at two strengths — view against edit~~ Two codes, plus permission.right_kind ∈ read \| write saying which side each sits on ~~decide whether a grant was enough for the code being checked~~ Nothing to decide. A grant names exactly one code, and the answer is yes or no ~~order two grants that both apply — locality, D-032~~ Nothing to order: two allows that apply produce one answer. Deny is absolute, and that half of D-032 survives untouched ~~carry revoked as the bottom rung~~ effect = deny on a grant row, and it is still asked first

Withdrawn by D-099. The rank integer it rested on went with it (D-012), and so did permission_level, the table that mapped levels onto codes: the famous bug it guarded — 'admin' < 'contribute' comparing alphabetically and inverting the model — cannot occur in a system with no levels, which is a better fix than the guard. The question that dies with the column is "what does manage give me on this event?": there is no such word, so there is no such lookup. The question it buys is "what exactly does this person have?", answered by reading grant rows.

Two columns moved onto permission itself, and only one of them is comfortable.

  • right_kind ∈ read | write survives only so that D-074's guardianship channel has something to compare a permission against now that the ladder is gone: none covers nothing, view covers read codes, write covers both. Nothing else in the system compares it. It is a column whose only job is one other mechanism, and saying so is cheaper than discovering it later (§6).
  • applies_to ∈ unit | unit_and_item is where a code may be granted at all, and it is checked when the grant is saved, not at check time: an item scope is refused for codes like event.create (an event cannot be created twice, so a creation permission attached to a thing that already exists answers no question) and membership.terminate (a membership is a fact about a person at the unit, not something an event owns). The example D-099 gives for the second half is membership.manage, and this catalog has never carried a code of that name — §12 records that rather than minting it. The system namespace is unit-only the same way, which is who enforces now for the old rule that system.admin can never arrive through an item grant (D-081).

Scope is two things, not a ladder. A grant at the unit — the organization, of which there is one, and which is a scope and never a row (D-097) — reaches every item of every type. A grant on one item reaches that item and nothing else. There is no tier between them and no relation on the item to test: no owner, no parent, no covering body.

docs.title: A grantee is an expression
docs.text:
Wherever this catalog writes a grantee, it is a legal expression in the selector language of D-101: the leaves EVERYONE, MEMBERS, PERSON(person), ROLE(name), GROUP(name), AUDIENCE(name), the two age sets OLDER(n) and YOUNGER(n), and the five event-bound sets ATTENDED, PLACED, CONFIRMED, ON_WAITLIST, ORGANIZERS — each writable with its argument spelled, or bound to the item being checked (D-102) — combined with + union, - difference, * intersection, and brackets. Those three operators are unchanged: round 12 added two operands and no operator (D-107), so (MEMBERS * OLDER(18)) - YOUNGER(6) — brackets printed as always, since * and - bind equally and the stored form never relies on a reader who memorized it — is an ordinary expression of the grammar that already existed, and nothing in this file's grant rows, in audience_operand, or in §11's tables is shaped differently for it. There is no comparison operator in the language — no >=, no <, no bare AGE — and after this round that, not any claim about what counts as a set, is the clause keeping eligibility rule engines out (D-060, as amended by D-107). A hand-written set of people is not a leaf and has no table: it is a sum, PERSON(a) + PERSON(b), because the leaf that used to hold one and the table behind it are both deleted (D-105).

Those thirteen leaves are the registry, not a sample of it — fourteen for round 12 alone, until D-113 removed a row that should never have been in the registry, and neither GUARDIANS nor GUARDIANS(p) is a selector in its place: "True, GUARDIANS should not be selectable in the audience, guardians can perform ANY action (their read/write perms grant) on behalf of the child." A guardian's authority is a right_level ∈ none | view | write over a child, not a set this language resolves (D-074). They are the seeded selector_type rows: the eleven that D-101 copied from the evaluator's arm list and that survived it, plus PERSON, which arrived as the thirteenth to repair a waiver expression that did not parse — the episode D-104 settles — minus LIST, which left in the round after (D-105), plus OLDER(n) and YOUNGER(n), which arrive this round and are the first operands whose argument is a number rather than a row of some table (D-107). So the count has been twelve, thirteen, twelve, fourteen and now thirteen, and it is still not a contradiction: the second number counted an arrival, the third a departure, the fourth two arrivals more, the fifth a row that should never have been counted, and only the last is a fact about today. This page has now printed the registry's size twice and been wrong twice, which is the lesson rather than an excuse: a page repeating a registry's row count is a copy of the registry, and a copy is stale the moment the original moves. This corpus already ruled that an ordinal and a count are different facts — "the thirteenth to arrive" and "one of the twelve that remain" were both true of PERSON at the same time — and round 12 is the round where one of them moved twice, so the rule now has a worked example rather than an assertion: the ordinals are durable and the counts are not. Every number in that sentence except the last is a true sentence about history and will stay true forever; the last one is a sentence about the seeded rows as of this round and is the only one the next round has to re-check.

Two of these leaves move with the calendar, and that is new. OLDER(n) and YOUNGER(n) read person.birth_date as of the date the check is made, so a person joins or leaves one of those sets with no write of any kind, one person at a time, at midnight — and a check asked about a past date answers for that past date, which is a question no snapshot design could answer. Exactly these two, and no others: the other dated operands — ROLE, GROUP, AUDIENCE — move when somebody makes a write with a date on it, which is a different claim and is not the one this sentence makes. Nothing is stored, so there is nothing to invalidate — and since round 14 there is no stored answer left to invalidate either: ~~the cache is rebuilt nightly in full, immediately on any write to the ruleset, and on explicit request, and an answer that moved without one of those is simply allowed to be a night stale~~ (D-111) is retired by D-114, which deletes the answer cache and with it the claim that anything could be a night stale. A check resolves against live rows, so a birthday moves an age set at the instant it happens, with no job standing between the birthday and the answer. What this costs the catalog is a sentence it used to be able to write: this is cheap because it is cached. It cannot write that any more, and the cheapness argument is now one indexed read of the checked person's grant rows per request, plus the two batch reads — can_many(person, codes[], item?) for a screen's affordances and which_of(people[], code, item) for a list's people. No table changes when a person turns eighteen, so there is no row to expire and no cache of membership to keep — which is exactly the property age bands would not have had, and why bands are not in this design. The editor's preview is a workbench and never was a record, and the record is the expression: the audit row logs the words, and the preview is logged as a rendering on a date rather than as a statement of who was in it (D-110, §12).

A leaf outside that registry does not parse, and that sentence is now the whole of what keeps a rule engine out: an operand must be a named operand — a row — and AGE >= 18 is not a row and cannot become one while the language has nowhere to put >=. The test this corpus gave for the same rule, from ../domain/06-authorization-model.md §6, is quoted here so that this file's rule is not read as resting on it again: ~~"an attribute is not a set of people; guardianship is (GUARDIANS(x) is a set), age is not, and the line falls exactly where D-060 already drew it."~~ That test is withdrawn, and it was never holding anything up: OLDER(18) is the set of people who are eighteen or older on the date being checked, exactly as MEMBERS is the set of people who pass is_current_member and ROLE(name) is the set of people who hold that office — every operand in the registry is a test with a set behind it, and reading one column is not a different kind of thing from joining one table — and MEMBERS would have failed the old test too, since nothing in this system stores the member list. D-060's decision stands; its sentence does not (D-107). The quoted sentence turned out to be wrong in a second way, and the quotation stands anyway: its parenthetical treated guardianship as a set the language resolves, and round 13 ruled that it is not one in either spelling (D-113) — which is a reason not to quote that sentence as a test, never a reason to rewrite what this file once printed. The refusals below are operands people ask for that the registry does not carry.

Every expression below is printed in the canonical stored form, which brackets every bracket, always. * and - bind tighter than +; * and - bind equally, left to right; and the stored string never relies on a reader who memorized that (../domain/06-authorization-model.md §6.2). So event.answer.view on an event is aimed at ORGANIZERS, an open camp is opened by MEMBERS, a gated office is MEMBERS * ROLE(treasurers), and the exemption for one named person is (MEMBERS * ROLE(treasurers)) + PERSON(jan) — a second grant aimed at a person is the other way to write the same thing, and keeps the exception off the expression everyone else reads.

Three refusals belong next to the language, because each is a temptation this catalog creates, and a reader could now mistake the first two for type errors. They are not, and never were (D-107): a selector is allowed to be a hard-coded computation in the resolver, because MEMBERS is one today, and an operand may read a column against a date, because OLDER(n) does. Nothing is kept out of the registry for what it is — the word that sounded like it did, ~~"not materializable"~~, is retired with the test it belonged to — so every refusal standing here is an argument about consequences, which is what all three have always been.

  • PRESENT(<event>) is not seeded, on the argument that always carried it. was_present is NULL until somebody takes a register, so an operand over it would revoke a child's access to their own camp photos — a leader's access to their own camp — because a volunteer forgot to tick a box. Presence stays a three-valued safeguarding signal (D-067), and nowhere in this file is it a set anyone may be granted over. The language would not stop anybody writing it now, and that is exactly why the consequence has to be the thing that says no.
  • WHITELISTED is not seeded because there is nothing stored to evaluate (F-20): no type system is objecting — there is no type system left to object — but an operand with no argument, nothing bound to the checked item and no column behind it is a word pointing at a state this system does not keep. F-20 is closed, and closed by that reasoning rather than by a decision about the feature: the operand stays unseeded because there is nothing to evaluate, and the feature it was wanted for arrives as grants anyway. Whether the feature is wanted at all is an events question, and this catalog no longer carries it — which is the closure's real content: a selector question that was really an events question went back to the events module instead of being answered here.
  • A bare name is one namespace across roles and groups (D-101), which makes §11's office names a load-bearing vocabulary, and makes every selector code a reserved name: an office called MEMBERS is refused when it is saved. Two more reserved names arrive with this round — an office, a group or an audience called OLDER or YOUNGER is refused on the same rule, and it is the parser rather than a review that saves a reader from OLDER(18) meaning an office with that name.

docs.title: There is no wildcard, except system.admin
docs.text:
Every capability in this catalog is narrow and explicit. A check for X.y is satisfied by an exact grant of X.y — or by system.admin, which is checked outright and is the only permission in the system that means everything.

A check for 'X.y' is satisfied by: an exact grant of 'X.y', OR 'system.admin'.

There are no per-resource admin permissions. The earlier convention that every resource should expose an <resource>.admin subsuming its narrower codes — a prefix match computed in the resolver — was reversed by D-068, which also deleted the resolver branch that implemented it.

"Someone who can do everything about events" is a role, not a permission — the organization composes it from the thirteen event.* codes. That is the division D-052 already drew: the code implements capabilities, the organization groups them. A per-resource admin was the code guessing at a bundle on the organization's behalf. Since D-100 the composition is literal: a role confers nothing, so the bundle is thirteen live grants whose expression names ROLE(x) — thirteen rows you can read, which is what D-068 was reaching for.

The cost, because it is real. A new narrow permission is not automatically covered by the offices that should imply it; someone must write the grant row. Integrity check 18 is the safety net the wildcard used to be — it lists permissions no live grant names, which is what a missed bundle looks like now that no role carries a permission list of its own. It fails closed: a capability goes unheld and somebody says so, rather than a capability going unmeant and nobody saying so.

docs.title: Two things named "admin", which are not the same thing
docs.text:
The word used to be ambiguous three ways. Three rounds of deletion left one, and the others are recorded as deleted rather than quietly dropped:

Shape What it is Status ~~access_level.admin (rank 40)~~ A grant level — how much authority a grant carries, in view < contribute < manage < admin. Used by permission_level to decide whether a given grant satisfies a given permission. Deleted — the whole ladder, top rung included, by D-099. This row read "real, untouched" until round 10, which is what "untouched" was worth system.admin The one wildcard permission: everything, carried by a grant at the unit and never on an item (applies_to = unit) Real, and the one named exception — the only code in this system allowed to end in a noun. Exempted by name in words by D-068, and named as an exception by D-104, because its meaning is defined by the resolver rather than read off the name. Not a precedent (§1) <resource>.admin A wildcard permission code implying every sibling on that resource Deleted — all sixteen, by D-068, and refused in advance for codes not yet written by D-104: a grade word, and a prefix read as a permission dependent.medical.admin, dependent.admin An action meaning "edit", paired against .view inside a sub-resource; plus a shorthand for the whole set Deleted — by D-074, which reduced a guardian's rights to none / view / write

D-068 exempted dependent.admin on purpose, and D-074 withdrew the exemption. The reason D-068 kept it was sound at the time: it was not a prefix match inferred by code but a value a person deliberately stored on one row about one child. What changed is not the reasoning about wildcards but the thing it was a value of — there is no longer a set of guardian capabilities for a shorthand to stand for. Read the two decisions together before reinstating anything that spells admin.

docs.title: Namespaces
docs.text:
Namespace Resolved against Channel (absent) access_grant — aimed at a person or at an audience — and ownership 1, 3 system access_grant at the unit only — applies_to = unit, so never on an item 1

The channel numbers are the three in ../domain/06-authorization-model.md §1: grants, guardianship, ownership. There used to be a fourth row in this table and a fourth channel above it — role_assignment, the channel a system permission could only be reached through. Withdrawn by D-100: role_assignment is role_holder, a role confers nothing, and every code in this catalog — system.admin included — arrives through the one grant channel now. Who enforces that a system code stays out of item grants: applies_to, checked on save (D-081), not the absence of a channel.

There is no dependent namespace (D-074); §9 explains what replaced it, and what was lost with it.

That leaves the guardianship channel with no prefix to dispatch on, which has to be answered rather than left implied. It used to route on dependent., and the reason for routing by prefix was that no caller should decide which channel applies — otherwise the same authorization rule gets implemented twice, once correctly. It now routes on a fact about the request instead of a fact about the name: the channel is consulted whenever the person the action is about differs from the person performing it. That is stronger than the prefix rule, not weaker — under the old rule a guardian asking to change their child's address with a person.contact.edit code would not have routed through guardianship at all, because the code did not carry the right prefix. Nobody chooses a channel; the shape of the request selects it.

The guardianship.* codes are additionally satisfiable by being a party to the row, and not only by a grant (D-073).

system permissions remain non-grantable on an item: system.admin must never be delegable to a single event, a group, or an office. What enforces it is no longer the shape of the channel that could carry it but a column on the code itself.

docs.title: Sensitivity marker
docs.text:
The Sens. column flags permissions that need extra care:

Mark Meaning ⚠ Granting it exposes personal data ⚠⚠ Granting it exposes children's personal data — or the same about an adult, where the code reads a whole person record rather than one field of it. Since D-083 there is no separate health data class to name: the mark grades what a grant exposes, not which field the code points at 🔒 Granting it confers authority over the permission system itself 🔒🔒 The escalating half of that family: granting it changes what other people can do, not merely what the holder can do. role.* is marked this way in D-100, which names it "the most sensitive code family in the catalog" ⛔ Granting it can end someone's membership or standing

These marks should drive UI warnings and the alerting in ../data-model/05-authorization.md. A mark grades what a grant exposes, not the table a code names (D-086), and the two new families are placed by that rule: person_group.member.manage takes ⚠ because a roster is a list of people, and role.* keeps 🔒🔒 because writing a holder row writes who may hold everything else.

docs.title: 2. People and identity
docs.text:
Code Namespace Sens. Grants person.view — ⚠⚠ See person records — all of them, including every descriptive value person.create — Add a person record person.edit — ⚠ Change person details, including descriptive values person.contact.view — ⚠ See contact points person.contact.edit — ⚠ Change contact points person.merge — 🔒 Confirm identity matches and merge people — and reverse a merge, and resolve a sign-up collision; there is no separate code for any of the three person.redact — 🔒 Perform a GDPR-style erasure attribute.define — Curate the vocabulary of descriptive data — create, rename, merge or retire a code

person.merge and person.redact are separated from person.edit deliberately: both have privacy consequences far beyond editing a record. This paragraph used to justify the separation by calling both irreversible in practice, and D-087 has withdrawn that premise for one of them — a merge can be reversed, and reversing it is a required operation. What survives the correction is the half the separation actually rests on: the merged window cannot be reversed, so the union of two people's permissions is real from the moment the merge commits, whatever is discovered afterwards. The separation stands on the narrower reason.

Three operations, and not one new code. Round 8 introduced two capabilities and, each time, checked whether the catalog needed a row for it (D-087, D-089):

  • Unmerge — reversing a merge a human approved: person.merge. Undoing an identity correction is the same act as making one, done by a named human, through the same queue, over the same rows. A person.unmerge code would grade undoing a mistake as safer than making one. Such a row stood in §2 until round 8 and is removed here; no seed role held it, so no role loses anything, and it is recorded rather than quietly deleted because a reader of an older draft will look for it.
  • Resolving a sign-up collision — working the claim a colliding registration files: person.merge. Resolving it is confirming or rejecting an identity_hypothesis, which is what person.merge already means (../domain/03-identity-and-legacy.md §4).
  • Linking a colliding sign-up to the person it matched: nothing, deliberately. There is no account.link and no account_claim table (§3). An automatic link once the e-mail verifies is D-004 under another name, and its failure mode is one human's descriptive data becoming another human's record.

The check itself is the point: this file is the only list of grantable codes, so a code minted while propagating a decision is a migration nobody decided.

Before D-068, the way to keep them apart was to carve them out of person.admin's prefix match — a special case in the resolver that was invisible in every role editor. Now there is no wildcard to carve out of, and the question moves somewhere reviewable: an office bundling all of person.* reaches them, and you can see it — since D-100 deleted role_permission, the bundle is the live grant rows naming ROLE(x), one row per code, dated and attributable. The guidance that replaces the special case is in §11 — no seeded office mixes person.merge or person.redact with routine person.edit, and one that does should be named for what it is. This is now a report a person can read, not a caveat about a resolver rule.

person.background_check.* is gone (D-043). The organization has no background checks handled by this system, so there is nothing to view and nothing to record. If that changes, the permission pair and a dated record with an expires_at are the natural shape — and it would belong here, next to person.*, because a clearance is a fact about a person and not about their membership.

docs.title: Descriptive data: two old codes and one new one
docs.text:
Everything the system knows about a person other than their name, their gender and their age is one class of data, in fields the organization defines while it runs (../domain/08-person-data.md, ../data-model/09-attributes.md, D-083, D-084). The catalog's whole involvement in that is one row added and none removed:

  • Read: person.view. Write: person.edit. That is the entire access story. No read or write code was added for descriptive data, because there is nothing left for one to gate — a code that separated, say, the allergy list from the rest of the record would reinstate the privileged subset D-083 refused on the merits. There is therefore no health.* or medical.* namespace and no per-field access rule, deliberately: category on a definition groups a form and grants nothing. If a narrower tier is ever genuinely needed, the route is a decision entry about a second grant scope over a defined set of data, not a code with a suggestive name.
  • attribute.define is the new one, and it is the narrow one (D-084): it creates, renames, merges and retires a code — deciding what the organization collects, which is what makes the data queryable. Recording a value against a code that does not exist needs no such permission: it saves as a proposed definition and waits in the curation queue. The mark column stays empty for it because it reads nobody's data — the vocabulary is rows about codes, and the values underneath it are reached through person.view like anything else.
  • person.view moved from ⚠ to ⚠⚠, and the reason is the same decision: the marker grades what a grant exposes, and this one now exposes everything known about a child — an allergy list, an insurance number, a note about who the child actually lives with — through a single code that used to be graded as ordinary personal data from when the record was smaller than the person.

person.redact reaches the layer too, and in the opposite direction from retiring a code: retiring one keeps the values, redacting a person erases theirs — in the audit trail as well as in the row, since a trail that still reads out an erased value has preserved it rather than missed it (../data-model/09-attributes.md §6).

docs.title: 3. Accounts
docs.text:
Code Namespace Sens. Grants account.view — ⚠ See account records account.create — Create an account for someone account.suspend — ⚠ Suspend an account account.close — ⚠ Close an account account.credential.reset — 🔒 Issue a credential reset

account.suspend is not membership.suspend. Suspending a login does not remove someone from the organization; the two are separate lifecycles and separate permissions.

Nothing in this namespace links an account to a person it already belongs to, and the absence is decided, not overlooked. A sign-up that strong-matches an existing person raises an identity_hypothesis and brings nothing into the world that a human has not approved — nothing merged, nothing linked, nothing activated; the account sits at pending_verification until a reviewer decides, and deciding is person.merge (§2, D-089). So there is no account.link code and no claim object for one to act on: the second live account those would manage is exactly what the rule forbids, and the case they would have been asked to solve most often is already handled underneath permissions — account_credential holds many credentials for one account, so a member with a new e-mail address is adding a credential to the login they have, not acquiring a second one.

docs.title: 4. Membership
docs.text:
Code Namespace Sens. Grants membership.view — ⚠ See membership records membership.request.create — Submit an application membership.request.review — ⚠ Read and work an application membership.request.approve — ⛔ Approve or reject an application membership.activate — Activate a membership membership.lapse — ⛔ Lapse a membership (administrative, non-payment) membership.suspend — ⛔ Temporarily suspend a membership membership.terminate — ⛔ End a membership for cause / expel membership.backdate — ⚠ Enter or correct historical membership periods

Two rows stood at the foot of this table and are gone. ~~unit_participation.view and unit_participation.manage — see who takes part in a sub-unit; add, move or end participation~~ were deleted by D-097 with the table they read and the sub-units that had rosters. Their work is retargeted, not lost: "who is in the organization?" is membership.view — one query over membership, with no depth in it — and "who is in this group?" and "write that group's roster" are person_group.view and person_group.member.manage (§5a, D-098). Everything D-095 said of unit_participation.manage — never self-scoped, the write is somebody else's act, the report is the control — transfers to the new code intact, and is written there.

membership.terminate is the most consequential non-system permission in the catalog. A lapse is administrative; a termination is a decision about a person's standing in a youth organization, frequently with safeguarding and reputational consequences. It should be held by very few people, and it must not be implied by membership.lapse. Grant it explicitly, per person — which since D-099 is the only thing a grant can be: one code, one effect.

membership.transfer is gone, and round 10 removed the sentence that pointed at a replacement. "Transfer a member between units" was an artefact of units holding memberships, and it was last answered by "moving between sub-units is unit_participation.manage — close one row, open another" (D-041). That replacement is now itself deleted (D-097). The discipline survives and the object moved: moving a person from one group to another is person_group.member.manage — close one dated row, open another (D-098, ../data-model/02-organization.md §4) — and it does not touch the person's membership at all. There is still nothing to transfer.

person_group.member.manage has no self-scoped variant, and none will be added (D-095, whose reasoning D-098 transfers intact). Every grant of it means "over this group's roster" or "over every group's roster", never "over my own row" — so "nobody writes themselves into a group" is not a check the write performs, it is the shape of the thing being granted: there is no smaller grant to make yourself. The same holds for role.assign (§7): nobody appoints themselves, and D-095's instruction was explicitly not to mint a code that could express either act. This is also where the safeguarding story moved to. org_unit_type.allows_minors was removed a round ago and the units it graded are now gone too, so no column anywhere says which sets are for children and nothing here refuses to place a minor in one; what is left is this code held by named adults at the unit, the write audited the way any business-table write is, its recorded values emptied after 24 months (D-088), and a report of who holds it (../domain/04-organization-structure.md §3). What is lost is not in this list: D-097 names it plainly — the named adult used to be somebody the body chose, and there is no body (../domain/04-organization-structure.md §1). The gate in front of a membership is the fee; a group has no fee and no second gate, so this permission is the only one (../domain/05-membership-lifecycle.md §1).

~~These permissions are gated by membership when held through a role that requires one (D-039). The gate is a property of the role, not of the permission, so it is not visible in this table. The single exception is system.gate_exempt (§7), which is the gate's waiver and is therefore exempt from the gate itself (D-051).~~ Withdrawn by D-100. Nothing about a code says whether it requires a paid-up holder, so this table has nothing to hide and nothing to warn about. Who performs the membership test now: the grantee expression, which says MEMBERS * ROLE(x) when the fee is meant to matter and omits it when it is not — evaluated live on the checked date (§11, ../domain/06-authorization-model.md §6.1).

docs.title: 5. Organization and positions
docs.text:
Nothing is granted here, because nothing described is left. Both halves of this title died in round 10 for different reasons: the six org_unit.* codes went with the unit hierarchy (D-097) and the two position.* codes went with positions (D-100). The heading stays so that a reader arriving from an old bookmark finds the reason and not an empty space, and because this catalog is the only list of grantable codes — a code leaving it silently is a migration nobody decided (§2).

~~Deleted code~~ Went with Where the act is now ~~org_unit.view~~ org_unit (D-097) Nowhere. The unit is a scope, not a row: there is no list of units to read, and no "which units exist" report to run ~~org_unit.create~~ ditto Nowhere, and nothing needs creating. The unit arrives as a code in grant_scope_type, not as data ~~org_unit.edit~~, ~~org_unit.rename~~ org_unit_name and its rename history (D-097) Renaming a group is person_group.edit (§5a), and it is cheap: a grant and an expression store kind + id, never a name, so a rename rewrites nothing (D-101) ~~org_unit.restructure~~ splits, mergers and successions (D-097) Nowhere, and the loss is stated once in D-097: a group that splits is an old group that ended and two that began, with no edge between them unless somebody writes one ~~org_unit.close~~ org_unit.status (D-097) person_group.end (§5a) — which ends a set, and is graded accordingly ~~position.view~~, ~~position.assign~~ position, position_assignment, is_leadership, max_holders, the appointment workflows (D-100) role.view and role.assign (§7). An elected leader is a holder of a role, and the audience rule that used to read unit_leaders is ROLE(leaders) — which, unlike the rule round 6 had to correct because it was silently matching nobody, means what its name says

Why position.assign was split from everything else, kept because the reasoning outlived the code. An appointment was made to a person by somebody else, was never self-scoped, and came with eligibility rules about the office rather than the appointment — position.min_age, max_holders, requires_membership (D-095). All three of those columns are deleted with the table, and none of them is a self-service door in the new model either: role.assign has no self-scoped form (§7). The reasoning that survives is the one that made role.assign 🔒🔒 — nobody appoints themselves, and no code in this catalog can be sharpened into that act.

"An appointment writes one row, not two" — and now nothing writes a second row either. The sentence existed to stop a leadership position silently deriving authority: the derivation from a position to a set of people lived in a group's filling rule, where it stopped covering the person on the day the assignment closed (D-091). Filling rules were superseded by D-101 and positions by D-100, so the derivation is gone rather than relocated: a holder row is written by a named person under role.assign, and the only thing that turns it into authority is a grant naming ROLE(x). What is genuinely lost is the elected-versus-appointed distinction as stored data (D-100): it survives only as offices the organization invents — elected_council beside appointed_it — or not at all (../domain/04-organization-structure.md §6).

org_unit.restructure was separated from routine editing because a split rewrites the answer to historical questions. Reparenting had already been taken out of it — a unit could not change parent at all (D-036, itself now reversed by D-097) — and the splits and mergers it did grant are gone too, so the separation is recorded here rather than kept anywhere live.

docs.title: 5a. Groups, roles and audiences
docs.text:
Three things the catalog used to describe with units, exposure rows and filling rules, and which are now three small tables: a group (person_group, dated member rows, a lifetime) is company (D-098); a role (role, role_holder) is an office, and confers nothing (D-100); an audience is an expression over named sets, and is what a grant aims at (D-101). Writing a group's roster and writing an office's holder list are different codes on purpose — that difference is the whole reason there are two tables — and the office codes are in §7.

Code Namespace Sens. Grants person_group.view — ⚠ See which groups exist, their lifetimes, and who is in them — a roster is a list of people, which is what ⚠ grades person_group.create — Create a group: a name, a description, a lifetime. applies_to = unit person_group.edit — Change a group's name or description. A rename rewrites no grant (§5) person_group.end — Set the group's valid_to. It ends a set, not anyone's standing — hence no ⛔, deliberately person_group.member.manage — ⚠ Add, move or end a member. Never self-scoped (§4); applies_to = unit_and_item audience.view — See the expressions a grant can be aimed at, and the people each one resolves to audience.manage — ⚠ Create an audience; change its expression — which is now the whole of it: the LIST this gloss used to add, and the table behind it, are deleted, so a hand-named person is a PERSON(x) leaf the same permission already reaches (D-105)

~~scope.expose and scope.exposure.review stood at the top of this section, and scope.expose was arguably the most consequential permission in the authorization model. It was the only door between unit levels: authority never inherits downward (D-031), and this was the single mechanism that crossed the boundary — graded 🔒 despite the obscure name, and made safe by who could write it, since every scope_exposure row was written by the unit it covers, so a parent's officer could not satisfy it for a child unit (D-049). There was no bulk variant, and every row was a deliberate, attributable decision about one assignment (D-045).~~ Deleted by D-097, with the table, the direction-of-authority check, and the nightly alert that was its only detector. They are kept here struck because the question they answered — may the center read what happens inside a body it does not run? — no longer has a subject, and someone who remembers the answer "no, unless the body says so" should find that fact rather than a silent gap. The same reasoning is worked through in ../domain/06-authorization-model.md §2.

person_group.member.manage is a ⚠ next to a 🔒🔒 two rows away, and the gap is the design. D-100 refuses to merge person_group and role into one table with a kind column precisely because one membership table gives a single code that both adds a child to the Thursday group and puts the holder into SYSTEM_ADMINS. Same columns, different codes, and GROUP(x) / ROLE(x) distinct in the grant text so the difference is visible to whoever reads the grant. A group additionally authorizes nothing by existing: no parent, no type, no leadership, no roles of its own, no fee — a member of a group can do nothing, which is D-005 one level down (../domain/04-organization-structure.md §2).

A group and a role are both items, which is what makes "these two may work this roster" a grant. Both are registered in grant_scope_type, so the code above can be held at the unit — reaching every group, existing and future, because nothing stands between a unit grant and an item after D-097 — or written on one group, reaching that roster only (../data-model/02-organization.md §3). Reaching the second requires the first: a grant on an item is written by someone who holds the code at the unit, or holds a grant on that item.

A live grant whose group has ended is a listed oddity rather than a failure: it applies to nobody, which is the safe direction, and the report of such rows is where the stale one surfaces (../data-model/02-organization.md §6).

audience.manage is the permission that creates a grant target, and it is wider than it was. Whoever holds it can assemble a set of people which a later access_grant may then address (D-042) — authority over who could be granted, one step removed from granting. Whether it belongs to a dedicated office or to whoever runs things is open (§12).

It used to be one code over three arms; it is now one code over a whole expression, and the hazard changed shape rather than leaving. D-091 let a group be filled by a rule, a hand-kept list, or an inclusion of other groups, and the inclusion arm was the one that worried, because "add the kitchen crew to everything the troop-staff group is used for" silently widened every grant aimed at anything including it. audience_include is deleted by D-101, along with include_depth_limit, the transitive walk and the write-time cycle check over a graph — an audience is a tree of + - * now, a tree cannot cycle, and composition happens in the grant (GROUP(kitchen) + ROLE(troop_staff)) instead of in an edge nobody could see the shape of. What did not get smaller: EVERYONE is a legal operand, so nothing in this table distinguishes "add these five people" from "this grant reaches the whole organization", and no separate code was invented to do it. That stays an open question, not an answer (§12), and until it is answered the only control is the one D-091 named and D-102 sharpened: the editor shows the people a grant reaches, expanded, computed for an item, rather than the expression's name (../domain/06-authorization-model.md §6.2).

The display is itself a read over people, and this catalog does not grade that yet. Showing a resolved set means enumerating which humans an expression currently covers — which is what audience.view is for, on a row carrying no sensitivity mark. Listing the holders of "everyone except the counselors in schuzka2026-1" is not the same kind of act as listing the kitchen crew, and the grading was written before the two could be one query (§12).

docs.title: 6. Guardianship
docs.text:
Code Namespace Sens. Grants guardianship.view — ⚠⚠ See guardianship relationships guardianship.create — ⚠⚠ Record a guardianship guardianship.end — ⚠⚠ End a guardianship guardianship.assign — ⚠⚠ Add another guardian over the same dependent guardianship.change_right — 🔒 Change a guardianship's right_level

These four are the only codes in the catalog that a private individual holds over their own household, without being granted them. D-073 makes the parties to a guardianship principals on the row: a guardian may end it, add another guardian, and change its level; the adult subject may end it over themselves. Staff hold the same codes and are an route, never the route.

guardianship.permission.grant is deleted — it granted individual codes from the dependent.* namespace, and there is no such namespace to grant from (D-074). guardianship.change_right replaces it, and does less: one value, three choices.

What the three choices are compared against, now that the ladder is gone. D-074's none / view / write used to be read off the access-level ladder — write reached contribute, view reached view. That comparison was deleted with the ladder by D-099, and the guardianship channel would have had nothing left to compare a permission against. It compares against a column instead: permission.right_kind ∈ read | write, where none covers nothing, view covers the read codes, and write covers both. That is the column's only customer in the whole system (§1), and it is why a code added to this catalog has to be typed read or write at all: the column is required, because a nullable one whose null-ness silently means something would let a permission arrive with a guardian's answer already decided by nobody.

docs.title: 7. Permissions administration
docs.text:
Code Namespace Sens. Grants role.view system See the offices that exist and who has held them, over what period (role_holder) role.create system 🔒🔒 Create an office: a code, a name, a description. It carries no permission — see the note below role.edit system 🔒🔒 Change an office's name or description role.delete system 🔒🔒 Delete an office. Only possible if it was never held and is not a system role role.assign system 🔒🔒 Write a role_holder row — make someone a holder. applies_to = unit_and_item: on one role, this is "manage the counselors roster" role.unassign system 🔒 Close a role_holder row — set its valid_to permission.view system See the permission catalog permission.edit system 🔒🔒 Change the permission catalog access_grant.create — ⚠ Create a grant — the act that turns a code into someone's authority access_grant.revoke — ⚠ End a grant early, or write a deny system.admin system 🔒🔒 Everything. Single top-level capability, applies_to = unit ~~system.gate_exempt~~ system ~~🔒~~ Deleted by D-100 — see the note below the table

A role confers nothing. That is the sentence that rewrites this whole section, and it is worth reading before the table above, because three of the six rows above used to mean something they can no longer mean. role_permission is deleted, and with it the answer to "what does this role grant?": the codes an office carries are the live grants whose expression names ROLE(x) (D-100, ../domain/06-authorization-model.md §4). What role.create and role.edit touch is a name, a description, an order — an office is a set with a label, and a set is not a grant (D-005). role.view used to read "see roles and their permissions", and what it shows now is the holder register, which is the question the table can still answer and the one F-12 was closed to keep answerable: who was treasurer in 2023?

role.assign is the permission to escalate privilege. Whoever holds it can write themselves a holder row in an office that grants them system.admin. It must be held by very few people and every holder row must be logged and alerted on. Note that system.admin is deliberately a single top-level permission rather than a per-resource one — concentrating the most dangerous capability and alarming on its holders is safer than scattering equivalents of it. role.assign has no self-scoped form and none will be added (§4, D-095): the reason it is not a check the write performs is that there is no smaller grant to make yourself.

Roles are runtime data, and these six permissions are how the organization administers them. role.create names a new office; role.edit renames one; role.delete removes one created by mistake; the reach of any of them is written by access_grant.create down the table. §11 is therefore a starting point to be edited, not a fixed vocabulary — which is why §11 no longer claims to answer "which roles are exempt from the membership gate". That question is not answered in configuration any more either: it is answered in the text of each grant, by whether its expression contains MEMBERS.

There is no role.retire, and a role cannot be switched off (D-053). A role is a definition and is valid always; the period lives on the holder row. Ending a role's use means closing holder rows, which is role.unassign — one person at a time, or a loop over the holders. This is still the right shape, and the round that deleted the role's own permission list left this alone on purpose: what ends is someone's authority, and that is a fact about a person, not about a definition. What died with the gate is the reassurance that used to come with it — the old note pointed out that a dormant authority would quietly expire anyway when the holder's fee lapsed. Nothing does that now, so the report of holder rows that never end (D-071, whose posture transfers from assignments to holder rows) is carrying all of the weight.

~~role.edit is a bulk privilege change wearing the clothes of a settings screen. Editing a role's permissions takes effect immediately for every holder, with no assignment touched and no notification. It is marked 🔒🔒 alongside role.assign for that reason. The two are different powers — role.assign escalates one person, role.edit escalates everyone holding the role — and neither is implied by the other.~~ Withdrawn in substance by D-100: there are no longer any permissions on a role to edit, so the screen this paragraph warned about has nothing dangerous left on it. The hazard it named did not go away — it moved to the grant. Whoever can save a grant aimed at ROLE(x) escalates everyone holding x, immediately, without touching a holder row and without notifying anybody: that is the new bulk privilege change, it is access_grant.create with an expression in it, and it is exactly why role.* stays 🔒🔒 while the composition of grants is the least-graded write in the catalog (§12). The two powers are still not each other, and neither is implied by the other.

role.delete only works on an office that has never been held and is not is_system — which is what protects the one seeded role, counselors, from an editor (§11). No delete may leave a role_holder pointing at a role that is gone: ../data-model/05-authorization.md §3 states the guard and the order it refuses in. The two halves are not equally strong, and the difference is the reason this permission is not self-policing. The first is referential integrity — role_holder.role_id references role.id, a migration-level constraint, so it refuses a delete that arrives from an import, from a manual fix, or from a second client as surely as from the screens. The second, is_system, is a property of the row being deleted and no index can see it: it is a check inside the transaction that deletes, and a model-layer guard there is a friendlier message, not the refusal. A role that has been held is left in place, so the answer to "what office did this person hold in 2019?" survives — which is precisely when someone asks it.

system.gate_exempt is deleted, and this is the round's largest deletion seen from here. It used to be the permission that waived the membership gate for one named person (D-051), alongside role.requires_membership, which waived it for a whole office, and both existed only because the resolver asked the question of every grant (D-039). The resolver no longer asks it, so there is nothing to waive and no exemption to be granted: the waiver is now the expression the grant was written with — MEMBERS * ROLE(x) where the fee must hold, ROLE(x) where it need not, and (MEMBERS * ROLE(x)) + PERSON(y) when one named person is to survive their own lapse. person_holds_gate_exempt goes with it, and so does the lockout hazard that came from performing a permission check through can() inside the exemption (§11, ../domain/06-authorization-model.md §6.1).

~~access_grant.create is scoped by permission_level: holding it lets you grant others access to items you have admin on, and only at a level at or below your own. Without that restriction, any item-grant holder becomes a universal grantor.~~ Withdrawn by D-099, which deleted the ladder the ceiling was drawn from. What bounds a grantor now: the code is one code, applies_to refuses it on an item it does not fit, the scope is the item the grant names or the unit, MEMBERS is the writer's act, and a delegation may not exceed the delegator's own authority — but that test is written only for delegations (../domain/06-authorization-model.md §9). For an ordinary grant, no decision in D-097..D-102 says you may grant only what you hold. D-099 noticed the hazard and answered a different half of it: the price of one row per code is paid in rows, and the report of dead-weight denies is the hygiene that came with it. The ceiling is therefore recorded as an open question (§12), not as a rule this catalog holds.

docs.title: 8. Audit and system
docs.text:
Code Namespace Sens. Grants audit.view — ⚠⚠ Read the audit log — including the before/after values it carries, which are person data like any other audit.export — ⚠⚠ Export audit records import.view — ⚠ See import batches import.stage — Stage an import import.apply — 🔒 Apply a staged import import.revert — 🔒 Revert an applied import report.view — ⚠ Run standard reports report.export — ⚠⚠ Export report data

audit.view is graded ⚠⚠, and the reason is a property of the trail rather than of any field it touches. audit_log carries the before and after images of what changed, which makes it a second copy of the person record — descriptive values included, on the same terms as a person_contact or a note change. There is no exclusion list doing that work, and there must not be one: a rule naming the person fields whose values may not be logged is a privileged subset of the record, which is precisely what D-083 refused — and it would hollow out D-085, whose entire justification for overwriting a value in place is that the trail holds the sequence. So reading the trail over a scope is reading person data over that scope, and reading more than person.view shows: the current row is the organization's present belief, the trail is every belief it has held. What protects the trail is therefore the guard on it — scope, this mark, and who is granted it — exactly as the guard on person.view protects the record. The grading rule this applies — the mark follows what a grant exposes, not the table a code names — is D-086, taken during propagation rather than from an answer, and reversible on one line.

The contents expire, which bounds this exposure without fixing it. A row lives for the life of the system; its old_values/new_values are emptied 24 months after they were written, by a scheduled job this corpus calls payload reduction — a third operation on the trail, distinct from redaction (a person's erasure, immediate and absolute, whatever the age of the row) and from an import revert (D-088). So "the trail is every belief it has held" is, since round 8, true only of the values less than two years old; about anything older the trail answers who touched this row, when, and were they allowed to and not and to what. For the risk this note is actually about — a grant graded wrongly, or simply held by the wrong person — that is a control worth having: it does not make the exposure impossible, it puts a horizon under it, which for an organization of this size is the realistic form the same protection takes. AT-4 stays open, because a window on the payload is an argument about how long a bad grant can do harm, not an answer to whether one permission should guard the trail.

Payload reduction needs no code here, and saying so is the check that it was considered. Nobody performs it interactively: it is scheduled, and the guard on it is a check that alerts when a row past the window still carries a payload (../data-model/06-audit-and-import.md §2.2). A permission for it would imply a person choosing not to run it.

The excluded-keys list survives, with a smaller and honest job. Values that must never be logged at all belong on it: credential secrets, tokens, session material. Personal data does not, because personal data is protected by who may read the table, not by a list of its names.

Erasure reaches the payload. A redaction that rewrote the business tables while the erased values stayed readable in the trail is a failed redaction, not a partial one (../data-model/06-audit-and-import.md §2, ../data-model/09-attributes.md §6).

audit.export sits at ⚠⚠ for a reason unrelated to what it reads. An export carries the payload outside every mechanism this catalog governs: scope stops at the file, revoking the grant does not recall the copy, and a later redaction cannot reach it. It is graded by where the data goes, not by what the code is allowed to see.

Whether one permission is enough of a guard for all that is itself open — tracked as AT-4 (../open-questions.md). The grading above is what is settled: the trail is read with the guard of person data, whichever permission or combination of permissions that guard turns out to be.

docs.title: 8a. Events
docs.text:
The per-item grant scope the whole authorization model was built toward — and since D-102, an item like any other. Nothing owns an event: event.org_unit_id is deleted, and with it can_event() — the unit-authority rule nearly every code below used to be reached through. A grant at the unit reaches every event because there is no tier between the unit and the item and no owner to test; every event check goes through the ordinary resolver and nothing else. Registration is eligibility — a live allow of event.register_self is the rule for who may sign up, and there is no separate eligibility mechanism (D-060). And there is no door code. The capability these thirteen codes are sometimes read as containing was never registered anywhere — not in this table, not in any other page (D-104, §12); arriving people are recorded by whoever holds event.presence.mark, with a clipboard if necessary, and D-075 keeps the only QR code in this system attached to a payment, where it is a rendering and not a row.

Code Namespace Sens. Grants event.view — See an event event.create — Create an event. Held at the unit — there is no owner to create one for since D-102 deleted the column that would have named one event.edit — Change an event's details, dates, capacity event.cancel — ⚠ Cancel an event — keeps registrations, notifies nobody by itself event.organizer.manage — ⚠ Add or remove organizers — a roster write, which aims ORGANIZERS at more people and so widens every grant pointed at that set event.register_self — Register yourself — this is the eligibility rule event.register_other — ⚠ Register someone else (a minor, a walk-in) event.manage_participants — ⚠ Manage the roster — add or remove registrations, work the waitlist, promote event.presence.mark — ⚠ Mark who turned up — nothing else, and never a set anyone is granted over (§1) event.answer.view — ⚠⚠ Read registrant answers (tent, dietary, …) — the note below, and the seeded grant event.question.manage — ⚠ Define what the event asks event.grant_access — 🔒 Grant access to an event. The level it used to demand is gone; what distinguishes it from access_grant.create now is the scope, not a rung (§12) event.delete — 🔒 Delete an event — only possible with no registrations

Where each of these may be granted, and what kind of right it is — the two columns D-099 added, replacing the table of required levels that stood here:

Code applies_to right_kind event.create unit write event.view, event.answer.view unit_and_item read every other event.* code unit_and_item write

unit_and_item is the whole of the old per-scope table, and it says less: at the unit a code reaches every event, on one event it reaches that event, and no level rides on top of either. The read rows are read because a guardian's view is meant to reach them (§6) — which is the only reason the column exists.

The five sets bound to an event are grantees, not codes. ATTENDED, PLACED, CONFIRMED, ON_WAITLIST and ORGANIZERS name the people connected to the item a grant is written on, and they belong to the audience language, not to this catalog: an operand is a set, and a set is not a grant (D-062 survives untouched — an event_organizer row grants nothing). Two refusals come with them and both land when the grant is saved: a bound (argument-less) operand is legal only on an item-scope grant, and only where selector_type.argument_type matches the item — PLACED on a group grant is refused because that item is not an event. And PRESENT(<event>) is refused outright (§1). The definitions, and the reason PLACED rather than ATTENDED is the capacity set, are in ../data-model/08-events.md §8.

event.presence.mark is split off event.manage_participants on purpose, and it used to sit a level lower. Marking presence is a task handed to whoever is at the door with a clipboard; managing the roster is a task for the event's leadership. One permission covering both forces the organization to hand the clipboard-holder the ability to delete a child from the camp roster. Splitting it costs two rows and makes the ordinary delegation ordinary. What the split was graded with is gone — the note used to add "and note the level: presence is contribute, the same bar as being able to register", and there is no bar to compare now (D-099). The split is worth more than the level was: the distinction the level made softly — this volunteer is not roster leadership — is now written as the only thing a grant can say, one code, and granting event.presence.mark on an event cannot smuggle in event.manage_participants the way contribute once sat underneath manage. It follows the shape of membership.lapse versus membership.terminate (D-022) — one routine, one consequential — and it is free to add because the catalog is a menu, not a fixed set (D-055). It was previously an open question (EV-5); it is resolved there as a split, and the split outlived the ladder it was graded on.

event.register_self is the whole of D-060. Opening an event to the membership is one row: an access_grant scoped to that event, of event.register_self, aimed at MEMBERS. One row is the point — nobody is enumerated, so nobody is left out when the roster changes, and nothing has to be re-run when someone joins. It used to be one row at contribute, and the level was doing a second job there that nobody assigned it: it made the eligibility grant the same size as the presence task. With the level gone the row says one thing, which is the smaller claim and the one that survives review.

An age-restricted camp is a narrower expression instead — MEMBERS * GROUP(camp_2026_junior) aimed at the same one code, or the same subtraction pattern read the other way. There is no age rule on the event and there will not be one — an open event with an age ceiling is accepted as a risk, on the grounds that a registration-time condition the capability model does not know about is the first rule-engine rule (D-070). If it ever needs closing, the shape is a new selector in the selector_type registry, not a column (../domain/07-events.md §4) — and note that GROUP(...) is a set somebody maintains, so "who is eligible" stays a roster with a person's name on every row rather than a predicate the resolver evaluates.

event.cancel is separated from event.edit deliberately. Cancelling is the most consequential thing anyone does to an event: it affects every registrant, it usually involves money, and it is a decision rather than an edit. It does not notify anyone — that is the communication module's job, and conflating the two makes "who cancelled this, and when?" harder to answer than it should be.

event.delete is on this list and nothing else has an equivalent, because events are the one thing in this data model that can be deleted. (The comparison used to be with org_unit, which had no delete permission and had six codes of its own; §5.) A draft event with no registrations is a mistake to be cleaned up; anything else is cancelled, not deleted (D-064). No event with even one registration row may be deleted — Guard 2 in ../data-model/08-events.md §8 is the rule, and cancelling is what to do instead. The obligation is not the permission's to carry: event.delete decides who may ask, and only a migration-level constraint — event_registration.event_id referencing event.id with no cascade — refuses the same delete when it arrives from an import or a hand-written fix instead of a screen. Enforcing this in the model layer alone would leave the record of who was coming deletable by everything except the intended route.

event.answer.view is where D-061 lives, and since round 10 it lives there as a grant. The sentence "answers are read by that event's organizers" used to be hard-coded prose beside the resolver, reached through the event's owning unit. event.org_unit_id is deleted, so the sentence is now said where permissions are said: a seeded grant of event.answer.view, scoped to the event, aimed at ORGANIZERS (D-102). Because a bound operand is legal only on an item-scope grant, this cannot be one row for every event: what ships is a template, and D-102 now says plainly that the event-creation path instantiates it beside the event row, in the same transaction as the event, and that the import owes one instantiation per event it writes (../data-model/08-events.md §8). What remains open is only the safety net: an event whose two writes were not one transaction has no organizer who can read its answers, and "these two rows exist together" is a report — events with no answer-view grant — that no layer of this project can express as a constraint (F-10). The rule itself is unchanged: whoever runs an event reads that event's answers with no additional gate, because holding an office grants nothing (§7) and leadership is not guardianship — guardianship authority belongs to the guardians (§9). That is a deliberate widening and it is recorded as one. The catalog's registered spelling is event.answer.view, singular — the arbiter for a spelling the round briefly had two of, and the reason §12 says a code is a row and prose is only prose (§12, F-19).

Its premise has since been narrowed, and not by reversing it (D-085). D-061 was written when an event form was the only route by which a camp leader learned a child has a nut allergy, because nothing else was readable. Descriptive data now exists (../domain/08-person-data.md) and a leader holding person.view over that unit reads a recorded allergy there, so the form is the fallback for a fact the organization has not recorded, not the ceiling on what an organizer may know. What survives unchanged is the decision itself, and the discipline below it.

This code is graded ⚠⚠, and it is the second time in this round that the marker followed the content rather than the category. It sat at ⚠ beside a paragraph conceding that the answers under it can be clinical, which is the same mismatch audit.view had one section above: a payload that is children's personal data, graded as though it were logistics. D-083 refuses a class of data more delicate than the rest, so either an adrenaline-pen answer is person data — it is — or the grading on the audit trail was wrong. The raise narrows nothing: D-061 stands, an event's organizers read that event's answers with no additional gate, and all that changed is what a reviewer should notice before ticking the box for the grant that reaches thirty volunteers — and since D-102 there is a box to tick: the seeded grant above, rather than a clause in a resolver nobody can read.

Which leaves the discipline exactly where it was, and says so plainly: the rule that only preference-level detail belongs on a form is guidance on the form's label and nothing more. No layer enforces it and no layer can: nothing distinguishes "vegetarian" from "carries an adrenaline pen" to a database (../data-model/08-events.md §7). It rests entirely on whoever writes the form — a convention, not a guard, and D-072's own sentence is the right way to read that.

docs.title: 9. There is no dependent.* namespace
docs.text:
Eighteen codes deleted by D-074. A guardian's rights are none, view, or write — one value on the guardianship row, not a capability list. Nothing in this namespace may be reinstated by pattern-matching the old names; there is no set of codes left for a name to stand for.

Old code Became dependent.profile.view, dependent.contact.view, dependent.membership.view, dependent.event.view, dependent.fee.view, dependent.medical.view, dependent.achievement.view, dependent.document.view view — all of them, together. They can no longer be separated dependent.profile.admin, dependent.contact.manage, dependent.medical.admin, dependent.consent.admin write dependent.membership.request, dependent.event.register, dependent.event.answer, dependent.fee.pay, dependent.consent.give write — an act is not a narrower category than an edit dependent.admin Nothing. There is no set left to be a shorthand for

What is lost, stated as plainly as it should be. A court order restricting one parent's access to a child's medical record while leaving everything else in place cannot be expressed. "Read-only, but not the medical file" cannot be expressed. A grandmother granted roster visibility and nothing else is now a view guardian, which reaches the fee history and everything else the system holds about that child. The old namespace existed for exactly these cases, and D-074 traded them for a vocabulary a volunteer treasurer can hold in their head.

The separation was then declined, not merely left unimplemented — and the difference matters to anyone reading this table as a to-do list. D-083 put the court-order story to the organization directly and it was refused on the merits ("medical data is not different in any way"), and the same answer removed the referent: there is no medical record inside the person record to be shut out of, because everything other than name, gender and age is one class of data reached by person.view and governed by the guardian's right level whole (../domain/08-person-data.md). So "read everything except the diagnoses" is not a sentence waiting on a mechanism somebody has yet to build; it is a sentence the organization declined to want, which is why E-7 closed as a dissolved question rather than an answered one. Read the inexpressibility above as settled, not as pending work.

What still holds:

  • ~~write ranks at contribute (20), not manage.~~ Withdrawn by D-099: there is no ladder for it to rank on, and the bullet's real content was never its rung. What it was guarding is untouched by D-099 — a guardian cannot do organization-wide things, and cannot reach a different dependent's records: authority is per guardianship row, because the channel is entered by whose record the act touches and answers only about that row (D-079). What write now means is this row's dependent, both kinds: it covers the write codes and the read ones, where view covers only read and none covers nothing — compared against permission.right_kind, not against a level (§6).
  • The deny is untouched. A live deny beats every allow that applies, at any scope, in any channel (D-032's first half, now its entire content, restated by D-099), so "this guardian, nothing" remains expressible — a deny at the unit aimed at the person, PERSON(x). There is no "that child's guardians" operand to aim one at, and round 13 settled that there never was one to have: the channel resolves no sets, so the name an expression can carry here is the person's (D-113). What was lost is a narrow deny, not the ability to refuse.
  • A guardianship at none grants literally nothing, so being a guardian still grants nothing by itself — the safeguarding property that motivated the eighteen codes survives without them.
  • Answers to an event's questions are still read through event.answer.view, which is a permission on the grant side, carried by the seeded grant to ORGANIZERS (§8a), and never was a guardian one (D-061).

If the split turns out to matter in operation it is still a new decision — one grant scope over a defined set of data, argued from the current documents — and not a restoration from this table.
