Underneath, integrity check 1 is the nightly net.

And this is F-10 shape 1, which is the problem. The overlap invariant needs an exclusion constraint over a range built from two columns; no ORM emits one (F-10), and F-10 is still open — nobody has ruled per shape which layer writes these. Three specific traps on the way to writing this one by hand:

  • Shape 1 is described in F-10 as "no two open rows overlap", and this rule is not that rule. Copying the shape as worded — a constraint scoped to rows with no valid_to — would permit a closed row and an open row for the same person and group to overlap, which is exactly the pair that makes "who was in this group in 2019?" have two answers. It is the same mistake §6a warns about from the other side: a conditioned constraint over unconditioned columns is a different rule. This one must be written over all rows.
  • valid_to is NULL for an open row, and the corpus refuses a sentinel date (03-membership.md §3), so the range cannot be built from the columns as they stand; it has to be built from an expression that supplies an upper bound. That is a second reason a generated schema will not have this constraint, and the reason the hand-written version is the deliverable rather than the annotation.
  • Half-open is part of the rule, not an implementation detail. A closed-open range ([from, to)) makes a leaving day and a joining day coexist, which is what §4's transfer relies on. An inclusive range refuses every transfer that happens on a single day and would be quietly loosened by whoever hits it.

Until that migration exists, this is a convention, not a guard — the phrase 00-conventions.md §6a reserves for exactly this case. It is stated here rather than softened because the alternative is a document that implies a database refuses overlapping rows when nothing yet does.

docs.title: 3. A group is an item: a grant can be written on one
docs.text:
person_group has a row in grant_scope_type, so a group is a thing a grant may be written on — which is how "these two people may work this group's roster" is said without inventing a scope (D-098). The scope types now are unit (not item-scoped, the organization itself), event, person_group, role, and document (deferred). role joins as an item for the same reason and by the same move (D-100).

Shape of grant on a group Reaches Written by at the unit, person_group.member.manage every group, existing and future — nothing stands between a unit-scope grant and an item after D-097 access_grant.create at the unit on one group, person_group.member.manage that roster only a holder of the code at the unit, or of a grant on that group either of the above, effect = deny defeats every allow that applies to that person, including ones written elsewhere, later, or by somebody else the same — denies are legal at the unit and on an item (D-099)

person_group.member.manage is therefore applies_to = unit_and_item on the permission row (D-099): the two arms above are what that value is for. There is no self-scoped variant and none will be added — nobody writes themselves onto a roster (D-095, transferred intact in D-098).

The same group is also a leaf in an expression. GROUP(name) names this table's set, and the set is the member rows live on the date being checked (D-101; storage of the expression tree is not this page's subject). Three consequences worth stating next to the table they touch:

  • Membership confers nothing. The group is a set; a set is not a grant, and reaching a person through GROUP(x) happens only because some grant's expression says so (D-005).
  • An operand that does not resolve is the empty set. A deleted group id, an orphaned argument, a broken expression: it reaches nobody, and the answer is denial. Fail closed in every direction, as the resolver's rules already require. GROUP(nonexistent) is not an error at check time and must never become a permissive default.
  • The polymorphic id has no foreign key, exactly as access_grant.scope_id accepted it (D-011), and the compensating orphan check is specified once in 05-authorization.md §11. This page does not re-state it.

Ending a group is refused at save while something live names it, and the reason is the subtraction, not the grant. D-103 rules it for audiences — an audience may not be ended or deleted while a live grant, or a live audience reachable from a live grant, names it — and extends the same refusal to person_group in the round after, on identical reasoning. The reverse lookup is the audience arm's own query, one index: audience_operand rows whose selector_kind = 'GROUP', together with the grants whose scope is the group. Why a refusal, and not the report this page first wrote: an empty set is not neutral. A grant that merely has an ended group as its scope reaches nobody and is dead weight on the allow side, of the kind D-099 already reports for denies that deny nothing; named inside an expression the same emptiness points the other way, because EVERYONE - GROUP(x) with an empty GROUP(x) denies everybody. One field set on one group's row would then silently widen a deny that somebody else wrote, inside a grant the person who ended the group may never open. The refusal has two arms and the second is the one people forget, because it is not about ending anything: saving a new grant whose expression contains GROUP(x) for a group that is already ended is refused by the same rule, since the writer is pointing a live grant at an empty set, and EVERYONE - GROUP(x) is the same mistake arriving from the other end. A rule written only around the end-date field would leave that grant savable and this page's own report populated with something that looked allowed. The write path refuses both saves and integrity check 5 in §6 is the net beneath it — the split D-081 asks for, since a refusal that no code implements enforces nothing.

ROLE(x) needs no equivalent rule, and the difference is the shape of the set, not the idea of naming one. An office cannot be emptied quietly: there is no role.retire, no status column, and deleting a role is already refused while holder rows exist, so ending an office means ending role_holder rows one at a time, on a screen that shows each person. A group has a lifetime, and valid_to is one field that empties a set in one save. That is why the refusal names groups and audiences and not roles (D-103, whose own exception row states the point: the hazard is a property of the shape).

A group's set is stable across items, and that is worth one sentence of contrast. GROUP(x) means the same people whoever is being checked, so the grant editor's expansion of a group grant is per grant; the operands that bind to the item (PLACED, ORGANIZERS, …) mean different people on different events and must be previewed per item (D-102). The presence operand is not among them: PRESENT(<event>) over was_present is refused, because a column that is NULL until somebody takes a register would revoke a child's access to their own photos because a volunteer forgot a tick box.

A deny that matches no live allow is dead weight and is reported — the check is specified in 05-authorization.md §11 and applies to group-scope denies as to any other, because a deny that denies nothing is how a stale restriction survives its reason (D-099).

docs.title: 4. Joins, leaves and transfers: close one row, open another
docs.text:
Every change to a roster is a period ending and a period beginning. Nothing on a member row is edited to move a person anywhere. The discipline is 03-membership.md §5.2's, retargeted at groups and otherwise unchanged, and it carries the same design rule the deleted participation section carried:

Never rewrite a member row to point at a different person or a different group. Close it and open a new one. Rewriting destroys the answer to "where was this child in 2003?" — and unlike most tempting edits, this one leaves no bad row behind, only a history that quietly stopped being true.

Change The write Rows afterwards Someone joins insert one row, valid_from = the day, added_by = the writer 1 Someone leaves set valid_to on the open row — the only in-place edit this table permits, and only on the row that is open 1 They come back later insert a second row. Never reopen the first, never extend it 2 They move from group A to group B on 1 June close A's row with valid_to = 1 June, open B's row with valid_from = 1 June 2, one in each group A group splits in two create the two groups, insert member rows for whoever is in each, move whatever grants name the old one, and only then end it — valid_to is refused while a live grant or expression names the group (§3). No edge connects them — see §1's absence table old group closed, two open A name comes back years later a new person_group row (§1) 2 groups, same name, no relation

Half-open is what makes the transfer row land on one day. A row ending on 1 June and a row beginning on 1 June do not overlap, so a handover has no gap and no double-count, and no one has to invent a midnight.

A row is written by a person, and that is the whole of how the roster gets populated. The import owes no member rows and nothing is inferred from attendance, from an event, or from a unit that no longer exists (D-092, D-097). The gate is person_group.member.manage, at the unit or on one group (§3), the write is audited, and the row names who wrote it — which is D-095's answer to do not place a child where nobody is responsible for them, retold with the table changed and the reasoning untouched (D-081).

Two things the deleted table could say that this one cannot, on purpose. No join_reason_code / leave_reason_code — so no transfer, promotion, reorganisation, unit_closed vocabulary to maintain, get wrong, or pretend is a safeguard (the eighteen-ticks-without-a-receipt shape D-095 removed). No role_in_unit display label, because a label like that always becomes an authorization check the moment somebody asks "can she edit the roster?". The note column is where any of that reasoning goes, as prose, unread by the resolver (D-098).

There used to be a second dated set of people beside this one, and the argument for keeping them apart is worth keeping even though one of them is gone. audience_member held the names somebody typed into one audience; it was the same shape D-080 teaches a reader to distrust, and this page argued at length that the two must never be merged, because merging them would make the permission table the system's roster. D-105 deleted that table and its LIST operand — a hand-named person is now a PERSON(x) leaf inside the expression itself — so the duplication is gone rather than reconciled, and one of the two tables D-080 would have flagged no longer exists to be flagged.

What did not go is the hazard, and it is the reason this paragraph survives its subject. The temptation when a grant needs one more person is to add that person to a group, because a group is the thing with a roster editor. That is still refused, and for the same reason D-098 gave: a group's rows are true when no grant points at them, so editing one to move one grant's reach edits a roster that other grants read, and it invents a group nobody talks about. Since D-105 the refusal has a clean alternative next to it instead of a competing table: write PERSON(honza) in the expression that needed him, where it is visible, dated by the grant that carries it, and meaningless outside it (D-101).

docs.title: 5. What this page held before round 10
docs.text:
The ledger, so that a reader who arrives from an old link or an old report knows what happened. Every row is a deletion, not a move, unless the last column says otherwise.

Deleted With it goes Who enforces the surviving rule now org_unit the root row, the single-root conditional uniqueness, path, depth, status, code, data_confidence, the closed-without-end-date check nothing enforces "there is one unit" — there is no row to violate it with. That is the replacement, not a gap org_unit_type, org_unit_type_rule the runtime vocabulary, is_leaf, max_depth, the seven-step ordered nesting check, allows_minors' last context no nesting to check. Do not place a child where nobody is responsible is person_group.member.manage (§4) org_unit_name rename and renumber history, change_reason, the denormalised org_unit.name and the write rule that paired them nothing. A group rename edits one column and the previous name is gone (§1) org_unit_relationship split_from, merged_into, successor_of, renamed_to, and D-096's only home nobody. A split is an ended group and two begun groups, with no edge (§4); where a claimed continuity goes is undecided (§8) unit_participation sub-unit rosters, the root participation row every membership owed, is_primary, role_in_unit, the reason codes, and the transfers between units person_group_member (§2) is the roster; the membership row in 03-membership.md is the membership. Moved, not deleted — the only row in this table that is scope_exposure, scope.expose, scope.exposure.review the only downward crossing, the direction-of-authority check, and the nightly alert that was its sole detector nobody. There is no "outside it" to be stopped from (D-097); what D-031's reasoning still supports is carried by deny-is-absolute and by the ownership and guardianship channels unit_ancestors(), unit_descendants(), the materialized path the recursive walk, the path-consistency check, and the CI assertion that the resolver never calls the function nothing, and an assertion about a function that does not exist is not a guard the reparenting guard on parent_unit_id F-10 shape 4, and with it the whole class — see below nothing, because there is nothing to guard position, position_assignment is_leadership, max_holders, min_age, requires_membership, appointment_reference, the holder-count check, and the appointment workflows (D-100) role_holder in 05-authorization.md §4; the membership test is an operand, not a resolver clause; the last stored eligibility rule in this module is gone, so eligibility is capability and age is nobody's check (D-060)

Shape 4 has no instance, and the sentence is worth its weight. F-10 shape 4 — a column that may not change once set — is the only shape in that list with no report at all, because a violation leaves every row individually valid and satisfies every constraint; nothing can be compared afterwards, so the guard in the write path is the entire enforcement and the test that attempts the update is the only remaining evidence it was meant to stay. Its one instance in the whole design was org_unit.parent_unit_id. It has none now. Two consequences, in both directions: this document no longer contains a rule that nothing can enforce, which is a real gain nobody counted (D-097 calls it the one thing that got easier); and F-10 loses its sharpest example, so the question stays open on the strength of shapes 1–3 alone — of which shape 1 has a fresh occupant, §2.

Checks 1–10 of the old §9, and where each went. The numbering restarts in §6 because almost none of them has a subject:

Old check Fate 1 stored path vs. actual tree dead — no path, no tree 2 live unit under a closed parent dead — no nesting 3 live unit with no current name row dead — no name table, no denormalised copy 4 org_unit.name disagreeing with the open name row dead — same reason. This pair was "the one to read every morning"; there is nothing left to drift 5 a live unit type with no nesting rules dead — no types 6 a position assignment pairing a position with a unit of another type dead — positions are deleted (D-100) 7 a unit with exactly one live child dead — no children 9 a position holding more people than its own limit dead with max_holders. Note what this retires: it was the report that was supposed to be the second half of F-10 shape 3's remedy, and the document's own sharpest admission of a rule that might not be enforced at all 10 the single-root constraint really exists in the schema dead with the constraint — the check whose peculiar job was asserting that a migration had emitted a guarantee rather than that any row was clean

(There was no old check 8; the numbering had a hole in it from an earlier round. The list below is numbered from 1 and is contiguous, which is the point of this note.)

Check 10's pattern survives even though check 10 does not. A CI assertion that a guarantee exists, rather than that the data looks fine, has a new occupant: names unique across person_group and role cannot be carried by any constraint, so the write path carries them and something has to assert that the write path still does (D-081's rule, D-101's requirement). That is check 4 below.

docs.title: 6. Integrity checks
docs.text:
Invariants to verify

  1. Two member rows for the same person and group covering the same date (§2). Counts overlapping pairs over all rows, half-open, so it agrees with the constraint it is the net beneath. §2 names the migration as the enforcing layer; this report is what notices if that migration was never written, which — F-10 being unanswered — is the state of things today.
  2. A member row lying outside its group's own period (§2). A list to read rather than a breach: the two periods are two facts and containment is assumed here, not ruled (Status: assumption — §8). A large count means people are editing old rows instead of opening new ones.
  3. A group name that collides — with another group, with a role, with a set audience.code, or with a reserved selector_type.code (§1). Reports the collisions the write path should have refused; a non-zero count means a path exists that bypasses it, which in a system with an import, a data fix and a second client is a question of when.
  4. The cross-table name rule is still carried by the write path (§1). Not a data report: an automated test that attempts to save a duplicate name, and a second that attempts MEMBERS, and expects both refusals. No constraint can hold this rule, so if the code loses it, nothing else notices — the same job the retired check 10 did for the single-root constraint, and the reason it is numbered here rather than left to the test suite's own memory.
  5. A live grant whose scope is a group that has ended, or a live expression with a GROUP(x) leaf on one. The same number, and a different kind of check: this one used to watch a rule nobody had made and now watches one that has been made. D-103 refuses the end date at save while a live grant, or a live audience reachable from a live grant, names the group; §3 states the rule, the query behind it, and why an empty operand on the - side is dangerous rather than merely inert. What the report still earns is D-081's half of the arrangement — the refusal is application code, and application code loses things. Two causes put a row on this list and both are now regressions: either the write path stopped refusing the end, which means fixing the code and then the rows; or the grant was written onto a group that was already ended — a direction the rule needed saying twice, because a constraint on ending alone would leave this report full of behaviour that looked permitted (D-103 refuses both). That second cause is why the question about hiding ended groups from pickers (§8) is not cosmetic. Read the leaves sitting inside a subtraction first: EVERYONE - GROUP(ended) denies everybody, where the same ended group as a plain scope denies nobody.
  6. An open group with no open member rows for a long period. A data-quality list in the family the old check 7 was: often legitimate (a project group between seasons), sometimes a group that ended and nobody set valid_to. Nothing should reject it; somebody should be able to see it.

Checks 1 and 4 fail on different things and must not be read alike. Check 1 finds bad rows; check 4 finds a missing guarantee while every row is still clean. Only check 4 belongs in CI.

What this section no longer contains, and why that is not an oversight: path consistency, nesting legality, name denormalisation drift, holder-limit overrun and the single-root constraint assertion — the five subjects are gone, and §5 says which decision took each.

docs.title: 7. Seed data
docs.text:
No group is seeded, and that is the decision rather than a gap. The seed ships zero person_group rows. The corpus names no groups, so there is nothing to import and nothing to infer (D-092); a seeded group would be an invented one, which is the exact error D-054 recorded about the unit vocabulary — a wrong vocabulary in seed data is harder to dislodge than an absent one. Groups are runtime data, exactly as role is (D-052): the organization creates them, names them in its own words, and ends them.

The one set people expect to find here is a role, and it is not on this page. counselors ships as a role with is_system so an editor refuses to delete it (D-100): a permanent, organization-wide population is the opposite of what a group is. The seeded grant event.answer.view on an event to ORGANIZERS is likewise not here (§3 explains why a group is an item; D-102 owns that row).

What the old seed said, for the record. Two rows and nothing else: one unit type for the organization itself, and the single root unit carrying it. Neither exists. There is no root row to create and no type to give it; the unit arrives as a code in grant_scope_type, which is a lookup row in the authorization module and not data this page seeds. The old §10's long note about the root type's allows_minors = false asserting the opposite of what the membership flow does — the correction D-095 made by deleting the column — is retired with the column, and the paragraph's real lesson survives where it was written: a seed that contradicts the runtime behaviour is worse than no seed.

docs.title: 8. Open issues
docs.text:
• Where a claimed group continuity is recorded. §1 states the default (a returning name is a new group) and D-096's method says the continuity is asserted, never matched — but the table that accepted the assertion is deleted and D-098 refuses group-to-group edges. Tracked in ../open-questions.md.
  • Whether a member row must lie inside its group's period. Assumed in §2, reported in §6 check 2, and nowhere ruled. A one-sentence decision either way; left open rather than decided by a document.
  • Which layer writes the no-overlap constraint. That is F-10, still open, and §2 spells out the three ways this particular instance of shape 1 gets written wrong if nobody answers it (../open-questions.md).
  • Whether an ended group is hidden from pickers, and whether it may be reopened. Closed units had a stated behaviour; person_group has a period and no rule about which screens read it. Reopening an ended group by clearing valid_to would also collide with §1's rule that a returning name is a new group, so the two questions are one question.

Resolved and no longer open, kept visible so the reasoning survives: the sub-unit vocabulary and the nesting rules (there is no structure — D-097, closing the question D-054 had left open); retroactive reparenting (the dimension is gone, so the question cannot be asked, let alone answered — D-036); organization-wide operational roles (the unit is the only scope, so there is no "wider" to be organization-wide against); whether the unit may read into what these docs used to call its sub-units (moot after D-097 — the question presumed two scopes and there is one, and it used to be this page's largest open item); whether allows_minors should also constrain positions (both columns are deleted — D-095, D-100); whether is_leadership should create a role assignment (positions are deleted, and a role now confers nothing at all — D-100); background checks (none are recorded — D-043); whether a group may be ended while a live grant, or a live audience reachable from one, names it (refused at save — D-103 wrote its audience row first and extended it to person_group in the round after, on the --widens reasoning; §3 and §6 check 5); whether a PERSON selector should exist so that D-100's one-person exemption is writable (it is one of the fourteen seeded rows — thirteen until D-105 removed LIST, twelve until D-107 added OLDER and YOUNGER — and it arrived late by D-101's amendment, because the registry had been copied from the evaluator's arm list and lost the arm, which D-104 is the answer to); and whether a hand-typed set of people needs a table of its own (no — D-105 deleted audience_member, and the round that added PERSON(x) had already removed the only reason it had for existing).

All tracked in ../open-questions.md.

docs.title: Data Model — Membership
docs.text:
membership_type, membership, and membership_request.

unit_participation used to be documented here and no longer is — the table is deleted, together with every sub-unit it pointed at (D-097). §5 is where that is recorded and where the discipline it carried is retargeted at groups. Belonging to the organization is a membership; belonging to a group is person_group_member, specified in the groups module.

Domain rationale: ../domain/05-membership-lifecycle.md.

docs.title: 1. membership_type — one row, kept as a table
docs.text:
Fields

Field Kind Notes code text, required 'member' — and nothing else, for now. name text, required description text, optional duration_months integer, required, defaults to 12 12: the fee is yearly. Kept as a column rather than a constant so a type with a different term could be added as a row, with no migration. expiry_month, expiry_day integers, required, both defaulting to 1 When the fee expires (D-047): 1 January. The organizational year runs with the calendar, so "a member this year" means what a reader expects, and the sweep, the campaign and the reports all land on a boundary nobody has to look up. These are columns, not a constant in a scheduled job, for the reason the user gave for the window below: the date is a parameter the organization may move, and moving it must not require a code change. Every lapse date, the yearly sweep and the renewal worklist derive from these two values. renewal_grace_days integer, required, defaults to 60 The renewal window after valid_to, during which a payment restores the membership without re-applying and backdates the new period to the expiry date. Dates, not a status: the person is expired throughout (D-040). 60 days (D-048). Read it from here; never hardcode 60 in a job or a front end (D-048). The requirement attached to that answer was precisely that the value stays tunable. is_self_registerable boolean, required, defaults to true requires_approval boolean, required, defaults to true sort_order integer rank, required, defaults to 0 valid_from, valid_to period (from/to, open-ended allowed); both ends optional created_at timestamp, audit time

Rules

  • code is unique over all rows.
  • expiry_month is between 1 and 12; expiry_day is between 1 and 31.
  • Where both ends of the period are set, valid_to is later than valid_from. Either end may be absent, and no comparison is attempted when one is.

docs.title: Why this table still exists with one row
docs.text:
There is exactly one membership (D-037). Everyone who is a member holds membership_type = 'member', the fee is flat and per person, and being a counselor or a leader is a role, never a type (D-100).

The table survives rather than collapsing into a constant for two reasons:

  1. Consistency with the design's own principle. Vocabularies are rows, not enums — the same argument that keeps the seeded registries as tables (grant_scope_type, selector_type; the two examples this bullet used to give, org_unit_type and position, were both deleted in round 10 by D-097 and D-100). A second kind of membership (a supporting or honorary one) would then be a data change.
  2. A place for the organizational calendar to live. The term, the expiry date and the renewal window are genuinely type-dependent parameters even when there is one type — and they are the parameters most likely to be tuned. Putting them in a row rather than in code is what makes "it should not be hard to modify" (D-048) true by construction rather than by discipline.

The cost is honest and small: an FK that currently always holds one value. Recorded here rather than hidden.

docs.title: What was removed, and why
docs.text:
Removed Reason category (child/adult/special) Membership is ageless (D-038). Age is a fact about the person. min_age, max_age No age floor, ceiling, or automatic age-out. requires_background_check The system records no background checks (D-043). requires_references, requires_guardian_consent Nothing gates a request but identity and payment (D-044). allows_concurrent With one type and a person-scoped overlap constraint, this cannot arise. grace_period_days (as a status) Replaced by renewal_grace_days — a window, not a state (D-040). fee_schedule_id The fee is flat and per person (D-037), so there is nothing type-specific to schedule. The schedule attaches to the obligation instead — 07-finance.md §2.

The age checks that used to sit on the type go with them (ck_membership_type_ages was their name). With no ages on the row there is nothing for a migration to express and nothing left for a report to verify, so the removal is complete rather than a rule left hanging.

docs.title: 2. membership_request
docs.text:
Fields

Field Kind Notes id surrogate id Internal only. public_id uuid, required, generated The identifier used outside the system; unique. person_id reference to person, required The subject: the person who would become a member. For a minor's application this is the child, not the parent. submitted_by_person_id reference to person, optional Who actually submitted it. Equals person_id for self-application; differs when a guardian (or staff) applies on behalf. This is the act-on-behalf record. requested_membership_type_id reference to membership_type, required status text, required, defaults to draft One of draft, submitted, under_review, approved, rejected, withdrawn, expired. submitted_at timestamp, optional decided_at timestamp, optional decided_by reference to person, optional rejection_reason_code text, optional rejection_note text, optional membership_id reference to membership, optional Set on approval. The reference is added only once membership exists (§3): this is the design's circular pair, resolved with a deferred reference. previous_membership_id reference to membership, optional Links a renewal or re-application to the prior membership. This is how a returning member's chain is expressed. expires_at timestamp, optional An unreviewed request eventually goes stale. Needed so the review queue does not accumulate abandoned drafts forever. notes text, optional source text, optional self, guardian, staff or import. created_at, created_by, updated_at, updated_by timestamp, audit time; reference to person The standard audit columns.

Rules

  • A request in approved or rejected has both decided_at and decided_by. There is no decision without a decider and a time.
  • Any request that is not draft has a submitted_at.
  • An approved request points at a membership. The one allowance is a request decided at a time still in the future, which is how the request and the membership are inserted in two steps inside one transaction; the link is not optional once that transaction is over.
  • At most one open request per person per membership type. Open means draft, submitted or under_review. Decided requests — approved, rejected, withdrawn, expired — are outside the rule, which is what lets a person apply again after being turned down.

Indexes

  • On person_id with submitted_at descending: one person's applications, newest first.
  • A partial index over the review queue only — rows in submitted or under_review, which is the whole queue and nothing else.
  • On submitted_by_person_id, covering only the rows where that optional column is actually set.

person_id vs submitted_by_person_id is the most important pair in this table. The subject is the child; the submitter is the parent. Collapsing them into one column — which is what most systems do — makes it impossible to answer "who applied for this child?" and falsely attributes the parent's action to the child. See ../domain/02-actors.md.

Why requests are a separate table from memberships. A rejected request produces no membership and must not pollute member listings; a person may submit several over time; and review data (who decided, why) has no meaning on a membership. See ../domain/05-membership-lifecycle.md.

A request asks for membership of the unit, and names nothing else. requested_unit_id is deleted (D-098), along with the index over it. ~~The applicant may express a preference, or the organization may assign the unit at approval.~~ Withdrawn by D-098, which also removed the thing the column could have referenced (D-097). The want behind it is real — a reviewer would like to know where the applicant expects to turn up — and it is served by the free-text notes the row already has, which is what the field always actually was: a sentence addressed to whoever reads the request, carrying no authority. Placing the person is a separate act and a separate row — one person_group_member row, written by a person holding person_group.member.manage — and an approved request with no group beside it is a complete, ordinary outcome. Which group a new member lands in is a write on the group, not a preference on the request.

A rejection requires a reason code (ck_request_rejection_reason is the rule's name): no rejected request may be written without one. Two columns of the same row, so a migration can state it directly as a check on the row — and it belongs there rather than only in the model layer, because the two paths that most need catching, an import and a hand-corrected row, never reach a model-layer guard. "Why was this application turned down?" is asked months later, sometimes by the family. A rejection with no recorded reason is an answerable question made unanswerable.

previous_membership_id is what makes the returning-member chain explicit rather than inferred from date arithmetic.

docs.title: 3. membership
docs.text:
Fields

Field Kind Notes id surrogate id Internal only. public_id uuid, required, generated The identifier used outside the system; unique. person_id reference to person, required membership_type_id reference to membership_type, required status text, required One of pending_payment, active, suspended, lapsed, terminated, completed. No default — the state is always chosen deliberately. valid_from date, required valid_to date, optional NULL = open / current. Never NULL on an imported row — both ends are what makes an imported membership safe, and check 1 of 06-audit-and-import.md §5 counts the rows that broke it (D-093). joined_via_request_id reference to membership_request, optional renewed_from_membership_id self-reference to membership (the previous one), optional Forms the renewal chain. See domain/05 §6. outstanding_balance money amount, optional Denormalised from fee_obligation/payment. 07-finance.md §3 recommends dropping this column in favour of v_fee_obligation_balance — a wrong balance suspends the wrong child. Kept here only until that decision is taken. NULL on every imported row, and since D-093 put memberships back into the import that is load-bearing rather than incidental: the export carries no payment data, and a zero would be a claim — settled — that the export does not support. There is no fee_obligation underneath these rows either, which is what makes the NULL unambiguous rather than merely uncomputed (07-finance.md §2, D-090). termination_reason_code text, optional termination_note text, optional ended_by reference to person, optional ended_at timestamp, optional data_confidence text, required, defaults to high One of high, medium, low. import_batch_id reference to the import batch, optional Set on imported rows. notes text, optional created_at, created_by, updated_at, updated_by timestamp, audit time; reference to person The standard audit columns.

Rules

  • Where both ends of the period are set, valid_to is later than valid_from.
  • A terminated membership has both a termination_reason_code and an ended_at.
  • A membership may not be renewed from itself: renewed_from_membership_id never points at its own row.
  • THE critical rule — one person, one membership, full stop. Two rows for the same person may not cover the same date while either of them is pending_payment, active or suspended. Periods are half-open, so one ending on a day and another beginning on that day do not collide. Statuses outside those three are outside the rule entirely, and the rule reaches every person regardless of membership type — the type is not part of it, and that omission is deliberate, as the next section explains.

Indexes

  • ix_membership_current — per person, over rows that are open and active. The membership gate reads through this, and it is the index a far-future sentinel date would defeat — see Why valid_to IS NULL and not a sentinel below.
  • On valid_to over active rows that have one. This drives the renewal worklist: who expires soon, who is in their renewal window.
  • On (status, valid_to) over active and pending_payment rows — the states anyone is actually queried in.
  • On person_id with valid_from descending, and a period index per person: one person's membership history, and the range scan the overlap rule and every point-in-time question use.

docs.title: The constraint dropped membership_type_id — that is the point
docs.text:
The old constraint was scoped to the type, to permit an honorary member who is also an active member. With one membership type (D-037) that case cannot arise, so the type is gone from the constraint and "one person, one open membership" becomes an enforceable invariant rather than a convention. It is conditional uniqueness — one open row per person — which is the shape 00-conventions.md §6a says a migration must emit by hand: a unique constraint over all rows is a different rule and the wrong one, because it forbids the second closed membership that the person's history requires.

This is what makes is_current_member() a question about one row, one status, one date, rather than one that has to reconcile three concurrent memberships. That is worth keeping in mind now that the predicate's consumer has changed: the resolver no longer calls it per grant, because the membership gate left the resolver for the MEMBERS selector (§6, D-100), but MEMBERS is evaluated live on the checked date and evaluates to exactly this predicate. The constraint is what makes that evaluation cheap and unambiguous either way.

docs.title: renewed_from_membership_id and the renewal window
docs.text:
When a person pays inside the renewal window (D-040), the new membership's valid_from is set to the previous row's valid_to, not to the payment date. Two consequences worth stating:

  • The history shows continuous coverage — no gap, no spurious "returning member".
  • The person is nevertheless expired during the window (D-040). The two facts are compatible because the window is a date range, not a status: they were not a member while it was open, and the record of that period is filled in retrospectively once they pay. Nothing needs backdating in the audit sense, because the new row's as-of start is the expiry date and its audit time is the payment date — the two-times distinction in 00-conventions.md.

A payment after the window opens the new membership at the payment date, and the gap is real.

docs.title: The exclusion constraint and status transitions
docs.text:
The overlap rule covers only pending_payment, active, suspended. A terminated/lapsed/completed row is excluded, so a new membership can be created with a valid_from inside an old one's period without violating the constraint. This is deliberate — a returning member's new membership may legitimately overlap the tail of a lapsed one if the dates were entered imprecisely. Historical imports rely on this.

Consequence: the constraint does not prevent two active memberships with overlapping periods if one was inserted while in another status and then transitioned. A status update re-evaluates the constraint (PostgreSQL does check exclusion constraints on UPDATE), so this is safe — but the transition from lapsed back to active can therefore fail with a constraint violation. That is correct behaviour: it means the person has two overlapping claims to membership and someone must resolve it. Handle it as a business error, not a crash.

Which layer carries all of that: the migration. A status transition that re-checks the overlap is only a violation if the constraint is in the database, and no ORM emits an exclusion over a period assembled from valid_from and valid_to scoped to three statuses — the migration writes it, as 00-conventions.md §6a requires. The same check performed in the model layer returns a friendlier message a moment earlier and guarantees nothing: a batch that imports the legacy people export writes memberships by the thousand again. D-090 took that sentence away last round, on the reading that the corpus produces participations only, and D-093 gives it back; §5 keeps the record of both readings. Round 10 removes the participations altogether (D-097), and the argument here never depended on them: it rests on the memberships the people export produces, and on the hand-corrected row that never passes through the model layer either. Both meet the constraint in the database; neither would ever meet a model-layer check.

docs.title: Why valid_to IS NULL and not a sentinel
docs.text: Repeated from the conventions because it is the mistake most likely to be made here. A '9999-12-31' sentinel breaks IS NULL checks, makes daterange spans enormous, and defeats the ix_membership_current partial index. Use NULL.

docs.title: renewed_from_membership_id
docs.text:
Renewal opens a new row (Shape A in ../domain/05-membership-lifecycle.md). The self-reference makes the chain explicit:

membership 501  member  1990-09-01 → 1991-06-30   completed
     ↑ renewed_from
membership 502  member  1991-09-01 → 1992-06-30   completed
     ↑ renewed_from
membership 503  member  1992-09-01 → 1993-06-30   completed
(The type is member on every row — there is only one type, and the person's age is not part of it: §1, D-037, D-038.)

"Why does this person have 15 membership rows?" is then answerable by following the chain rather than by reasoning about dates. And a gap — a missing link — is visible as data.

docs.title: Current-membership queries
docs.text:
Five questions the membership table has to answer, each with the exact rule that decides it. The wording of each is load-bearing; the differences between them are the design.

  • Is this person a member right now? is_current_member(person) — true when they have a membership whose status is active and whose period covers today: valid_from on or before today, valid_to absent or after today. No grace coalescing: a lapsed membership is lapsed, and the renewal window (domain/05 §6) is a date range for rejoining, not a state in which the person is a member. This predicate is what the MEMBERS selector evaluates on the checked date (§6) — it is no longer called by the resolver on someone else's behalf, which changes its callers and not its meaning.
  • Was this person a member on a given past date? was_member_on(person, date) — true when a membership of theirs covers that date, on the same half-open terms, and its status is anything except pending_payment. Note the asymmetry with the question above: now demands active, then admits every terminal status, because how a membership ended does not change that it existed.
  • When does the organizational year containing a date expire? membership_expiry_date(as_of) — expiry_month and expiry_day read off the member row, applied to the year of as_of. Always derived from those two columns and never from a constant (D-047).
  • May this person renew without re-applying? in_renewal_window(person, as_of) — true when they have a membership of theirs that has ended (valid_to set) with valid_to on or before as_of, and valid_to plus that type's renewal_grace_days still after as_of; in other words the window is [expiry, expiry + grace), half-open like every other period here. No status is consulted — this is arithmetic on dates alone. D-040: expired, but inside the window. This is the distinction a grace_period_days membership status would have blurred: they are not a member, and they may rejoin cheaply. 60 days, read from the row (D-048). Not a member during the window: this answers "may they rejoin cheaply?", never "do they have access?".
  • How long has this person been a member? membership_years(person) — the sum of the lengths of their memberships, with today standing in for an open valid_to and any pending_payment row left out, expressed in years of 365.25 days.

membership_years sums the periods rather than subtracting the first join date from today. The difference is the 14-year gap in the returning-member case, and getting it wrong mislabels a returning member as having 36 years of service.

current_member_category() is gone. It existed to answer "is this person currently a child or an adult?", which is no longer a question the membership table can answer, because membership is ageless (D-038). Age is a fact about the person:

Is this person a minor? is_minor(person, as_of) — true when person.birth_date is recorded and as_of falls before their eighteenth birthday. A person with no recorded birth date is not a minor by this test; nothing guesses one. A fact about the person, never about their membership.

This matters for guardianship and safeguarding, which are where age legitimately bears — not for whether someone may be a member.

docs.title: 4. No request requirements — removed entirely
docs.text:
requirement_code and membership_request_requirement do not exist (D-044).

Why. Your answer, asked what a membership request must contain in order to be accepted: "Just identity and the fee — nothing to verify." The option of keeping the mechanism as empty infrastructure was offered and not taken, so it is gone rather than left dangling.

What a request therefore is: a person, a submitted timestamp, a reviewer, a decision, and a payment. The membership_request table in §2 is complete as it stands — it never referenced requirements except through this table.

Guardian consent is unaffected. It was never a membership requirement; it belongs to the guardianship layer, where it is a relationship fact rather than a checklist item. See 04-relationships.md.

If a requirement ever appears — a form, an interview, a document — the honest starting point is to add the table back deliberately, with the requirement that made it necessary recorded as a decision. The removed design was general enough to carry one; it is recorded in the decision log rather than deleted from history.

docs.title: 5. unit_participation — deleted by D-097
docs.text:
Deleted by D-097. There is one unit, it is the organization, and it is a scope rather than a row — so there is no body below it to belong to, and no table to record belonging in. Everything the table carried goes with it: the sub-unit rosters, the root participation row every membership owed, the transfers between units, role_in_unit, the join_reason_code / leave_reason_code vocabulary, is_primary, and the data_confidence value those rows carried into an import.

Why it existed, kept because the reasoning outlives the table. ~~Belonging to a sub-unit is participation, not a species of membership~~ (D-041). The name unit_membership had been asserting otherwise, and the rename was the fix: a "unit membership" read as a second species of membership, which raised questions about which membership was which and whether a fee was owed twice, and participation removed the questions. That distinction is still true one level down — membership of a group confers nothing and owes nothing, no more than belonging anywhere else does, because participation is not authority and the fact that it is now stored in a tidier table does not quietly promote it (D-098, restating D-005). The same holds for the column this document argued hardest for: person_id, never membership_id, because a person may belong somewhere with no membership behind them and a row about 1998 must not become unrepresentable because the record of 1998 status is thin or absent. person_group_member is keyed on a person for that same reason and inherits the argument whole.

Where each question goes now (D-098) — two shapes, and no longer one shape with a depth in it:

Question Read Who is in the organization on date D? membership — one query over the period and status of §3 Who is in group G on date D? person_group_member — a point-in-time read over the dated rows, 02-organization.md §1

The one thing the deleted §5.1 bought was a single query shape for both rows of that table, and that is what is given up. What is given back is the redundancy: two tables kept in step only by an obligation on every writer, and a report watching for the writers who forgot.

docs.title: The write obligation is retired, and so is the check that watched it
docs.text:
The import owes no participation rows to anything (D-097). The old §5.1 required that no write may change a membership's period, or open or close one, without making the matching change to that person's root-unit participation row in the same transaction — two rows holding one fact — and integrity check 1b was the report that found whoever skipped it.

Who enforces that rule now: nobody, because there is nothing left to enforce. The second row is deleted, so the pairing is not a rule running without a guard, it is a redundancy that has been removed; membership is the single record and cannot disagree with a copy of itself. Both the obligation and check 1b retire rather than being restated somewhere else, which is the outcome D-081 asks for stated plainly rather than left as a silence.

Marked withdrawn rather than deleted, because this obligation was reversed twice inside three rounds and a reader is entitled to the whole record. ~~When a membership is created, a matching unit_participation row for the root unit is created over the same period, and similarly closed when the membership ends.~~ Round 8 corrected the section to say an ordinary import "touches neither arm of this pair", because a roster produced participations and no memberships; round 9 reversed the correction (D-093), because the corpus turned out to state membership periods after all; round 10 deleted the arm both readings were arguing about. Every step of round 8 was true of the input it was describing, and the input was described wrong (D-092). What each round got right and keeps is the framing rather than the conclusion: the obligation was never about one batch — import, renewal, extension and hand-corrected row each owed the paired write exactly as much — and the reason the answer moved twice is that nobody had read the file. That is worth remembering about imports in general, and the reversals are recorded against D-093 and the round-10 block rather than being quietly unwritten here.

~~The root row was the only participation row that is extended rather than closed and reopened~~ (D-050): the yearly sweep moved its open end to the expiry date and a renewal inside the window stretched the same row to the new period's end, so a person who lapsed and renewed looked exactly like one who never had. Withdrawn with the table, and the condition that made the match exact — the renewal beginning exactly where the row was swept to, matched by person and date because the row carried no membership reference — goes with it, as does the accepted cost that the lapse stopped being visible in the roster. What is worth keeping is why the trade was acceptable: the roster answers who was in this body when, and for that question a child who was there across the lapse has exactly one answer, while membership remains the authority on payment. With the row gone both facts live in membership alone; the renewal rule that backdates the new period is untouched (§3, and ../domain/05-membership-lifecycle.md §6).

docs.title: Moving between groups closes one row and opens another
docs.text:
D-098 retargets this section's discipline at groups and changes nothing else: moving a person from one group to another is two writes, closing one person_group_member row and opening another, never an edit of the group on the existing row. Close-and-open is what preserves "where was this child in 2003?"; an in-place update destroys it, and the whole temporal design exists to answer that question. Nothing about the person's membership, their fee, or their standing as a member changes, because moving was never a membership event — which is exactly the expense D-041 removed when it made belonging below the organization a different fact from being a member, and which is why the same discipline survives the move to a different table.

Who enforces it now. The close-and-open pair is the write path's, behind person_group.member.manage, audited and naming who wrote the row; the invariant underneath it — no two rows for one person and one group overlap, counted over all rows and not only the open ones, half-open so a row ending on a day and one beginning that day do not collide — is open question F-10 shape 1, which a hand-written migration emits and the ORM will not. A person who left in 2020 and came back in 2024 is therefore two rows, never one row edited in place: the edit destroys the answer to "was she in the group in 2019?". The groups module owns both, and this document does not re-specify them — 02-organization.md §1–§2 and ../domain/04-organization-structure.md.

What died with the unit version of this, named as a loss. A group that splits is an old group that ended and two that began, with no edge between them unless somebody writes one: org_unit_relationship's split_from / merged_into / successor_of are deleted, so restructuring has stopped being a recorded event (D-097's third loss). The bulk unit-reorganisation transfer — close and open across every member, with join_reason_code = 'reorganisation', as one named procedure with a dry run because it will be run over hundreds of rows — goes with it. There is no reorganisation to perform in one statement, and the lineage it recorded is now a thing a person would have to write down on purpose.

The other columns, given up rather than moved (D-098 lists them, and "no special features" was the instruction): no join_reason_code / leave_reason_code and so no transfer / promotion / reorganisation / unit_closed vocabulary to maintain or to get wrong, no is_primary saying which of a person's groups to show first, no role_in_unit display label, and no data_confidence with nothing left to import into — the corpus names no groups either, so every group member row is typed by a person, which is also the only way one can be true (D-092).

docs.title: 6. Membership and the authorization system
docs.text:
The resolver no longer asks whether you are a member. The grant does. This is the round's largest deletion (D-100), and it is still the single largest coupling between these two modules, so it is stated in full rather than in a footnote. What was withdrawn:

~~A role grants access ONLY IF the holder has a current membership,~~
    ~~unless  role.requires_membership = false    (appointed counselors, local leaders)~~
    ~~or      the channel is guardianship         (a legal relationship, not a membership)~~
    ~~or      the channel is ownership            (your own record — see below)~~

Withdrawn by D-100. The clause above ran on every grant the resolver examined, and it needed two escape mechanisms to be livable. MEMBERS is now a selector operand, evaluated live on the checked date, and the question "must this person be a current member to hold this?" is answered by whether the expression says so:

Old mechanism New expression The gate applied to a role with requires_membership = true MEMBERS * ROLE(x) The gate waived for a whole role ROLE(x) — write it without MEMBERS The gate waived for one named person (system.gate_exempt) MEMBERS * ROLE(x), plus a second grant for that one person

role.requires_membership, system.gate_exempt and person_holds_gate_exempt are all deleted, together with the resolver's membership clause and the special-case path that had to be carefully kept out of can(). Who enforces the rule now: whoever writes the grant, by putting MEMBERS in the expression or leaving it out, and the expression is a row that can be read.

Corrected in this round: an earlier draft of this page read D-100's PERSON(y) as shorthand for the audience's own LIST, on the grounds that the seeded selector_type registry did not carry the code. The registry was the side that was wrong — PERSON was seeded then, as the thirteenth row (data-model/05 §8, D-101's amendment), so MEMBERS * ROLE(x) + PERSON(y) parses as written. LIST was never a substitute, which was the part worth remembering at the time: it is one set belonging to one audience, so + LIST brings everybody on it and nothing on that list can except one person from itself. That confusion can no longer recur, because D-105 deleted LIST and its table in the round after this correction was written, leaving twelve seeded rows — fourteen since D-107 put age in the language — and one way to name a person by hand — which is the outcome the paragraph was arguing for, arrived at by deleting the thing it had to argue against. Writing the waiver as a second grant aimed at the person is still legal and still clearer for something permanent, and is now the only way to date it (D-105 §2).

Two of the three carve-outs were never carve-outs. Guardianship (a parent's authority comes from a legal relationship, and an unpaid fee must not stop a parent acting for their child) and ownership (otherwise a lapse locks a person out of the very screen they renew on) stay channels and are unaffected — they were never gated, whatever the shape of that block suggested. Only the third, the appointed counselors and local leaders the organization needs present regardless of their own fee status, was a real waiver of a real gate, and it is now the second row of the table: write the office without MEMBERS.

The posture reverses, and the new failure mode is named rather than buried. The gate was default-on, so forgetting it was impossible. It is now opt-in per grant: a grant written ROLE(TREASURERS) with no MEMBERS authorizes a lapsed member, silently, forever. Three controls, none of which is the resolver:

  • A standing report of live grants naming a ROLE(...) operand whose expression does not contain MEMBERS — check 1 of §7. An office held by a non-member is the case worth a human eye, and the report is narrow enough to actually be read.
  • Seeded grants and any grant template carry MEMBERS, so the path of least repetition is the safe path.
  • Import completeness. MEMBERS * COUNSELORS is only as correct as the counselor roster: the gate used to fall out of membership alone, so an import that misses 300 counselors silently un-gates them. It fails closed — nothing breaks, which is exactly why nobody notices — and the import reconciliation report of D-090 must count people marked as counselors in the corpus against role_holder rows written.

What still costs, unchanged by the move:

  • ~~The permission cache must be invalidated on every membership transition — including the yearly expiry sweep, which is a bulk event touching every member at once.~~ ~~The coupling did not leave with the resolver clause: MEMBERS is evaluated live, so a transition still changes who an expression reaches. The cache design has to be built for this from the start; retrofitting it is where the bugs will be.~~ This requirement is discharged by deletion, and it has to be struck rather than left as history, because it was a live instruction aimed at a table that no longer exists (D-114). Read it against the page it was aimed at. This sentence was written in the round that moved the membership gate out of the resolver, three rounds before D-111 wrote the cache policy — and when that policy was finally written, membership was not on its invalidation list, while membership.terminate is precisely the ⛔ action a concerned guardian waits for. The sentence here was right, the page it was asking for did not hear it, and the way to close a coupling like this one is not a louder requirement but an invariant that has nowhere to be violated: MEMBERS is evaluated live at the checked date, there is no answer stored to go stale, and D-111's claim that "the safeguarding case is immediate" is true here by construction instead of by trigger. ~~D-101 helps rather than excuses it — a cache may key on an operand and reuse it across every grant~~ — and the yearly expiry sweep keeps every other thing it had to do; what it no longer has to do is invalidate anything, because §11's invariant 19 forbids the row that would need it.
  • A lapse silently removes access — from exactly those grants whose expression names MEMBERS, and from none of the others. "Why can't I see this?" now has an answer that is a date and a line of grant text.

The "leaver with access" report remains valuable, and it is now two reports. D-071's posture transfers intact to role_holder: nothing forces a holder row to end, and the control is the report. Checks 1 and 2 of §7 are that control — one for grants that gate nothing, one for offices held by people who are not members.

Dormant authority is a real hazard, and slightly larger than it was. A membership that lapses and is renewed a year later resurrects every still-open role_holder row the person accumulated in the interim, including ones a human had quietly decided not to reinstate — and where the grant behind that role was written without MEMBERS, it was not dormant at all in the meantime, it was live. Closing the holder row at the same time as the membership is the honest fix; the reports find the ones that were missed. A role holder row should not outlive the membership that justified it.

A role is held at the unit and nowhere else. role_holder carries no scope columns, because D-097 left one scope; there is no body to hold an office of. The table, the ROLE(x) selector and the codes an office carries belong to 05-authorization.md §3 role and §4 role_holder.

docs.title: 7. Integrity checks
docs.text:
Invariants to verify. The numbering restarted at 1 this round. Every check below old 3 either lived or died with unit_participation, and leaving holes in a renumbered list is only honest while the surviving numbers still mean what their citations claim — which they no longer would. The retired numbers, and what happened to each, are listed after the live ones, because the decision log cites "integrity check 2 of 03-membership.md §7" by name and that citation should land on an explanation rather than on a gap.

  • 1. Live grants that gate nothing. Counts live grants whose audience expression names a ROLE(...) operand and does not contain MEMBERS — D-100's standing report, restated here because this is the module whose data it reads. Enforced by no layer, and no layer can: whether an office is written with MEMBERS is a choice made in the grant text, so the controls are this report, plus seeded grants and any template carrying MEMBERS so the common path is the gated one (§6). A non-zero count is not a fault — it is the list of offices worth a human eye, and it is narrow enough to actually be read.
  • 2. Non-members holding an office. Counts open role_holder rows whose holder is_current_member() says is not a member (§3). Enforced by nothing, deliberately: D-071's posture transfers to role_holder, so no constraint and no sweep ends a holder row and this report is the control. Read it with check 1, which says whether that role's grants are gated: on a gated role this is dormant authority that springs back to life at the next renewal, and on an ungated one it is access that is live today (§6). The old wording of this check — "the resolver blocks these, so it is not an access breach" — is the sentence the round retired, and it must not be copied forward.
  • 3. Approved requests that never produced a membership. Counts requests that are approved, carry no membership_id, and were decided more than seven days ago. Non-zero is an approval that went nowhere. Enforced by the §2 requirement that an approved request points at a membership once the deciding transaction is over — a deferred reference rather than a suggestion, and one a migration can state on the row.
  • 4. Memberships expiring soon. Counts active memberships ending within the next 90 days — the renewal campaign worklist (domain/05 §6), not a fault. Run by whoever runs the campaign; nothing here guards it, because there is nothing to guard.
  • 5. Renewal chains with a broken link. Counts memberships whose renewed_from_membership_id names a row that does not exist. Non-zero means the chain is followed into nothing. Enforced by the ordinary foreign key on that column, which any migration emits; the check survives as the assertion that the key is there, which is the form 00-conventions.md §6a prescribes for a constraint this project's ORM does not generate on its own.
  • 6. Renewals inside the window whose new period does not start at the previous expiry date. Counts renewals whose valid_from differs from the previous membership's valid_to and begins less than 91 days after it. The renewal rule (D-040) backdates the new period, so a mismatch means either a genuine post-window rejoin or a bug. Enforced by nothing: both answers are legal data, so only a report separates them, and only a reader decides which one it is looking at.

Checks 1 and 2 are the ones that matter now, and they are what the old check 3 became. The old check could assume the resolver had already handled access and confine itself to the stale row behind it; that assumption was the gate, and with the gate in the grant text the same predicate splits into a report about grants and a report about people. Neither one alone is the control.

Check 4 is operational (a worklist for the renewal campaign). The rest are data-quality checks for cases no constraint rejects at the write.

Two checks this module deliberately does not hold. The one D-099 asks for — a live deny whose grantee, scope and code match no live allow, and so denies nothing — is a report over grants, not over memberships, and belongs to 05-authorization.md §11. The no-overlap invariant over person_group_member belongs to the groups module, 02-organization.md §6. Naming both here is to stop either being written twice and drifting.

Retired with unit_participation (§5), listed so that a citation of an old number lands somewhere:

Old Was Where it went 1 participation rows with no membership at that time Deleted with the table (D-097). Its reasoning survives as a caution rather than a query: the check spent two rounds carrying an import exclusion because every imported row satisfied the predicate by design, which is the shape of a report whose floor is thousands of meaningless findings — worth remembering before writing any "row without its obvious partner row" report here 1b the root participation row disagreeing with the membership it mirrored Deleted with the redundancy it watched (§5). There is no second row, so there is nothing to disagree and no writer left to name 2 ⚠ participants in units that do not allow minors Withdrawn by D-095 one round before the table itself went. Who enforces the rule now: person_group.member.manage, held at the unit — which reaches every group — or granted on one group as an item, audited and naming who wrote the row (D-098). What is lost is unchanged and unrecoverable: no column says which groups take children, so the system can neither answer the question nor report on it

docs.title: 8. Seed data
docs.text:
The organization starts with a single membership type — member, named and described in plain words, open for a person to register themselves for, and left to requires_approval at its default of true. The term and the calendar parameters on that row are §1's, not constants anywhere else.

One row, and that is the whole vocabulary (D-037). The fee is flat and per person, so there is nothing to vary by type; being a counselor or a leader is a role, not a type (D-100); and membership is ageless, so there are no age limits to seed (D-038).

Nothing else is seeded here. The counselors role that D-100 seeds — shipped is_system, so an editor refuses to delete it — is a row of the authorization module (05-authorization.md §12) and not of this one, and it is a set that confers nothing until a grant names it: no more than a membership type has ever conferred.

All three are settled, and all three are §1's columns — 12 months, 1 January, 60 days (D-047, D-048). The sentence this one replaces called the 12-month term "a placeholder that nothing currently depends on", and that was stale in two directions at once. It is §1's duration_months default, stated there as a value with a reason attached (the fee is yearly), and things do depend on it: the yearly lapse sweep (07-finance.md §4) and the period a renewal opens both read a term, and a term of the wrong length produces a membership that ends on a date nobody chose. What survives the correction is the part that was always the point — none of the three is a constant, so tuning any of them is an UPDATE, not a release, and the difference between a settled value and a hard-coded one is exactly that difference.

The one rule about these four values: read them from the row. A scheduled job, a front end or a report that contains the literal 60 or 1 has quietly reverted a parameter to a constant, and the organization will discover it the first time it changes its mind.

No requirement_code seed. That table does not exist (D-044). The formerly seeded rows — guardian_consent, background_check, medical_form, references, previous_unit_transfer, photo_consent — are all gone: consent moved to the guardianship layer where it belongs, background checks are not recorded at all (D-043), and the rest were never required.

docs.title: 9. Open issues
docs.text:
• Nothing about the type-level parameters is open any more (§1, §8): 12 months, 1 January and 60 days are all settled and all three are columns read from the row. What is left of this bullet is a question about the values rather than about the mechanism — whether 60 days is the right window for an organization whose renewal campaign is a handful of people, which only a year of real lapses can answer.
  • Whether outstanding_balance should exist as a denormalised column or be computed (§3) — depends on the finance design in 07-finance.md.
  • Which offices are written without MEMBERS. The membership gate left the resolver for the grant text (§6, D-100), so somebody has to decide, per office, that a lapsed member may still hold it — and nothing in the model records who decided it or why, only whether the expression contains the word. The standing report of §7 check 1 is the control over the outcome, not over the choice. Assumption: this is left to whoever writes the grant, which is the honest reading of D-100 rather than a ruling in it.
  • Whether a group is ever allowed to state an age rule of its own — the question position.min_age used to answer for offices, which D-100 deleted along with positions, and which nothing in the round-10 model answers for groups either: a group carries no eligibility, and D-098 refuses it one. Left as a question for ../open-questions.md rather than answered here; today the answer is a report over person_group_member and is_minor().

Resolved and no longer open, kept visible so the reasoning survives: whether a person may hold several open memberships (no — one type, person-scoped constraint, §3); whether membership activates on payment (yes, §3); whether permissions depend on membership state (it did, through a resolver clause — D-039; since D-100 the grant says so itself with MEMBERS, §6, and the carve-outs turned out to be channels that were never gated); the age limits and age-out (§8); the grace period as a status (§6 of domain/05); the whole requirement mechanism (§4); whether unit_participation should reference the membership for referential integrity (moot — the table is deleted, D-097, and open question D-8 retires with it. The argument is kept because it recurs: the pointer was refused because participation had to survive without a membership, which is precisely why person_group_member is still keyed on a person and not on a membership, §5); what the root-unit participation row did when a membership was renewed inside the window (extended across the retrospectively filled period, never closed and reopened — D-050. The row is gone, D-097, and the answer is kept because the reasoning about backdated periods is what the renewal rule in §3 still rests on; the same rule had reached the imported consecutive periods D-093 introduced); and whether the legacy import may create a membership at all (yes, bounded at both ends, data_confidence = 'low', one row per period the source states — D-093, after a round in which the answer was no; the reasoning either way is 06-audit-and-import.md §3.1).

All tracked in ../open-questions.md.

docs.title: Data Model — Relationships
docs.text:
guardianship, and the single right level that travels with it.

Domain rationale: ../domain/02-actors.md.

This document describes requirements. It contains no DDL (D-072); the ORM decides how each rule is enforced.

docs.title: 1. guardianship
docs.text:
Fields

Field Kind Notes id internal identifier Never appears in a URL or an external reference guardian_person_id reference to person, required One side of the relationship dependent_person_id reference to person, required The other side. Must not equal the guardian relationship enum: parent / legal_guardian / foster_parent / step_parent / grandparent / sibling / other, required sibling and other exist because the organization will meet cases that do not fit, and forcing them into parent corrupts the data. A 19-year-old legal guardian of a 12-year-old sibling is real right_level enum: none / view / write The whole of the guardian's authority (D-074). Current value, denormalised for the read that happens on every authorization check; history in guardianship_permission (§2) valid_from date, required valid_to date, optional NULL = current. Set by a person — a party to the row (§1 "Guardianship ends"), or a staff member asked to record it. Never by a job: the system takes no position on majority (D-069) is_primary_contact boolean, required, default false Who the organization calls in an emergency. Independent of right_level — a grandparent with no system access at all can still be the emergency contact. See ../domain/02-actors.md §6 is_legal_decision_maker boolean, required, default false Distinguishes who may make legal decisions — consent for medical treatment, travel — from who provides day-to-day care. Often different people lives_with boolean, optional Deliberately optional: false means guardianship without cohabitation (shared custody, a guardian in another city), which is a different fact from unknown. Relevant to contact routing, never to authority custody_arrangement free text A description, not a computable fact, and kept that way on purpose (§7) source enum: self / staff / import / court_order Decides the starting right_level (§2 defaults, D-046) verified_at timestamp, optional verified_by reference to person, optional evidence_reference free text Where the proof of guardianship is filed. For legal guardianship this matters: the organization must be able to show that it checked ended_reason_code free text / reason code ended_note free text created_at, updated_at timestamps created_by, updated_by reference to person import_batch_id reference to import batch Legacy rows only

Rules

  • A person may not be a guardian of themselves: the two person references must differ.
  • valid_to, when present, must be after valid_from.
  • At most one current guardianship per (guardian, dependent) pair. Their periods may not overlap. Past ones are unlimited and expected: a court order lapses and is renewed.
  • A dependent may have any number of simultaneous guardians, each with its own row and its own right_level.
  • is_primary_contact is not unique per dependent. A child can have two primary contacts.

Indexes

  • Lookups in both directions by person and valid_to — "who is this person's guardian" and "who does this person guard" are equally common.
  • A partial index on current rows only, and a second on current rows that are primary contacts: the emergency-contact lookup must not scan history.

docs.title: The relation is a general graph, not a two-level hierarchy
docs.text:
The requirements permit:

  • One guardian → many dependents. Multiple rows with the same guardian. This is "one parent can manage multiple children".
  • Many guardians → one dependent. Both parents, brothers' grandparents, a legal guardian plus a step-parent. Nothing assumes a child has exactly two guardians.
  • A person being both. Person A is guardian of B and dependent of C. Costs nothing to allow, and avoids a rewrite when a member reaches majority and becomes guardian to a younger sibling.

You specified the first two explicitly. The third is free.

docs.title: Per-dependent authority
docs.text:
Authority is per guardianship row, never per person. A parent can hold write for one child and view for another — a realistic shared-custody arrangement, and one the model must represent without inventing a second parent identity.

What changed with D-074 is the grain, not the location. Per row it used to be a set of capability codes; per row it is now one of three values. See §2 for what that costs.

docs.title: Guardianship ends — and who is allowed to end it
docs.text:
valid_to is set when:

  • a party to the row ends it. The guardian, or the adult who is the subject of it (D-073);
  • a court order changes the arrangement, which staff record;
  • the guardian dies — and note the organization does not record death (D-034), so this too arrives as a person ending a row, with whatever reason the organization uses.

Staff may always do it when asked. Staff may never be the only way it happens.

The parties are principals, not third parties with a grant. A guardianship row is not the guardian's record, and it is not the subject's record. It is a record of a relationship between them, and both hold it.

This claim used to borrow its justification from a rule that no longer exists. It was written as scope authority — ~~the rule that authority over a nested thing originates at that thing~~ (D-031), "applied to a household instead of a unit" — which was a good analogy right up until D-097 deleted the nesting it was borrowed from, along with the crossing mechanism that made it a rule rather than a sentiment. The claim does not need the borrowing. A relationship row belongs to the people in it is a statement about this channel and stands on its own, and it is the reason neither party needs a grant to act on the row. What the deleted rule was really doing on this page was answering who may end it, and that answer is already given locally, a paragraph above: a party to the row, or staff acting on a request — with staff never the only way it can happen.

It is not the ownership channel, and the distinction is worth keeping. Ownership is your own record. Ending a guardianship over yourself is not editing your own record; it is dissolving a relationship you are one half of.
