Mechanically this is the guardianship channel gaining a direction: it already asks "may guardian G act on D's records?", and it now also answers "may a party act on the guardianship row itself?", for exactly three acts — ending it, adding another guardian, and changing the right level. The resolver still has four channels (D-010, and the channels' dispatch changed in D-079).

The three acts a party may take, and no others:

Act Guardian Subject (adult) Staff End the row ✅ ✅ ✅ Add another guardian over the same dependent ✅ ❌ ✅ Change right_level downward ✅ ✅ ✅ Change right_level upward ✅ ❌ ✅ Edit the dependent's records per right_level own record per role

Read the last row against the first four, because an implementation will get this backwards. The four acts above are not gated by right_level: a guardian whose right is view, or even none, may still end the guardianship, and a person who has never been a guardian at all may not. The level ranks what you may do to the child's records, which is the fifth row and nothing else — it is not a general competence over the relationship, and reading it as one would mean that lowering someone's access to a medical file also locked them out of leaving the arrangement. The party direction follows the same rule as the record direction: it can only say yes (D-079). Being a party grants the act; not being one leaves the actor's own guardianship.* role permissions to be tried, which is how staff in the table above get their ✅s. An explicit deny still runs first and beats both.

The asymmetry, stated plainly. A guardian may appoint a guardian: anyone with authority over a child can give a second person that same authority with no approval from the organization. The ordinary case is a mother adding the father. The design does not prevent the non-ordinary case; it attributes it instead — who added whom, when, from which account, is audited, and the other party is notified. That is a deterrent and an evidence trail, not a wall. See E-6.

The system does not notice birthdays in this connection. No job, no review queue, no computed candidate date (D-069, reversing D-024 and closing E-2).

Why not, including why the gentler version was also refused. The legal reasoning is unchanged and still correct: in many jurisdictions a parent's authority over health and school records does not end at 18, and in some it ends at a different age, so any computed date is a claim the system cannot support. What D-069 adds is that a review queue makes the same claim more quietly. A queue asserts this arrangement is now suspect, in every case, for every family, including the ones where the adult child actively wants their parent to keep handling the paperwork. Deferring a decision is not declining to make one, and the queue was a decision.

D-069 refused, D-073 supplies. Read as one decision in two halves: a legal relationship between two people ends when one of those people says so, and the organization's job is to be told rather than to permit it. Without D-073, D-069 was a refusal with no alternative; the exit it assumed had no door.

What is lost, precisely: a prompt, not a record. valid_from/valid_to mean "who is listed as my guardian, and since when?" is a query with a complete answer including the date each ended. What replaces the prompt is the report in §6, run by a person on purpose.

docs.title: is_primary_contact vs is_legal_decision_maker
docs.text:
Two distinct questions that a single "is primary parent" flag conflates:

Question Column Who do we phone at 2am when the child is injured at camp? is_primary_contact Who may sign the consent form for that treatment? is_legal_decision_maker

They are often different people, and conflating them means either the wrong person is called or an invalid consent is accepted. Both are separate flags rather than one is_primary, because a child can have two primary contacts and one decision maker.

docs.title: 2. The guardian's right: none, view, or write
docs.text:
A guardian either cannot see the child's records, can see them, or can change them. That is the entire vocabulary (D-074).

guardianship_permission survives as the history of that value, not as a capability list. One row per change, exactly one row open at a time, so "what was this guardian allowed to see in March 2024?" stays answerable — the same current-value-plus-temporal-history shape that person uses for names.

Field Kind Notes guardianship_id reference to guardianship, required Scoped to the row, never to the (guardian, dependent) pair right_level enum: none / view / write, required The value being recorded valid_from date, required valid_to date, optional NULL = current. Ending this row without ending the guardianship changes the right; a new row starts it again changed_reason free text e.g. default for self-registered guardianship, court order 2026-03-14, guardian request changed_by reference to person, optional NULL when the default was applied by the application at creation

Rules

  • Exactly one row per guardianship may be open at a time.
  • Every change is a row; the value on guardianship.right_level is always the open row's value. If the two disagree, the row is authoritative and the copy is wrong.
  • Scoping to the guardianship row and not to the person pair is deliberate (D-020): when a guardianship ends and a new one begins — a renewed court order, a lapse and re-establishment — the rights must not silently carry over. A new relationship is a new row and a new, deliberate level.

docs.title: Three values, two kinds, and no scale
docs.text:
This section used to argue that the guardian rights were not a second authorization model by mapping them onto the shared level ladder — none → 0, view → 10, write → 20, so the resolver would never need to know which ladder it was standing on. The ladder is deleted (D-099), so that argument is gone and the requirement underneath it is still met, by a different mechanism: the level is compared against a column on the permission, permission.right_kind ∈ read | write — none covers nothing, view covers the codes marked read, write covers both. There is nothing to order and no rank to keep in step, because three values against two kinds is a lookup, not a scale. The column exists for exactly this comparison and for no other customer in the system (05-authorization.md §1).

What the ladder was really buying survives, and it never was the numbers. A guardian was never a staff member, and that was expressed by write landing on contribute rather than manage. It is now expressed by the shape of the request: the guardianship channel is entered only when the check is about somebody other than the actor (D-079), so the widest guardian right in the system reaches the child's record and cannot reach a roster, a fee schedule or another family — not because its rank was too low, but because those checks are not about the child and the channel is never asked. Losing the ladder costs the comparison; the boundary moved into the one place that was always enforcing it.

docs.title: What the collapse gives up, written down rather than discovered later
docs.text:
Before D-074, a guardianship carried a set of capability codes — dependent.profile.view, dependent.medical.view, dependent.consent.give, dependent.fee.pay, and thirteen others, with dependent.admin as a shorthand for all of them. Every dependent.* code is deleted.

The consequence is specific and should not be softened: it is no longer expressible that this guardian may register the child for events but may not read the medical record. The case the old model existed for — a court order restricting one parent's access to medical information while their other access continues — cannot be represented. A grandmother who was granted roster visibility and nothing else is now a view guardian, which means she can see the fee history and the medical file too.

What still holds:

  • write is not manage, and since D-099 there is no manage to be short of: the ceiling on a guardian is the channel, which answers only for checks about this child. A guardian cannot do organization-wide things because those checks are not about the child, not because a rank was too low.
  • Authority is per row, so a guardian of one child sees nothing of another's.
  • The organization-wide deny channel is untouched: a guardianship row granting write can still be refused by a deny, because deny is absolute and scope-independent (D-032). What was lost is a narrow deny — "not medical" — not the ability to say no.

If the split turns out to matter in operation it is a new decision, not a permission to be re-added quietly (E-7).

docs.title: Defaults still depend on how the guardianship arose
docs.text:
D-046 survives, with one value where it used to have a set:

source Starting right_level Why self — a parent registering their own child write They created the record and are asserting the relationship. There is nobody better placed to hold authority over it staff, import — recorded by someone else view, chosen at creation and raisable A person who did not assert the relationship is not handed authority by a default court_order view, and raised only by the person who filed the order The document says what the authority is; the system should not guess above it

Applied by the code that creates the row, at creation — and this is the correct layer, not a compromise. A default depends on why the row is being created, which is a fact about the user's intent that no database rule can inspect. What must not happen is the default being applied only by a form: an import that omits it produces a view guardian where the person meant full rights, and nothing objects. And nothing in §6 catches this either, which is worth being plain about: a default that was never applied leaves no inconsistent row behind — only a quiet view where a write was intended, indistinguishable from a deliberate restriction. That gap is a consequence of §2's collapse. Before D-074 an omitted bundle of grants was visible as an empty set, and an empty set is reportable where view is not. What closes it is not a report but the shape of the write path: one place creates guardianships, it reads source, and it does not accept a right_level from a caller who is not entitled to choose one. The staff and court_order paths need a human choosing a value, and a default that fires before anybody is asked is not a default, it is a decision made on someone's behalf — the same refusal D-069 and D-076 make elsewhere.

Why source and changed_reason are both kept. The same word — "guardian" — now means two different starting scopes depending on paperwork, and the record has to say which was chosen and why. A guardian with read-only access and a guardian with full access are indistinguishable in the domain language and must not be in the data.

docs.title: 3. There is no household table
docs.text: Removed (D-057). An address is a person_contact row of type postal (01-identity.md §6), which already exists, already keeps history (valid_from / valid_to), and already carries a purpose — 'billing' for the address an invoice goes to. A separate household table was duplicating it under a different key, and the duplication had gone stale: its postal_address column was documented as denormalised from the billing contact's postal contact, with nothing keeping the copy true.

docs.title: Shared address still grants no access
docs.text:
Living at the same address does not grant any permission over another person at that address. A stepparent with no guardianship row has no access to the children's records. A grandparent at the address has no access. This is deliberate and it is a safeguarding property, not an oversight.

This was true when household existed (D-019) and it is true now, for a simple reason worth stating so nobody re-derives it: the access never came from the household tables. All authority over a child's records comes from guardianship (§1–2). Removing a table that granted nothing cannot grant anything.

docs.title: What replaced it
docs.text:
Household feature Now Billing address person_contact of type postal with purpose billing "Which children lived at this address in 2003?" A query over the temporal person_contact history (domain/03 §4) One invoice for three siblings The fee is flat and per person (D-037); there is no family price to invoice fee_obligation.household_id Column and its index removed (07-finance.md §2)

What was genuinely lost, recorded rather than glossed: a household was a group with a name and its own lifetime. Two people at one address are now related by a query, not by a row, so there is nowhere to hang "the Novák family" as a first-class thing and no valid_from for the grouping itself. Accepted, because nothing was using it — no code set fee_obligation.household_id, and household.name had no consumer. If family-level communication or a family discount is ever wanted, this is the decision to revisit, and the shape to bring back is a group with a period, not a fake person.

docs.title: Why not a family person row
docs.text: Some systems model a household as a fake person so that memberships and payments can attach to it. Do not. It creates rows in person that are not people, which breaks identity matching, produces nonsense in name searches, and — because it is a person — can receive a membership, an account, and eventually permissions.

docs.title: 4. How the resolver uses these tables
docs.text:
The guardianship channel is step 4 of the resolver (../domain/06-authorization-model.md).

How the channel is selected — a change D-074 forces, and it is an improvement. It used to be selected by the permission code's namespace: a code beginning dependent. routed here, and the point of routing by prefix was that no caller gets to choose which channel applies, which is what stops one authorization rule being implemented twice, once wrong. With no dependent.* codes there is no prefix, so the channel is now selected by a fact about the request: the person the action is about is not the person performing it. Nobody picks a channel; the shape of the call picks it. And it catches what the prefix missed — a parent editing their child's address under a person.* code previously did not route through guardianship at all, because the code's name said otherwise.

Asked about another person, it resolves in this fixed order, and it produces one of two outcomes: an allow, or no answer at all. It never answers "no".

  1. Is there a current guardianship row between this actor and this subject, at the date being asked about? If not, this step is not the channel's business and says nothing — the resolver continues to the actor's own roles and grants. Silence, not refusal (D-079).
  2. Is there an explicit deny covering this check? Deny wins here as everywhere else, and independently of how broad the underlying grant is (D-032) — but note that this deny is found by channel 0 of the resolver, before this step runs, so nothing in this list can override it. It is listed second only because it is the other reason a guardian with a sufficient right_level still gets nothing.
  3. Read the row's right_level and rank it: none 0, view 10, write 20.
  4. Compare against what the action needs. Reading a profile needs 10; editing a contact needs
  5. At or above the requirement → allow. Below it, or none → no answer, and the actor's own roles are tried.

Why step 1 and step 4 fall through instead of refusing, when refusing is what this channel used to do. It used to be entered only by codes no role could hold, so its refusal was the whole answer. Now it is entered by ordinary codes that a role may also carry, and finality produces an absurd result the moment one person wears two hats: the parent who is also the event registrar, holding view over their own child, refused the right to mark attendance. The relationship should not be able to revoke a job. What is not given up: none still grants nothing (that is what D-074 promised, not a power to block other bases), and an organization that genuinely must stop a specific person touching a specific child's records uses an explicit deny, which runs first, everywhere, at any scope. The prohibition survives; it simply lives in the channel D-032 built for it rather than in a capability level.

Two further properties:

  • An ended guardianship never opens this channel again. For every question, forever, the row is not current, so step 1 does not fire and no guardian authority flows. What a former guardian may still do is what any other member may do — through their own assignment, on its own scope, with the guardianship row doing nothing at all. That distinction did not exist while the channel was the only road to a child's records, and it is the honest version now.
  • The date is a parameter of the question, not read from the clock. So "could this parent have seen this record on the day they did it?" stays answerable, which is what auditing a past action requires. As-of must be threaded into every step above, including the deny lookup — a check that reads today's denies against a 2024 action invents history.

Asked about the guardianship row itself rather than through it, the same channel answers for a party to it, and only for the three acts in §1's table. That branch is not a fifth channel; it is this one, pointed the other way.

docs.title: 5. Acting on behalf — recording it
docs.text:
Every operation performed for a dependent must record both parties. This is not optional: without it, the audit trail attributes the parent's actions to the child.

Every access-log row for an act-on-behalf carries, together:

Field Records actor_person_id the guardian who acted subject_person_id the child whose record was affected on_behalf true, explicitly — not inferred from the two ids differing authorization_channel guardianship guardianship_id which row authorized it result allowed or refused

Concretely, when a parent registers their child for an event, the record must answer:

  • Who did it? The parent.
  • For whom? The child.
  • By what authority? A specific guardianship row, and the right_level it held at the time.
  • Is that authority still valid? Re-checkable from the row's dates.

A row that records only "the child registered" is not merely incomplete — it is wrong, and it is the kind of wrong that matters when someone later asks whether a parent consented to something.

docs.title: 6. Invariants to verify
docs.text:
These were executable queries. They are now requirements stated in prose, and nothing runs them (D-072).

  1. Adults still listed under a guardian. Every open guardianship whose subject is past majority by person.birth_date. Expected in the ordinary case and not an error — this is the periodic human review D-069 names as the entire control, and it exists precisely because no job acts on that date. Run it deliberately, never nightly: a report nobody reads is a queue, and the queue was withdrawn.
  2. Rights outliving the relationship. A guardianship_permission history row still open while its guardianship has ended. This is the exact failure that scoping to the row was meant to prevent; worth verifying because an application bug or a hand-edit can still create it.
  3. A dependent with no primary contact. A current guardianship set in which nobody is flagged as the emergency contact.
  4. A minor member or participant whom no guardian can see. Two shapes, one report, because they are the same gap arriving by different routes: no guardianship row at all, and a full set of guardians with every one of them at right_level = none. Age comes from person.birth_date — there is no membership category to read it from, because membership is ageless (D-038). This is a safeguarding gap, not a data-quality nit: the organization holds a member it cannot contact in an emergency and cannot obtain consent from. It should alert, not log. This check is one of the reasons guardianship is a required part of the model rather than an optional convenience.

The second half was added by D-082, and it is not a hypothetical refinement. A direct message to a minor is mirrored to the guardians at view or write — deliberately not to a guardian at none, because none means the organization already decided that party sees nothing about the child. Without this half of the check, a child whose guardians are all none would look, in every report, like a child with guardians, while in fact nobody outside the child receives a copy of anything sent to them. A right level that silently removes the only safeguarding net is a right level nobody understands anymore, and this report is what keeps none meaning what it says. 5. A guardian younger than the dependent, where both birth dates are known. Almost always a data-entry error, and detectable only when both dates survived the import. 6. guardianship.right_level disagrees with its own open history row. A new invariant created by D-074's current-value-plus-history shape. If it is ever non-empty, the copy is wrong and the row is right.

Deleted with the model that needed it: "a guardian permission outside the dependent.* namespace" — there is no dependent.* namespace any more. "Households with no address" went with D-057; the nearest surviving signal is a live billing purpose with no postal address behind it, which is a finance problem.

Note what changed when membership became ageless. Check 4 used to read membership_type.category = 'child'; with one membership type (D-037) that column does not exist, and the question is now answered from person.birth_date. The signal is arguably better than it was: "this person is under 18 today" rather than "this person's membership row was categorised as a child when it was opened", which could be years out of date.

docs.title: 7. Open issues
docs.text:
• ~~Whether guardianship should auto-expire at majority, or always require review.~~ Neither — the system takes no position on majority, and the review queue this file recommended was withdrawn with it (§1, D-069).
  • ~~How does an adult end a guardianship over themselves?~~ They end it, themselves, as a party to the row — D-073.
  • New: a guardian may appoint a guardian, with no approval from the organization. Attributed and notified, not prevented. E-6.
  • New: one right level cannot separate the medical record from the profile, which is the case the deleted capability codes existed for. E-7.
  • Resolved: household is removed entirely — answered "drop household entirely", now D-057 (§3). Addresses live on person_contact.
  • Whether a guardian may act for a dependent who is also a member in their own right — e.g. can a parent register their adult child for an event, if the child consents? Recommend an explicit consent-based delegation rather than a guardianship, since the legal basis differs. The group version of this is now answered by audiences (D-042).
  • Whether custody_arrangement free text should be structured. Recommend not — custody orders vary too much to model, and a wrong model is worse than honest prose.
  • Confirm that the membership gate's guardianship carve-out is intended. A lapsed parent keeps their right_level (D-039), which means an unpaid parent and a paid one are indistinguishable inside that namespace. It is almost certainly right — guardianship comes from a legal relationship, not a membership — but it should be a stated choice, not a side effect of where the gate was placed.

Resolved and no longer open, kept visible so the reasoning survives: the default grant at guardianship creation (now one level, chosen by source — D-046); whether fees are per person or per household (per person, flat — D-037, which retired the load-bearing half of household and led to its removal — D-057); and background checks (none are recorded — D-043).

All tracked in ../open-questions.md.

docs.title: Data Model — Authorization: permissions, offices, grants
docs.text:
permission, role, role_holder and access_grant — the four tables an answer is made of — and the shape of the check they add up to. Design rationale, in plain language: ../domain/06-authorization-model.md.

Section numbers are shared across the five parts and never renumbered, because other pages cite them by number and their anchors are built from them: 05-authorization.md holds §1–§7, 05a §8 (the audience table, the grammar, the selector registry), 05b §8 continued (the tree and what each operand costs), 05c §9–§10 (access_log and the resolver), and 05d §11–§13 (invariants, seed data, open issues).

docs.title: 1. The shape of the answer
docs.text:
permission ─────────────── the atomic capability.       'membership.request.approve'
                            + where it may be granted:  applies_to  unit | unit_and_item
                            + read or write:            right_kind

access_grant ───────────── THE ONE TABLE THAT GRANTS.   grantee (person | audience),
                                                       scope ('unit' | exactly one item),
                                                       one code, effect (allow | deny),
                                                       period

role ───────────────────── an office, conferring nothing.     'treasurers'
role_holder ────────────── who holds it, for a period.        person X, 'treasurers',
                                                              2026-03-01 → open

selector_type ──────────── the language: every operand that   'ROLE', 'MEMBERS', 'PLACED',
                          may appear in an expression.          'AUDIENCE'
                          Seeded, is_system, read-only.

audience ───────────────── a set a grant aims at, nameable     MEMBERS * ROLE(treasurers)
                          by code from another audience.
audience_operand ───────── one node of that expression        (a tree, not a string; an
                          — an AUDIENCE leaf doubles as       AUDIENCE leaf is also the
                          the reference edge to another tree)  edge to another audience)

guardianship ───────────── authority over one PERSON: right_level   (04-relationships.md)
access_log ─────────────── what was decided, and by what authority.

One table grants. access_grant is the only place authority is written (D-005), plus the guardianship channel over one person, whose authority is guardianship.right_level (data-model/04, §10). Everything else here decides whom a grant reaches, which is not the same question — a role holder, a group member and an audience operand are all sets of people, and being in one is worth exactly what the grant aimed at it says (D-100). A hand-written set of people is written in the expression too, as PERSON(a) + PERSON(b), where every other set is written (D-105).

And the rule that answers every check (D-099):

allowed when some live allow applies, and no live deny applies.

That is the entire precedence rule. "Live" means the row has started as of the checked date, has not ended on it, and has not been revoked; "applies" is decided per channel in §10. There is no level to reach, no rank to compare, and no nearer grant that beats a further one; a deny is absolute (D-032, D-099). Why there is no ordering: an ordering could only ever rank one allow against another, and a boolean answer has nothing to rank.

Authority is written at exactly two sizes — the unit, or one item — because there is one unit and it is not a row (D-097), and the widest read permission in the system reaches every member from the unit. What that costs is stated once, in domain/04 §1.

role_holder and access_grant are different mechanisms, and only one of them grants. What they have in common is the temporal pattern every dated row in this system uses:

role_holder access_grant Says this person holds this office in this period this grantee may, or may not, do this one thing here Carries authority No — confers nothing (§3) Yes; it is the only thing that does Scope None. A role is held at the unit, because there is nowhere else The unit, or exactly one item Decides Whom a grant naming ROLE(x) reaches Everything, for one code Typical row "is the treasurer, from March" "may read this event's answers" Rows per broad capability One One per code — a broad office is a couple of dozen of them

The row count is the price, and it was paid deliberately (D-099). One grant per code is what buys "what exactly does this person have?" answered by reading rows, and it costs the question "what does manage give me on this event?", which has no answer because there is no such word.

docs.title: 2. permission
docs.text:
Fields

Field Kind Notes id integer identity Surrogate key. code text, required, unique The stable identifier — membership.request.approve. The code never changes; display_name can. resource text, required What the permission is about — membership_request. action text, required What may be done to it — approve. applies_to enum: unit, unit_and_item Where this code may be granted at all: at the unit only, or at the unit and on an item. Checked when the grant is saved, never at check time — see applies_to below. right_kind enum: read, write Exists for exactly one customer: the guardianship channel's none / view / write (D-074). Say the one customer out loud — see right_kind below. namespace text, optional system, or absent. What the column does is its own subsection below. description text, required What it means, for whoever has to read it. display_name text, required Human label for the permission editor. is_system boolean Default false. True: seeded by the platform, cannot be deleted or have its code changed. is_assignable boolean Default true. False: a permission no grant may name directly — a deprecated code kept only so historical audit rows still resolve to something readable. created_at timestamp, audit time

The one question this table does not answer is "may this code be granted on an event at all?" — that is applies_to, and it is answered on the save rather than in the resolver. Nothing else in the row constrains where a grant may sit.

Rules

  • code is well-formed: two or more dot-separated segments of lowercase letters and underscores.
  • resource equals the first dot-separated segment of code, so the code's prefix is never a second, drifting copy of the resource column. One exemption, deliberate: codes beginning system., whose resource is the thing being administered rather than the word system. It is the only one, and a code under any other namespace prefix with two meaningful segments (dependent.medical.view is the shape) means reopening this rule.
  • code is unique.
  • applies_to and right_kind are both required. A required enum with two values is cheap; a nullable one whose null-ness silently means something is how the guardianship channel would have acquired an answer that depends on a value nobody typed.
  • A code seeded as system. is seeded applies_to = unit. This is not decoration; see What namespace does.

docs.title: There is no wildcard permission
docs.text:
A check for X.y is satisfied by an exact allow of X.y, or by system.admin, which is checked outright and is the only permission meaning everything.

A check for permission 'X.y' is satisfied by:
    - an exact allow of 'X.y', OR
    - an allow of 'system.admin'   (NULL-namespace permissions only)

There are no <resource>.admin codes — no prefix matching in the resolver, and none to come by (D-068). "Can do everything about events" is an office composed from the thirteen event.* codes — which is to say, a role some grants name, each grant naming one code (D-052) — because that composition is runtime data the organization edits, and a wildcard was the code guessing at it instead.

The cost is accepted: a new narrow permission is not automatically covered by the offices that should imply it. Integrity check 13 (permissions no live grant names) is the net, and it fails closed (D-007, reversed by D-068).

is_assignable = false exists for permissions that only make sense as part of a bundle — a deprecated narrow permission kept for historical audit readability, for instance. A bundle is a role's set of grants, and nothing else bundles.

docs.title: applies_to: where a code may be granted, and when that is asked
docs.text:
What the column encodes: event.create and membership.manage are nonsense on an event. unit means the code may be granted at the unit and nowhere else; unit_and_item means it may be granted at the unit or on one item of a registered type.

It is checked when the grant is saved, not when a permission is checked (D-099). A grant of event.create written on one event is refused, with the reason in the error: an event cannot be created twice, so a creation permission attached to a thing that already exists answers no question — and a refusal at save time is one human conversation, where the same shape discovered at check time is a rule inside the resolver that every future reader has to re-derive.

What enforces it is the write path, and the direction of its failure is worth knowing. No database rule spans permission and access_grant columns, so integrity check 3 (§11) reports any row that got through — a row there means the check was skipped, not that a constraint was disabled. And because the rule sits on the save, a check that names an item for a unit-only code is not refused by it: the mismatched shape cannot be stored, so the check simply gets the unit's answer. That is a caller bug rather than a data bug, and §13 registers the question of whether the API should refuse it out loud.

docs.title: right_kind: a column with exactly one customer
docs.text:
Saying so is cheaper than discovering it later (D-099). D-074 fixes a guardian's rights at three values — none, view, write — and the guardianship channel has to compare a checked permission against something. This column is that thing, and it has no other consumer anywhere in the design:

Guardian's right_level Covers none Nothing. view Codes marked read. write Codes marked read and codes marked write.

The alternative was to store permission codes on the guardianship row, and D-074 refused it on the grounds that a volunteer cannot maintain a 74-code checklist per child. A two-valued column on the catalog side keeps that refusal intact: the organization grades each code once, when it is written, rather than per child, forever.

A new code is seeded write unless someone marks it read, because write is the narrower guardian reach: an unconsidered new code is then unreachable by a guardian with view, which is the direction this model fails in everywhere else. This is a seeding convention derived from D-074's fail-closed posture rather than a ruling in D-099, and §11 has no check for it — a code mis-marked read is visible to a human reading the catalog and invisible to the database, which is worth knowing before trusting it.

docs.title: What namespace does
docs.text:
namespace What it means Example absent An ordinary code. membership.request.approve system A code about the system itself. It is seeded applies_to = unit, so no grant on an item can carry it, and the resolver no longer branches on the prefix. system.permission.edit

There used to be a third value, and this subsection was about it. dependent. prefixed every guardian capability, and the resolver dispatched on the prefix: a code beginning dependent. went down the guardianship channel, everything else went down the ordinary path. D-074 deleted all eighteen of those codes, and with them the only thing the namespace column was being used to route on.

So the namespace column no longer selects a channel, and the guardianship channel is now selected by something the namespace could never express: whether the action is about a different person from the one performing it. A parent editing their child's address is checked under person.address.edit — an ordinary, un-prefixed code — and reaches the guardianship channel anyway, because the subject of the act is not the actor. See §10. The old prefix rule silently missed exactly that case: a guardian acting under a person.* code looked like a person acting on themselves.

What the column was also guaranteeing, and who guarantees it now. The surviving sentence in the old design read "a system. permission is resolved against role assignments and never against an item grant", and it was load-bearing: no one could hand someone authority over the permission system by sharing an item with them. Its mechanism died twice over — there is no role channel (D-100) and no item-scope path it needs excluding, because applies_to = unit already refuses the grant at save time. So the guarantee survives as a seeding rule plus integrity check 3, and the layer is named because the difference matters: it is no longer structural, and a system. code seeded unit_and_item by someone in a hurry would put the old hole back with nothing in the schema to catch it. A new namespace remains a data change rather than a resolver branch; it just has one tenant and no routing left.

docs.title: 3. role — an office
docs.text:
Fields

Field Kind Notes id integer identity Surrogate key. code text, required, unique among roles, and unique across roles and groups registrar, treasurers, counselors. The cross-table half of the rule is §8's namespace rule; a single constraint cannot span two tables, so the write path carries it (§8, Names are one namespace). name text, required What the office is called on screen. description text, optional is_system boolean Default false. True: seeded — cannot be deleted, and its code cannot be changed. False: an ordinary office the organization created and may delete. sort_order integer, required Default 0. created_at timestamp, audit time updated_at timestamp, audit time updated_by reference to person Who last changed it.

Deleted with their mechanisms, in one list, because D-081 requires each one to be answered:

Gone With it Who answers the question now scope_required "is this office held org-wide or at a unit?" Nobody — the question has no subject. There is one scope (D-097), so a role is always held at the unit (§4 has no scope columns). requires_membership the membership gate, default-on, enforced in the resolver (D-039) The expression, per grant: MEMBERS * ROLE(x) gates on a current membership, ROLE(x) alone does not (§8, §10). The posture is opt-in, and §11's report is the control. max_term_months the prefilled term, and with it the "expiry is the default" nudge Nothing. Nothing forces a holder row to end, and §11's report of offices held past their end date is the control (§4, D-071). is_delegatable the refusal to let an office's authority be delegated (domain/06 §9) Nothing about roles. Delegation of authority survives only on a grant row (is_delegated + delegated_from), where the grant's own expiry is the control (§6).

role is runtime data, not a fixed vocabulary. The organization creates offices, names them, fills them, and deletes the ones nobody ever held. Two rows ship with the platform, and the list is deliberately short: counselors, marked is_system (D-100; a permanent, organization-wide population is the opposite of D-098's definition of a group, and the table is what decides the sensitivity that protects the set). §12 states what is seeded and what is starter material.

role has no valid_from / valid_to, deliberately (D-053). A role is a definition — a named office — and a definition does not come into and out of force. It is valid all the time, for as long as the row exists.

The period belongs on the holder row. role_holder.valid_from / valid_to is where "this person holds this office from March until December" lives (§4). The distinction is between what the office is and who holds it: the first is not a historical fact, the second is.

There is no retirement mechanism. No role.retire permission, no resolver check on a role's period. A role the organization no longer uses is one nobody holds any more, and §11 reports the offices still held past their holder row's end date.

docs.title: An office confers nothing
docs.text:
The codes an office carries are the live grants whose audience names ROLE(x) (D-100). That is not a relabelling: an office's power lives in grant rows that are individually visible, individually dated, individually auditable and individually revocable. "What may a treasurer do?" is therefore a query over rows a screen can show. Roles and audiences are the bundle, and nothing else is (D-068, D-100).

Three rules this table has to get right:

  • role.edit edits a name, a description and a sort order. The sharp edge is role.assign. Adding one person to treasurers inherits every grant that names ROLE(treasurers), including ones written later, by other people, for reasons whoever is doing the assigning has never seen. That is the invisibility §8 records for composition, arriving through the office door instead of the expression door — which is why role.* is the most sensitive code family in the catalog (🔒🔒) and why §11's report of ROLE(...) grants written without MEMBERS is worth reading.
  • A role that has ever been held cannot be deleted, for three reasons: role_holder.role_id is a foreign key and D-003 forbids taking the history with the row; "what authority did this person have in 2019?" must survive the office being abolished, which is exactly when someone asks; and an is_system role must survive regardless, because deleting a row some grants name would silently widen or narrow whatever they aim at. The guard runs row by row, in this order, and both refusals are absolute:
  • any role_holder row references the role — refuse, with a message in terms the operator can act on: this office has holders, end the holder rows instead, so the history survives;
  • otherwise, is_system — refuse outright. A role that clears both was created by mistake and never held, and deleting it is legitimate.
  • There is no permission inheritance between roles. A unit_leader does not get the assistant_leader permissions by being implicitly senior: inheritance chains produce authorization answers nobody can predict by reading the configuration, which is what makes such systems undebuggable. Composition is available and visible instead — an expression says ROLE(x) + ROLE(y), in the grant, where whoever reads the grant sees it (§8).

role is registered in grant_scope_type, so an office is an item (D-100): "these two people may manage the counselors roster" is a grant of role.assign on one role, which is D-098's move applied to an office as well as a group. Without it the only way to say that is a grant at the unit, which reaches every office — the exact over-reach this table's sensitivity exists to avoid.

Why a role and a group are two tables when they are technically the same shape is answered where the difference bites — D-100 puts it in one line: the difference decides who may edit the membership, and one table would merge those two permissions into one. role.* is the most sensitive family in the catalog (🔒🔒); writing a group's roster is person_group.member.manage (⚠). One table with a kind column gives a single code that both adds a child to the Thursday group and puts the holder into the office whose grants reach everything. The groups themselves are person_group, in 02-organization.md — this document describes only the selector that reads them.

docs.title: 4. role_holder — who holds an office
docs.text:
A role_holder row is an office, a person, and a period (D-100). It carries no scope columns and no resolver channel: a holder row grants nothing by existing, and what it changes is whom a grant naming ROLE(x) reaches (§10).

Fields

Field Kind Notes id integer identity Surrogate key. person_id reference to person, required Who holds the office. One person, never a rule — F-12 is closed by D-100 and its answer is no, for the reason the register always gave: a derived holder list cannot answer "who was treasurer in 2023", and an office record that cannot answer that is not an office record. role_id reference to role, required valid_from date, required Default today. valid_to date, optional Absent = open-ended. Nothing forces it to end — see below. granted_by reference to person, required Who appointed this person. Kept, and not the provenance column this section deletes elsewhere — see What granted_by records and what audit_log records, immediately below. The arrow of this column goes to person and never to audit_log: it is a fact about the holder row, readable by anyone who may read the office, and reconstructing it from the trail would put the answer behind audit.view. granted_at timestamp, audit time Set when the row was written. Redundant with created_at in the ordinary case and kept because an appointment can be entered retrospectively, which is the only case where the two differ and the one where the distinction matters. note text, optional Why, in the writer's words. The only place the reason survives the audit trail's payload window (D-088). created_at timestamp, audit time updated_at timestamp, audit time updated_by reference to person

This table has no scope columns (D-097: a role is always held at the unit, and there is nothing else to hold it at), and no columns recording who ended a row. Who ended one, and when, is the audit trail's answer; the why is note, on the row that opens. The one thing with no answer is a typed, countable reason code for ending a holding — refused for the same reason D-098 refused it one table over: ticks nobody counts.

What granted_by records, and what audit_log records. The two look like duplicates and answer different questions, so the line is worth drawing properly. audit_log records an act: that a particular person, in a particular session, from a particular address, asked to appoint someone, and whether they were allowed to. It is the record of the writing. granted_by records a fact about the row: who appointed this person, which is a property of the office holding in the same way valid_from is. Who is entitled to say is the audit's question; who said it is the row's.

Two reasons the fact cannot live only in the trail, and the first is decisive.

  • The trail's payloads do not last (D-088); the before-and-after images are emptied after 24 months. "Who put her in charge of the money?" has to be answerable in year five, from the same screen that shows when the appointment started, and an answer that requires audit.view, a date range and an intact payload is not an answer to a question about the current officer.
  • The row's readers are not the trail's readers. role_holder is read by whoever administers offices; the trail is read by whoever holds audit.view 🔒🔒, and D-086 graded that deliberately. Making the ordinary screen reach into the audit trail to show an ordinary field either widens audit.view or leaves the field blank, and neither is acceptable.

The same argument decides access_grant.granted_by, and what separates the columns that stay from the ones that go is whether the value is a property of the row that still exists. An ending describes a row nobody is looking at, and "who closed this" is a question about an act — the trail's subject. An appointment describes a holding somebody is looking at now.

One diagram rule follows from it. The relationship drawn from granted_by points at person. There is no edge from role_holder to audit_log and there must never be one: the trail is written about the act, by the same transaction, and the holder row neither refers to it nor depends on it.

Rules

  • valid_to is either absent or strictly after valid_from.
  • At most one open holder row for a given person and role. There is no scope term left to distinguish two concurrent holdings, because there is no second scope. A person may have been treasurer three times, and be treasurer once.
  • Rows for the same person and role may not overlap, counted over all rows and not only the open ones, half-open so a row ending on a day and one beginning that same day do not collide. Dating rows imports this invariant set whether the author wants it or not — it is D-098's argument for the identical rule on person_group_member, D-002, and F-10 shape 1, which says a hand-written migration must emit it and the ORM will not.
  • A person who left the office in 2020 and returned in 2024 is two rows, never one row edited in place, because the edit destroys the answer to "was she treasurer in 2019?" — and that is the question this table exists to answer. Moving from one office to another closes one row and opens another.

Indexes

  • over open rows only, by role — the read that answers "who is in ROLE(treasurers) today", which is now an operand of a grant rather than a tier of the resolver, and runs on every check that names the office;
  • over open rows only, by person — the read that answers "what offices does this person hold", for the screen where someone is about to be given one more.

docs.title: Nothing forces a holder row to end, and the report is the control
docs.text:
This is D-071's posture, and it is now load-bearing rather than backstopped: a membership lapse no longer silently withholds anything from a holder row. A holder row that nobody closes authorizes for as long as a grant naming the office lives, and the only things between an overdue treasurer and a written authority are:

  • the report — open holder rows, oldest first, with the grants each office is named by;
  • role_holder.valid_to where a human typed one, and §13 keeps the question of whether it should be mandatory for high-authority offices; and
  • the audience expression, which is where a lapse now matters: MEMBERS * ROLE(x) stops reaching a lapsed member the day the membership ends, and ROLE(x) never noticed.

The mirror-image failure is the more likely one. A holder row that outlives the person gives that person authority they should not have; a grant written as ROLE(x) with no MEMBERS authorizes a lapsed member silently, forever, and looks fail-closed so nobody notices. Integrity check 6 (§11) is the standing report of that shape, and the seeded grants carry MEMBERS so the path of least repetition is the safe path (D-100).

docs.title: 5. scope_exposure — deleted by D-097
docs.text:
There is no such table, and this section exists because four pages link to its number. D-097 left one unit, and a unit is a scope rather than a row, so there is no boundary for authority to cross and nothing for an exposure row to sit on. D-031 was not weakened; it was deprived of its subject.

What is lost, stated once. Access to a body's children used to have to be granted by that body — by the people who recruited its leader, who can be asked, and who chose the person being let in. Nothing in this model reproduces that, and what stands instead — a permission held by a named adult, an audit trail whose payloads expire after two years (D-088), and a report of who holds the write — is missing exactly the half where the named adult was somebody the body chose. domain/04 §1 states the same cost where the unit is defined, and this document does not repeat the argument.

Who answers each deleted question now. scope.expose and scope.exposure.review are not in the catalog. The direction-of-authority check has no enforcer and needs none: a row has no direction when there is one unit. org_unit, unit_participation, unit_ancestors() and unit_descendants() are gone with the hierarchy, and with them every rule about paths, depths, nesting and reparenting — 02-organization.md describes groups. D-078's rule, that an exposure extends an assignment and never a grant, has no subject: a holder row has no scope to extend.

A caution that outlives the table. A write-path rule whose only guard is a report, and a report that stops running, is a rule that quietly stops existing: the nightly exposure alert was that check's only detector. Every rule in this document that has no enforcer says so, and §11 is where those reports are listed.

The way back is a decision, not a migration. The plausible reason is that the organization has outgrown one center's visibility, and taking it would mean re-arguing D-031 from its own premises — D-097 deleted the table that made the old rule work, so there is nothing to switch back on.

docs.title: 6. access_grant — the per-item layer
docs.text:
This is the "per-item permission" table. You specified it means a capability on that item: "person X may act on item Y". After round 10 it is also the unit-level table, because the unit is now one of the scope types rather than a different kind of thing, and there is no other grant table to hold the difference. The heading is deliberately unchanged — it names only half of what the table is now, and it is kept because pages across the corpus and in the decision log link to this anchor.

One grant is: a grantee, a scope, one permission code, an effect, and a period (D-099).

Fields (grant_scope_type)

Field Kind Notes code text, required, unique unit, event, person_group, role, document. The key a grant points at. name text, required item_table text, required The table scope_id references — event. For the unit, nothing: the row exists so the scope type has a name, and is_item_scoped is what says so. is_item_scoped boolean Default true. False for exactly one row: unit. A grant at a non-item scope has no scope_id, and that single fact is what "the unit is a scope, not a row" means in the schema (D-097). description text, optional

Seeded rows, and the list is short on purpose:

code Item-scoped Means unit No The organization. There is exactly one, and it is not a row anywhere else. event Yes One event. Nothing owns it (D-102); a unit grant reaches every event and an event grant reaches one. person_group Yes One group (D-098) — how "these two may work this group's roster" is said without inventing a scope. role Yes One office (D-100) — the same move applied symmetrically. document Yes Deferred; a document layer still to be designed. It stays in the registry because the registry's whole point is that a new grantable thing is a row here rather than a migration.

supports_levels is deleted with the ladder, and so are the organization and org_unit rows: the first is unit renamed (a scope with no item under it, which is all it ever was), the second is deleted with the hierarchy. membership is not in the seed. Nothing in this design writes a grant on an individual membership row — the thing a membership is protected by is membership.* codes held at the unit — and if that ever changes, adding it is one row here, which is what the registry is for. That the row is gone rather than merely unused is an inference from D-097's and D-099's lists of what is seeded, and §13 records it as one.

Rules (grant_scope_type)

  • Every access_grant.scope_type names a row here. This is the one piece of referential integrity the polymorphic scope does get.
  • Exactly one row — unit — has is_item_scoped false.

Fields (access_grant)

Field Kind Notes id integer identity Surrogate key. person_id reference to person, optional The grantee, when the grant names one person. audience_id reference to audience, optional The grantee, when the grant names a set (§8). Evaluated against the person being checked, per person, as a predicate — never as a list of ids. scope_type reference to grant_scope_type, required unit, or an item type. scope_id integer, optional The concrete item id. Absent exactly when the scope type is not item-scoped — that is, exactly at unit. No foreign key: polymorphic by design. See the note below. permission_id reference to permission, required One code, not a bundle (D-099). What level used to stand in for, without the ladder. effect enum: allow, deny, required Allowed iff some live allow applies and no live deny applies. D-013's deny survives as an effect on a row rather than as a level called revoked, and its reason for existing is unchanged: a court-ordered restriction must not be beatable by a broader grant. valid_from date, required Default today. valid_to date, optional Absent = open. Discouraged; see below. is_delegated boolean Default false. delegated_from reference to person, optional The person whose authority this delegation carries. granted_by reference to person, required granted_at timestamp, audit time grant_reason text, optional revoked_by reference to person, optional revoked_at timestamp, audit time, optional revoke_reason text, optional created_at timestamp, audit time updated_at timestamp, audit time updated_by reference to person

Rules

  • Exactly one of person_id and audience_id is set. A grant to neither is meaningless; a grant to both would be ambiguous — any person in the audience, or only this one?
  • valid_to is either absent or strictly after valid_from.
  • scope_id is absent exactly at unit scope — and that is the whole of what the rule says. It constrains the absent case alone; grant_scope_type.item_table is what states which table an id belongs to.
  • effect is allow or deny. There is no third value and no ordering between them: deny is absolute and is checked first, which is D-032 entire surviving content.
  • permission_id names a permission whose applies_to permits this scope shape — a grant at an item requires unit_and_item. Refused at save with the reason (§2, applies_to).
  • is_delegated and delegated_from agree in both directions: the flag is true exactly when a delegating person is named.
  • A grant is never a delegation from the person it is granted to: delegated_from does not equal person_id.
  • A revocation names who made it: if revoked_at is set, revoked_by is set.
  • A delegation must expire: if is_delegated is true, valid_to is set. With delegation_of deleted (§4) this is the only remaining guard against a delegation outliving its reason — the old second half, re-validating a source assignment at check time, has no assignment to re-validate. Integrity check 11 (§11) reports an open-ended one.
  • An audience grant cannot be delegated. is_delegated requires delegated_from, which is a person, and delegating "everyone" is not a coherent act: if audience_id is set, is_delegated is false.

docs.title: Inheritance, stated once
docs.text:
A grant at the unit reaches every item of every type. A grant on one item reaches that item and nothing else. That is the whole of it (D-099), and it follows from two deletions rather than from a new rule: after D-097 there is no intermediate scope left between the unit and an item, and after D-102 there is no ownership relation to test.

This is D-006 with the unit tier left standing — per-item permissions are capabilities on the item — and it deletes can_event() outright, along with the unit-authority rule that nearly every event permission in this corpus was reached through. What that rule was doing, so that its absence is noted rather than assumed: it asked whether the actor had authority over the event's owning unit before honouring an event grant. There is no owning unit, so there is nothing to ask, and the question "who is connected to this event?" is answered by the operands of §8's language instead — ORGANIZERS, PLACED, CONFIRMED — each of which is a set the item itself defines.

A unit grant of system.admin therefore reaches everywhere on its own. The old resolver needed a special clause for that ("system.admin qualifies whatever the checked scope is"); it existed because organization scope and unit scope were different tiers. With one unit scope and plain inheritance, the clause has nothing to fix.

docs.title: The uniqueness rule has to be careful with audiences
docs.text:
The obvious index — one live grant per (grantee, scope) — never worked, because a person can legitimately hold a personal grant and be covered by an audience grant on the same item, and those are different rows with different lifetimes. Round 10 adds a second reason it cannot work: one code per row, so one person legitimately holds a dozen live allows on one item. A broad office is a couple of dozen rows (D-099), each a different code, and a rule that permitted one live grant per grantee and item would refuse the second of them.

Rules

  • At most one live allow per (grantee, scope, permission) — counted over the rows that name a person and are open, unrevoked, and effect = allow.
  • At most one live allow per (audience, scope, permission), counted the same way over the rows that name an audience.
  • A person and an audience are different grantees, so the same code on the same item may exist once for the person and once for a set they are in. It grants nothing extra and it is not an error; it is two people's decisions about the same capability, which is what the grantee pair has always meant.

Indexes

  • person, audience and scope lookups, each restricted to open rows;
  • a deny-only index over open rows with effect = deny, keyed by grantee, scope and permission — the deny lookup runs on every check, at every scope, and it is the first thing the resolver does.

Denies are excluded from both unique indexes, so a deny may coexist with an allow on the same grantee, scope and code — which is exactly what makes an explicit deny meaningful. A personal deny beats an audience allow, because the deny check runs first and is scope-independent (§10).

docs.title: effect, and why a - in an expression is not a deny
docs.text:
Two mechanisms that both subtract, and are not interchangeable (D-099):

effect = deny - in an audience expression Narrows Every grant that applies to the person, including ones written elsewhere, later, or by somebody else One grant's reach Says "she must not have this, whatever else she is given" "this grant is not for the people in that set" Beatable by Nothing. Checked first, absolute, scope-independent Yes — any other grant that reaches her Lives on A grant row An operand of the grant's audience (§8)

The first cannot be expressed by the second, which is why denies stay — that is D-013's whole reason for existing. And denies are legal at the unit as well as on an item, since "exclude her from what the unit grants everyone" is exactly the case an expression cannot serve: subtracting her from one grant leaves every other grant aimed at the same set intact.

A deny is a real row and can therefore be wrong in a way an allow cannot be. A live deny whose grantee, scope and code match no live allow is dead weight, and a deny that denies nothing is how a stale restriction survives its reason — integrity check 5 (§11) reports the shape, as D-099 requires.

docs.title: Live-grant uniqueness excludes denies — deliberately
docs.text:
A deny must be able to coexist with an allow on the same scope, because that is the only way to express "this person has access to the unit's events, except this one". So the rule that keeps one live grant per grantee, item and code — carried here as uq_access_grant_live — covers allows only; a deny row is outside it by design, and the resolver checks denies first.

This is the rule's shape, not an implementation detail of an index (D-072), and the distinction is load-bearing here rather than pedantic: "unique among live allowing grants" is a conditional rule, so the migration must emit a partial unique index whose predicate excludes deny. A plain unique constraint over the same columns is a different and wrong rule — it would refuse the deny beside the allow, which is precisely the pair the domain requires. See open question F-10, shape 2.

The condition also excludes revoked_at, which is easy to write wrongly in the other direction. A revoked grant must not occupy the unique slot — that is what lets a grant be revoked and re-made rather than edited. So the predicate is "open and unrevoked and allow", three tests, and a partial index that gets one of them wrong is invisible until the day someone cannot save a grant they should be able to.

docs.title: What is refused when a grant is saved
docs.text:
Five checks, one transaction, each with the layer named — because none of them is a database rule, and D-081 forbids writing them as if one were:

  1. The code may be granted at this scope. permission.applies_to permits the scope shape (§2). Refused with the reason in the message, per D-099's example: a grant of event.create on one event is refused because an event cannot be created twice.
  2. The code is assignable. is_assignable is true (§2's deprecated-code case).
  3. Every bound operand in the grant's audience may bind here. An operand whose selector_type.binds_to_item is true is legal only on an item-scope grant, and only where selector_type.argument_type matches that grant's item type. PLACED on a person_group grant is refused because that item is not an event; ORGANIZERS on a unit grant is refused because at the unit there is nothing to bind it to, with the operand named in the message (D-102).
  4. The audience's expression is well-formed and acyclic (§8) — and "acyclic" is measured over the expanded tree, so this check follows the AUDIENCE leaves into the audiences this one names (D-103). Saving a grant is not where a cycle is created, but it is where a person is standing to be told about one, and a grant must never be saved pointing at an expression that cannot be evaluated. There is no depth bound to check here — D-105 left the tree unbounded — so this check carries no size rule at all, and the cycle walk is its only structural refusal.
  5. Every AUDIENCE leaf names an audience that exists and that has a code (D-103). Both halves read a second table, so neither is a constraint on this row: the dangling case is the orphan check of §11 item 2, and the null-code case is that item's neighbour in item 12. A leaf pointing at an unnamed audience is refused rather than resolved-at-read, because resolving it later would make a grant's reach depend on whether somebody had typed a code into a different screen.

Why the save path and not the check path, said once for all five. A grant that cannot mean anything is a data-entry mistake, and a data-entry mistake is refused where the person making it is standing. The resolver's job in the same situation is the opposite and is already fixed: an operand that does not resolve is the empty set, so anything that slips past these checks denies rather than widens (§8, Evaluation) — except through -, where an empty operand widens, which is why these are refusals and not warnings. Checks 3 and 4 (§11) report what got through, and a row there means the write path was skipped — there is no constraint to have disabled.

A sixth refusal lives on the other screen. Ending or deleting an audience is refused while a live grant, or a live audience reachable from one, names it (§8, Rules). It is listed here only so that a reader of this section does not conclude the grant save is the whole write path.

docs.title: No foreign key on scope_id — the accepted trade-off
docs.text:
scope_id has no FK because it is polymorphic. This is a deliberate choice, and D-101 extended it to audience_operand.selector_arg_id, which is polymorphic for the same reason and takes the same four mitigations:

Polymorphic scope_id grantable_item supertable Adding a grantable type One row in grant_scope_type New table + FK from supertable + migration Referential integrity None — can point at a deleted item Full Query cost Direct Requires a join Risk Orphaned grants after an item is deleted Migration churn on every new feature

Polymorphism is what makes a new grantable thing — an event, a group, an office, a document that does not exist yet — a configuration row rather than a schema change, which matters a great deal given how much of this system is not yet specified.

The mitigations are mandatory, not optional:

  1. grant_scope_type validates the scope_type value (FK above).
  2. Deleting an item must close its grants — an application obligation, and tested.
  3. A nightly orphan check per scope type, and the same scan over selector_arg_id (§11, check 2).
  4. scope_id is BIGINT and ids are never reused.

To overrule this, add a grantable_item(id, item_type) supertable and give every grantable entity an FK to it. Tracked in ../open-questions.md — it is a real fork and worth a deliberate decision.

docs.title: Why valid_to is discouraged here too
docs.text: An item grant is typically for one event, so an open-ended item grant is nearly always a mistake. Application validation should require valid_to for item-scoped grants, with access_grant.grant_reason explaining any exception. The sentence stays an application rule, because D-071's posture applies here too: nothing in the schema forces a grant to end, and the report of long-lived open grants is the control. Nothing backstops a forgotten grant. There is no prefilled term and no membership gate between a forgotten row and an answer, so a forgotten grant is simply live.

docs.title: 7. permission_level — deleted by D-099
docs.text:
There is no such table, and this section exists because one page links to its number (D-099). permission_level mapped (permission, scope kind) → the level a grant had to reach, so that one access_grant.level could serve many codes without a mapping hidden in application code. Its two surviving jobs sit on permission itself: applies_to (§2) says which scope kinds a code means anything at, checked on save, and right_kind (§2) is compared by exactly one channel — guardianship (§10). The third job, "how much of this permission does this grant carry", has no answer: a grant is one permission, and the row exists or it does not.

The table's job Where it is now Which scope kinds this permission means anything at permission.applies_to (§2), checked on save How much of this permission a given grant carries Nowhere — a grant is one permission The comparison the level made possible permission.right_kind, used by the guardianship channel alone (§10)

What is lost, said once. A level was a bundle with a name, and a named bundle is something you can ask about: the audit trail could say "she held contribute". The answer to "what did she have in 2024?" is now the set of grant rows that were live then — more precise, less quotable, and a broad office is a couple of dozen rows. That price was paid deliberately, and D-068 had already refused the same idea once. Roles and audiences are the bundle, and nothing else is.

How an ordering could come back, and what it would cost. Names for sets of codes cost nothing — that is what a role already is. A real ordering means re-importing this table, the rank-comparison rule (D-012) and locality's tie-break (D-032's other half), all deleted with their only consumers. The door is wide on the naming side and narrow on the ordering side.

Decisions behind this page: D-002, D-003, D-005, D-006, D-007, D-012, D-013, D-031, D-032, D-039, D-052, D-053, D-068, D-071, D-072, D-074, D-078, D-081, D-086, D-088, D-097, D-098, D-099, D-100, D-101, D-102, D-103, D-105.

docs.title: Data Model — Authorization: the audience table, the grammar, the selector registry
docs.text:
What an audience is as a row, how an expression is written and rendered, and which operands the language has.

Section numbers are shared across the five parts and never renumbered, because other pages cite them by number and their anchors are built from them: 05-authorization.md holds §1–§7, 05a §8 (the audience table, the grammar, the selector registry), 05b §8 continued (the tree and what each operand costs), 05c §9–§10 (access_log and the resolver), and 05d §11–§13 (invariants, seed data, open issues).

docs.title: 8. audience — grants that target a set of people
docs.text:
A grant can name a person or an audience (D-042). An audience is an expression over named sets, stored as a tree (D-101): MEMBERS * ROLE(treasurers) - GROUP(schuzka2026-1) is one grant's grantee. One grant composes a rule and a roster — "the kitchen crew, plus whoever leads this pack" — in the same expression, and it intersects and differences as well as unions.

Fields (audience)

Field Kind Notes id integer identity Surrogate key. code text, optional, unique where set Two jobs. (1) A stable handle for the seeded rows (everyone, all_members) and for reports — an audience is aimed at by a grant through access_grant.audience_id, a reference. (2) The only thing another audience can name: AUDIENCE(<code>) resolves through this column, so naming an audience is what makes it composable, and an unnamed audience is simply not one (D-103). Naming stays opt-in — there is no reason to force a handle onto a grant's private addressee list — and the leaf may not point at a null code, which is a check reading another table and therefore not a constraint (§11, check 12). code joins the shared namespace of roles, groups and reserved words; name does not, and the two are different columns serving different questions. name text, required What a human calls it in the editor. description text, optional Why it exists, for whoever finds it in three years. is_system boolean Default false. Set on the seeded rows so an editor can refuse to delete one. valid_from date, optional valid_to date, optional Absent = open. An ended audience reaches nobody, and that is the one test that gates the whole expression (§Evaluation). Ending one is therefore a save-time refusal once anything names it (rule below): under - an emptied operand makes the result wider, so "ended" would otherwise be a way to widen a grant by editing a different screen. created_at timestamp, audit time created_by reference to person

Rules (audience)

  • The expression is the audience. An audience with no root operand row is an empty set, and a freshly created one is exactly that — not a misconfiguration, and how an expression gets built one node at a time. What is not legal is a grant aimed at one being reported as granting something, which is the editor's job (§The cost of composition) and integrity check 7 (§11).
  • An audience is aimed at by reference and named by code, and those are different relations. A grant points at audience.id; another audience points at audience.code. The name collision problem therefore does reach this table, and §Names are one namespace is where the rule lives (D-103).
  • Bare names do not resolve to audiences. MEMBERS * COUNSELORS names a role or a group, and the audience arm has to be written AUDIENCE(veterans). Why: letting a bare name reach a third table would silently change what stored expressions mean — D-103 keeps bare resolution at its two kinds.
  • code is unique among the rows that have one, and joins the shared namespace (§Names are one namespace).
  • An audience may not be ended or deleted while something live names it — a live grant aimed at it, or a live audience reachable from a live grant through any number of AUDIENCE leaves. Refused at save, and the reverse lookup is one indexed query over audience_operand rows whose selector_kind is AUDIENCE. Why: without this, "ended" is a way to empty an expression from a screen nobody associates with it, and under - an empty operand makes the answer wider, not narrower (D-103). No foreign key does this job: the reference is a code inside a polymorphic column, not a foreign key (§The expression tree).
  • Naming an audience requires the right to read it — audience.view over it, in the catalog's vocabulary — and grants nothing to the people it contains (../appendix/permission-catalog.md). Fail closed. Why: AUDIENCE(veterans) in a grant someone else saves is how one person's composition decision becomes another's authority, and the read permission is the only place that asymmetry is visible to the writer — see what you name is D-091's requirement.
  • The row carries no size rule. There is no depth limit, no width limit and no node budget on an audience, and nothing replaces them on this row (D-105) — the tree is stored exactly as the writer wrote it. What a large expression costs is a report's job (§The cost of composition), and a report with nothing behind it is a convention and not a guard (D-081).
  • Where both ends of the period are set, valid_to is later than valid_from.

This table carries no rule key, no kind, no scope parameter and no configuration column: an audience has no kind and no rule key, only an expression. Which operands exist, whether they take an argument and what type it is live in the selector_type registry (§The selector registry), and no bound on an expression's size is configured anywhere (D-105).

docs.title: Author in sets. Evaluate per person.
docs.text:
p ∈ (A ∩ B) ∪ C is by definition (p ∈ A ∧ p ∈ B) ∨ p ∈ C: the set notation and the per-person boolean test are the same function read from two ends. The choice decides what gets stored and what a writer is allowed to say, not what the machine computes:

  • Sets are the source language, and they are the closed one. - is complement against EVERYONE and * distributes over +, so the set form is no weaker than a boolean one — it buys zero expressive power and everything in the way of safety. The operators are +, - and *, one spelling each; there are no boolean spellings — no &, no |, no !, which were offered with the age operands and declined (D-107). D-060 refused a rule engine, and a per-person boolean language is the door to one.
  • An operand must be a named registry row — a row of §The selector registry — and a writer may compose seeded operands and nothing else. Every row denotes a set of people: MEMBERS denotes the people who pass is_current_member and stores nothing; OLDER(15) denotes the people who are fifteen or older on the checked date, the same shape of thing. What an operand requires is the name, not a table behind the set — an attribute may be an operand (D-107). OLDER(18) is a row, seeded, shipped with its evaluator arm like every other row; AGE >= 18 is not a row and cannot be, because the language has no >= to put anywhere.
  • Eligibility is capability (D-060): no eligibility rule table, no prerequisite system, nothing evaluated outside can(). There is no gate the system applies on its own, and the language holds a vocabulary a person may use to write one.
  • A check never materializes a set. The resolver compiles the expression down to a predicate for the person being checked. An implementation that evaluates MEMBERS as a list of ids and then tests for containment pays three thousand rows per request — the one way to get this wrong, and the reason the requirement is written here rather than left to whoever builds it. Integrity check 16 (§11) is the CI assertion of that sentence.
  • The workloads this corpus promises need sets, not predicates. "Who does this grant reach?" must be shown, expanded, in front of a human — a requirement on the screen (D-091), and a predicate can only report true while a set is the answer. "What may a treasurer do?" (D-100) needs the person→set index, and role_holder and person_group_member are it; an expression is unindexable. And naming an operand is what makes a compilation reusable: a compiled predicate is keyed by the expression it came from and the ruleset version, so one edit to a shared name refreshes every grant that embeds it (§10, D-114).

docs.title: Grammar, precedence, and the canonical rendering
docs.text:
expr    := term ( '+' term )*
term    := operand ( ( '*' | '-' ) operand )*
operand := EVERYONE | MEMBERS
         | OLDER '(' n ')' | YOUNGER '(' n ')'
         | ATTENDED | PLACED | CONFIRMED | ON_WAITLIST | ORGANIZERS
         | ROLE '(' name ')' | GROUP '(' name ')'
         | PERSON '(' person ')'
         | AUDIENCE '(' code ')'
         | '(' expr ')'

  OLDER(n) and YOUNGER(n) read person.birth_date AS OF THE DATE THE CHECK IS MADE,
  so `MEMBERS * OLDER(13) * YOUNGER(19)` reaches different people on different
  dates with no write, and can(..., on date) for a past date answers for that
  past date. Their argument is an INTEGER — the only operand argument in the
