  registry that is not an entity reference (§*The selector registry*). There is
  no comparison operator anywhere in this grammar: no '>=', no '<', no bare AGE
  -- which is where D-060's refusal of a rule engine lives.  See the prose
  under this block, and D-107.

  '+', '-' and '*' are the whole operator set, each with one spelling. OLDER
  and YOUNGER are ordinary named operands, composed by the same three
  operators as every other row.

  Each of ATTENDED, PLACED, CONFIRMED, ON_WAITLIST and ORGANIZERS appears either
  bare — bound to the item the grant sits on — or written '(' event ')'.  A bare
  bound operand on a unit-scope grant is refused (§6, *What is refused when a
  grant is saved*).

  PERSON takes a person and names a set of one.  A hand-written set of people is
  therefore a sum, not a leaf: `PERSON(a) + PERSON(b)`
  ([D-105](../decisions/round-11-12.md#d-105--there-are-no-lists-a-hand-written-set-is-an-expression-like-any-other)).
  AUDIENCE names another saved audience by its
  `code`; an audience with no code cannot be named, and a bare name never
  resolves to one ([D-103](../decisions/round-10b.md#d-103--an-audience-may-name-another-audience)).
  • + union, * intersection, - difference — three operators, one spelling each. MEMBERS * OLDER(13) * YOUNGER(19) is an ordinary term.
  • There is no comparison operator in the language. No >=, no <, no bare AGE: an operand is a registry row and AGE >= 15 has no row to be, which is the whole of D-060's protection now (§Author in sets, and D-107).
  • * and - bind tighter than +; * and - bind equally, left to right; brackets override.
  • The canonical rendering prints every bracket, always. The rendering is derived from the rows and is what every screen shows; if it is also kept as a column for search, it is a copy and the rows win (see §The expression tree).

Printing every bracket is not a courtesy, and the example is the proof. Under this precedence, the unbracketed MEMBERS - GROUP(schuzka2026-1) * COUNSELORS means "everyone except the counselors in that group", which is not what its author meant — they meant "all counselors not in that group", whose stored form is (MEMBERS - GROUP(schuzka2026-1)) * COUNSELORS. The editor rewrites what is typed into canonical form before saving, so no expression in this system is ever read bare; and once everything is stored fully bracketed, changing what binds tighter later changes nothing already stored.

A hand-typed sum of twenty people is a left-to-right chain, so it prints as nineteen nested pairs of brackets. That is what "storage and display both say what was written" buys, and it is asked for. If it turns out unreadable, the answer is that a set of people big enough to be unreadable is a person_group — not a flattening rule invented in advance (D-105).

docs.title: The selector registry
docs.text:
selector_type is a seeded table, not an enum (D-101): the language becomes data. The parser reads its reserved words from it, the editor builds its dropdown from it, and the write path checks arity against it. It is the shape grant_scope_type already has.

Fields (selector_type)

Field Kind Notes code text, required, unique The reserved word: MEMBERS, ROLE, PLACED. name text, required For the editor's dropdown. takes_argument boolean, required Whether the code may be written with an argument. The arity check reads this column and nothing else. binds_to_item boolean, required True exactly when the argument-less form means "relative to the item being checked" (D-102). argument_type text, optional Which table the argument names a row of — role, person_group, person, event, audience — or a scalar: integer, the argument kind OLDER and YOUNGER take (D-107). Six values, five of them entity kinds and one of them not an entity. Absent exactly when takes_argument is false. This is what the save path compares against the grant's item type, which is a reason the registry is doing real work and not merely tidying. It is not always a grant_scope_type: person never was and audience never will be, because a grant is never about an audience — it is aimed through one. The two coincide for exactly the item-scoped operands, which is the set the binding check reads. A scalar argument is never in that set, since OLDER binds to nothing. description text, optional The sentence a writer reads before using it. AUDIENCE carries its gloss here, because the name misleads without one. is_system boolean, required Default true, and every seeded row is true with no row planned false. This column exists to make the table refuse an edit, not to mark a category.

Seeded selectors, in full, because this table is the language — thirteen rows, all of them shipped. The number is only the cheap form of the real check: this list is the language, so an operand appearing anywhere other than here — in a screen's dropdown, in a resolver's switch, in a decision entry that never reached this table — is a bug, and §13 keeps the document-level report that hunts exactly that. Every seeded row is either a rule about people or takes an argument, so the registry carries no special case left to explain; OLDER and YOUNGER are the only rows whose argument is not an entity reference.

code Argument Binds to item Means EVERYONE never no Any person, including those with no account and no membership. MEMBERS never no Holds a membership live on the checked date — the same predicate the membership gate applied (D-039). OLDER required (integer) no The people who are n years old or older on the date being checked, from person.birth_date — the only operand in the registry whose argument is a number rather than a row (D-107). It is a row here for the reason the whole table exists: it is a named operand, and it denotes a set of people — the same shape of thing MEMBERS denotes, which is a test over membership rows and stores nothing either. A person with no birth date is not in the set, as a person with no membership row is not in MEMBERS: that is an ordinary answer, not a resolution failure, and §11's report of unresolved leaves must not page about it (§Evaluation). Its membership moves at midnight with no write — see §The cost of composition. YOUNGER required (integer) no The people strictly younger than n on the date being checked — OLDER's mirror, n and up against under n. Each is the complement of the other, and the language has no complement a bare leaf can carry (only -, which needs something on its left), so both are seeded rather than one being spelled out of the other; that is the whole of their relationship, and it is why there is no AGE_BAND row and none is wanted — a band is composed out of the operators every other row is composed with, and OLDER(13) - OLDER(18) is thirteen to seventeen. Same argument kind, same date rule, same non-failure for a missing birth date. PERSON required (person) no One named person — a set of one, which is a set, so it is a named operand like every other row: the exception for a named individual lives inside the expression that granted the rule, next to the thing it exempts (D-100). A hand-written set of several people is written the same way, as a sum of these — PERSON(a) + PERSON(b) — because a set of one is a set, and a set of three is the same thing three times (D-105). There is no separate "hand-typed list" operand and no table behind one. ROLE required (role) no Holders of that office live on the checked date (role_holder). GROUP required (person_group) no Members of that group live on the checked date (person_group_member). AUDIENCE required (audience) no The value of another saved audience's expression, evaluated live on the checked date — the one operand whose argument is a decision about access rather than a roster, and so the one that makes a rule namable (D-103). ATTENDED optional (event) yes, event response = attending. PLACED optional (event) yes, event Attending and not waitlisted — the capacity set, the one the events module counts and the index already serves. CONFIRMED optional (event) yes, event PLACED and is_confirmed — holds a paid place. ON_WAITLIST optional (event) yes, event Attending and waitlisted. ORGANIZERS optional (event) yes, event Runs the event (event_organizer).

Two operands a reader might reach for are not in this table. LIST is not an operand: a hand-written set of people is a sum, PERSON(a) + PERSON(b), written inside the expression like every other set (D-105). GUARDIANS is not a selector either: guardianship is a channel carrying a right_level over a child on the guardianship row, not a set a grant may be aimed at, and an operand naming it would re-grant, one code at a time, what that channel grants whole (D-113).

Rules (selector_type)

  • Rows are platform-seeded. Adding an operand is a decision entry plus a seed row, never a row somebody types into a screen: each operand is a branch of the evaluator and a fact about stored data, and an editor that could invent one would produce an expression nothing evaluates — which then resolves to the empty set and denies quietly forever (§Evaluation).
  • The registry is organization-read-only, and saying that out loud is what makes "a closed language" true of a table rather than merely asserted. Every row ships with the platform, every row is is_system, no screen edits this table, and no organization adds to it (D-103). The language becomes data means the parser and the editor read one place instead of three; it does not mean the language is extensible at runtime. A code in this table with no shipped resolver arm is a deployment bug, and it surfaces as an empty set — an operand that reaches nobody, an allow that allows nobody, and a deny that on the - side denies everybody. That is the whole hazard of calling a closed set "data", and it is why the seeding of this table is release engineering rather than configuration. There is no third kind of row — the taxonomy is shipped and seeded, and "seeded, marked system, but not implemented" is not a category this model allows, however useful it would be as a roadmap marker.
  • Every code is a reserved name in the shared role / group / audience namespace (§Names are one namespace).
  • argument_type is absent exactly when takes_argument is false, and names a real table exactly when it is true — one exception: the scalar domain integer, which OLDER and YOUNGER take and which names no table because it names no row (D-107). Anything reading this column has to know the scalar case exists, and has to know what the scalar is not — it is not a reference. That is why §11's assertion that exactly two polymorphic keys in this design go without a foreign key (access_grant.scope_id, audience_operand.selector_arg_id) holds: an 18 sitting in selector_arg_id points at nothing, so there is nothing for a merge to repoint, nothing for a cascade to find, and nothing for the orphan scan to walk. The check counts references, and 18 is not one (§A hand-named person is now a keyless reference, where the argument kinds are enumerated).
  • The four attendance tiers name columns of event_registration and nothing else. That is the requirement that keeps the writer's choice honest — picking between tiers only means something if the choices are the stored facts.

Three operands are not in this table, and each absence is load-bearing.

  • PRESENT(<event>) over was_present is refused, and this paragraph is the whole reason. The reason is the failure direction: was_present is NULL until somebody takes a register, so an operand built on it would revoke a child's access to their own camp photos because a volunteer forgot to tick a box. That column is a safeguarding signal, three-valued on purpose (D-067), and keeping it out of the selector language is what keeps it meaning "a person recorded this" rather than "this is who may see things". It is refused because of what it would do on the - side of an expression when a volunteer forgets a tick box — not because of what it is: a predicate over a column is an ordinary kind of operand (D-107).
  • GRANTS is refused. It was wanted so that an expression could name "the people reached by these grants" — a bulk-editing affordance dressed as an operand. An operand must resolve to a set of people, and a set of grants is not one: the moment an expression can name the grant table, MEMBERS - GRANTS(...) is expressible, and a language in which a grant can subtract a grant is a language in which the answer to "who may do this?" requires evaluating the whole expression tree of every other grant to answer one check — the closure property of §Author in sets doing the job it exists for. The bulk edit it was asked for is real and is an editor affordance — select the grants, change their grantees, in one screen, which changes rows and leaves every stored expression meaning what it meant. Refusing it here is what keeps that screen a UI feature instead of a resolver feature.
  • WHITELISTED is not seeded, and the reason is that there is nothing to evaluate. The nearest facts are source = staff (an organizer entered them) and promotion off the waitlist. Either it means one of those or it is a new column on event_registration, which is an events decision and not a selector decision, so it stays an open question rather than being implied by a word in a grammar. An operand that reads no state is not a vocabulary item but a syntax error wearing one's clothes. F-20 is a question about whether the feature is wanted, not about whether the language could hold the word.

PERSON(x) is a registry row, and a hand-named person is a set nobody maintains: PERSON(a) is created by being typed. That is tolerable for exactly one operand, at the size of one person, because the alternative — a second grant aimed at that person, which stays legal and is arguably clearer for a permanent exception — leaves the exception invisible next to the rule it exempts. A grant aimed at one person is the ordinary expression of a temporary exception, and its cost is not the typing: a typed person is a selector_arg_id with no foreign key behind it, and §A hand-named person is now a keyless reference is where the repointing requirement that hangs on that lives.

docs.title: What LIST is, said plainly — withdrawn by D-105
docs.text:
LIST is not an operand and audience_member is not a table. The answer to "plus Honza" is PERSON(a) + PERSON(b), written in the expression where every other set in this language is written (D-105).

Naming three people inside a grant must not mean making them members of a person_group. A group's members are true when no grant points at them (D-098), so editing a roster to move one grant's reach edits a set that other grants read — and it invents a group nobody talks about. The answer to "plus Honza" is PERSON(honza), and the answer is not a roster edit. An exception written this way is invisible to every other grant until somebody opens this one and has no name of its own, and AUDIENCE(x) still resolves to another audience's whole expression and nothing less, so nobody can reach into the middle of it from outside.

The limits of writing people in the expression. There are no per-person dates: audience_operand carries no period and gains none, so a June-to-August exception is its own grant with its own period (D-099) — where there is one audience and one grant there are now two grants, and a reviewer asking "what does Honza have?" must find both. There is no per-name provenance: created_by on a node answers "who last saved this tree" and not "who added Honza". "Who was on this audience in 2026" is a recomputation over audit payloads that expire after 24 months (D-088), so the question stops being answerable in 2028. And two writers can collide: a hand-written set is one expression edited as a whole, so whoever builds the editor owes this an optimistic-concurrency check or a queue — a silent lost update here quietly removes somebody's access, and nothing in the schema will notice.

Decisions behind this page: D-039, D-042, D-060, D-067, D-081, D-088, D-091, D-098, D-099, D-100, D-101, D-102, D-103, D-105, D-107, D-113, D-114.

docs.title: Data Model — Authorization: the expression tree and what each operand costs
docs.text:
The storage half of §8: the audience_operand tree itself, the namespace rule, what each operand costs, and how a tree is evaluated.

Section numbers are shared across the five parts and never renumbered, because other pages cite them by number and their anchors are built from them: 05-authorization.md holds §1–§7, 05a §8 (the audience table, the grammar, the selector registry), 05b §8 continued (the tree and what each operand costs), 05c §9–§10 (access_log and the resolver), and 05d §11–§13 (invariants, seed data, open issues).

docs.title: The expression tree
docs.text:
Each row of audience_operand is one node — a binary tree: two operands and one operator per row. Why: one evaluator of about fifteen lines answers every operand, and the tree keeps the writer's brackets instead of silently rewriting them (D-101).

Fields (audience_operand)

Field Kind Notes id integer identity Surrogate key. audience_id reference to audience, required Denormalized onto every row so that the whole tree is one indexed fetch. The read path never walks a parent chain; it selects by audience_id and assembles in memory. One indexed read per audience in the closure, not one per check (D-103): an expression naming AUDIENCE(veterans) has to fetch that audience's rows as well. No transitive walk over audience_operand rows, and no recursive query. The closure's size is discovered by walking it at save, not bounded by a number — the walk that checks acyclicity has already counted the audiences, so the cost is known before the first check runs, and it is not known in advance of the expression (rule below, and §The cost of composition). Every row also carries its parent's audience_id, so a node never belongs to a different audience than the one above it (checked on save, asserted by check 10). parent_id reference to audience_operand, optional On the child, so a node belongs to exactly one expression. Absent on the root. operator enum: +, -, *, optional Set on a node, absent on a leaf. left_id reference to audience_operand, optional Set on a node. Left and right are not interchangeable: - is not commutative, and the pair is the expression's meaning. right_id reference to audience_operand, optional Set on a node. selector_kind reference to selector_type, optional Set on a leaf, absent on a node. selector_arg_id integer, optional Polymorphic, and deliberately without a foreign key — it points at role, person_group, person, event or audience depending on kind — or it points at nothing: OLDER and YOUNGER write their integer into this same column (D-107), because the column is an integer and the value is one. An integer in this column is not a reference: nothing to repoint on a merge, nothing for a cascade to find, nothing for the orphan scan to walk — which is precisely why that scan filters on the selector's kind and walks the five entity kinds rather than every row in this column (§A hand-named person is now a keyless reference). A reader who takes "polymorphic" to mean "always a row id" will write that scan wrong, which is why the sentence is here. §11 asserts that exactly two polymorphic columns in this design go without a foreign key, and it holds at thirteen operands; the count is of keys, so a scalar sitting in a key's column does not move it, and an operand arriving or leaving cannot move it either. D-011's accepted trade-off, with its compensating orphan check (§11, check 2). Absent exactly when the selector's takes_argument is false. An AUDIENCE leaf stores the referenced audience's row here and is therefore also the reference edge (rule below), and the extra condition on that leaf is that the audience it names has a code — a check reading another table, which is why it is an integrity check and not a constraint (§11, check 12). created_at timestamp, audit time created_by reference to person Who wrote this node. An expression is a decision about how far a grant reaches, and the person who saved it is the answer to the question asked afterwards.

Rules (audience_operand)

  • Exactly one shape. A node has operator, left_id and right_id, and no selector_kind; a leaf has selector_kind (and selector_arg_id where the registry says it takes one) and no operator and no children. Expressible on the row, so this one stays a real constraint — the only rule in this section a migration can state by itself, which is worth noticing among the ones that cannot.
  • One parent, never a DAG. parent_id lives on the child. A side table letting two expressions share a node is refused. Why: editing the shared node would silently widen every grant using it — the inclusion hazard re-imported through the back door (D-091). Check 15 (§11) is a CI assertion that no such table exists.
  • Cycles are refused when the row is saved, and the two walks below are the only structural guard this module has. Nothing else stands between a saved expression and one that never terminates, so they are not relaxed for any reason: an expansion that never terminates is precisely what they refuse.
  • Inside the tree: walk the parent chain from the row upward — refuse a revisit. The tree shape makes a cycle structurally hard to build (a node cannot be its own ancestor if it did not exist when its parent was written), and it is refused rather than trusted for D-091's own reason: a hand-fixed row, a restore from before the guard existed.
  • Across audiences: follow every AUDIENCE leaf in the closure and refuse a cycle through them. Why: a tree cannot cycle, and an expression naming audiences is a forest of trees pointing at each other (D-103 is what makes this half necessary). Half 1 is cheap; half 2 is a write-time reachability walk over a graph built at save time from rows that already exist, and it is the walk that also counts the closure whose size the read path pays for, since it is already visiting every audience in it. No size is measured here: the walk refuses a cycle and nothing else.

Application layer for both walks, and the layer is named because each spans rows rather than columns of one row, which is F-10 shape 3, so no migration can emit either. - There is no edge table and no depth parameter. audience_include and include_depth_limit are not in the model: the edges are the AUDIENCE leaves, so there is nothing to maintain and no transitive walk over rows at read time (D-101, D-105). - The tree is stored exactly as the writer wrote it: one row per node, two operands and one operator, left to right, and no rebalancing (D-105). Why: a rebalanced tree is a different expression from the one a person wrote — which is the whole reason this storage exists rather than a normalized union of terms — and a quietly flattened tree is one whose canonical rendering does not print what its author saw. A balanced tree is cheaper to walk and nothing here wants a cheaper walk badly enough to pay for it. - Nothing bounds how big an expression may get, and this page calls that what it is: a convention, not a guard. There is no depth bound, no width bound and no node budget on an audience; selector_depth_limit is not a parameter and nothing replaces it (D-105), so the size of an audience's expansion is bounded only by acyclicity — height was never bounded across a closure and breadth was never bounded at all. "A check costs a bounded amount" is therefore not a property of this system; that property came from a bound and nowhere else. What stands in place of the check is a standing report of the widest and deepest audiences, their closure size and their cost per check, kept running rather than computed once at save, and its home is the tab on the permissions page (F-21). Nothing refuses a save on size, no CI job fails, and the report stops being a control the moment nobody reads it — D-081's convention rather than a guard, and the third control of that shape this module depends on. The cost it reports is paid per check: there is no stored answer to pay it once (D-114), a request memoizes it, and a compilation is cached once per version and holds no person and no item (§10) — so compiling removes the parsing and the name resolution from the cost, not the reads. A wide EVERYONE is therefore nobody's problem only until somebody checks it. - Arity and binding are checked against selector_type on save: an argument present exactly when the registry allows one, and a bound (argument-less, binds_to_item) operand legal only on an item-scope grant whose type matches argument_type (§6, What is refused when a grant is saved). - An operand that does not resolve is the empty set — including an AUDIENCE leaf whose target has gone (D-103). A dangling selector_arg_id, a selector kind the evaluator does not implement, a role or group whose row has been deleted — each is the empty set, and an expression that cannot be evaluated reaches nobody (§Evaluation). Fail closed on the allow side, and note that the same rule is fail-open looking, which is why it is stated with its two halves rather than as a slogan: a failed operand on the + or * side narrows the set, and a failed operand on the - side widens it (D-106). - is the only operator whose failed operand can grant, so fail closed names a direction and not a safe state: EVERYONE - PERSON(x) with a dead x is fail-closed and a lockout of everybody in one breath. Why the answer stays the empty set: a silent widening is discovered in an audit two years late, so the visibility goes on a page instead — an audience carrying a leaf that does not resolve is listed for its owner, in a second column of the report F-21 already asks for. No save is refused because a leaf is broken, and no expression is pinned to the set it resolved to when it was saved — pinning would make the stored expression a ceiling on truth, and a grant would freeze at the shape it had on the day somebody typed it. The report is a query with an owner and is a convention, not a guard (D-081). The line is narrower than it looks: an operand that resolves fine and simply does not contain the person is not on that list. A person with no birth date is not a failed OLDER(18) — the operand resolves to the people who are that age on the checked date, and the person is not among them, exactly as a person with no membership row is not a failed MEMBERS. A missing attribute on the person being asked about is an ordinary answer, not a resolution failure, and a report that conflated the two would page about every incomplete import in the country. What keeps the wide case from arriving by ordinary administration is that an audience a live grant names cannot be ended or deleted (§8, in 05a). - The AUDIENCE leaves are the reference edges, and there is no edge table (D-103). Every question about nesting — does this cycle, how deep does this get, which grants name this audience, may this audience be deleted — is answered by selecting rows from this one table where selector_kind = 'AUDIENCE'. The two-directional index that makes that cheap is (selector_kind, selector_arg_id), and it is the second reason the reference is stored as a row rather than parsed out of a rendering: an edge inside a string answers none of those questions without a table scan. - A node belongs to exactly one tree, and to exactly one audience. Every row's audience_id equals its parent's; there is exactly one row with no parent; no row is its own descendant. Check 10 (§11) counts these. Nesting does not soften this: AUDIENCE(x) points a whole tree at another whole tree. It is not a node shared between two expressions, and the rule above about one parent and no sharing table is exactly what keeps AUDIENCE() from being a node-sharing design by another name. - The whole tree is written together. An expression is one act of authorship, so inserting a grant's audience inserts its nodes in one transaction, and deleting an audience deletes them. A node whose parent arrives in a later transaction is an orphan, and an orphan is check 10, not a transient state to be tolerated.

Why a tree and not a string, and why not a normal form. A string would have to be re-parsed on every check and would make the arity rules text-processing rather than row-writing. A union of terms needs the normalizer — distribute, dedupe, sort, survive blow-up — and would rewrite the writer's brackets behind their back. The tree needs one fifteen-line evaluator and keeps the brackets; (A + B) * C costs nothing.

What that costs. Two expressions with the same meaning are two different row sets, so "you already granted exactly this set on that row" does not fall out of storage — and that is accepted, not mitigated: nothing computes the semantic equality of two expressions, so no warning fires when a second audience means what a first one means (F-14, D-110). The same reasoning is why "this selector reaches nobody" belongs to the editor preview that has to exist anyway (§The cost of composition) rather than to a syntactic check the tree cannot perform — a tree catches X - X on one node and nothing else.

docs.title: audience_member, re-roled as the LIST leaf — deleted by D-105
docs.text:
audience_member is not a table and LIST is not an operand (D-105). A hand-written set of people is written in the expression, as PERSON(a) + PERSON(b), in the same place every other set in this language is written; a set that is dated and shared between grants is a person_group. The heading is kept so that pages linking here land on the guardrail rather than on nothing. None of these are in the system: a per-person valid_from / valid_to half-open period with its no-overlap rule, an added_by naming who put one person there, an editor rendering an operand as LIST (this audience), and a refusal to add a person to a seeded is_system audience — adding somebody to everyone is a category error, and with no list there is no row left to refuse, so that one retires instead of becoming a report. What an expression carries is one period — its grant's — and created_by on a node, which answers who last saved this tree.

Not a roster edit. The refusal to solve a grant's exception by editing a group roster stands, because the hazard is real: making three people members of GROUP(kitchen) in order to reach one grant edits a roster that other grants read, and it creates a row in the group browser that is not a group anybody talks about. D-098 is the rule that says so — a group's members are true when no grant points at them — and PERSON(a) + PERSON(b) is the answer that respects it. person_group_member is the only dated set of people the system keeps. The hazards a hand-named person now carries — no per-name date, no per-name adder, and two writers editing one expression at once — are stated once in 05a, §What LIST is, said plainly.

docs.title: Three named sets, and the one question nesting cannot answer
docs.text:
GROUP(x), AUDIENCE(x) and PERSON(x) are all "some people" and none of them is the same kind of thing (D-103). A hand-written set of people is not a fourth kind of thing: it is a sum of PERSON() leaves (D-105).

GROUP(x) AUDIENCE(x) PERSON(x) What it is A dated roster somebody maintains A saved expression, evaluated live One named person, typed into this expression Who may change who is in it person_group.member.manage audience.manage on that audience Whoever may edit this expression Does it exist outside a grant? Yes — D-098: a group's members are true with nothing pointing at them No — it exists to aim a grant No — and it is not a set anybody maintains "Was she in it on 1 June 2024?" Answerable, from the dated rows Not answerable past the audit window Not answerable past the audit window Sensitive as ⚠ company 🔒🔒 authority 🔒 one named person

The fourth row is the honest cost. GROUP(x) is materialized, so its past is reconstructable from its own rows; AUDIENCE(x) is a live rule, and its past shape survives only in the audit trail — where D-088 empties the payloads after 24 months. So "who could see this child's data in 2024?" is answerable when the grant pointed at a group and is not answerable when it pointed at a nested audience. A rule whose reach cannot be reconstructed is still the right tool for a rule — MEMBERS is not going to be replaced by a roster of everyone — but the gap gets closed by a report, not by pretending the question has an answer. The report is the save-time listing in §The cost of composition, kept over time rather than shown once; whether that is worth building is registered in §13 and is the same question as F-7, which is dissolved (§The cost of composition). A saved snapshot of whom a grant reached is the only thing that could answer about 2011, and the system keeps none — the expression is the record, and it is a rule, not a snapshot (D-110).

docs.title: Names are one namespace, and reserved words are the other half
docs.text:
Bare COUNSELORS resolves against roles and groups together, since ROLE() and GROUP() do not have to disambiguate — which makes the name namespace load-bearing: a name in this system is not a label, it is what resolves (D-101). Five rules, and the layer each one lives in is the point:

  1. Names are unique across role, person_group and audience.code — the third of them because code is what resolves and audience.name is what a screen displays, so name is not in the namespace (D-103). No single constraint spans three tables, so the write path carries it and integrity check 12 (§11) asserts the write path exists — D-081 wording, because a rule with no database backstop is a convention until a check says otherwise.
  2. Case, whitespace and separators are folded on write, so Schuzka 2026-1, schuzka_2026_1 and SCHUZKA2026-1 are one name and not three sets that look different in an editor.
  3. Every selector_type.code is reserved. A group called MEMBERS is refused at the save rather than silently rewriting every expression in the system.
  4. Bare names resolve to exactly two kinds: a role or a group. An audience is reachable only through its own keyword, AUDIENCE(veterans) — naming the namespace a third way without widening bare resolution. Why: bare resolution is what keeps stored expressions meaning what they meant when they were written (the audience rules at the head of §8).
  5. What is stored is always kind + id, never a name — so a rename never rewrites a grant. A role renamed still carries everything aimed at it. AUDIENCE obeys this like every other leaf: the resolution happens once, at save, into selector_arg_id, and renaming the audience afterwards rewrites nothing. Read the rule for exactly what it says: a rename rewrites nothing, because a rename leaves the row and its id where they were. A person merge is not a rename — it retires an id — and every hand-named person in the system is a leaf holding one, which is the next section.

What is given up: a name is a security-relevant string. Two organizations that both call something leaders and one of them a group and the other a role get one namespace deciding which leaders a grant meant, and the answer is that they cannot, because the write path refused the second one at the save. An audience code colliding with an office code is in that namespace too, and it is not cosmetic: something can name an audience, so a collision is a silent grant.

docs.title: A hand-named person is now a keyless reference
docs.text:
Every hand-named person in the system is a selector_arg_id, and that column deliberately has no foreign key — D-011's accepted trade-off, extended to this column by D-101 and backstopped by an orphan scan rather than by the database. This is what makes the requirement below load-bearing.

Requirement: a person merge, and a redaction, must repoint every audience_operand leaf whose selector_arg_id names the absorbed or erased person, in all five argument kinds that name an entity. The merge reassignment table carries the row, the erasure path carries the scan, and the nightly orphan check (§11, check 2) is the backstop rather than the mechanism — a scan that runs the following morning is not a reassignment, and by the time it reports, an expression has already resolved wrong. It belongs to F-10's register for precisely the reason that register exists: the ORM cannot express it, because the column has no key to follow.

Why this is not housekeeping. A leaf that resolves to nobody is the empty set, which narrows the result on the + and * sides and widens it on the - side (D-106), and this module's own recurring worked example is a subtraction: EVERYONE - PERSON(x). Un-repointed, x stops subtracting anybody and the grant denies everybody — reachable by an ordinary merge rather than by a hand-edited row.

Why all five kinds, and not just person. The scan is over one column, and the column does not know what it points at. A merge is the case that made the requirement, but an erased event, a deleted group, a retired office or an ended audience leave the identical orphan behind them, and writing the rule as "PERSON leaves only" would put the hazard straight back where it is sitting. The five kinds a scan walks are person, role, person_group, event and audience. selector_type.argument_type takes six values: five of them entity kinds, and the sixth integer, the argument of OLDER and YOUNGER (D-107) — and the scans walk the five. This is the one place to say why, because it looks like an omission and is not: an 18 in selector_arg_id is not a reference, so there is no row behind it to merge away, none to erase, none for a cascade to find and none for the orphan scan to report. The number this section is about — that exactly two polymorphic columns in this design go without a foreign key — is therefore two, and it is a count of keys: a scalar stored in a key's column is not one. Nobody has to add a person.birth_date branch to a merge script, and anyone who does has misread this paragraph.

docs.title: What each operand costs
docs.text:
What is worth comparing is whether a set is derived or kept. Every operand in the registry reads a fact that exists independently of the expression:

A derived operand Which Twelve of the thirteen — EVERYONE, MEMBERS, OLDER, YOUNGER, ROLE, GROUP, ATTENDED, PLACED, CONFIRMED, ON_WAITLIST, ORGANIZERS and AUDIENCE — are derived from another expression rather than from a fact table, which makes AUDIENCE the odd one and the reason this table has a footnote below. The thirteenth, PERSON, is neither derived nor kept: see below. OLDER and YOUNGER sit here on the strength of the row below them — a live read of a stored fact at the checked date, exactly like MEMBERS reading membership — but they are the first whose answer to "when does someone join?" is not "when a row is written": the row was written at birth, and the set changes on its own. §The cost of composition carries what that costs How evaluated A live read of the fact that defines it, at the checked date When someone joins They are in it immediately — automatically Maintenance None. It cannot rot. Membership stored? No — and therefore not retrievable after the facts move (§The cost of composition) Examples "everyone who holds a place on this event", "the counselors", "anyone thirteen or older"

Nothing is kept. No operand's members are rows somebody maintains, so there is no per-person date, no no-overlap rule and no staleness warning anywhere in this module: LIST, the one operand whose members were maintained rows, is not in the model (D-105). A set that is dated, shared and maintained by hand is a person_group (§audience_member, re-roled as the LIST leaf).

PERSON(x) is not a kept operand either, and pretending it is would lose the distinction. It is a constant: the answer is written into the leaf itself, so it reads no fact table and maintains no roster. It cannot rot the way a kept set rots — nobody has to remove anybody, because nobody is in it except the one person named. What it can do is dangle, which is a different failure with a sharper edge, and §A hand-named person is now a keyless reference is where that is handled.

Prefer a derived operand where one exists. A grant to PLACED gets the right answer forever: a new registrant is covered the moment they are placed, and someone who withdraws stops being covered, with no rows to maintain. A grant listing names by hand does not do that: a sum of PERSON() leaves goes stale, one leaf at a time. So the choice is a size question and not a question about the kind of set: a set of people big enough to be a roster is a person_group, and a set small enough to type is a sum of PERSON() leaves, and one expression may hold the derived set and the names it cannot reach in one grant (D-105's judgement, registered where missing operands are registered in ../open-questions.md).

Composition is written in the expression, not in an edge. GROUP(kitchen) + ROLE(troop_staff) composes as much as an inclusion edge ever did, because a group's membership is its dated rows (D-098), and reusing a whole saved expression is AUDIENCE(<code>) (D-103). So there is no transitive walk over a graph and no include_depth_limit to enforce it with — the guard that came back is the write-time reachability walk across audiences (§The expression tree), which is smaller machinery than the table it replaced. AUDIENCE() is also the only arm that names a decision about access rather than people, so it is the only one that can say "the same people that grant may see the fee ledger, plus the accountant".

AUDIENCE is derived, and it is derived from something nobody maintains, which is its one genuinely new property. Every other derived operand reads a fact table someone is already keeping — a membership, a holder row, a registration. AUDIENCE(x) reads an expression. So the "maintenance: none, it cannot rot" row of the table above is true of it in the sense that there are no rows to maintain, and misleading in the sense that the thing it is derived from is edited by whoever holds audience.manage on it, for their own reasons. That is the hazard of §The cost of composition, and it is why this operand is graded as authority rather than as company.

docs.title: Evaluation
docs.text:
An audience grant is evaluated as part of the person's own permissions — the resolver expands it, so a grant to an audience is checked as if the person held it directly. The expansion is a predicate, not a set (§Author in sets).

A grant applies when one grant row satisfies all of these. These are conditions on a single row, tested together — their order carries no meaning:

  1. The grant names an audience; a personal grant is not this question's business.
  2. Its scope_type is the scope type being checked, and its scope_id matches the scope id being checked, with an absent id counting as equal to an absent checked id.
  3. Its effect is allow — denies belong to the channel that runs first (§10).
  4. It has not been revoked.
  5. It has started as of the checked date and has not ended on that date.
  6. Its permission_id is the checked permission — or is system.admin, the one code that means everything (§2). There is no permission_level row to consult and no rank to compare: a grant answers one code (D-099).
  7. person_in_audience(person, audience, at, item) puts the person in that audience on the checked date, for the item being checked — because a bound operand means different people on different items (D-102).

person_in_audience() is where the language lives. It takes the item so that bound operands have something to bind to, and it answers one question: is this person in the value of this expression, evaluated as a predicate?

  1. The audience itself must not have ended — no valid_to, or a valid_to after the checked date. An ended audience covers nobody, and this is the one test that gates the whole tree: the expression belongs to the audience that has ended, not to one of its operands.
  2. Evaluate the tree bottom-up, as a predicate. A leaf asks its selector; a node combines its two children with its operator; p ∈ A - B is p ∈ A ∧ ¬(p ∈ B), and so on for + and *. No set of people is ever built — the same fifteen lines answer every operand, and the cost of a check is one indexed read per operand, not one per member. AUDIENCE(x) is the one leaf that recurses (§Three named sets): it hands the same person, at and item to the other audience's tree and returns that answer, predicating all the way down (D-103). Nesting does not turn the evaluator into a set-builder; it turns one fifteen-line function into the same function with one more branch. The recursion is bounded by nothing, and the read path gets no depth cap and no cycle check of its own. Why: a cap applied while reading becomes the thing that decides who a grant reaches, so the refusal is deliberate (D-105) — which is why the acyclicity walk at save (§The expression tree) is the only thing standing between a saved expression and one that never finishes evaluating.
  3. A leaf's selector is one read — except AUDIENCE, which is one read per audience in the closure. MEMBERS is the membership predicate at at; ROLE(x) is one open role_holder row for this person and this role at at; GROUP(x) likewise in person_group_member; PERSON(x) is the cheapest leaf in the language — it is the comparison x = p against a value already stored in the row, so a hand-written sum of twenty names is twenty of those and no fact table is consulted; PLACED is this person's event_registration row for the bound event with response = attending and is_waitlisted false; EVERYONE is true. OLDER(n) and YOUNGER(n) are the two cheapest reads in the language after PERSON: one row already in hand — person.birth_date — compared against n at at, no join and no fact table. They are also the only operands whose answer at changes on its own: every other leaf asks whether a row was live at at, and these two ask arithmetic about one, which is why a check for a past date has a right answer here (can(p, view, doc, on 2024-05-01, about q) computes the age that day) and why the set can move with no write to invalidate (D-107). A person whose birth_date is null is not in either set, and that is this rule answering, not failing — item 5 below is about leaves that resolve to nothing, and this is not one of them.
  4. A bound operand binds to the item under check. PLACED with no argument means the event in the check's scope. At the unit there is nothing to bind it to, and such a grant could not have been saved (§6's save-time list) — so an unbound-at-unit shape reaching here is a fault, and it resolves to the empty set rather than to "everyone at the unit", which is the direction a helpful implementation would get wrong.
  5. Failure is denial, in every direction. An operand whose selector_arg_id names nothing, whose selector_kind no evaluator implements, or whose tree cannot be assembled reaches nobody, and a leaf whose argument names a person who has been merged away is on this list too — which is why §A hand-named person is now a keyless reference makes repointing a requirement rather than a nicety. An absent selector is a fault, not a hint. Nothing here falls back to "so it probably includes everyone", and nothing here guesses the half of a tree it could resolve: an expression that cannot be evaluated is an empty set, which is the direction this model fails in everywhere else — default deny (§10), deny absolute (channel 0), and an audience whose rule was quietly wrong reaching nobody rather than everybody. A cycle through AUDIENCE leaves is refused where it is written, so an evaluator meeting one is meeting data that should not exist, and the rule that covers that is this one — reach nobody, do not recurse forever and do not guess. The reason the write-path check has to be a cross-audience reachability walk and not a parent-chain walk is exactly here (check 15): if the read path is ever the thing that notices a cycle, some grant has already been evaluated wrong.

Note that ORGANIZERS and ROLE read their tables without themselves being authority grants. Membership in an audience confers nothing on its own — it only decides whether this grant, which someone already created deliberately, reaches this person. An appointed organizer does not become able to do anything by being on the roster; they become able to do exactly what the grant aimed at ORGANIZERS says, on that event. This is D-062 standing untouched, and it is the sentence D-102 leans on: the appointment is aimed at by grants rather than special-cased inside the resolver.

docs.title: What audiences do not do
docs.text:
• They are not a permission. Being in an audience is not authority; it is membership of a set. All authority still comes from a grant.
  • They cannot reach guardianship at all. A guardian's authority is not a set of codes an audience could extend one at a time: it is a right_level of none / view / write on the live guardianship row (§10, D-074), and it reaches any action about that child — wider than any grant could assemble, and narrower in the only direction that matters, because it reaches nothing that is not about the child. Neither GUARDIANS nor guardianship_permission is in the model (D-113). So an audience neither opens nor closes guardianship: a deny still overrides the channel, because the deny channel runs first and is scope-independent (§10) — which is the one thing an audience can do to it. What an audience can do with a guardian is be a group the organization keeps: the six contact adults of these children are GROUP(x), a roster with a lifetime and no authority (D-098) — a different fact, written down, about different people.
  • They nest, through AUDIENCE(x) alone (D-103). A cycle is impossible to store and possible to write, so the guard is a cross-audience reachability walk on the save path rather than a shape argument (§The expression tree, check 15), and the thing to remember is that nesting buys reuse of a composite rule: "the kitchen crew plus whoever leads this pack" is one grant either way, and AUDIENCE() adds the case that could not be expressed without it rather than undoing it.
  • Nesting is not sharing. AUDIENCE(x) evaluates the whole of another audience's expression; it does not splice one of its nodes into this tree. Two expressions never share a row, so editing a node inside veterans changes exactly the grants that name veterans and no others — which is the distinction that keeps this from being the node-sharing design this corpus refuses.
  • everyone is genuinely everyone, including people with no account and no membership. It is the right target for a public event page and the wrong one for anything else. And it is reachable by + from inside any expression: nothing stops an expression from unioning the seeded EVERYONE operand, and a writer with audience.manage can widen a grant to the whole world in one edit. That is not a hole in the model — holding EVERYONE directly is already legal and already alarmed (check 8, §11) — it is that a language with union in it makes the same reach available without even pretending to compose it carefully. The mitigation is the editor's expanded set below, not a rule about which operands may appear where.
  • A role cannot be held by a rule. role_holder names one person, and F-12 is closed by D-100, and its answer is no — a derived holder list cannot answer "who was treasurer in 2023", and an office record that cannot answer that is not an office record. Grants aim at roles; roles are not filled by grants.
  • An expression cannot compute with a person's attributes, in the one direction that is still a negative. OLDER(15) says something about an attribute and it is a row of the registry (D-107), so what is refused is a term and not a subject matter: AGE >= 15 is not an operand, is not expressible, and there is still no open question asking for it, because there is no comparison operator for it to use and no way to add a row from a screen. What an author may write is what shipped; that, and not the type of the thing written about, is the closure property §Author in sets protects. Eligibility is capability (D-060): no rule is evaluated outside can(), no eligibility rule table exists, and the system gates nobody on its own — an age rule is a grant somebody wrote, visible in the grant list, revocable like one.

docs.title: The cost of composition
docs.text:
A grant's reach stops being visible in the row that grants it. Derived membership is not stored — D-042 accepted that, and these documents recommend it, because a rule does not rot the way a list does. Most of the permission answer is therefore recomputed rather than recorded, and composition makes that sharper.

  • The editor must show the set a grant actually reaches, expanded — the people, not the expression's text — and it is a requirement on the screen rather than a nicety. Composition turns a three-deep expression into a silent widening, and the person saving the grant is looking at one row that mentions no person at all. This is the same posture as the resolver's in §10: the answer exists, it is just not stored, so somewhere has to compute it in front of a human — and here the human is the only control there is.
  • The preview is per-item, which it structurally cannot be from the grant alone (D-102). PLACED means different people on different events, so "who does this grant reach?" is unanswerable as written when the expression contains a bound operand. The preview is therefore computed for an item and says so on screen — an honest screen names the event whose people it is showing — and a bound operand may never answer for another item: the item is a parameter of the compiled predicate (§10), which is one requirement with one fewer place to get it wrong. This is the one place where D-102's convenience costs a screen an editor's design has to notice, and §13 keeps it open rather than assuming it away.
  • Editing an audience changes grants you did not make, and the screen has to say so before it commits (D-103). Add a person to AUDIENCE(veterans) and every grant naming it now reaches them — including grants their owners wrote for another purpose, and including grants this editor cannot see because they are not theirs. This is not a new failure mode: GROUP(x) has the same property (D-091), and the reason for accepting it there is the reason for accepting it here — a named set is worth being reusable, and a reusable thing has more than one user. The mitigation is D-091's, extended to the second user: saving an edit to a referenced audience shows which grants name it, and at what depth, before it commits. It is one indexed query over the leaf rows (§The expression tree), and it doubles as the report that partially closes the history gap in §Three named sets. D-103 registers this as an assumption rather than a measured fact — cheap at this organization's size because the edges are indexed rows in the table that already holds every expression, unverified at any size, and a slow save screen is a real risk if the import corpus's row-count estimates turn out wrong. §13 keeps it.
  • "Who could read this in 2023?" has no owner. The audit trail holds the change that made it true only until D-088 empties those payloads after 24 months, and derived membership is not stored at all. After two years the question is answered by re-running expressions against state that has itself moved on, and it is answered with today's confidence. That is the flat statement of the limitation: a historical check is re-running today's expressions over whatever state survives. F-7 is dissolved, not answered: a nightly rebuild of cached answers and a nightly materialized effective_permission table turned out to be one job with two names, and neither would have made history answerable — a table of today's answers, rebuilt nightly, is as blind to 2011 as no table is. Nothing computes a snapshot of whom a grant reached (D-110). History has no owner, and that is recorded as a limit rather than a to-do.
  • Something has to keep count of how big expressions get, because nothing refuses them (§The expression tree states the rule and what replaced the check). The standing report of the widest and deepest audiences, their closure size and their cost per check is kept running rather than computed once at save, and it has no CI behind it — a convention, not a guard (D-081); the failure mode of a report nobody reads is that it stops being read and nothing else happens. Who reads it is answered with the cheapest object available: not a report and not a job, a tab on the permissions page. The answer to who reads it is therefore nobody, necessarily — a tab is read by whoever opens it — and that is a decision rather than an oversight, with D-112's stated size underneath it and a trigger on top. The save-time walk that computes the numbers is the same walk that checks acyclicity (§The expression tree), so the number costs nothing extra to obtain; what costs something is deciding to look at it.

Decisions behind this page: D-011, D-042, D-060, D-062, D-074, D-081, D-088, D-091, D-098, D-099, D-100, D-101, D-102, D-103, D-105, D-106, D-107, D-110, D-112, D-113, D-114.

What a check writes down, and the one place in the system that computes an answer.

Section numbers are shared across the five parts and never renumbered, because other pages cite them by number and their anchors are built from them: 05-authorization.md holds §1–§7, 05a §8 (the audience table, the grammar, the selector registry), 05b §8 continued (the tree and what each operand costs), 05c §9–§10 (access_log and the resolver), and 05d §11–§13 (invariants, seed data, open issues).

docs.title: 9. access_log
docs.text:
The audit trail. Append-only; no updates, no deletes.

Fields

Field Kind Notes id integer identity Surrogate key. occurred_at timestamp, audit time Default now. actor_person_id reference to person, optional Who performed the action. Absent for system actions. subject_person_id reference to person, optional Whose data was affected. Differs from the actor when acting on behalf. on_behalf boolean Default false. True when the actor and the subject differ and the action was performed for the subject — guardianship, delegation. See 04-relationships.md §6. authorization_channel enum: deny, ownership, guardianship, unit_grant, item_grant, none, or absent Which channel answered this. Makes the audit answerable: "by what authority did this person do that?" deny records that a deny row defeated the allows; none records that nothing answered at all. Six values, and role is not one of them: there is no role channel to name (D-100), and system was never a channel rather than a namespace. An answer of role in an old row is now unreadable by the model that reads this table, which is the honest state of a historical value: the audit trail keeps the word that was written, and nothing can keep a channel that no longer exists. authorization_ref_id integer, optional No foreign key: it names a row in one of several tables — access_grant.id or guardianship_permission.id. Lets an auditor go directly to the grant that permitted the action. permission_code text, optional The permission checked, as its code. Absent for pure read events that are logged for access-trail purposes rather than permission decisions. scope_type text, optional unit, or an item type. scope_id integer, optional Absent for a check at the unit. action text, required membership.request.approve, person.view. entity_type text, optional entity_id integer, optional result enum: allowed, denied, error Required. denial_reason text, optional session_id text, optional Acting context, for forensics. ip_address an IP address, optional Acting context, for forensics. user_agent text, optional Acting context, for forensics. request_id text, optional Acting context, for forensics. before_state free-form jsonb, optional For write actions. after_state free-form jsonb, optional For write actions. Redacted fields must be stripped before logging — an audit log that leaks the data it audits is worse than none.

Rules

  • A denied result carries a denial_reason. There is no unexplained denial in this table.

Indexes

  • the subject lookup covers only rows that name a subject;
  • one index over denied rows only, newest first;
  • one over acting-on-behalf rows only, newest first.

authorization_channel and authorization_ref_id are what make this an audit trail rather than a log. A record saying "person 100 changed person 200's address" answers what and who. A record that also names the guardianship_permission row that authorized it answers why they were allowed to — and whether that authority was valid at the time. When a custody dispute arises eighteen months later, that is the question asked.

Every value in that enum names a row the auditor can open. unit_grant and item_grant are the two ways a permission is granted, and a grant names one code, so the row answers "by what authority" with the authority itself. Why that is worth stating: an audit answer naming a bundle is not an answer — the reader still has to expand it into codes to learn what the person could actually do, and the table that used to do the expanding holds nothing (D-099).

denied results are logged too. A series of denials is the signature of someone probing for access they do not have. Logging only successes discards the signal.

before_state/after_state must be redacted before the insert. Copying a value out of a guarded record into a table guarded by different people, on a different path, for longer than the record is kept, produces a copy with less protection than the original — and the copy is the one that gets read by auditors, exported for reports and mirrored into backups. Redaction therefore happens before the insert, in the logging function, and never in a job that might not run — the ordering is the part of this rule with teeth. No database constraint can carry this one, because a constraint sees the row after the values are already in it, and this rule is about never letting them in: it is the application's obligation, and it is stated with the redactor itself in 06-audit-and-import.md §2.2. This is a rule of 00-conventions.md §6a's last kind — no automatic enforcement reaches it — so it is written as an obligation, not as a guarantee.

A retention window does not weaken this rule, and it is worth seeing why. If F-8 is confirmed, this table's state columns expire on the window D-088 proposes for the change trail, so the copy is shorter-lived than the business row it was copied from. The conclusion is unmoved, because what the rule guards is the audience. A window decides how long a copied value is readable; it does not decide who may read it while it is readable, and the readers here are whoever holds audit.view, not whoever may see the record. A sensitive value copied into a less-protected table is a protection failure on the day it is copied, not only for as long as it then survives.

How far the argument reaches. It is an argument about the copy's guard, not about the copy's contents, so it is not an instruction to empty payloads. D-083 refused the subset a field list would select from — everything about a person beyond name, gender and age is a value in person_attribute (09-attributes.md) — which rules out name-keyed scrubbing of personal data for good: there is no list, and allergy is not on it. It leaves two conclusions, and they point in opposite directions from the obvious one:

  • The credential case stays, and it is the only one a name list can serve. Values where being in a log at all is the harm — secrets, tokens, credentials — are stripped on the way in, by key name, everywhere a listed key turns up (06-audit-and-import.md §2.2).
  • The person-data case is answered by grading the copy, not by thinning it. audit_log holds before and after images of a child's descriptive values, because D-085 made that trail the only history those values have. So "the copy must not be less guarded than the original" is a requirement on audit.view's sensitivity mark — the top tier, beside person.view — and not a rule about which keys may appear in a jsonb column. Written as a requirement in 00-conventions.md §8 item 7 and demanded of the catalog in ../appendix/permission-catalog.md §8; erasure reaching those payloads stays absolute (06-audit-and-import.md §4).

Append-only enforcement:

Any update or delete against access_log is refused row by row, before it happens, with an error saying the table is append-only. Nothing is left to the application remembering this.

Two operations are excepted, and a blanket refusal would defeat the retention policy. Emptying a row's payloads once it passes the window below is an update, and so is scrubbing one person's values out of a row after an erasure. Neither is a correction: nobody is making a version of this table right, and the answer the row gives to who, what, when, by what authority is untouched in both cases. So both fall inside what "append-only" forbids in spirit and outside what it may forbid in practice. State the guard as a refusal of rewrites rather than a refusal of writes — the only actor allowed to change a row is the erasure or the reduction, the only columns either may touch are the state columns, and every other field on the row is immutable. The literal version of this rule is the more dangerous one, because it fails silently and what it fails is the policy. The same reasoning applies to audit_log and is stated with the operations themselves in 06-audit-and-import.md §2.2.

Retention: a proposal, not this document's position. The window that D-088 puts on audit_log's payloads is proposed here too — 24 months on the state columns, rows kept, 12 months as the floor — and it is recorded as F-8, which still needs confirming. Whether an audit trail is bounded at all is a legal question rather than a technical one, so until someone confirms it this is a default awaiting a person.

Why the question is weaker here, which is structural and not luck: this table does not hold the contents of reads. before_state and after_state are populated for write actions only, so a read records who asked, for what, under which permission, through which channel, and whether it was allowed — and stops. Recording what the read saw would copy every record a permitted glance touched into a table read by a wider audience than the record itself, which is the exact act the redaction rule above exists to prevent. So the window here protects considerably less than it protects over in audit_log, and what survives it is everything this table was built to answer. The valuable fact about a read is that it happened and by what authority, and that is precisely the part no reduction touches.

Consider partitioning by month once volume justifies it, and moving old partitions to cheaper storage. Rows are not deleted on either answer; the window is carried out by emptying the state columns, which is the job and the over-age check described for the change trail in 06-audit-and-import.md §5. If F-8 is confirmed, that check has to be written for this table too — a reduction with no check under it is a reduction that quietly stops happening, which is the failure mode §2.2 of that document names as the only one this operation has.

Assumption: access_log may be queried by staff with a specific permission, but writing is automatic. If the organization needs human annotation of audit entries, add a separate access_log_note table rather than making this table mutable.

docs.title: 10. The resolver
Steps the resolver leans on
docs.text:
Three helpers keep can() readable, and one of them is fifteen lines long.

grant_satisfies(person, scope_type, scope_id, permission, at) — does the person hold a live allow of this code on this exact scope? Exact match only. It covers both a personal grant and one made to an audience the person is in. Any one grant row meeting all of these satisfies it:

  1. Its scope_type equals the checked scope type and its scope_id matches the checked scope id, with an absent id equal to an absent checked id.
  2. Its permission_id is the checked permission, or is system.admin.
  3. Its effect is allow — denies are handled by the channel that runs first.
  4. It has not been revoked.
  5. It has started as of at and has not ended on at.
  6. The grantee is this person, or an audience containing them at at for this item (§8).

The question has a yes-or-no answer, not a threshold. There is no rank to compare and nothing to join in order to get one: a grant carries exactly one code and either it is the checked code or it is not (D-099).

person_in_audience(person, audience, at, item) — is the person in the value of this audience's expression on this date? The item argument is there because a bound operand means different people on different items, and there is no other way to tell it which event it is asking about (§8, Evaluation). An unresolvable operand is the empty set; an expression that cannot be evaluated reaches nobody.

operand_holds(person, operand, at, item) — the evaluator's one recursive step: a leaf asks its selector, a node combines its children. It is written once and it is short; the requirement inside it is that every selector is evaluated as a predicate about this person and never as a set of ids (§8, Author in sets).

One leaf does not ask a selector, it asks this function again. AUDIENCE(x) calls person_in_audience(person, <the audience x names>, at, item) and returns what comes back (D-103) — the same three arguments carried straight through, because a nested audience means the same people on the same date for the same item, and the same predicate shape, because nesting is the moment at which a lazy implementation would most plausibly decide to materialize the inner set and test containment. That is §11's check 16 and it covers recursion explicitly. What the recursion costs: within one request the memo resolves a recurring named operand once, so a screen that asks the same question about the same person several times pays the depth once; across requests it runs to whatever depth somebody typed, every time (D-114). That is the honest price of a tree with no bound on its height, which is why §What each operand costs and the width report of §The cost of composition are the controls here. The recursion terminates by construction, not by a counter: a cycle through AUDIENCE leaves cannot be saved (§8), so a read-path depth cap would be a thing that decides who a grant reaches in exactly the case where the data is already wrong. The save-time cycle walk is therefore the whole guard, and it must not be relaxed: "the recursion terminates by construction" is a claim about a write-path check, not about a number.

No channel of can() consults membership, and that is a guardrail rather than an omission. A membership test performed inside the resolver is an invisible lockout: somebody whose membership lapsed is denied by the rule that was supposed to exempt them, with no error message, on the one day of the year it would hurt most. Nothing in this function asks the question, so nothing can be mis-routed — membership is MEMBERS, an operand in an expression, evaluated where expressions are evaluated (§8).

The single authorization entry point. One implementation, used everywhere. Algorithm: ../domain/06-authorization-model.md.

can(person, permission_code, scope_type, scope_id, at, owner_person_id) returns allowed or denied. scope_type and scope_id are optional, at defaults to today, and owner_person_id is supplied only where the ownership or guardianship channel is in play.

The order of these steps is a rule for one reason and not the other. Each step either returns or falls through, so a step never gets to contradict an earlier one. The deny step must run first, and that is the only ordering with a consequence for the answer. The allow steps are alternatives producing the same boolean, so their order decides which channel the audit names and how quickly the answer arrives — never what the answer is. That is what having no locality means (D-099): the allow steps are not ordered by strength, and "the nearest one wins" is not a sentence about this function.

  1. Look the permission up by code. If no permission carries that code, return false — an unknown permission is a deny, and it is settled before anything else is considered.
  2. Resolve merge chains. Replace the person with the survivor of any merge, so permissions are never evaluated for a tombstoned person.

  3. Channel 0 — explicit deny. Absolute and scope-independent. A live deny grant of this code applicable to this person blocks access no matter what scope it sits at: a per-event grant can never restore access that a unit-wide restriction removed (D-013). A deny counts when it is itself unrevoked, has started as of at, has not ended on at, and applies to the person — where "applies" means it names them or names an audience they are in at at for the item being checked. A personal deny and an audience deny are equally absolute, and a personal allow cannot beat an audience deny, because channel 0 has already returned. Its scope applies when either of these holds:

  4. it sits at the unit, and then it applies everywhere — every item of every type, because a unit grant reaches every item and a unit deny is the same shape with the opposite effect;

  5. it sits on the exact thing being checked — same scope type, same id.

A deny matching either bullet is the whole answer: return false. There is no case in which a deny at the unit reaches less than everything under it, because there is nothing under it to reach — the unit is a scope and there is exactly one of it (D-097) — so no walk between scopes stands between a restriction and the item being checked. 4. Channel 1 — a grant at the unit. grant_satisfies(person, 'unit', NULL, permission, at). Because a unit grant reaches every item of every type (§6), this one step covers every item the organization has. 5. Channel 2 — a grant on this exact item. grant_satisfies(person, scope_type, scope_id, permission, at), reached only when both a scope type and a scope id were supplied. Nothing is consulted before it: a unit grant reaches the item, an item grant reaches the item, and there is no owner to ask (D-102). 6. Channel 3 — ownership. If an owner was supplied and that owner resolves to this same person, return true. Your own data. 7. Channel 4 — guardianship. Consulted when the check is about someone other than the actor; answers with an allow only. The test is a comparison, not a name: an owner was supplied, it resolves to a real person, and that person is not the actor. The question is whether the actor holds a live guardianship over that subject at at whose right_level covers the checked permission — and this is where permission.right_kind is read, by its only customer: none covers nothing, view covers codes marked read, write covers both. If such a guardianship exists and covers the permission, return true. In every other case — no guardianship, none, or a right that does not cover this code — the channel returns nothing at all and the resolver continues. It does not deny. Defined in 04-relationships.md §4; the reasoning for both halves is D-079.

Two properties of this channel:

  • Entered by shape, not by namespace (D-079, following D-074). A parent correcting their child's address is checked under person.address.edit — an ordinary, un-prefixed code — and still routes here. A permission added next year for a field a guardian must edit is covered the day the field exists, provided it is marked write, which is the seeding default (§2).
  • Silent rather than final. The channel never takes the last word: a guardian whose right does not cover the code simply does not answer, and the actor's own grants get their turn. There is no partial answer to fall through either, because the channel returns a yes and nothing else. A real prohibition is still possible and still absolute — it is a deny row, step 3.

Two refusals belong to this channel. The guard must not be weakened into "the subject is a minor": the existence of a guardianship row is the whole test, and an age lookup would put a branch in the resolver that D-070 and D-077 rule out. And personal attributes reach this resolver through no new door — everything beyond name, gender and age is descriptive data read by person.view and written by person.edit through the channels above, with no attribute.* read permission, no fifth channel, and no branch on what a value is about (09-attributes.md §4, D-083). The temptation this channel is offered — "a leader may see allergy data, but only for the children in their unit" — is refused twice. There is no "their unit" for such a rule to refer to (D-097), and the older reason stands on its own: a branch on what a value is about is the privileged medical subset walking back in through the resolver after D-083 refused it through the permission list. 8. Default deny. Return false.

There is no membership gate anywhere in this function. MEMBERS is an operand a writer types into an expression, and no channel of the resolver consults membership: a check is about grants, not about whether the actor is a paid-up member (D-100). The predicate is_current_member exists only inside the evaluator, evaluated live at at like every other operand. Every intent a gate would have served is written in the expression that carries the rule:

Intent Expression The office counts only while its holder is a member MEMBERS * ROLE(x) The office counts whatever their membership looks like ROLE(x) — written without MEMBERS The office counts, but one named person is an exception MEMBERS * ROLE(x) + PERSON(y) — the exception sits inside the grant that carries the rule, so it is read next to the thing it exempts. A second grant aimed at that person alone is equivalent, and arguably clearer for something permanent; what is never allowed is a row that does not parse (§8, PERSON)

The posture is opt-in, and the failure mode is named rather than buried (D-100). Forgetting MEMBERS is invisible, silent and permanent, and nothing in the resolver can see it. Three controls, none of which is the resolver: the standing report of ROLE(...) grants with no MEMBERS (check 6, §11); seeded grants carrying MEMBERS so that the path of least repetition is the safe path; and import completeness — MEMBERS * COUNSELORS is only as correct as the counselor roster, so an import that misses 300 counselors silently un-gates them, and the reconciliation report of D-090 must count people marked as counselors in the corpus against role_holder rows written. It fails closed — nothing breaks, which is exactly why nobody notices.

docs.title: The cache is deleted: nothing in this schema holds a permission answer
docs.text:
Nothing in this schema holds the answer to a permission question. No row, table or field anywhere maps a person — or a person and a code, or a person and an item — to an answer. That is §11's invariant 19, and it is why no later optimization can reintroduce such a table rather than merely disliking it. A check resolves, a request memoizes, and the only thing ever cached is a compilation (D-114). The rule is unconditional on purpose: the expansion of an audience is a predicate and not a set (§Author in sets. Evaluate per person., §Evaluation), and a design that forbids a materialized answer in one path and permits it in another spends the rest of its prose explaining the difference.

What the checks use instead, and what may be held in memory:

  1. A compiled expression. Parsed once, operand kinds resolved once, a parameterized predicate emitted once, keyed by the expression's root and ruleset_version, holding no person and no item.
