A rule written for a recurring process is too strict for a one-time one, and the safety that mattered is not the ban but the review.

Four consequences, in the order they arrive.

  • The root participation obligation now points at the import again. 03-membership.md §5.1 had just been corrected to say that an ordinary import "touches neither arm of this pair". With memberships arriving by the thousand it does: every imported membership owes its root-unit participation row in the same transaction, which is what keeps who is in unit X one query (D-041). Consecutive imported years for one person therefore stretch one root row rather than opening a second, and a gap in the source is a lapse that produces two — the same rule as a renewal, and the same accepted cost: the lapse stops being visible in the participation table.
  • No obligation, no payment, no balance. An imported membership creates no fee_obligation. The corpus has no money in it (D-090), so an obligation per historical year would arrive as unpaid and turn a decade of members into a wall of debt on a ledger that has never heard of them, with a due_date in 1999 for the lapse sweep to choke on. The sweep is already safe — it acts on active memberships with a positive-balance obligation, and an imported row is neither — but the absence becomes a rule, because the alternative failure is silent and enormous.
  • outstanding_balance is NULL on these rows, and that is now load-bearing rather than incidental (07-finance.md). A zero would be a claim — settled — that the export does not support.
  • These rows are the oldest layer of the skeleton D-088 keeps forever. That decision held named membership periods indefinitely on legitimate interest, on an unverified legal basis (assumption 49). From this round the indefinite-retention half of D-088 covers thousands of named people with birth dates who were never asked and never used the system. It is the same judgement, applied to a much larger population, and the review commissioning it is unchanged in kind and much changed in scale.

What this makes true about reports. Every cross-decade member count is now a mix of an export and a register, distinguished only by data_confidence and import_batch_id. A membership-rate chart that spans the import boundary is comparing a source that states membership with a system that records it, and nothing in the query knows the difference.

Closes: C-5 (together with D-092).

See: data-model/06-audit-and-import.md §3.1, data-model/03-membership.md §5.1, domain/03-identity-and-legacy.md §7.

docs.title: D-094 — The root unit owns every imported event
docs.text:
Status: decided (from your answer) Date: refinement round 9

Deleted rather than reversed by D-102: there is no owner column for an imported event to have. The import still owes one event row per event in the corpus, and now owes the per-event grant instantiation D-102 added with it.

Follows: D-058, D-092, D-067

Your answer. Asked what owns an imported event, given that every event belongs to exactly one unit (D-058) and that unit assignment is out of scope: the root unit owns them all.

Decision. event.org_unit_id on an imported event is the single root unit, as a rule rather than a judgement. D-058's "exactly one owning unit" is satisfied without inventing a unit, without a per-event decision, and without the import touching the unit vocabulary at all — which is what makes this compatible with the instruction that decided D-092. The root is the only unit the corpus speaks of, so it is also the honest answer, not merely the convenient one.

Attendance becomes registrations, and the three-valued rule decides what is not written. An attendance export lists the people who came. Each one becomes an event_registration with attending and was_present = true (D-067). Nobody else gets a row: a person who might have come and did not is not in the export, and inventing not_attending rows from silence would put words in a source that said nothing (D-059). So imported events have a population exactly as large as the evidence for them, and the historical attendance figures these documents will be asked for are arrived, not registered.

Three costs, one of which is the reason this decision was worth recording separately.

  • The root's event list becomes mostly history. "What's on" stops being a unit filter and has to be a date filter — and the unit-scoped report that asks "our events this term" shows an imported camp because the root is its owner, which is the same class of misreading D-049 recorded for unit_participation.view at organization scope.
  • Imported events have no organizers, so nobody holds them at unit scope: event_organizer is empty on them by construction, and editing one takes organization-scope authority (D-062). An imported event is therefore read-only for the people who would ordinarily run an event, which is correct and will still surprise somebody.
  • Correcting an owner is one column, and it moves the audience. Unlike participation history, which is never rewritten, event.org_unit_id is editable — and because an event is an artifact of its unit (D-063), moving an event from the root to a pack silently changes who can read it. So corrections are allowed and expected, and each is an audited write with a reason; and the audit record of who moved it is readable for 24 months (D-088) while the event itself is kept indefinitely.

Closes: C-5 (together with D-092).

See: data-model/08-events.md §2–§4, data-model/06-audit-and-import.md §3.

docs.title: D-095 — Units carry no restrictions; joining one is somebody else's act
docs.text:
Status: decided (from your answer) Date: refinement round 9 Follows: D-038, D-043, D-081

Your answer. Asked whether a unit that declares it does not supervise minors should refuse a minor's position as it refuses their participation: a unit does not have any restrictions — however, persons can't assign themselves. They will be assigned to the unit by the counselors. And on the shape of entry: into the root unit, there is a fee for entry; into the sub-units, there is no fee, it is entirely managed by the organization, including adding more members.

Decision. Two entry paths, each with exactly one gate, and no third control:

The root unit A sub-unit How you get in You pay. The membership flow is the only self-service entry in the system, and it opens the membership and its root participation row (D-041, D-050) Somebody else writes the row What stops you The fee unit_participation.manage at that unit — held by the people who run it, with no self-scoped variant, and none will be added Money The yearly fee Nothing. There is no fee for taking part in a pack, and no model wants one

The same holds for position_assignment: nobody appoints themselves. There is no code in the catalog that could express either, and D-095's instruction is not to add one.

org_unit_type.allows_minors is removed. It was introduced as a safeguarding flag — the thing that let the system refuse to place a minor in a unit that does not supervise them without hardcoding which type codes those are. After this answer it enforces nothing about positions, and a flag that is documented as a safeguard and enforced on one of two write paths is precisely the thing these documents elsewhere refuse to keep: a list of eighteen ticks nobody read is not a safeguard, it is a receipt (domain/08 §4). What goes with the column: its check in 03-membership.md §7 (check 2, participants in units that do not allow minors), the root type's allows_minors = false in the seed, and the sentence in 02-organization.md §1 that explains why there is no allows_adults sibling.

D-081 requires naming who enforces the rule now, and the honest form of that answer is a shift in kind. The rule the flag existed to express — do not place a child where nobody is responsible for them — is now enforced by who is allowed to write the row: a person able to add a child to a unit is a person the unit's leadership trusts with its roster, the write is audited, and the assignment names who made it. That is a stronger control than a boolean on a type, because a boolean only ever refused a placement nobody had thought about and the permission refuses every placement by the wrong person regardless of the child's age.

What is genuinely lost, and it is the safeguarding story in one paragraph. The system no longer knows which units are for children. allows_minors was the only machine-readable answer to that question; nothing replaces it, because "entirely managed by the organization" is a statement about people rather than data. Combined with D-043 — no background checks recorded anywhere — the organization module's safeguarding story after D-095 is: a permission held by named adults, an audit trail whose values expire after two years, and a report list of who holds the write. If that turns out to be too little — after a real incident, or an insurer's question — the route back is a rule about who may be placed where, argued once as a decision, with its enforcement layer named in D-081's terms, and not a resurrected column whose name implies it enforces something.

Not changed by this, because it was never about units: membership stays ageless (D-038), position.min_age stays a real eligibility constraint about the position (a scoutmaster must be an adult), and the guardianship channel is untouched.

Closes: C-6.

See: domain/04-organization-structure.md §1, §4, data-model/02-organization.md §1, domain/05-membership-lifecycle.md.

docs.title: D-096 — A reused unit number is a new unit unless someone records the continuity
docs.text:
Status: decided (from your answer, and one question back) Date: refinement round 9 Follows: D-036, D-054, D-092

Question, put back to you, and the answer's shape. Asked whether a unit number appearing twice — one unit closed in the 1990s, another carrying the number now — is the same unit or a new one, the answer was "what is a unit number?". That question is the useful part of this entry, so it is answered before the decision is. A code is a short human label typed by somebody: T12, 4. oddíl. It is not the unit's identity, which is the row; it is not its name, which is a temporal row of its own (org_unit_name); and it is not unique, deliberately — uniqueness is per parent and among live rows only, which is exactly why a closed unit's number is free again (02-organization.md §3). Once it is described as a label, the question answers itself in the direction the docs already argued.

Decision. A reused number is a new unit. One org_unit row per unit that existed, each with its own period; the continuity between two of them is not a property of the label but an assertion somebody makes and records as an org_unit_relationship with successor_of (§5). The opposite default — reuse the row and let a thirty-year gap show inside one unit's life — is what a system drifts into if nobody says, because it is what "match on code" does. And the two cases the docs separate are unchanged and are not this case: a renumber is one unit with two name rows (same participants, continuity asserted by the rename itself), while a unit that moves parent is a new unit (D-036).

The cost is a decision the organization has to make in words, occasionally, and it is cheap. When a number really does come back — a troop refounded after a decade dormant — someone writes down that this unit is the successor of that one, and "who was in Pack 12 in 1984?" follows the relationship instead of guessing from an overlapping name. Refusing to default either way was considered, and it is what domain/04 §6 used to say ("record which was chosen and why on the unit"); what D-096 adds is the direction the record goes in when nobody records anything, because a default that is unstated is a default that gets implemented by whoever writes the matching screen.

Closes: C-3.

See: domain/04-organization-structure.md §3, §6, data-model/02-organization.md §4–§5.

Superseded by D-097. There are no sub-units left to number, close, or declare a successor of, and no org_unit row for a code to sit on. The reasoning survives as a method — a label carries no identity, so continuity is asserted and never matched — and it transfers intact to person_group, where a group name that comes back after a decade is a new group unless somebody says otherwise.

docs.title: Decision Log — Refinement round 10 — the deletions, part 1 (D-097 … D-100)
docs.text:
The unit becomes a scope rather than a row, and a grant becomes one permission that either allows or denies.

Refinement round 9 — organization (D-091 … D-096) ← | All decisions | Refinement round 10 — the deletions, part 2 (D-101 … D-104) →

docs.title: D-097 — There are no sub-units. The unit is a scope, not a row
docs.text:
Status: decided (from your answer) Date: refinement round 10 Reverses: D-008, D-035, D-036, D-041, D-049, D-050, D-054, D-078, D-096. Amends D-031 and D-095, whose subject was always the nested unit.

Your words. "I want to remove the sub-organizations completely. They are more of a 'group of people'. They are useful in permission groups, however they should not hide any information or have any special features. I have over-specified the system and this complicates things." Asked whether anything below the organization should still scope authority, the answer was no — and asked whether the root unit is still a table, the answer was "no table — the unit is a scope", with the vocabulary settled in the same breath: unit means the root, the organization itself, of which there is one; group means a set of people, which is where D-098 goes.

Decision. The organization has no internal structure in this system. There is one unit, it is the organization, and it is not a row: it is the non-item scope that grant_scope_type already carries (is_item_scoped = false, a grant at it has no scope_id). Its code is unit. Everything that existed to describe the inside of an organization is deleted:

Deleted With it goes org_unit the root row, the one-root partial unique index, path, depth, status, code, data_confidence on units org_unit_type, org_unit_type_rule the runtime unit vocabulary, is_leaf, max_depth, the seven-step nesting check, and the whole of D-054's argument about not guessing words org_unit_name rename and renumber history, change_reason, and the denormalised org_unit.name it fed org_unit_relationship split_from, merged_into, successor_of, renamed_to unit_participation sub-unit rosters, the root participation row every membership owed, and the transfers between units scope_exposure, scope.expose the only downward crossing, the direction-of-authority check, the scope.exposure.review code, and the nightly alert that was its sole detector unit_ancestors(), unit_descendants() the recursive walk, the path-consistency check, and the CI assertion that the resolver never calls it role_assignment.scope_type / scope_id a role is always held at the unit; there is nothing else to hold it at the resolver's unit tier the ladder of D-032 drops from four tiers to the ones D-099 states

Why this is affordable now, when it was not affordable in round 1. Because of D-092, which your own answer supplied: the legacy corpus names no units. Two exports — people with their membership period at the root, and events with attendance — and no unit column anywhere. So the hierarchy has no recorded history to lose; "who was in pack X in 2011" already had no answer at go-live, and was already written down as a consequence rather than a bug. A structure that describes nothing imported and (per D-095) restricts nothing is a structure that carries no information, which is the definition of the over-specification you were pointing at.

The rule that dies hardest is the founding one. D-031 —"authority over a unit originates at that unit and cannot be claimed from outside it"— existed to stop the center deciding permissions inside a body it does not run. With one unit there is no "outside it" to be stopped from. The rule is not weakened by this decision, it is deprived of its subject: every permission is held at the unit or on an item, and the unit's people are the only people there are. What D-031's reasoning still supports is carried forward by D-099 (deny is absolute) and by the ownership and guardianship channels, neither of which was ever about units.

What is genuinely lost, said once and not argued away.

  1. The unit is no longer a locus of accountability for a child's records. D-031's safeguarding property was that access to a pack's children had to be granted by that pack, by people who recruited the leader and can be asked. That property is gone, and nothing in the remaining model reproduces it: a permission held at the unit reaches every member, and person.view was already the widest read permission in the system (D-083, D-086). What is left of the safeguarding story is the same three things D-095 was left with — a permission held by a named adult, an audit trail whose payloads expire after two years (D-088), and a report of who holds the write — minus the part where the named adult was somebody the unit chose.
  2. "Who was in the Thursday group in 2011?" stays answerable, because D-098 dates its member rows. What is lost is the unit framing: there is no "and everything nested under it" left to ask about, so the subtree question that justified the materialized path has no subject.
  3. Restructuring stops being a recorded event. Splits, mergers and successions were the organization module's whole history problem (domain/04 §3) and they are simply gone: a group that splits is an old group that ended and two that began, with no edge between them unless somebody writes one.
  4. Unit-scoped reports — a pack's roster, a pack's events, "which units exist" — have no subject to report on. The organizational-year reports that mattered are membership and fee reports, which live at the unit and are unaffected.

One thing gets easier that nobody counted. F-10 shape 4 — a column that may not change once set, the only shape with no report at all because a violation leaves every row individually valid — had exactly one instance in the whole design, org_unit.parent_unit_id. It has none now. The single-root conditional uniqueness (shape 2) goes too, along with integrity checks 1–10 of data-model/02-organization.md §9 and check 10's peculiar job of asserting that a migration had emitted a constraint.

Import, restated. The one-off import owes person, membership (D-093) and — since D-102 — events and registrations. It owes no participation rows to anything, which retires D-093's knock-on about the root participation row and 03-membership.md §5.1's write obligation with it. Group membership is never inferred from anything: the corpus does not name groups either, so every person_group_member row is typed by a person, which is also the only way it can be true.

Two-way door? No. This is a deletion of a dimension, not a flag. The route back is a decision with a reason attached — most plausibly "the organization has grown past one center's visibility" — and that decision would have to re-argue D-031 from its own premises, because the mechanism that made it work (scope_exposure, written by the covered unit) no longer exists.

See: domain/04-organization-structure.md (rewritten as the groups module), data-model/02-organization.md, data-model/05-authorization.md §6, data-model/03-membership.md §5.

docs.title: D-098 — A group is a person_group: explicit members, a lifetime, and no authority
docs.text:
Status: decided (from your answer) Date: refinement round 10 Follows: D-097 Supersedes the subject of: D-041

Closes: —

Your words. "A group defined by display name and an audience… A group is just an audience, but it is visible to the users of the system (if the permissions say so)." Then, when the choice was put back as group-is-an-audience or audience-is-a-selector: "person_group, but let's make it upside down — a group will have explicitly stated members and a person_group can be used as an audience selector", and "a group will have explicitly stated members (all members live, while the group lives). The group can have a lifetime (start and end date)."

Decision. person_group — a name, a description, its own valid_from/valid_to, the standard audit columns. person_group_member — (person_group_id, person_id, valid_from, valid_to, who wrote it, when). The member row is dated: assignment, removal and re-assignment are all periods on the same pair, so the roster has a history of its own rather than borrowing the audit trail's. person_group is registered in grant_scope_type, so a group is an item and a grant can be written on one — which is how "these two people may work this group's roster" is said without inventing a scope (D-099).

What a group is not, in one list, because this is the part the previous design got wrong. It has no parent and no children, no type and no vocabulary of types, no code, no path, no nesting rules, no rename history, no split or merger edge, no leadership of its own, no roles (your words: "screw them, the groups don't have any roles, only the root unit"), and no fee. It holds no permissions over its members by being a group: a member of a group is not able to do anything, which is D-005 and D-019 restated one level down — participation is not authority, and the fact that the participation is now stored in a tidier table does not quietly promote it.

Why the word "audience" survives at all, and where the line is. You named the inversion, and it is the load-bearing part of this entry: a group states its members; a selector picks them. person_group is the domain fact — a thing a user sees, names, opens, and ends. audience is the grantee a grant names, and one of its operands may be a person_group (D-101). Two tables answer "who is in it", which is precisely the shape D-080 teaches to be suspicious of, so the difference is stated rather than implied: a group's members are a list of people that is true whether or not any permission points at it; audience_member rows are an addition to a rule, meaningful only inside the selector they complete. A group exists to be talked about; a selector exists to be aimed at something.

Membership of the unit is unchanged and is not a group. One membership per person, at the unit, paid for yearly (D-037, D-040, D-047). unit_participation is deleted with the units (D-097), including the root row every membership used to be issued with, so "everyone in the organization" is now one query against membership and "everyone in the Thursday group" is one query against person_group_member — two shapes, and no longer one shape with a depth in it. D-050's renewal mechanism narrows to exactly what it always claimed to be about: the membership row, per D-016.

Joining a group is still somebody else's act, and D-095's reasoning transfers intact. The gate is person_group.member.manage, held at the unit (which reaches every group, per D-099) or granted on one group as an item. There is no self-scoped variant and none will be added: nobody writes themselves onto a roster, which was the whole of D-095 and is unchanged by moving the roster. membership_request loses requested_unit_id — a request is for membership of the unit, and which group a new member lands in is a write on the group, not a preference on the request.

So the history question has an answer, and it is the same answer every dated row in this system gives. "Who was in schuzka2026-1 on 14 March 2026?" is a point-in-time read over person_group_member, exactly as domain/05's query 3 was for a unit, and it survives the audit trail's 24-month payload expiry (D-088) because it does not depend on the trail. The group's own valid_from/valid_to and the member rows' periods are two different facts and both are kept: the first says the group existed over that span, the second says who was in it. An open group with dated members answers the historical question just fine, which is the whole reason the rows are dated — the naming in your own example (schuzka2026-1) becomes a habit the organization may or may not keep, rather than the mechanism history depends on.

Dating the rows imports the invariant set that dating always imports, and naming them here is the work: where both ends are set, valid_to is later than valid_from; no two rows for the same person and group may overlap, counted over all rows and not only the open ones, half-open so a row ending on a day and one beginning that same day do not collide (the D-002 shape, and F-10 shape 1, so a hand-written migration emits it and the ORM will not); a person who left in 2020 and came back in 2024 is two rows, never one row edited in place, because the edit destroys the answer to "was she in the group in 2019?"; and moving from one group to another closes one row and opens another — 03-membership.md §5.2's transfer discipline, retargeted at groups and otherwise unchanged.

The duplication is now real, which is why the two tables are said apart by their rules and not only by their names. person_group_member and audience_member are both dated sets of people, which is precisely the pair D-080 teaches a reader to distrust — two statements that can drift, one of which will be the one the screens read. They stay apart because the maintenance differs, and the dated shape makes the difference sharper rather than softer: a group's members are the organization's record of who attends, kept by the people who run the group, and it is true when no grant exists; audience_member rows are a selector's additions, kept by whoever composes permissions, and are meaningless outside the selector they complete. Merging them would make the permission table the system's roster, which is the same mistake D-062 refused when it declined to answer "who is running this camp?" by reading the grant table.

Amended by D-105, which deleted one half of the pair. There is no audience_member any more, so the distrust this paragraph arranges is aimed at a table that no longer exists — and the duplication it feared is gone rather than reconciled. What survives is the distinction, now carried by a leaf instead of a table: a group's dated roster is the organization's record of who attends and is true when no grant exists, while PERSON(x) inside an expression is an addition made by whoever composes permissions and means nothing outside it. The closing refusal survives, and is cheaper to honour than it was. The temptation to answer "who is running this camp?" from the grant table was always resisted by saying use the roster instead; when the roster was the only dated set of people, that was a real constraint on the composer. Now there is a second way to name the same people — a run of PERSON(...) leaves written beside the grant — so the hazard this entry named has moved from "two tables drift" to "the composer chose the wrong one", which is what data-model/02-organization.md now says out loud, and what a MEMBERS * ROLE(...) expression exists to make the obvious answer.

What is actually given up against unit_participation is small and worth listing, because "no special features" was the instruction. No join_reason_code / leave_reason_code (and so no transfer, promotion, reorganisation, unit_closed vocabulary to maintain or to get wrong), no is_primary saying which of a person's groups to show first, no role_in_unit display label, no data_confidence and nothing to import into: the corpus names no groups, so every member row is written by a person (D-092, D-097).

Two-way door? The periods are the door and they are open. What to refuse later is the vocabulary that used to hang off them — a controlled leave_reason_code list is exactly the eighteen-ticks-without-a-receipt shape D-095 removed, and a role_in_unit column is the thing that always turns into an authorization check the moment somebody is asked "can she edit the roster?"

See: domain/04-organization-structure.md, data-model/02-organization.md §1–§2, data-model/03-membership.md §5.

docs.title: D-099 — A grant allows or denies one permission. There is no level, and no locality
docs.text:
Status: decided (from your answer) Date: refinement round 10 Reverses: D-012 (including the reason it was written), D-013 as a level, D-032's second half, D-074's level form, D-010. Amends D-055, D-068 and D-079.

Your words. "This is more complicated. I said that there are read, write, none permissions. This is not correct. What would make the most sense is if items would inherit all unit-scope permissions and would have their own item-scope permissions in the same format (e.g. event.edit). Both of those permissions are essentially the same, however in the item-scope some of them don't make sense (e.g. on an event, membership.manage, or event.create, make no sense). On the item-scope there should also be a deny-permission, not just allow-permission." And on whether anything still needs a ladder: "only allow/deny on the same permissions as on the root unit."

Decision. One grant is: a grantee, a scope, one permission code, an effect, and a period. The grantee is a person or an audience (D-042, unchanged). The scope is the unit or exactly one item (D-097). The effect is allow or deny. The answer is:

allowed when some live allow applies and no live deny applies.

That is the whole of the precedence rule. What it replaces, item by item:

Deleted Was Why it goes access_level revoked 0, view 10, contribute 20, manage 30, admin 40 A level is a bundle of permissions identified by one word. D-068 already refused that idea once, when it deleted <resource>.admin and said roles are the bundle. This finishes the same thought: roles and audiences are the bundle, and nothing else is permission_level which level satisfies which permission at which scope type Its two jobs move to two columns on permission itself (§below) The rank integer D-012 There is no ordering left to compare. The famous bug it guarded — 'admin' < 'contribute' — cannot occur in a system with no levels, which is a better fix than the guard Locality D-032: a nearer allow beats a further one Locality only ever ranked allows against each other. With a boolean answer, two allows that both apply produce one answer; there is nothing to order. D-032's first half — deny is absolute — survives intact and is now its entire content revoked as a level resolver channel 0 Deny survives as an effect on a grant row. D-013's requirement — a court-ordered restriction must not be beatable by a broader grant — is unchanged and is still checked first

permission gains two columns, and only one of them is comfortable.

  • applies_to ∈ unit, unit_and_item — where a code may be granted at all. This is your observation that event.create and membership.manage are nonsense on an event, written as data instead of as prose. It is checked when the grant is saved, not at check time: a grant of event.create written on one event is refused with the reason in the error, because an event cannot be created twice, and a creation permission attached to a thing that already exists answers no question.
  • right_kind ∈ read, write — and it exists for exactly one customer. D-074 fixes a guardian's rights at three values, and with the ladder gone the guardianship channel has nothing left to compare a permission against. This column is that thing: none covers nothing, view covers read codes, write covers both. It is a column whose only job is one other mechanism, and saying so is cheaper than discovering it later. The alternative was to store permission codes on the guardianship row, which D-074 refused on the grounds that a volunteer cannot maintain a 74-code checklist per child.

Inheritance, stated once. A grant at the unit reaches every item of every type, because after D-097 there is no intermediate scope left between the unit and an item, and no ownership relation to test. A grant on one item reaches that item and nothing else. This is D-006 — per-item permissions are capabilities on the item — with the unit tier left standing, and it deletes can_event() outright (D-102).

- in a selector is not a deny, and the two are not interchangeable. An audience expression may subtract a set (MEMBERS - GROUP(x)), which narrows one grant's reach. A deny defeats every grant that applies to that person, including ones written elsewhere, later, or by somebody else. The first cannot express "she must not have this, whatever else she is given", which is D-013's whole reason for existing, so denies stay — and they are legal at the unit as well as on an item, since "exclude her from what the unit grants everyone" is exactly the case the selector cannot serve.

The round silently upgraded deny, and the upgrade needs naming because it changes an operator's job. D-013 did not say a deny beats everything; it said revoked beats deny, which left an escape hatch — a stale denial could be outranked by a newer act, and revoking it was a decision somebody could take late and still take. Deleting the ranking deleted the hatch. A live deny now beats every live allow with no tie-break of any kind, and the only thing that removes one is a person ending its period. That is why the integrity check below is a requirement rather than a nicety, and why a deny is the row on which access_grant.valid_to earns its keep: everywhere else an open-ended grant that outlived its reason costs a tidy database, and here it costs a child who cannot see their own camp photos. A date is the only remedy that works without somebody remembering to act.

What it costs, in rows. A role that used to be one grant at manage is now one row per code. The catalog holds 66 codes; a broad office is a couple of dozen rows. That is the price of the question you are now able to ask — "what exactly does this person have?" answered by reading rows — and the price of the one you can no longer ask, which is "what does manage give me on this event?": there is no such word, so there is no such lookup. Integrity check to add: a live grant whose effect is deny and whose grantee, scope and code match no live allow is dead weight and should be reported, because a deny that denies nothing is how a stale restriction survives its reason.

Two-way door? Cheap in one direction, expensive in the other. Levels can come back as names for sets of codes with no comparison defined — which is what a role already is, so no new mechanism is needed to approximate one. A real ordering coming back means re-importing permission_level, the rank rule, and locality's tie-break, all of which were deleted with their only consumers.

See: data-model/05-authorization.md §2, §6–§7, domain/06-authorization-model.md, appendix/permission-catalog.md.

docs.title: D-100 — A role is an office and a group is company: two tables of the same shape
docs.text:
Status: decided (from your answer) Date: refinement round 10 Follows: D-097, D-098, D-099

Reverses: D-039's resolver clause, D-051 entirely, D-033 and the position module, D-009's remaining subject.

Closes: F-12.

Your words. "A role_assignment is no longer necessary, as it can be supplemented by a ROLE selector in the audience string." Then, when asked whether roles go too: *"Role and group are technically the same, but not semantically. A role was meant to be for a single person / a small couple of individuals that are visible as the leaders / financial / IT managers of the organization, while the group is a temporary set of members that do e.g. events together." And on the gate: "This should be sortable with the audiences, right? Some permission (e.g. event.create) can be assigned to MEMBERS * COUNSELORS."

Decision. Three things, of which the first is the one that looks like nothing.

1. role_assignment becomes role_holder. (role_id, person_id, valid_from, valid_to, granted_by, note) — no scope columns, because D-097 left one scope. role keeps code, name, description, is_system, sort_order. role_permission is deleted: a role confers nothing by itself, and the codes an office carries are the live grants whose audience names ROLE(x). What that buys is the question the old design could not answer cleanly — "what may a treasurer do?" — which is now a query over visible grant rows rather than a walk through a bundle table nobody reads. This is where D-068 was already going; it just went the rest of the way. role.create, role.edit, role.delete, role.view, role.assign, role.unassign survive, retargeted: the last two write role_holder. role.scope_required and role.requires_membership are deleted with their mechanisms. role joins person_group in grant_scope_type, so "these two may manage the counselors roster" is a grant on one role, which is D-098's move applied symmetrically.

2. Positions are deleted. position, position_assignment, is_leadership, max_holders and the appointment workflows go: with no units there is no body to be a leader of, which is the only thing a position recorded and a role does not (D-033's own reasoning for why leadership is a position-assignment fact and not a role fact). An elected leader is now a holder of a role, and the audience rule that used to read unit_leaders — which round 6 had to correct because it was silently matching nobody — is ROLE(leaders) and means what its name says. What is genuinely lost is the elected-versus-appointed distinction as stored data: it survives only as a role the organization invents (elected_council next to appointed_it) or not at all. F-12 is closed and its answer is no: role_holder names one person. The reason the register refused it — a derived holder list cannot answer "who was treasurer in 2023", and an office record that cannot answer that is not an office record — is untouched, and the grantee pair that F-12 contemplated is no longer even tempting, because grants now aim at roles instead of roles being filled by grants.

3. The gate moves from the resolver into the selector, and this is the round's largest deletion. D-039 made the resolver ask, for every grant, whether the holder currently holds a membership; D-051 then needed system.gate_exempt and person_holds_gate_exempt to let appointed people through anyway, with the documented hazard that a permission check performed through can() there means a lockout with no error message. Now MEMBERS is a selector operand evaluated live on the checked date, and:

Old mechanism New expression The gate applied to a role with requires_membership = true MEMBERS * ROLE(x) The gate waived for a whole role ROLE(x) — write it without MEMBERS The gate waived for one named person (system.gate_exempt) MEMBERS * ROLE(x) + PERSON(y)

role.requires_membership, system.gate_exempt and person_holds_gate_exempt are all deleted, the resolver's membership clause is deleted, and the special-case path that had to be carefully kept out of can() goes with it. Ownership and guardianship stay channels and are unaffected — they were never gated. D-071's posture transfers to role_holder: nothing forces a holder row to end, and the control is the report.

The posture reverses, and the new failure mode is named rather than buried. The gate used to be default-on, so that forgetting it was impossible. It is now opt-in per grant: a grant written as ROLE(TREASURERS) with no MEMBERS authorizes a lapsed member, silently, forever. Three controls, none of which is the resolver:

  • A standing report of live grants naming a ROLE(...) operand whose expression does not contain MEMBERS. An office held by a non-member is the case worth a human eye, and this report is narrow enough to actually be read.
  • Seeded grants and any grant template carry MEMBERS, so the path of least repetition is the safe path.
  • Import completeness. MEMBERS * COUNSELORS is only as correct as the counselor roster: the gate used to fall out of membership alone, so an import that misses 300 counselors silently un-gates them. It fails closed — nothing breaks, which is exactly why nobody notices. The import reconciliation report of D-090 must count people marked as counselors in the corpus against role_holder rows written.

PERSON(y) is a selector, and this entry is the reason it had to become one. The grammar D-101 first shipped did not include it — LIST and GROUP(x) cover the enumeration cases, and a language with no attribute operands has no obvious place for one person — which left the third row of the table above unparseable in the very entry that wrote it down. It is seeded in selector_type like every other operand, it takes a person, and it passes the materializability test for the plain reason that a set of one is a set. The workaround the membership module reached for before this was repaired — write a second grant whose grantee is that person — stays legal and is arguably clearer for a permanent exception; what was not acceptable is a control that does not parse.

A consequence of moving the gate that no entry in this round had named: the expiry sweep can lock the organization out of its own system. D-040 lapses memberships on a date, to everyone at once, and whoever runs that sweep is a member too. Under D-039 the collision existed but system.gate_exempt was the purpose-built hole in it, and that mechanism is deleted above. So an administrative office whose grants read MEMBERS * ROLE(...) stops working at the instant the sweep lapses its holder — including the office that would have been asked to fix it. What carries the case now is the second control: the seeded grants for offices that must survive a lapse are written ROLE(...) with no MEMBERS, which turns a flag nobody read into a written expression with an outage attached to getting it wrong. Assumption: the seeded is_system role set contains at least one such office; nothing in the catalog requires it to, and if it does not, 1 January is a support call.

Why two tables, when you said they are technically the same. Because the difference decides who may edit the membership, and one table would merge those two permissions into one. role.* is the most sensitive code family in the catalog (🔒🔒); writing a group's roster is person_group.member.manage (⚠). One person_group table with a kind column and one membership table gives a single code that both adds a child to the Thursday group and puts the holder into SYSTEM_ADMINS. That is the merge to refuse, and it is the answer to D-080's lesson about two same-shaped tables: these are not two statements of one rule, they are two different grants of power. Same columns, different codes, and ROLE(x) / GROUP(x) distinct in the grant text so the distinction is visible to whoever reads the grant — which is where you asked for it.

COUNSELORS is seeded, as a role. A permanent, organization-wide population is the opposite of your own definition of a group ("a temporary set of members that do events together"), and the table decides the sensitivity that protects the set every safeguarding convention hangs from. It ships is_system so an editor refuses to delete it. Consistent with D-005: this is a set, and being in it confers nothing until a grant names it — audience membership has never been authority (D-042, restated in D-091). Bare COUNSELORS is legal in an expression, which makes the name namespace load-bearing (D-101).

Two-way door? The gate is the expensive half. Restoring a default-on membership test means re-adding a resolver clause and re-deciding which permissions it applies to, because a system where every expression is explicit has no record of which grants were meant to be gated. The role/group split is a cheap door in both directions: the tables have the same shape, so merging them is a migration, and the only thing to re-argue is the permission separation this entry records.

See: data-model/05-authorization.md §3–§4, domain/06-authorization-model.md, domain/02-actors.md, appendix/permission-catalog.md §11.

docs.text:
Offices and groups as two tables of one shape, and the audience rebuilt as an expression tree over named sets.

Refinement round 10 — the deletions, part 1 (D-097 … D-100) ← | All decisions | Refinement rounds 11 and 12 (D-105 … D-108) →

docs.title: D-101 — An audience is an expression over named sets, stored as a tree
docs.text:
Status: decided (from your answers) Date: refinement round 10 Follows: D-098, D-100

Amends: D-091 in its third arm. Confirms: D-060, D-011.

Your words. "A group can be used as a selector in the audience rule (e.g. MEMBERS - GROUP(schuzka2026-1) * COUNSELORS — meaning all counselors that are not part of the group schuzka2026-1)." Asked which of two notations to build on: "Would it be easier for the system if we wrote an evaluator for each person (MEMBER & COUNSELOR | ROLE(TREASURER)) or as a union/difference of groups?" — and then: "I dislike the lack of operand precedence. I would like to be able to use brackets." — and then: "Can we not store it as expressions? Each row has two operands and one operator, and the operands can be either another row or a selector."

First, the reframe that makes the notation question smaller than it looks. p ∈ (A ∩ B) ∪ C is by definition (p ∈ A ∧ p ∈ B) ∨ p ∈ C. The two notations you were offered are the same function written from two ends, so the choice does not decide what the machine computes; it decides what gets stored and what a writer is allowed to say. The answer is therefore both, split by direction:

Author in sets. Evaluate per person.

A check asks about one person, so the resolver compiles the expression down to a predicate and never materializes a set. An implementation that evaluates MEMBERS as a list of ids and then tests for containment pays three thousand rows per request, which is the one way to get this wrong and the reason the requirement is written here rather than left to whoever builds it.

Why the set form is the source language, in one argument each.

  • It is no weaker. - is complement against EVERYONE, * distributes over +, so every boolean formula has an equal expression here. The predicate form buys zero expressive power.
  • It is the closed one, and that is the whole case. D-060 refused a rule engine, and a per-person boolean language is the door to one: once &, | and ! exist, the next operand somebody wants is AGE >= 15 or FEE_PAID, and there is a parser standing there to accept it. A set language closes it by rule instead of by discipline: an operand must be a named, materializable set of people. An attribute is not a set of people. Guardianship is (GUARDIANS(x) is a set), age is not, and the line falls exactly where D-060 already drew it — eligibility stays capability.
  • The three workloads the corpus already promises. "Who does this grant reach?" must be shown, expanded, in front of a human — D-091 made that a requirement on the screen, not a nicety, and a predicate can only report true, while a set is the answer. "What may a treasurer do?" (D-100) needs the person→set index, and role_holder and person_group_member are it; an expression is unindexable. ~~Caching (F-6) can key on an operand and be reused across every grant, and role_holder changes are the invalidation.~~ This third workload was argued on a cache that D-114 deleted, and it survives the deletion for a different reason: what a named operand makes reusable is a compilation, which is keyed by the expression and the ruleset version and therefore shared across every grant and every person, while the rows an operand reads are fetched live. The workload itself — showing a grant's reach to a human — was never the cache's job; the preview does it on open (data-model/05 §The cost of composition).
  • It is the schema that exists. An audience's manual arm, its included groups, and everyone / all_members / guardians_of are already named sets; the only genuinely new symbols are * and -. Today's audience has no intersection and no difference at all, which is why your example was not writable in any notation.

Grammar.

expr    := term ( '+' term )*
term    := operand ( ( '*' | '-' ) operand )*
operand := EVERYONE | MEMBERS | LIST | PERSON '(' person ')'
         | GUARDIANS [ '(' person ')' ]
         | ATTENDED [ '(' event ')' ]     | PLACED [ '(' event ')' ]
         | CONFIRMED [ '(' event ')' ]    | ON_WAITLIST [ '(' event ')' ]
         | ORGANIZERS [ '(' event ')' ]              argumentless = bound, [D-102]
         | ROLE '(' name ')' | GROUP '(' name ')' | AUDIENCE '(' code ')'
         | name                                      bare; the shared namespace below
         | '(' expr ')'

MEMBERS names a set the membership module already defines, and does not define it here. It evaluates is_current_member(person) — status active with a period covering the checked date, no grace coalescing, because the renewal window is a date range for rejoining and not a state in which somebody is a member (data-model/03-membership.md §3, domain/06-authorization-model.md §6.1). That is the whole reason the language works: an operand is the name of a set somebody else already provably owns, which is what "materializable" has to mean for this to stay out of rule-engine territory.

(The AUDIENCE arm is D-103's, added the same round this entry was written, and it is the reason this grammar is marked as amended rather than final: an entry that ships a grammar and then grows an arm is worth seeing to have grown one.)

(The LIST arm is since gone. D-105 deleted it, and a hand-written set is now written the way every other set in this grammar is written — as an operand, PERSON(a) + PERSON(b). The arm is left printed here because this entry shipped it; the registry that has to be true today has thirteen rows — twelve for the round that deleted LIST, plus the two attribute rows D-107 added, minus the GUARDIANS row D-113 deleted. This footnote said "fourteen rows, not thirteen" until round 13, and a footnote whose number has to be re-typed by whoever changes the table is the same defect the footnote itself is describing — which is why it keeps its own history rather than just its new number.)

(Two arms have been added since this entry shipped, also by D-107: OLDER(n) and YOUNGER(n). No operator was added. The boolean spellings &, |, ! were proposed along with them and declined — + - * are still the only three, and a negation is still written EVERYONE -. This entry's grammar is therefore amended twice, and the second amendment is the one that changes what a writer may say: an age test is now statable in this language, which this entry's own appeal to D-060 said it was not. The materializability test this entry leaned on is corrected there too — it was never what was doing the work.)

Two arms the first draft of this grammar omitted, and both were load-bearing elsewhere in the round. PERSON(x) names one person — a set of one, so it passes the materializability test, and it is how the membership gate's "except Honza" is written inside the expression that granted the rule in the first place, which keeps the exception visible next to the thing it exempts. (This entry's first draft credited that pattern to system.gate_exempt, which D-100 had already deleted in the same round: the waiver is an expression now, not a permission code. A live pattern pointed at by a dead code is F-19's defect wearing a decision entry's clothes, so it is named rather than quietly corrected.) And bare name, because the round's own control is written MEMBERS * COUNSELORS: an expression that does not parse is not a control. ROLE() and GROUP() remain as explicit qualification, required in the canonical rendering.

Both arms were still missing from the seeded registry when the registry was written, and that is worth recording rather than fixing quietly. data-model/05-authorization.md §8 was written from the evaluator's arm list, not from this grammar, and an arm list copied from an implementation is exactly the kind of source that loses an arm nobody had implemented yet. The registry carries thirteen rows and PERSON is one of them: takes_argument true, argument_type person, binds_to_item false. Its distinction from LIST is real and is why both survive — PERSON(x) is an argument, so it composes and can be subtracted on its own, while LIST is one set of several people belonging to one audience and subtracting it removes everybody on it. D-103's kitchen example needs both, which is the proof that they are not the same operand wearing two names. The class of defect is F-19, it arrived here in a second registry inside the same round, and D-104 is the answer to it.

Amended by D-105, which deleted the half of this paragraph's distinction that was not PERSON. The registry carries twelve rows; LIST is a tombstone where its row was. The finding stands on its own — an arm list copied from an implementation is what lost the arm — but the closing proof left with the thing it proved. PERSON(x) and LIST were never the same operand wearing two names, and they no longer have to be distinguished at all, because one of them was a table. What PERSON carries now, alone, is every hand-named person the language can name: the "except Honza" in MEMBERS * ROLE(x) + PERSON(y) — the expression that replaced the deleted gate's waiver, not a permission code of its own, and the run of leaves that spells out the set a list used to hold.

* and - bind tighter than +; * and - bind equally, left to right; brackets override. The rule is arithmetic-shaped so nobody has to learn a table, with one deliberate departure from arithmetic: - does not sit beneath *. The reason is the first expression anybody writes in this language — MEMBERS - GROUP(schuzka2026-1) * COUNSELORS, meant as "all counselors not in that group" — which is what left-to-right gives and is not what *-tighter-than-- gives. Precedence was chosen to match the reading the writer already had, not to be defensible on other grounds.

The canonical form prints every bracket, always. Not for legibility, so that the paragraph above is never load-bearing when somebody reads a grant two years from now: the stored form of the example is (MEMBERS - GROUP(schuzka2026-1)) * COUNSELORS, the editor rewrites what is typed into that before saving, and an implementer who reaches for arithmetic precedence in their parser builds a different expression than the one the writer meant. This entry's first draft got its own rule wrong — it asserted that the bare form had changed meaning, which is the *-tighter reading this entry then refused — and the correction is worth keeping in place of the claim, because the mistake is exactly the one the always-bracketed canonical form exists to make impossible: two precedence rules can sit in one document, agree with each other in the abstract, and disagree the moment an expression is written without brackets.

Storage: the tree you described, not a normal form. Each row is a node: operator + left_id + right_id, or a leaf's selector_kind + selector_arg_id. My alternative was to normalize to a union of terms on save; yours is better and the reason is the round's thesis — the normalizer is the code (distribute, dedupe, sort, survive blow-up), and a binary tree needs one evaluator of about fifteen lines and keeps the writer's brackets instead of silently rewriting them. It also makes the depth limit the only complexity bound, since (A + B) * C costs nothing. The rules that come with it:

Rule Where it is enforced Exactly one shape. A node has operator, left_id, right_id and no selector; a leaf has selector_kind and no operator or children. A check on the row — expressible, so it stays a constraint One parent, never a DAG. parent_id lives on the child, so a node belongs to exactly one expression. A side table letting two expressions share a node is refused: editing the shared node would silently widen every grant using it, which is D-091's inclusion hazard re-imported Structure, plus a CI check that no such table exists Cycles and depth refused when the row is saved — walk the parent chain, refuse a revisit, refuse past selector_depth_limit. Structurally hard to build; refused rather than trusted, for D-091's own reason: a hand-fixed row, a restore from before the guard existed. Amended by D-103: the parent-chain walk sees one tree, and AUDIENCE() makes cycles possible between trees, so the guard is a reachability walk over the reference closure and the depth bound is counted there too. Amended a second time by D-105, which deleted the depth half of this row: no parameter, no save-time bound, nothing to count — the walk stays and now guards termination alone, so this row is the cycle check with a history as a size check The write path, exactly as uq_audience_include_acyclic was selector_arg_id has no foreign key — it points at role, person_group, audience, person or event depending on kind D-011's already-accepted trade-off, with its compensating orphan check An operand that does not resolve is the empty set. Fail closed, in every direction, as §Evaluation of data-model/05 already rules for audiences The resolver The whole tree is fetched in one indexed read by denormalizing audience_id onto every row, then assembled in memory. The read path never walks a parent chain. Amended by D-103: still one read per audience, but an expression that names another audience needs one per audience in its closure, so the honest claim is "no parent-chain walking", not "one query" A stated implementation requirement

A naming ruling, written down because the table sits outside the naming conventions and somebody will notice. data-model/00-conventions.md §2 admits two shapes — a junction table named <a>_<b> alphabetically, and a lookup table named for the vocabulary it is — and audience_operand is neither: it is a recursive structure, which the conventions have no rule for because until now the model had none. It is kept for the reason the two existing rules exist: the name should tell a reader what a row means. Operand is the word the grammar itself uses, so the table teaches the language; audience_node was weighed and refused, because it names a graph shape and would leave a reader who has not met the grammar no better off than audience_thing. Worth marking anyway, because it is the reading that gets a migration wrong — singular-for-an-aggregate invites someone to build one row per audience, when the aggregate is the tree and a row is one node of it. The diagram caption and the data model's first line both say rows of one audience's expression tree for that reason. This entry's first draft justified the name by citing a naming decision that turned out not to exist — the rule is a conventions table, not a numbered decision, and a citation invented to settle an argument is the kind of thing this log keeps a record of.

selector_type is a seeded registry, not an enum. Which operands take an argument, which may bind to the item, and what type their argument is — that was three hard-coded lists (the resolver_key enum written out in prose, the reserved-word list, the "meaningless without a resolver_key" rule). It becomes one seeded table in the shape grant_scope_type already is: code, takes_argument, binds_to_item, argument_type. The parser reads its reserved words from it, the editor builds its dropdown from it, and the write path checks arity against it. The language becomes data. audience.resolver_key and scope_parameter are deleted into it.

Two sentences this paragraph needed, and did not have. The registry is data, so say what is not thereby open: every selector_type row is seeded and is_system, and the organization may not add one at runtime. "Closed language" and "the language is a table" are contradictory unless the table is read-only to tenants, and the read-only version is the one that keeps D-060's line — an operand is a shipped predicate, not a thing a well-meaning registrar invents at 23:00. One consequence of that rule is a refusal worth naming because it was nearly built: a set of grants is not an operand. GRANTS(<ids>) — "all the people these grants reach", wanted as a way to move a bundle of grants at once — cannot be one, because an operand must resolve to a set of people, and that is what a grantee is; the bulk operation it was wanted for is a screen over the grant list, not a meaning a stored grantee can carry. Refusing it on the type rather than on permissions is also what removes the awkward status such a row would have had: with this rule, every seeded selector is a shipped selector, and there is no third kind. What the deletion of resolver_key does leave unsaid is where a code meets its implementation: the resolver dispatches on code, and a seeded row with no shipped resolver is a deployment bug that shows up as an empty set, fail closed like everything else in the round. Second: this is what makes the age question answerable at all. Attribute operands are refused above, so "13 and over" cannot be typed by a writer; under D-070 the answer stays "open the event to the set whose members are that age" — a group somebody maintains — and an AGED_13_PLUS-style operand becomes legal only as a shipped selector, which is the one route this paragraph allows and the events document was right to guess. Nothing of the kind is seeded at go-live, because one shipped age band is the first step onto a ladder nobody asked for.

The inclusion arm dies, and composition survives by changing hands. D-091 let a group pull in other groups through audience_include, because a group could otherwise not be composed. Under D-098 a group's membership is its dated rows, and composition now lives in the expression: GROUP(kitchen) + ROLE(troop_staff) composes as much as an edge ever did. What goes with the edge table is a great deal of machinery — the transitive walk, include_depth_limit, the write-time cycle walk over a graph, and integrity check 20's job of asserting that the walk exists — because a tree cannot cycle, so the only acyclicity guard left is the cheap parent-chain one. ~~That sentence is the second-most-durable claim in this entry.~~ D-103, written the same round, lets an operand name another audience, and a forest of trees pointing at each other does cycle: the save-time reachability walk comes back — and the depth bound that came back with it has since left again, D-105 deleting the parameter and the save-time check with it, so the walk returns alone and bounds termination rather than cost. What stays deleted is the edge table and the materialized closure check 20 asserted — the edges are AUDIENCE leaves in the table that already exists. What is genuinely lost: "add the kitchen crew to everything the troop-staff group is used for" is no longer one edit. The answer is that named sets are the composition mechanism now — name the composite once, aim grants at it — which is D-091's outcome reached without a graph nobody could see the shape of.

~~audience_member stays, re-roled as the LIST leaf.~~ Did, for one round, and D-105 deleted it and the operand with it, so what follows is kept as the argument it was and is now an argument about a table that does not exist. It is the audience's own dated list of people, reachable in an expression as one operand. Merging it into GROUP(x) was weighed and refused twice over: naming three people in one grant would create a row in the group browser that is not a group anybody talks about, and D-098 already wrote the rule that keeps the two dated-member tables apart (a group's members are true with no grant pointing at them; a selector's additions are meaningless outside the selector). The duplication D-080 would flag is therefore kept on purpose, and the mitigation is the one D-091 already required: the editor shows which mechanism each person arrived through.

Names are one namespace, and that is a new dependency. Bare COUNSELORS resolves against roles and groups together, since ROLE() and GROUP() no longer have to disambiguate. So: names unique across role and person_group — and audience.code joins them in D-103, so it is three tables and no single constraint spans three of them — which means the write path carries it and an integrity check asserts it exists, per D-081; case, whitespace and separators folded on write; and every selector_type.code is a reserved name, so a group called MEMBERS is refused at the save rather than silently rewriting every gate expression in the system. What is stored is always kind + id, so a rename never rewrites a grant.

Given up, once. Storing a tree means two expressions with the same meaning are two different row sets, so "you already granted exactly this set on that row" no longer falls out of storage. The route back is a normalized fingerprint computed on save as a derived value used only for a warning — and if the expansion overflows, skip the warning rather than refuse the write: normalization informing a human, not gating one. Registered as an open question rather than promised. Similarly, DNF could have flagged term-matches-nobody syntactically; the tree catches only X - X on a single node, so "this selector reaches nobody" belongs to the editor preview that already has to exist.

Two-way door? The language is a wide-open door — it is one seeded table plus an evaluator, and an operand can be added by any later decision. Precedence is the closed half: once expressions are stored in canonical fully-bracketed form, changing what binds tighter changes nothing already stored, which is a nice property and the reason the canonical rendering is a requirement rather than a convenience.

See: data-model/05-authorization.md §8, domain/06-authorization-model.md §6, glossary.md (Audience, Selector, Filling rule, Locality).

docs.title: D-102 — Nothing owns an event. The people connected to it are named by selectors that bind to it
docs.text:
Status: decided (from your answer) Date: refinement round 10 Follows: D-097, D-099, D-101

Reverses: D-058's ownership, D-063, D-094.

Amends: D-061, D-062, D-065, D-067.

Your words. "The events are owned by the root unit, so anyone with a permission to create an event can create an event." Then: "I also want to include ATTENDING(<event>) (meaning is registered to an event)", and on the tiers: "let the user pick which they mean — mainly 'registered and confirmed', or 'registered and is confirmed or whitelisted or waiting for confirmation'", and on the argument-less form: "unparameterized form is great, I like that."

Decision. event.org_unit_id is deleted and there is no owner of an event. An event is an item in grant_scope_type like any other: event.create is held at the unit and creates an event; a unit-scope grant reaches every event, because after D-097 there is no tier between the unit and the item and nothing left to test. That deletes can_event(), the unit-authority rule that every event permission in this module was reached through, and the integrity checks that guarded the owner column. D-063's famous artifact, not child distinction has no artifact-and-unit pair left to distinguish, so it goes too.

1. Bound operands. Some selectors name a set relative to the item being checked, and write it without an argument:

Operand On the item checked means Explicit form ATTENDED said yes to this event ATTENDED(<event>) PLACED said yes and is not waitlisted — the capacity set, the one §5 counts and the index already serves PLACED(<event>) CONFIRMED holds a paid place on this event CONFIRMED(<event>) ON_WAITLIST is waiting for a place on this event ON_WAITLIST(<event>) ORGANIZERS runs this event ORGANIZERS(<event>) GUARDIANS are the guardians of the person this item is about GUARDIANS(<person>)

Every one of these is a seeded is_system row of selector_type, and is_system is not decoration here. D-101 made the registry read-only to an organization, so no tenant action can add an operand; what is_system guards is the platform's own delete path, and it is also the flag that tells a reader this code is vocabulary rather than content. The alternative — seeded but deletable — is a grant breaker with no crime attached: remove ORGANIZERS and every event.answer.view grant in the system silently resolves to nobody while the audit trail goes on reporting them live. ROLE and GROUP are the only kinds an organization populates, and it does so by writing role and person_group rows, not registry rows.

The argument-less form is the important half, and it exists to kill a specific flaw: ATTENDING(<event 1204>) — attending being this round's starting word for the idea, refused above in favour of four tiers that each name a stored column — written on event 1204 is one grant per event with the event's own id typed into it, so "every participant may see the other participants" is a thing you do 400 times and forget on the 401st. Bound, it is one expression written the same way every time. Two rules make it safe:

  • A bound operand is legal only on an item-scope grant. At the unit there is nothing to bind it to, so it is refused when the grant is saved, with the operand named in the message.
  • A bound operand is legal only on a matching item type. PLACED on a person_group grant is refused because that item is not an event. This is selector_type.argument_type checked against grant_scope_type — which is a reason the registry of D-101 is doing real work and not merely tidying.

2. ORGANIZERS is what replaces unit authority over an event, and it is not a contradiction of D-062. With the owning unit gone, "the people running this event" has no other expression, and D-061's rule (answers are read by that event's organizers) has to be said somewhere now rather than hard-coded in prose. It is said as a seeded grant: event.answer.view on an event to ORGANIZERS. D-062 and its "an event_organizer row grants nothing" both stand untouched, because an operand is a set, not a grant — the same sentence §8 of the authorization model already repeats twice for unit_leaders and audiences generally. What changed is only that the appointment is now aimed at by grants instead of being special-cased inside the resolver.

And a seeded grant carrying a bound operand is not one row — a sentence this entry omitted and the events module then had to assume. A grant's scope is the unit or exactly one item, and a bound operand is legal only on an item-scope grant, so there is no row that says "every event's answers go to its organizers": the one row that would say it needs the unit as its scope, which is precisely where the operand is refused. What is seeded is therefore a template, and the event-creation path instantiates it beside the event row. Two consequences, both kept:

  • The import owes one instantiation per event row it writes — this module's share of D-093's shape, and cheap, because it is the same insert the event row already needs.
  • An event whose creation failed between the event row and the grant has nobody who can read its answers. So the two writes are one transaction, and the check is a report — events with no answer-view grant — because "these two rows exist together" is F-10 shape 1 and no layer this project owns can express it.

What the per-event row buys, and it is not accidental: answers-view is revocable on one event without touching anyone's appointment, which is the kind of thing an organizer asks for the week before a camp.

3. Four attendance tiers, and the refusal of a fifth. You asked the writer to pick; picking requires that the choices be the stored facts and not four new ideas, so each tier names columns of event_registration and nothing else. PRESENT(<event>) over was_present is refused, and the reason is the failure direction: was_present is NULL until someone takes a register, so an operand built on it would revoke a child's access to their own camp photos because a volunteer forgot to tick a box. That column is a safeguarding signal — three-valued on purpose, per D-067 — and keeping it out of the selector language is what keeps it meaning "a person recorded this" rather than "this is who may see things". WHITELISTED has no stored state to name: the nearest facts are source = staff (an organizer entered them) and promotion off the waitlist. Either it means one of those or it is a new column on event_registration, which is an events decision and not a selector decision, so it stays an open question rather than being implied by a word in a grammar.

4. The set a grant reaches is now per-item. D-091's requirement that the editor show the expanded people — "the person saving the grant is looking at one row that mentions no person at all" — can no longer be answered from the grant alone: PLACED means different people on different events. So the preview is computed for an item and says so on screen, and the cache key for a bound operand must include the item (F-6 amended). Import consequence: the one-off import owes event rows and event_registration rows (D-090, D-093's shape), and it owes no owner column, which is the import-side saving D-097 already counted. D-094 is deleted rather than reversed: there is no column for an imported event to have.

Two-way door? Narrow and expensive. Re-introducing ownership means the owner column, the resolver tier that reads it, and every check that the module deleted — but the selectors added here are not in the way, because an ownership grant and a bound operand answer different questions and can coexist. That is the difference between this and D-097: that entry deletes a dimension, this one removes a test and leaves the vocabulary intact.

See: data-model/08-events.md §2, §8, domain/07-events.md, data-model/05-authorization.md §10.

docs.title: D-103 — An audience may name another audience
docs.text:
Status: decided (from your answer) Date: refinement round 10 Follows: D-091, D-098, D-101

Amends: D-101's grammar, its "a tree cannot cycle" claim, and its one-indexed-read fetch.

Your words. "What is a LIST? Also it should allow nesting AUDIENCEs." The second sentence is the decision; the first is the reason this entry has to be written at all, and §1 below is its answer.

docs.title: 1. What LIST is, said plainly
docs.text:
LIST is this audience's own hand-typed list of people — the rows of audience_member, which is the one table in the module that holds persons rather than rules. It is the only operand that is not a rule about people: MEMBERS is a test, ROLE(vedoucí) is an office with dated holders, PLACED is a join against an event, and LIST is the names somebody typed into this one grant.

It exists so that a grant can carry its own exceptions without creating a thing everybody can see. "Everyone in the kitchen crew, plus Honza, minus the two people who left" is (GROUP(kitchen) + LIST) - PERSON(a) - PERSON(b). The alternative — making Honza a member of GROUP(kitchen) to reach one grant — edits a roster that other grants read, which is D-091's hazard, and it also invents a group nobody talks about, which is the rule D-098 wrote. So LIST is scoped to the one expression that contains it, is invisible in the group browser, and dies with the audience.

The name is the weak part of this design and the question you asked is the evidence: nothing in LIST says whose list. The registry entry carries the gloss "the people written into this audience", and the editor renders the operand as LIST (this audience). Renaming the code was refused only because the round has already propagated it through four files and the gloss costs nothing; if it keeps causing this question, the replacement is ADDED, which says where the rows came from.

Amended by D-105, which deleted the operand this section exists to explain. Read it as the answer to the question that was asked; what it describes is now a table that does not exist. Two things in it survived, and one of them is why the deletion was cheap. "A grant can carry its own exceptions without creating a thing everybody can see" is still true, and still the requirement — a run of PERSON(…) leaves scopes exactly as LIST scoped, is invisible in the group browser exactly as LIST was, and dies with the audience. D-105 removed a table without removing a capability, which is the test this round should have applied to LIST before keeping it. The hazard paragraph is now the load-bearing one: the choice in front of whoever composes a grant is between editing a roster that other grants read and writing the names into the expression, and D-105 turned that from a theoretical choice into the only choice, by deleting the third option where somebody could have both. What is moot is this paragraph: LIST needs no better name, and ADDED is not coming, because there is nothing left to call.

docs.title: 2. The decision, and the hole it closes in D-101
docs.text:
An operand may name another saved audience: AUDIENCE(<code>). It is an ordinary selector — one row in selector_type, takes_argument = true, argument_type = audience, and it therefore costs one seeded row plus a resolver arm of about the same length as GROUP's.

The stronger reason is that D-101 did not deliver the answer it claimed to. Having deleted audience_include, it answered "add the kitchen crew to everything the troop-staff rule is used for" with "named sets are the composition mechanism now — name the composite once, aim grants at it." But under D-101's own grammar the only names available were GROUP() and ROLE(), and both name a roster, not a rule: a group's members are its dated rows. The rule you wanted to reuse had no name to point at, so the composite could be named only by copying its rows into a second audience — which is audience_include with the copy step done by hand. Nesting is the half of that answer that was missing: AUDIENCE() is what makes a rule namable.

It is also the arm that composes the two things the round kept apart. ROLE() names an office, GROUP() names company, ATTENDED() names attendance; only AUDIENCE() names a decision about access, so it is the only arm that can say "the same people that grant may see the fee ledger, plus the accountant".

docs.title: 3. The three named sets, which are not the same thing
docs.text:
Printed with four columns, because that is what this entry compared. The LIST column is dead — D-105 deleted the operand and its table, and the honest reading of the column is that everything in it is now either in the GROUP(x) column (a roster somebody maintains, with dates) or in the expression itself (a run of PERSON(…) leaves, with none). The three-way version that replaced this is in data-model/05-authorization.md; this one is kept four-wide so the deletion has something to be measured against.

GROUP(x) AUDIENCE(x) LIST What it is A dated roster somebody maintains A saved expression, evaluated live Rows on this one audience Who may change who is in it person_group.member.manage audience.update on that audience whoever may edit this audience Does it exist outside a grant? Yes — D-098: a group's members are true with nothing pointing at them No — it exists to aim a grant No "Was she in it on 1 June 2024?" Answerable, from the dated rows Not answerable past the audit window Not answerable Sensitive as ⚠ company 🔒🔒 authority 🔒

That fourth row is the honest cost and it is the D-100 distinction replayed one level down. GROUP(x) is materialized, so it keeps a history you can be asked about; AUDIENCE(x) is a live rule whose past shape survives only in the audit trail, and D-088 expires those payloads after 24 months. So "who could see this child's data in 2024?" is answerable when the grant pointed at a group and is not answerable when it pointed at a nested audience. A rule whose reach cannot be reconstructed is still the right tool for a rule — the roster is the wrong tool for everyone over 13 — but the gap should be closed by the report in §5, not by pretending the question has an answer.

docs.title: 4. Rules that come with it
docs.text:
