docs.title: D-109 — Nothing a rule names is deleted: deprecated, hidden, disabled — and a tab instead of a report
docs.text:
Status: decided (from your answer) Date: refinement round 13 Supersedes: the report D-106 added, the merge-repoint duty D-105 recorded, and part of F-21

Decision. Anything a stored expression can name — a selector_type row, a role, a person_group, an audience — is never deleted while a rule may name it. It is given a state instead. Three states, and they must stay three different things or one of them will silently become the other:

State Does it still resolve? Is it offered when writing a rule? Is it flagged? deprecated yes, unchanged no — it cannot be added to a new rule, and editing a rule cannot introduce it yes, highlighted in the editor wherever it appears hidden yes, unchanged no no — it is not obsolete, it is not everybody's business disabled no — the empty set no yes, and this is the only state that changes an answer

No standing report. There is a tab on the permissions page listing every live rule whose expression names a deprecated, hidden or disabled thing, or fails to resolve at all.

Why. Your answer, in full: "There should be no deleted selectors, only deprecated/hidden/disabled. In that case, the original resource is still referenced and applied, BUT it cannot be added to new or edited rules AND it is highlighted in the rule editor. No real report is needed, there can be a tab on the permissions page listing all the 'broken' permissions."

This deletes the reason the report existed, which is the elegant part of it. D-106 added a report to catch an unresolvable operand; F-21 asked who would read the report of the widest expansions and could not name anybody. Both are answers about a failure whose cause is now removed: a leaf broke because the thing it named was deleted, and here nothing is deleted. F-21's reader question resolves to nobody, because there is nothing to read — and what replaces it is better than a report for the ordinary reason that a report has to be remembered and a tab is where the person already is. The tab is not a control either, in D-081's sense; it is a control that has a decent chance of being seen, which is all the difference between a convention and a decoration.

Two duties this withdraws, and one it leaves standing. Round 11 recorded that a person merge or a redaction must repoint every audience_operand leaf, because a leaf naming nobody is the empty set and on a - side that widens. For the resources in the table above that duty is gone — retiring a group is now one write to the group, not N writes to N expressions, and the expressions keep meaning what they meant until somebody edits them. It survives for exactly one argument kind, and that is the collision this entry has to name: PERSON(x) names a person, and D-088 lets a redaction require the row to actually go. Erasure wins. A person is not a selector, and no convenience owed to an expression author survives a former member's right to be deleted. So the corpus now has exactly one remaining way to produce a broken leaf — a redacted person — and D-106's semantics cover it unchanged: the empty set, narrowing an allow and widening a deny, now visible in the tab rather than in a report nobody opens. That is a much smaller domain than D-106 assumed, and stating it that way is the point.

What disabled costs, said plainly, because it is the loudest switch in this system. Disabling a group, an office or an audience stops every rule that names it, in every scope, at once, and re-enabling it restores all of them — a widening in which nobody edited a grant, so the audit trail would show one flag write and a hundred permissions appear if it were logged as anything less. Therefore: disabling and re-enabling are audited writes that print the rules they touch, resolved before and after, which is the same report D-104 and D-105 adopted for their own migrations; and the tab lists the rules currently dead for this reason, so the state is reversible knowingly. disabled is also the answer to a question this corpus kept meeting — "how do I turn off that whole naming without editing forty grants?" — which until now had no answer except a deny per grant.

The invariant that keeps deprecated from drifting into disabled: deprecating or hiding what an expression names must not change the set the expression resolves to. That is check-worthy, it is cheap, and it is the precise failure this whole design is meant to make impossible — a rule that quietly stops granting because somebody tidied a list. The editor's reserved-name rule (D-101) keeps a deprecated or disabled name reserved, so nothing new can quietly claim the word and split its meaning in two.

See: D-106 (whose semantics now apply to redacted people only), D-105 (the repoint duty, halved), D-088 (why erasure wins), and F-21, closed as "no report; a tab; nothing bounds a check, deliberately".

docs.title: D-110 — The expression is the record of whom a grant reached
docs.text:
Status: decided (from your answer) Date: refinement round 13 Closes: F-23, and the reconstructable-past half of F-17

Decision. The audit record of a grant's reach is the expression. The preview still prints a resolved set before a save (D-091) and that printing is logged as a rendering on a date, not as a statement of who was in it. "Whom did this grant reach in May?" is answered, if at all, by evaluating the words against the data of May — and these documents do not promise the answer.

Why. Your answer, four words: "Words only — the expression is the record." The alternative was to keep the preview's list beside the audit row, and that list is the roster table this corpus has deleted twice (D-105, and assumption 58's history of it). It would also store, indefinitely and against D-088's window, a per-person record of people who were never granted anything — a list of everyone a rule happened to cover, kept after the rule was withdrawn. Storing that to make a historical question comfortable is the trade this corpus has refused every time it has been offered.

Why words-only is cheap now rather than brave. It was nearly untenable an hour ago and it is sound now, because of D-109: if nothing a rule names is deleted, the words stay evaluable long after their reason is gone. A role that was retired still resolves; a group that was deprecated still resolves; a name stays reserved. The two rulings are one design — refuse to delete the nouns, and then keeping only the words is not an amputation. Without D-109, this answer would mean "the past is usually unanswerable"; with it, the past is usually computable, and what is left is honestly bounded.

What is conceded, named so nobody finds it later. Editing a shared audience changes what every grant that names it has meant all along, because those grants hold a word, not a copy — and a re-evaluation for a past date uses today's inner expression. An edit to a shared audience is therefore a retrospective edit to every rule that names it. That is not new (D-103 accepted it as the price of reuse) but until now it was only implied; here it is the reason a past-date answer can be wrong rather than missing, and the control is D-103's existing one: the editor prints the resolved set before an edit to a shared expression saves, so the person editing sees, at least once, the thing they are changing backwards in time. What is not kept is a history of inner expressions; the audit trail records the edit, not the meaning that existed before it.

A consequence worth holding onto: the audit trail gets smaller and more honest. A row says this person wrote these words on this date about this item, which is a fact that cannot go stale, rather than this grant reached these 214 people, which starts decaying the night somebody's birthday falls.

See: D-107 for why a set now moves on its own, D-109 for why the words keep resolving, and F-17, whose premise about materializing this removes.

docs.title: D-111 — The permission cache is rebuilt nightly, on any ruleset change, and on request
docs.text:
Status: decided (from your answer) Date: refinement round 13 Closes: F-6, and F-7 by absorption Superseded in part by D-114: the cache is deleted, so there is nothing to rebuild. What survives of this entry is the integer — ruleset_version, now keying a compiled expression instead of a cached answer, with its bump set cut from the eight kinds of write listed below — six tables, this entry's own D-109 flag and a merge — to audience_operand and selector_type. What went is the object, the schedule and both invalidation lists. Reading this entry as wrong would be the mistake it does not deserve: it removed a TTL question by removing the need for a TTL, which was the right move against the problem it could see, and what D-114 found is that the rebuild had quietly inherited the staleness window the TTL was for — the answer moved on a schedule instead of on a clock, and a schedule is a harder place to notice that than a column. Its "the safeguarding case is immediate" argument is true now by construction rather than by trigger, which is the best outcome a superseded ruling can have.

Decision. There is one cache policy and three triggers. Every cached authorization answer is rebuilt (a) nightly, in full; (b) immediately on any write to the ruleset; (c) on explicit request — an administrative action, which belongs on the same permissions page as the tab. No TTL per entry, no asymmetric TTL, no partial invalidation list to get right.

Why. Your answer, verbatim: "All cache is represhed at night every day OR on manual request and ruleset change." F-6 had spent four rounds on which write invalidates how wide a fan-out, and on an asymmetric TTL that would make a deny visible sooner than an allow. This replaces the whole invalidation table with a rebuild and a rule about what counts as a ruleset change, which is a smaller thing to be right about — and the fan-out question was only hard because per-entry invalidation was assumed.

What counts as the ruleset, because the boundary is now the whole design: a write to access_grant, audience_operand, guardianship_permission, or permission; to role_holder and person_group_member; to the deprecated | hidden | disabled flag of anything in D-109's table (that flag must be a ruleset write — if it is not, "turn off this naming" waits until midnight, which is exactly the failure the flag exists to prevent); and a person merge or unmerge. An answer that moves without one of these is allowed to be up to one night stale: a birthday crossing OLDER(n)/YOUNGER(n), the 1 January membership sweep, a role or group period that ends by its own date, attendance writes behind the event tiers.

That residual window is the ruling, and it is the same ruling as D-107's. A withdrawn permission keeps working until the nightly rebuild only if the withdrawal was not a write — and every withdrawal a person performs is a write: revoke, add a deny, close a grant's period, end a guardianship, end a role assignment. What waits for the night is what nobody does: an expiry arriving on its own, an age arriving on its own. The safeguarding case is immediate; the calendar case waits at most one refresh, and the refresh is what fixes it. This is D-107's "I know, that the time will change, how the rules resolve and IT IS FINE" with the mechanism attached — until now the sentence described a behaviour, and now it describes a policy.

What "immediately" means when you cannot enumerate the affected people — the mechanism, added the same round because the ruling was incomplete without it. Found while propagating this entry: the cache key is (person_id, permission_code, scope_type, scope_id, at_bucket), and an audience appears in it nowhere. So the writes that need global invalidation are exactly the ones that name nobody. Ending one role_holder row names its person; ending one person_group_member row names its person; an edit to a shared audience_operand tree names nobody at all — the people it stops reaching are whatever the expression happens to resolve to, and finding them means evaluating it for everyone, which is the job, not a way around it. Per-entry invalidation had no answer to that, which is why F-6's table spent four rounds pretending the fan-out was tractable. The answer is a ruleset version: one integer, bumped by any write in the ruleset set above, carried in every cache entry, and an entry is valid only while its version matches. "Rebuild immediately on a ruleset change" then means bump the version, which is one write to one row and never needs to know whom a rule reaches; the nightly rebuild stays as the correctness backstop for everything the version does not cover (the calendar cases); and the manual request becomes "bump it and warm it". This is also what makes the deprecated | hidden | disabled flag safe in D-109's sense: flipping disabled on a group is a ruleset write, so it bumps the version, so no cached true survives it — and if the flag ever stops bumping, D-109's "deprecating or hiding must not change the answer" invariant still holds while "disabling takes effect now" silently does not, which is a failure worth having a check for. What the version does not buy: it is not a per-audience version and not a version per grant. A system large enough to want that is the system D-112 says this one is not, and the trigger there is what reopens this.

What F-7 was, and why it is answered rather than decided. F-7 asked whether to keep a cache or materialize an effective_permission table. A nightly full rebuild of cached answers and a nightly materialized effective_permission table are the same job with two names. There is now one job; the question was not resolved between two designs, it was dissolved by the design being chosen for a different reason — which is worth recording as such, because a dissolved question is the kind that comes back if nobody writes down that it dissolved.

The constraint this does not lift. The rebuild may evaluate expressions per person — that is what a cache warm is, and at the size in D-112 it is cheap. What stays forbidden is the failure domain/06 names as the one way to get this wrong: inside a check, an expression is compiled to a predicate on the person being asked, never materialized as a set — otherwise the nightly job is correct and every request still materializes the whole set instead of testing the one person in front of it. That clause used to end "…and every request still costs three thousand rows," and the number is gone on purpose: it was an estimate of the whole grant table, written three rounds before D-112 stated a size and said plainly that nothing in these documents had measured anything. It is in the same order of magnitude as that size, so nothing computed here changes — but a load-bearing number in a decision entry has to be one somebody counted, and this one was not.

See: F-6 and its invalidation table, which this replaces, and data-model/05 §10's cache section.

docs.title: D-112 — The system's scale is stated: hundreds of people, tens of registrants per event
docs.text:
Status: decided (from your answer) Date: refinement round 13 Closes: F-15, F-16, and the cost half of F-21

Decision. The system is specified against a stated size, and the size is now written down instead of being assumed differently by every page that reasons about cost: a few hundred people in the organization, a few dozen registrants on a typical event, a big camp on the order of two hundred. Every "is this cheap enough?" question this project has carried — the per-item preview, listing the grants that name an audience, an unbounded audience expansion, a nightly full rebuild — resolves at that size, and resolves only at that size.

Why. The pair chosen was "Hundreds of people, tens per event" — asked because two questions had stayed open for three rounds for the reason that nobody had stated a number, and a cost argument without a number is not an argument, it is a mood. Nothing in these documents measured this. No page carried a headcount before this entry, including the import pages that describe the legacy export row by row — so the number is stated, not observed, and it is the answer to a question rather than a finding. That is the whole reason the trigger below exists: a stated size is a load-bearing assumption with no evidence under it, which is exactly the shape this corpus has repeatedly had to come back and pin down.

What it closes. F-15: a preview that resolves an audience for one item is, at this size, evaluating a couple of hundred predicates — nobody will feel it, so the preview stays per-item and lazy (assumption 60) with no cap and no background job. F-16: listing the grants that name an audience is a scan over a small table with a handful of referencing rows each; pagination is a UI nicety, not a requirement, and D-103's assumption that listing is cheap is true, now on stated grounds. F-21's cost half: nothing bounds what an expression can cost, and at this size that is accepted rather than merely unaddressed. ~~D-111's nightly rebuild: people × 66 permission codes × a small number of items is a bounded, short job — "rebuild everything nightly" is affordable here specifically, and would be a different decision at ten thousand people, which is the honest reason it was chosen.~~ This half of the entry's affordability arithmetic was overtaken by D-114, which deleted the job whose cost was being estimated — so the answer to "is the rebuild affordable at this size?" is that there is no rebuild, and this entry's other four answers (preview, listing, expression cost, F-16) are the parts that stand. The method here is what matters and it is unchanged: a stated size is what makes a cost claim checkable, and a claim that stops applying says so.

The trigger, since a stated assumption without a trigger is just a guess with more confidence. If the population reaches a few thousand people, or a thousand registrants on one event, reopen F-15, F-16, F-7 and F-21 — in that order, because the preview is the first thing a user will feel and ~~the nightly rebuild the last~~ the nightly rebuild was last in that list and is now deleted; what sits in its place is nothing, so the order below it is unchanged and one shorter. Nothing in the design depends on the number, on purpose: the two rules that must survive any growth are the ones already written — a check compiles its expression to a predicate and never materializes the set, and a listing is paginated — so the system gets slow before it gets wrong, which is the only graceful failure this module can promise.

See: F-15 and F-16, both closed against this entry, and D-111.

docs.title: D-113 — The guardianship channel has no expression: GUARDIANS is not a selector
docs.text:
Status: decided (found while closing F-5) Date: refinement round 13 Closes: F-5's last live bullet, and with it the contradiction F-6 recorded about where a bound GUARDIANS could be written.

How it was found, since both the method and the mistake in it are useful. F-5 had one live bullet left — does GUARDIANS bind to the item? — and answering it needed every claim the corpus makes about that operand, so a read-only sweep went out to collect them. What came back was a confident report that the registry has no GUARDIANS row at all, fourteen rows and none of them guardianship. That was false: the row is the sixth in data-model/05 §8's table, takes_argument optional, argument_type person, and round 12's count of fourteen was a correct count of a table that includes it. The report also named a file that does not exist and a membership kind that does not, so its claims became leads and nothing more. What survived checking was better than what was claimed.

The real defect, which no count could have shown. The row's third column reads binds_to_item = "yes, person" — the one row in a table where that column means the item this grant sits on using it to mean a person, and its gloss promises a bound form: "Bound: the guardians of the person this item is about." That form cannot be written. F-6 found it independently while being closed: the save path refuses any bound operand on a unit-scope grant, and the only item scope that could host one is an event, which is the and the registry's own argument_type entry says the deciding sentence in passing — "person never was" a grant_scope_type — so a bound operand whose argument is a person can never satisfy the type match, at any scope, ever. The bound half of the row was illegal by the registry's own fields, while §12 was saying it may be "bound as GUARDIANS on a grant about that person". So the fourteenth row was a row whose advertised half no grant could hold, and the count agreed with itself the whole time.

Which is the opposite lesson to the one this entry was going to record. It was drafted as "a count is a good alarm" — an uncounted name pointing at a defect. Here the count was not the alarm, it was the camouflage: fourteen was arithmetically true of a table containing a row that could not be used as described, and every page that repeated "fourteen" was reinforcing a fiction with arithmetic. A registry checked against itself is not a registry checked against the rules that write it; that is D-104's finding again, one layer up, and it is why the checks that matter here are on the save path rather than on the row count.

Two things about this round's own conduct belong in the same section, because the entry is about method. The unsavability of the bound form was found twice, independently — once while closing F-6, once by an agent sweeping for this operand — which is the only reason I trusted it after this round's reports had already been wrong four times over. And this round wrote two false claims of its own while deleting the fiction: a quotation attributed to a page that does not contain it, and an invented role_holder "kind" whose enum I wrote out of nothing in a page I was editing to be tidy about D-100. The second was repaired by the agent that found it, in domain/04, and the correction says so on the page. The pattern across all six cases is one line: a confident claim with a line number is the most dangerous object in this repository, and the check is two seconds of grep. Which is worth more here than in most projects, because in a repo that is only documents, the grep is the test suite.

Decision.

  1. The registry drops to thirteen: the GUARDIANS row is deleted, and nothing replaces it. Neither the bound form it advertised nor the GUARDIANS(p) form it actually supported is a selector. Fourteen was a true count of a table with a row that should not have been in it — clause 4 is the argument for deleting the usable half along with the unusable one, and it is also the part of this entry that changed after the entry was written.
  2. The guardianship channel contains no expression, and never did since D-074. A check asks whether a live guardianship row links the person asking to the person the action is about, and reads right_level ∈ none | view | write off it — a lookup over a relationship, not a set that something resolves. guardianship_permission is that value's history: guardianship_id, right_level, valid_from, valid_to, changed_reason, changed_by. It has no grantee, no permission code, no audience and no expression column, so there was never anywhere in it for a selector to be seeded.
  3. What the corpus did was describe a channel with a selector's syntax. The word GUARDIANS appeared in tables and prose across domain/06, glossary, data-model/05, data-model/08-events, domain/07-events, appendix/erd, appendix/permission-catalog and open-questions — 31 occurrences outside this log, counted with grep rather than remembered, and deliberately not all of them live claims: several are struck quotations of the round that introduced the word, which stay struck and stay wrong in place because that is what keeping history means. The live ones all state a set where the model has a relationship. In a table listing seeded values the word meant "the guardians of this ward, via the guardianship channel", which is a true and useful thing to mean and the wrong notation to write, because D-107's test for an operand is a named registry row and no such row exists. Worse than a typo: a notation that parses reads as a decision someone made. The fix at each site is to name the channel and the value — a guardianship.right_level of view or write — which the same tables already do in their prose one line away, and which several of them do in the very next sentence.
  4. GUARDIANS(p) goes too, and this clause is the one that changed after the entry was first written. My first version removed the empty form and kept the parenthesised one as a narrowing operand — "the set of guardians of the named child", useful, I argued, for granting a ward's guardians something the three right_levels do not contain. That was wrong, and the reason is a fact about the channel I had described twice without drawing its consequence:

"True, GUARDIANS should not be selectable in the audience, guardians can perform ANY action (their read/write perms grant) on behalf of the child."

A guardian's authority is not a list of codes; it is a level over a child. write does not mean these six permissions — it means any action about this child. So an operand aiming a grant at a child's guardians offers, one code at a time, a subset of what those people already hold, and it can only ever be used about an item the channel would have reached anyway. It is not redundant by accident; it is the long way round to something the model grants outright. The reason it took a round to see is that GUARDIANS(p) looks like a perfectly ordinary narrowing operand — the ROLE(x) of family relationships — and the reason it is not one is that what it narrows is not a permission set but a relationship that carries its own authority, which nothing else in the registry is. That is the whole content of "a channel is not a selector"; clause 3 was only the half I had got.

What a real need looks like instead. "Send the parents of these six children the newsletter" is not a permission question — it is a set of people with a lifetime, which is what person_group is for (D-098): name the group, put the six guardians in it, aim the grant at GROUP(x). If the list must be derived rather than kept, the honest sentence is that this system stores a guardianship row and no query over it as an audience. A derived guardian list is a feature this system does not have — checked, not assumed: nothing anywhere in the model derives a set of people from the guardianship rows except the channel itself, not as a group's membership kind, not as an office's holder, in no table — and a missing feature is a question or a decision entry, not an operand nobody checked for. 5. binds_to_item keeps its meaning and loses its exhibit. D-102 introduced the column to settle a question about guardianship — it "records whose guardianship is being asked about, which is the only thing GUARDIANS ever needed and could not say" — and the thing it was introduced to classify turns out not to exist. The column is undamaged: ATTENDED, PLACED, CONFIRMED, ON_WAITLIST and ORGANIZERS are true because they cannot be evaluated without the event the grant sits on, and everything else is false because it can — five true rows, and this clause first printed four, having written the four attendance tiers and forgotten the roster, which is the same slip in the same entry that exists to record slips of exactly this kind: a count written from the shape of a sentence instead of from the table. ORGANIZERS is true on the registry's own row (yes, event) and is named in the same save-path rule in data-model/08-events.md. What changes is that the column is now justified by the event operands, which is a large and ordinary reason, instead of by one strange case that was never real. Where the confusion actually lived, because the two sentences are the evidence: data-model/05's registry row read Binds to item = "yes, person" — the one row in a table whose third column means the item this grant sits on, using the column to say something the column cannot say, and adding "Bound: the guardians of the person this item is about" — asserting a bound form the registry could not produce. data-model/08-events.md then counted it as the sixth attendance tier: "The sixth is GUARDIANS, which binds to the person an item is about rather than to an event." An operand with no seed row, listed among five that have rows, declared bound by a page while its own row used a column whose definition excludes it. Corrected at both sites: nothing guardian-shaped is bound to anything, because nothing guardian-shaped is an operand. What is left is four attendance tiers plus the organizer roster — five operands that bind, and no sixth, which is the naming data-model/08-events.md uses and the one this entry should have used the first time: "five tiers" and "five binding operands" are different claims wearing the same number, and only one of them is about the tiers.

The lesson is not about guardianship, it is about registries that are copied. A row can be wrong in a way no check catches, because the check compares the row's fields to each other and a field used to mean two things agrees with itself. binds_to_item needed a third value, or the sentence needed a different column, and neither happened for eleven rounds because the sentence was doing a good job in prose.

Why this is not merely a naming cleanup, and what class of error it is. SCHOOL was refused (D-108) for naming a fact no table stores. This is the same refusal one level up: a selector naming a mechanism the model implements somewhere else entirely. The grammar is closed and its vocabulary is checkable, so a word that parses without a row behind it is the only way to say something false in it — and this corpus has now been caught doing exactly that with a word nobody hand-typed, which means the vocabulary's open half was not the only place the check was needed. The general rule, for F-10's list: every selector name that appears in a document must be a selector_type row, and a check should be able to say so. That is a lint over documentation against a seed list, which is a strange thing to want until the fourteenth selector turns out to be a prose idiom.

What this costs, and why the answer is "less than it looked like from the clause above". Deleting the operand removes no capability, which is worth being precise about because the first draft of this entry thought otherwise and minted an open question for the loss. The worry was: nothing can now denote "whatever guardians the person this item is about has", so a guardian could never be given a permission wider than view/write over their ward. That worry presumes view/write is a ceiling on codes, and it is not — it is a ceiling on acts about that child. A guardian at write may already perform any action whose subject is their ward, which is a larger grant than any audience operand could have assembled from single codes, and smaller in exactly the direction that matters: it reaches no item that is not about the child. The channel is both wider and narrower than the operand it replaces, which is what makes it a channel. The residual case — guardians of this child should get at something that is not about the child — is not a permissions question and never was: it is a list of people, and lists are groups. So there is no F-24 and there is no new row — this sentence printed "the fifteenth row" while GUARDIANS still held slot fourteen, and at thirteen the next operand would be the fourteenth, so the number has been replaced by the words rather than corrected: an ordinal in this entry turned out to be a count in disguise, which is the collision this entry exists to stop — and no third binding kind is needed: binds_to_item keeps its two operands' worth of justification on the event side and never has to mean the subject.

Recorded because the pattern is the point: the open question I minted for this entry's supposed loss was emptied by the same ruling that caused it, ten minutes later, and an entry that had shipped in between would have put a real-sounding question in front of somebody who could not answer it. A question written against a capability should be checked against the channel that grants it before it is written down.

The seam this entry leaves open, and whose it is. D-109 says a selector that a rule may name is never deleted — it is deprecated, hidden, or disabled — and this entry deletes a row. The two are reconciled by a fact about dates, not by an exception: the row is unseeded in the same round it is criticized, in a spec that has shipped no release, so the set of stored expressions naming it is empty by construction. It would not have stayed empty. The argument-less form was unsavable on every scope (person never was a grant_scope_type), but the explicit GUARDIANS(p) form — legal arity, an argument type that column can hold, and no item-type check because an explicit argument binds to nothing — was savable, and one writer finding it in a dropdown would have made this deletion illegal. That is the whole of the reconciliation, so it is also a standing instruction: a deployment that does hold such a leaf must hide the row, rewrite the leaves, and only then unseed it, because deleting a row under a live leaf produces precisely the failing leaf D-109 retired deletion to prevent, and D-109 said the only remaining way to make one was a redacted person. If this entry is ever re-read as licence to delete a seeded operand, the reading is wrong: what licenses the deletion here is the emptiness of the set of grants that could name it, and that set has to be checked, not assumed.

See: D-074 (why there is no capability list to select from), D-085 (the view/write level on the live guardianship row, which is what actually serves the need — this line first named that thing OWN_WARD, a token invented in this line and found nowhere else in the corpus — the second name this entry manufactured after the F-24 question it disowns above, and the one that reached a reference, where it looks like a row someone seeded. It is named here in prose and linked from nowhere, which is the smallest honest repair: deleting the words would hide the invention, and leaving the link would keep it. D-102 (binds_to_item, whose definition this entry keeps and whose prose it corrects), D-107 (the test that caught it), D-108 (its neighbour: a selector naming a fact that is not stored, this one naming a mechanism that is stored elsewhere), D-098 (where a kept list of contact adults actually belongs), and F-5, whose last live bullet was exactly this question.

docs.title: Decision Log — Refinement round 14 (D-114)
docs.text:
The permission cache is deleted. A check resolves, a request memoizes, and the only cached thing is a compilation.

Refinement round 13 (D-109 … D-113) ← | All decisions

docs.title: D-114 — There is no permission cache: a check resolves, a request memoizes, and the only cached thing is a compilation
docs.text:
Status: decided (from your answer) Date: refinement round 14 Supersedes: D-111's storage half — the cache, the nightly rebuild, and both invalidation lists. **Its ruleset_version integer survives, with its bump set cut from the eight kinds of write D-111 named — six tables, the D-109 flag and a merge — to two tables (below), which is the part of it worth keeping. Amends rather than reopens: F-6's key dies with the cache it keyed; F-7's dissolution needs a new reason now that one of the two things it dissolved between has been deleted; D-112's "the rebuild is affordable here specifically" was a reason for choosing D-111 and is retired, while its population figure and its trigger both stand.

Decision. No permission answer is ever stored. permission_cache is deleted from the schema, and with it the key (person_id, permission_code, scope_type, scope_id, at_bucket), the at_bucket truncation, the nightly full rebuild, and the two lists that decided what bumps a version. Three things do the work the cache was supposed to do:

  1. A compiled expression is cached. Parse once, resolve operand kinds once, emit the parameterized predicate once — keyed by the expression's root plus ruleset_version, holding no person and no item, because both arrive as parameters. This is exactly why a compilation survives across people and an answer cannot: nothing in it depends on whom or where it is asked about.
  2. A request memoizes. One indexed read fetches the checked person's live grant rows; every code, item and date in that request is evaluated against them in memory. Within the same request, a named operand that recurs (ROLE(leader), GROUP(cubs)) is resolved once. Lifetime is the request, so there is no invalidation policy for it and no staleness window at all.
  3. The bulk screens batch. can_many(person, codes[], item?) answers a screen's worth of affordances from one resolution, and which_of(people[], code, item) answers a list's worth from one pass. The per-item preview (F-15) and the permissions tab (D-109) are written against these, not against a loop of single checks.

Named rosters may still be cached across requests, keyed by the name — ROLE(x) over role_holder, GROUP(x) over person_group_member. Two conditions, and they are the whole difference from what is deleted: the key is the thing the write touches, so invalidation is local to the row that changed and never global; and the cache holds the dated rows, or the set with its validity ranges, never the set as of today, so the checked date is still applied at check time and a period ending at midnight needs no job to be seen. A roster is also named and addressable — it is a row someone maintains and can point at — which an answer never was. And a roster is only what those two are. MEMBERS is not one: it is not a row anybody writes but the read predicate over membership, whose dated rows the 1 January sweep rewrites for every member at once, so caching it would put that bulk event straight back on the invalidation list this entry deletes (03-membership.md §6). ORGANIZERS is not one either, and not for want of holder rows — it has them — but because it is bound to an item (D-102), so its key would name an event and the cache would be a stored answer to "who was at this one", which is what D-102 refused to make a permanent set. Of the five operands that bind to an item none is a roster; of the seeded selectors only ROLE and GROUP name a holder table that a person maintains by name. That is the whole extension of the exception, and it is closed rather than open-ended.

Why the design as written was ineffective, in the order the numbers say it. The key's space at D-112's stated size is a few hundred people × 66 codes, order tens of thousands of entries, and a full rebuild of that is one short job — so the cache was saving a thing whose replacement costs about as much as it does. Worse, the bump set included person_group_member and role_holder, which are the two most ordinary writes in this organization — a child joins the Thursday group, an office hands over at camp — so every one of them dropped the entire cache, and the effective hit rate was time since the last group edit in a place where group edits never stop. A cache whose invalidation is free and total is one step from no cache, and D-111 had already made it free.

The decisive finding is not the hit rate; it is that the boundary was wrong in the sensitive direction. §8 said "the line between those two lists is the entire safety property", and the lists were: access_grant, audience_operand, guardianship_permission, permission, role_holder, person_group_member, the D-109 flag, and a merge or unmerge. membership is on neither list as a table whose writes matter. But membership.terminate ⛔ is a real code in the catalog, held by safeguarding_officer, whose stated reason is "whoever finds the problem and whoever ends a membership over it are the same person, and nobody else". So an officer terminates a member, MEMBERS shrinks, nothing rebuilds, and every cached true behind MEMBERS * … stands until midnight. One tier lower and the same shape: event_registration was declared not a ruleset write, so a family cancelling a place left the child inside PLACED and CONFIRMED until the nightly job. D-111's defence was "what waits for the night is what nobody does: an expiry arriving on its own" — and a termination and a cancellation are precisely things people do, one of them the most safeguarding-shaped act in the catalog.

The corpus had warned about exactly this, in the other file. data-model/03-membership.md §6, "What still costs, unchanged by the move", carried as its first bullet: "The permission cache must be invalidated on every membership transition — including the yearly expiry sweep, which is a bulk event touching every member at once. … The cache design has to be built for this from the start; retrofitting it is where the bugs will be." That sentence was written three rounds before D-111 drew the two lists, in the module that has the coupling, and the lists were drawn in the module that owns the cache — which is the whole failure in one sentence: a requirement stated where the dependency is felt is not read by the page that has to satisfy it. The prophecy was right about the mechanism and about the size of the hole. This entry deletes both the cache and the bullet's obligation, which is the only way the two files can now be made to agree.

How this entry's own finding got here, because the route matters more than the finding. The first version asserted that membership appeared in the caching discussion with "zero occurrences in the corpus" — and that was true, checked two ways: no file names membership beside the ruleset boundary, and no file describes a membership transition as rebuilding anything. What is not true is how nearly it was overwritten: a report reached me during this round asserting the claim false and supplying a quotation to a page, a sentence beginning "the change lands in the cache's one-night staleness window … that is the designed behaviour of the cache … not an oversight". That quotation does not exist anywhere in this repository. It was written into two files before the grep that should have preceded it was run; the grep found nothing, and both insertions came out. The lesson has two halves, and the second is the one that stung. (i) Grep the claim, not the phrasing — the requirement here is real and it hides behind the words "must be invalidated", not behind "ruleset", so a narrow grep nearly talked me out of a correct finding. (ii) A correction arriving from anywhere — an agent, a diff, a quotation with a line number — is a claim, and the check is the same two seconds it always was. A report that flatters its reader by catching the reader's error is the version of this that gets through, because the temptation is to accept it without looking.

The general form, which is why editing the list was never the fix. A correct invalidation set is every table any operand can read transitively: membership, role_holder, person_group_member, event_registration, event_organizer, the person row's birth date and status, the guardianship rows, plus the rule tables. That is not a policy boundary, it is the read path, and a hand-maintained copy of the read path is a second source of truth about what an expression means — D-081's class and D-104's in one object: a list whose membership contradicts the operands' read set is a fiction, and it had already contradicted it in the one place where being wrong is worst. Completing the list would make the version bump on nearly every write, which is this entry's answer with extra machinery bolted on first.

What D-111 actually got wrong, said precisely enough to be useful. It did not make an error inside its own frame; it never questioned the object that created the problem. Given a stored answer, "whom does this change reach?" is unanswerable without evaluating, so a global version was the right answer — and the sentence that turned the boundary into the safety property was written by this round, one round ago, into four files, and no check can read a list like that. ruleset_version was sound and is kept. What is retracted is the claim that the two lists were a safety property at all: a safety property that has to be re-derived from the grammar every time an operand is added is a chore with a reassuring name.

The version integer, narrowed rather than deleted, and the shrink is the point. A compilation depends on an expression's shape and on the seeded vocabulary and nothing else, so the bump set is audience_operand and selector_type — two tables, down from the eight kinds of write D-111 named: six tables, the D-109 flag and a merge. access_grant drops out because grants are not compiled: a check reads the person's live grant rows, so adding, editing or revoking one changes what that read returns and leaves nothing stale to drop, and a grant created together with a new audience is an audience_operand write, which stays in the set; the deprecated | hidden | disabled flag drops out because a state is not compiled in — resolution consults it live, once per request, memoized — which is also what makes disabled still mean now, by reading the flag rather than by dropping the world; guardianship_permission drops out because the channel is read live; role_holder, person_group_member and a person merge drop out because they move rosters and grant rows, which are read live or invalidated locally. Concretely: adding a child to a group, which used to drop the whole cache, now drops nothing. And because a compilation is finite and enumerable over the audience tree, "an edit to a shared audience invalidates everything" becomes "it invalidates the compilations that embed it", which is a bounded walk over rows that already exist, and the direction is worth stating rather than glossing: the save path walks the other way. Cycle refusal walks forward from the tree being saved, while invalidation needs the reverse direction — the one the delete-refusal check already runs when it asks whether a live grant, or a live audience reachable from one through any number of AUDIENCE leaves, names the audience being edited (D-103, and data-model/05 §The expression tree with §11's check 15). So it is a new use of a direction the design already needs, not a free ride on a query that already runs, and the listing's cost is registered as unverified at any size in data-model/05 §13 — this entry inherits that registration instead of resolving it, which is the honest form of "bounded". The claim that survives all of this is the narrow one, and it is the one that mattered: the fan-out that defeated F-6 was only hard because it fanned out to people. The name ruleset_version stays and its meaning is redefined here, in place, because a term whose scope just narrowed by an order of magnitude will be re-inflated by the next reader otherwise: "ruleset" now means the text of the rules, not anything an expression can read.

What is gained, and it is more than the deletion. "The safeguarding case is immediate" stops being a property of a list and becomes a property of the read path: a termination, a revoke, a cancellation or a closed period is visible on the next check, with no job in between and nothing to remember to mark as a ruleset write. And D-107's accepted drift ceases to exist. What D-107 waived was the calendar moving an answer between rebuilds — a birthday crossing OLDER(n), a period reaching its own valid_to — and D-111's own residual list widened that to the 1 January sweep and the attendance writes behind the event tiers, which is how a schedule ends up covering things that are not the calendar at all. Under live resolution every one of them moves the answer at the instant it happens, so the ruling stands and its mechanism is no longer needed: "up to one night stale" is deleted from this corpus, and the sentence that survives is "IT IS FINE" with nothing left for it to be fine about. A ruling that turns out to be unnecessary is a better outcome than a ruling that had to be defended.

What may never be stored again — invariant 19, TIME-BOMB: no row, table or field may map a person (or a person-and-code, or a person-and-item) to a permission answer. Enforcement is first structural, which is the best kind this corpus has: the schema has nowhere to put one, since the only table that could hold it was just deleted. The residue is honest and named — a future implementer adding a cache is stopped by this entry and by review, not by a constraint, so for them it is a convention, not a guard (D-081). If a cache is ever added back it must arrive as a decision entry, and it must carry three things this one lacked: a per-person invalidation handle alongside the global one, an explicit statement of which tables it watches, and that statement derived from the operand registry rather than from a list of ideas — on pain of this entry repeating one round later with a different table in the hole.

Cost, stated as arithmetic and not as a measurement. A check is one indexed read of the person's live grant rows — a few dozen rows at the stated size — plus, per expression, a handful of indexed point lookups against the operand tables. The cost that made a cache look necessary was never this arithmetic; it was the N+1 across a screen, and the memo and can_many remove that directly, so the deleted cache and the replacement differ mostly in when the work happens. What is genuinely lost: a nightly job used to pre-pay the expensive screens, so the per-item preview, the tab and the "who holds this" listing now do their work on open. At the stated size that is affordable, and D-109 already ruled the tab is computed when opened — that ruling now has no fallback, which is worth recording as a dependency rather than as a risk. D-112's trigger stands, and its reopen answer is now named instead of vague: at a few thousand people, materialize effective_permission per person and call it that — a real materialization with a per-person invalidation handle and a stated staleness window, which is the honest shape of the object being deleted here.

The second loss is the one nobody was counting, and it lands on a control that was already the weakest kind. Cached answers were the accidental mitigation for unbounded expression size: a wide expansion got paid once per person per night, so the cost of a thousand-person EVERYONE stopped being anybody's problem between rebuilds. D-105 deleted the depth bound and refused to mint a size bound in its place, and data-model/05 §The cost of composition registered what replaced the retired invariant — a standing report of the widest and deepest audiences and their cost per check, which is a convention, not a guard in D-081's vocabulary. Deleting the answer cache moves load onto that convention: after this entry an expansion is paid per check, memoized inside a request and cached nowhere wider. This does not reopen D-105's ruling; it changes what the ruling costs, and the honest record is that round 14 made the report this module is worst at reading carry slightly more. It is written into that bullet rather than softened here.

See: D-111 (what this keeps and what it retires), D-107 (the ruling whose mechanism this removes), D-110 (why nothing here needed a stored answer for the record's sake), F-6 and F-7 (both amended, neither reopened), D-102 and D-103 (the binding the roster exception respects, and the walk whose direction the narrowed bump set needs), D-105 (the ruling whose cost this changes without reopening it), and D-081 — a rule that outlives its mechanism must say who enforces it now, and this entry deleted the mechanism on purpose and wrote the answer down. The invariant lives in data-model/05 §11 as check 19, and the read path it protects is §10 of the same page. And the finding that decided it came from another module's file (data-model/03-membership.md §6), which is where a reader should look for the shape of this failure again.

docs.title: Domain Overview
docs.text: What the organization is, who interacts with the system, and how the core lifecycles flow. Read ../glossary.md first — this document uses its terms strictly.

docs.title: 1. The organization
docs.text:
A youth organization (Scout-like: uniformed groups, trained adult leadership, camps and weekly meetings) with:

  • Child members — youth participants, who join one another in groups.
  • Adult members — counselors and leaders who run the programs, hold offices, and put people into groups.
  • Caretakers — parents and legal guardians of child members. They may or may not be members themselves.
  • Non-member supporters — people who interact with the organization (donors, volunteers, alumni) without holding a membership.

"Child" and "adult" are how the organization talks about people. They are not two kinds of membership: there is one membership type and it is ageless, so "is this person a child?" is a question about person.birth_date and the date being asked about (§2). Only three things downstream key off the difference: guardianship, eligibility an organizer writes for one event, and the mirroring rule for messages.

The system models no internal structure of the organization. There is one unit, it is a scope rather than a row, and the nested bodies the organization has been reorganized into over four decades are not stored, not versioned and not imported — an absence decided on purpose, whose cost is written down in D-097. What remains of "the inside of the organization" is groups: named sets of people with a lifetime, in 04-organization-structure.md. A reader arriving expecting a hierarchy should learn that here, on the first page, because the absence changes every later answer about scope.

docs.title: 2. Actors
docs.text:
The system distinguishes actors by what they can do, not by what they are. The full treatment is in 02-actors.md; the summary:

Actor Has account? Has membership? Can do Anonymous visitor no no see public info, submit a registration or a membership request Registered person yes no maintain own profile, submit/renew a request, view own history Member yes yes own profile, event signups, own history Caretaker yes maybe view and act on their dependents — only as the guardianship row allows Staff / registrar yes maybe organization-wide administrative permissions Historical record no a bounded period, if the export states one nothing. Data only, never a login.

A minor is not an actor row. One row above is a member, and whether that member is a minor today is person.birth_date against the date of the check — a fact about a person that changes on its own, never a kind of account. What a minor genuinely cannot do alone is a guardianship question (02-actors.md).

Imported rows create person rows with no account, and import must never be blocked by a "users must have email addresses" rule. They also create membership rows: bounded ones, both ends dated, only for the periods the people export states, data_confidence = 'low', marked with the batch that wrote them (D-093). An imported period is never open-ended and never inferred from presence — an open membership satisfies is_current_member(), so inferring one would make every 1998 attendee a current member today. No sub-unit row is ever imported, because neither export names a sub-unit (03-identity-and-legacy.md §7).

docs.title: 3. The three lifecycles
docs.text: Almost everything in the system is one of three multi-step processes. They are separate because they succeed and fail independently: you can register without applying, apply without being accepted, be accepted without paying, and pay without ever joining a group.

docs.title: 3.1 Account lifecycle
docs.text:
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
                  │                                             │
 (none) ──register──> pending_verification ──verify──> active ──┴──> suspended
                                                            │              │
                                                            └──> closed <──┘

An account is about authentication only. It says "this person can log in". It says nothing about membership. A person can hold a verified, active account for years and never become a member — a parent who only ever manages their child is exactly this case.

One gate the arrows do not draw: an account may not reach active while an unresolved identity_hypothesis names its person, which is what a sign-up that strong-matches someone who already exists runs into (D-089). Verification is necessary and not sufficient; a human decision is the second condition. Because that makes a stalled queue a person who cannot log in, a hypothesis that blocks activation is age-checked and alerts. One live account per person is the rule doing the underlying work (02-actors.md §3).

docs.title: 3.2 Membership lifecycle
docs.text:
(none)
   │
   ├─ request submitted ──> under_review ──accept──> approved ──payment confirmed──> active member
   │                             │                                                    │
   │                             └──reject──> rejected                                 │
   │                                                                                   │
   │                                     ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
   │                                     ├──> lapsed (fee expired at the yearly date)   │
   │                                     ├──> terminated (cause, with reason)          │
   │                                     └──> suspended (temporary hold)               │
   │                                                                                   │
   │      ┌──────────────── renewal (no new application) ────────────────────────────┘
   │      │        inside the renewal window → the new period opens at the expiry date
   │      │        after it                  → the new period opens at the payment date
   │      ▼
   │   active member again
   │
   └──────────────────────── re-apply ─────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Every transition creates or closes a row; nothing is overwritten. A person who was a member 1990–2010 and again from 2024 has two membership rows, and the gap is visible as data rather than inferred from a date.

Two properties of the lapse are worth naming before the detail. There is no completed status: nothing ages out of a membership, so there is no state for having finished one. And the lapse happens to everyone at once, on a fixed date — the yearly expiry — which is why the renewal path matters more than the word "grace" suggests (D-040).

Detailed in 05-membership-lifecycle.md.

docs.title: 3.3 Authorization lifecycle
docs.text:
(none) ──grant──> active ──end date reached / period closed──> inactive
                     │
                     └──delegate──> delegated grant (with end date, provenance recorded)

Every grant has a start, an end, a granter, and a reason. Nothing is permanent by default and nothing is revoked by deletion — closing a period is the act, and the row stays. Detailed in 06-authorization-model.md.

docs.title: 4. The relationships between people
docs.text:
Four relationships, deliberately not merged:

Relationship Direction Example Grants access? Guardianship guardian → dependent parent → child No by itself — only the right_level (none / view / write) carried on the live guardianship row is authority, and that row is the whole of it (D-074). Membership member → the organization anyone → the unit No. Being in a group person → group child → the Thursday group No — a person_group_member row is a dated roster entry. Holding an office person → role adult → counselors No — a role_holder row says who holds it, and an office confers nothing by being held.

Being a member and being in a group are two rows, not one. A person is a member of the organization and on a group's roster: different facts, different lifetimes, and different guards on who may change them — which is why someone who stops attending on Thursdays is still a paid-up member, and someone who is paid up may turn up to nothing. The two rows are edited by different people for different reasons, which is the whole case for keeping them apart.

The recurring theme: participation is not authority. A person can be deeply involved — a parent of three members, a twenty-year veteran, the founder of a group — and still have no administrative access. Access comes only from an explicit grant. This separation is what makes the permission system auditable, and what prevents the classic failure where a relationship ends (custody changes, a leader steps down) and access silently persists.

docs.title: The counselor who is also a parent
docs.text:
This case is not special:

  • One person row.
  • One open membership, of the one membership type, member — the same shape as the child they lead.
  • One role_holder row: they hold the office counselors over a dated period.
  • A person_group_member row or two, dated, for the groups they actually turn up to.
  • Two guardianship rows (to their own children), each carrying its own right level.
  • Whatever access_grant rows somebody wrote whose grantee names them — as ROLE(counselors), or MEMBERS * ROLE(counselors) where membership is required of the holder.
  • No row of its own for "is a counselor". The role_holder row is all of it.

There is no counselor membership type, and being a counselor is an office held for a period — not a kind of membership, and not a grade of person. This person's membership is identical to that of the child they lead, which is exactly the point.

Their grants reach the unit's members, which is the whole organization: there is no smaller body to scope inside, so a unit-scope grant is the broadest thing a person can hold. Their guardianship reaches their own children through a different channel entirely — entered by the shape of the request (subject ≠ actor) rather than by any permission they were given (D-079), and capped by the right level that row records. Being a leader does not give them access to other people's children's records, and the reason is mechanical: no rule could imply it, so the access exists as rows or not at all.

That is a safety property, not a convenience. Child-protection practice requires that a leader's access to minors' personal data be bounded by their function, and two properties carry it here: an office, a roster, a membership and a guardianship each confer nothing by being what they are (D-100), and a grant is one code, one scope, one effect per row (D-099), so "what exactly does this person have over minors?" is answered by reading rows rather than by evaluating a rank. What the design does not do is guarantee that the reach was written by the body it governs — see rule 5 in the overview. The boundary is enforceable and reportable; who is obliged to read the report is a convention, not a guard.

docs.title: 5. Multiplicity, in both directions
docs.text:
Specified directly: one parent can manage multiple children; multiple children can be managed by the same parent. The model generalizes both:

  • One guardian → many dependents (many guardianship rows).
  • Many guardians → one dependent (both parents, stepparents, legal guardians — no assumption that a child has exactly two, or exactly one).
  • A guardian's authority is per-dependent, so a parent can hold write for one child and view only for another — a realistic custody arrangement.

The same person can be a guardian of someone and a dependent of someone else: the relation is a general graph, not a two-level hierarchy. This costs nothing to allow and avoids a rewrite when a member's sibling needs a guardian and the member is the one who has them.

docs.title: 6. The four decades of history
docs.text:
This is the constraint that most shapes the schema.

The system must answer, correctly and indefinitely:

  • "Was this person a member when they attended that camp in 2003?"
  • "This person registered in 2026 claiming they were a member in the 90s — is that true?"
  • "Who was on this group's roster on 1 June 1998?" — if somebody recorded the roster; the import supplies no group history.

It must not answer, and does not try to:

  • "Who was in Pack 12 on 1 June 1998?" and "what was that unit called in 2001, and what is its successor today?" There are no units, no nesting and no successor relations to traverse.

Consequences, which the data model implements:

  1. Everything temporal is a period, never a boolean or a single date.
  2. Nothing is hard-deleted, except by three named acts, each somebody's decision rather than a cleanup job. Erasing a person redacts their values wherever they were copied, including in the audit payload, immediately and at any age. Payload reduction empties an audit row's values 24 months after they were written and leaves the row standing, so the trail keeps answering who changed this, when, and were they allowed to and stops answering and to what (D-088). Reverting an import batch removes the rows that batch created. Reduction is not redaction: one answers to a person and is absolute, the other answers to a calendar and is bounded. The accounting skeleton — membership, fees, payments — is deliberately outside all three and kept indefinitely as the organization's own history. Assumption: that this "forever" has a legal basis is exactly what this document cannot establish for itself; the claim is recorded as an assumption awaiting review, not as settled law.
  3. People's names change, so a name is a child-table row with a validity period and never a column that gets overwritten. A group's name is a column, and nothing replaces the deleted name-history table: a rename edits it and the old name is gone. What survives a rename is the identity beneath it, because grants and expressions store a kind and an id, never a name.
  4. Imported data is low-confidence. The people export carries a name, a birth date, and the period each person was a member of the organization. Where an export also carries the organization's legacy member number — the number its paper records are keyed on — that number is imported verbatim into person_identifier under the legacy scheme, is never reissued, and makes a match exact rather than probable: same number, same person. Every other identity claim the import makes is a proposal a human confirms. See 03-identity-and-legacy.md.

docs.title: 7. What this design does not decide yet
docs.text:
Referenced by the schema but not designed, pending your specification:

  • Fees and payments — a provisional shape exists in ../data-model/07-finance.md because membership activation depends on it. Expect to rewrite it.
  • Communication — its shape is decided (direct by default, broadcast an ordinary scoped permission, the recipient chooses the channel, a minor's guardians get a mirror of a direct message), and its codes are in the catalog. There is no message or message_recipient table yet, and no design for templates, opt-out granularity, retention or moderation.
  • Notifications — the renewal window made them dated rather than status-driven, which is a design note, not a design.
  • Documents, reporting, API and UI.

docs.text:

  • Accounts and registration → 02-actors.md
  • Historical data → 03-identity-and-legacy.md
  • What the system knows about a person → 08-person-data.md
  • Groups, offices and the unit → 04-organization-structure.md

docs.title: Actors, Accounts, and Self-Registration
docs.text: How a human being gets into the system, what an account is (and is not), and why registration is deliberately separate from membership.

docs.title: 1. The core separation
docs.text:
person ─────────── the human being. Exists even with no account and no membership.
     │
     ├── account ──── the ability to log in. Optional. Zero or more per person over time, one live.
     │
     └── membership ─ the state of being a member. Optional. Zero or more periods.

These are three independent things. Any combination is legal:

State Example person, no account, no membership 1994 roster entry imported from paper. person, account, no membership A parent who registered to manage their child. person, account, membership An active member. person, no account, membership An adult member who never uses the system; staff manage them. person, account, lapsed membership Someone who let their membership lapse but still logs in.

The schema must not reject any of these. In particular there must be no requirement that a person has an email address, or that a member has an account — otherwise the historical import is impossible.

docs.title: 2. Who registers, and why
docs.text:
People register on their own to get access to the system; a person becomes a member only by requesting a membership, being accepted, and paying the yearly fee. So registration produces an account, not a membership. The person is then a registered non-member — able to log in, maintain their profile, view their own history, and submit a membership request.

The split gives the system a clean place to hang capabilities that must work before membership exists:

  • A caretaker registering to manage a child before deciding whether to join themselves.
  • An adult applying to become a counselor, who needs to fill in an application first.
  • A returning member from the 90s reconnecting to their history.

docs.title: Registration paths
docs.text: Path Actor Result Self-registration adult, or a minor with guardian involvement person + account Registration on behalf caretaker registers a minor who has no account person (child) + guardianship Staff-created account registrar creates one for an adult who is not self-sufficient with computers person + account, flagged created_by_staff Legacy import no account created person only, record_origin = 'legacy_import' Self-registration claiming history adult registers and asserts a past membership person + account + identity_hypothesis Sign-up colliding with an existing person adult signs up again through an address the system did not know, and strong-matches someone who already exists person + account, both held at pending_verification, + identity_hypothesis — and no merge, no link, no activation. The address typed survives as the credential it was offered as, and the hypothesis is what holds the account out of active (§3)

docs.title: Minor registration — the consent problem
docs.text: Assumption: a minor may not create an account unattended. The schema supports requiring a guardian's confirmation before a minor's account becomes usable, via account.guardian_consent_at. See ../open-questions.md for the age threshold and whether consent is required at all in your jurisdiction.

docs.title: 3. Account state machine
docs.text:
Status Meaning pending_verification Registered; email/phone not yet confirmed. Minimal capabilities. active Normal. suspended Temporarily blocked (security, disciplinary). Membership unaffected. closed Voluntarily or administratively closed. Retained for audit; login refused.

Two deliberate choices:

  • Suspending an account does not suspend a membership. They are separate lifecycles; a person can be an active member with a suspended account (they'd interact by phone).
  • Closing an account does not delete the person or their history. The account row is closed and retained. person and all membership rows are untouched.

And a gate this table cannot express. active has a second condition beyond verification: an account may not reach it while an unresolved identity_hypothesis names its person. One live account per person is the rule doing the underlying work — uniqueness says a person may not hold two live accounts, and the gate says the second arrival waits for a human rather than being merged into the first or quietly linked to it.

Why a human, and not an automatic link: a merge made by machine turns one person's false positive into one person's record becoming another's. Making a queue state block a login buys two obligations, and both are checks rather than intentions:

  • A hypothesis that is blocking an account is age-checked, and it alerts. A queue that stalls is not a data-quality problem with no victim you can name: it is a specific person who cannot log in, whose only remaining channel is to telephone someone.
  • The message the person sees confirms nothing. Not that the name matched, not that the birth date did, not that anyone by that name exists — because a sign-up form that can answer "yes, that person exists" is an existence oracle, and this system's roster is children.

The trigger is a strong match only — exact legacy member number, or exact birth date together with a normalised name. The scored band below that raises nothing at sign-up: blocking a stranger's registration on a fuzzy score is the failure this rule would most deserve (03-identity-and-legacy.md §4).

Why: D-089.

docs.title: Credentials
docs.text:
account holds authentication material. Two rules worth fixing now:

  1. The password hash lives in account_credential, not in account. This leaves room for multiple authentication methods (password, passkey, OAuth via a national Scout identity provider, staff-issued one-time links) without restructuring.
  2. Never share an account between a parent and a child. The temptation is real — "the parent will just log in as the kid" — but it destroys attributability. The correct mechanism is acting on behalf, which records who acted and as whom. An account shared between people makes every audit entry worthless, and in a youth organization the audit trail is the point.

docs.title: 4. Contact points and identifiers
docs.text:
A person's email, phone and address are rows, not columns. Each row carries its type, its purpose, its value, whether it is the primary one for that type and purpose, when it was verified, and the period it applied for.

Why not just person.email:

  • People have several emails (personal, school, work) and which one is primary changes.
  • A caretaker's contact details are often the effective contact for a child; the system needs both the child's own contact and the adult's.
  • Addresses change, and history is kept: an address row with a validity period answers "where did this member live in 2003?", which a column cannot.
  • Changing an email must not lose the old one, because historical records may reference it.

Purpose is the field that makes this useful operationally: login, membership, emergency, billing, guardian_contact. A person can have one address for billing and another for emergency contact, and the permission system can treat them differently — emergency contacts are visible to whoever holds the roster read on that camp; billing details are not.

docs.title: External identifiers
docs.text:
One row per identifier held against a person: a scheme, a value, and when it was verified if it ever was. (scheme, value) is unique among the identifiers that are still current — a superseded number may be reused, a current one may not be shared.

Identifiers issued outside the system belong here: a national Scout registration number, a government ID, an old membership card number from a previous system, a school ID. Keeping these separate from contact points is what gives the legacy import somewhere to put the old system's member numbers — which is precisely what makes reconnecting 1990–2010 members possible. See 03-identity-and-legacy.md.

docs.title: 5. Acting on behalf
docs.text:
Both read and write access for a caretaker are explicit:

  • A guardianship row establishes the relationship.
  • That row carries one right — none, view, or write. Being the parent implies nothing; a row at none grants literally nothing.

The right is one value, not a capability list, compared against permission.right_kind ∈ read | write: none covers nothing, view covers the codes marked read, write covers both. A court order that lets one parent register the child for events but not read the rest of the record cannot be written, and neither can "roster visibility and nothing else": a guardian at view reads the child's record whole, because the record has no compartment inside it to be excepted from (D-074, D-083). What the right is, and keeps: explicit, dated, revocable, audited — one deliberate value per row rather than an inference from who someone is.

write is not a license over the organization. The ceiling is the channel, not a rank: the guardianship channel is entered only when the check is about somebody other than the actor, so the widest right in the system reaches this child's record and cannot reach a roster, a fee schedule or another family — those checks are not about the child and the channel is never asked (D-079). Authority is per row, so a guardian of one child sees nothing of another's. A deny still refuses a guardian holding write, absolutely and regardless of scope — what is unavailable is a narrow deny, not the ability to say no. There is no per-resource admin wildcard either; a role that needs broad reach lists what it grants (D-068).

History is kept: every change of the value is a new guardianship_permission row, and the value on the guardianship row is always the open one's.

How a check resolves. A check about a dependent is evaluated against the guardianship row for the (guardian, dependent) pair and the right level it holds, not against roles. This keeps the two authority channels distinct:

  • Grants answer "what may this person do in the organization?"
  • Guardianship answers "what may this person do regarding this child?"

An office confers nothing by being held (D-100), so holding one gives nobody a guardian's right over a child and leadership has no channel of its own: a leader reaches data the way every other non-guardian does, through grants. If the organization needs its leaders to see a camper's emergency contacts, that is said, as a grant of person.view, and the scope chosen is the entire decision — every member of the organization or the people on one event, with nothing between them (D-097), and person.view has no narrower cousin to reach for if the first one turns out to feel like what it is (08-person-data.md). Audited either way; never through a fictional guardianship.

docs.title: Recording acts on behalf
docs.text:
Every operation performed on behalf of another person writes to access_log with both parties: actor_person_id is the parent, subject_person_id is the child, and on_behalf records that the actor acted for the subject rather than as themselves.

This is not optional bookkeeping. When a parent changes a child's address or registers them for a camp, the record must show that the parent did it, not the child. Without this, the audit trail falsely attributes the parent's actions to the child.

docs.title: 6. Effective contact for a minor
docs.text:
A recurring operational need: "who do we call about this child?" The answer is usually a guardian, but not always the same one, and not always the one with the most permissions.

Resolve it as three conditions on guardianship, applied in this order: the row's dependent is this child; the row is still open today, meaning valid_to is absent or later than today — a guardianship that has ended is not an answer, so the date is checked on the row rather than assumed; and is_primary_contact is set. The answer is the contact points of those guardians whose purpose is emergency.
