is_primary_contact on guardianship is separate from the guardian's right level on purpose: a guardian with no system access at all can still be the emergency contact. Do not require login capability to be reachable in an emergency.

docs.title: 7. Open issues
docs.text:
• Minimum age to hold an account; whether guardian consent is legally required.
  • Whether staff-created accounts are allowed for children, or only adults.

All tracked in ../open-questions.md.

Decisions behind this page: D-068, D-074, D-079, D-083, D-089, D-097, D-099, D-100.

docs.title: Identity Resolution and Legacy Data
docs.text:
How the system decides that two records describe the same human, and how four decades of paper and spreadsheet history gets brought in without corrupting live data.

This is the highest-risk area of the project. Get it wrong and either the history is unusable, or worse, two people's records get merged and you leak one member's data to another. The design below is deliberately conservative.

docs.title: 1. Why this is hard
docs.text:
A 1994 row has: a name, maybe a birth date, the period that person was a member, and, on most rows, a legacy member number (D-090), with free text — an address, remarks — in columns beside it. None of it can log in: the number keys the organization's paper, not a session, and it is missing from precisely the rows that most need the heuristics below — those predating the numbering, and those where it was written illegibly. Meanwhile:

  • Names change (marriage, adoption, correction of a misspelling).
  • Names repeat. In a youth organization spanning decades, "Jan Novák" is many people.
  • Diacritics and transliterations vary across decades of manual entry (Novák / Novak).
  • Birth dates are often wrong by a digit, or recorded as year-only.
  • The same human appears in multiple rosters under slightly different spellings.

So: automatic matching will produce both false positives and false negatives. False positive (two people merged) is a privacy incident. False negative (one person split) is a data-quality annoyance. The design must therefore bias hard toward false negatives — never merge on a guess.

This document is about one half of a person. Everything it resolves is identity: the fields that make a row a particular human — names, birth date, the account, contact points, issued identifiers. Everything the organization records about that human beyond those is descriptive data, and it is deliberately absent from every table below: no descriptive value is a match signal, and none may become one. A clothing size or a dietary habit identifies nobody, and making matching depend on one would make the reliability of a person's history depend on what the organization happened to collect about them (08-person-data.md, D-085). The line between the two halves is drawn by what a machine may act on without a human, not by how delicate a fact feels; the test is stated in 08-person-data.md.

docs.title: 2. The three record classes
docs.text:
Every person row carries record_origin:

Origin Meaning Confidence Has account? self_registered A human created this by registering high yes staff_created A registrar entered this person high maybe legacy_import Imported from historical records low no

Legacy-imported people are provisional. They are fully queryable — a member who left in 1998 is findable by name and birth date — but they are marked as unverified, they cannot be logged into, and they are the only rows eligible to be absorbed by a merge.

Rule: a merge always absorbs the lower-confidence row into the higher-confidence one. An import can never overwrite a self-registered person's data.

docs.title: 3. Identity hypotheses, not merges
docs.text:
The core mechanism. An identity hypothesis is a proposal that two person rows are the same human. It is a first-class table row, with a confidence score, evidence, a status, and a human decision.

The row holds the pair as person_a_id and person_b_id, stored in one order: person_a_id names the lower id, and the two are never the same person — a pair has one canonical spelling rather than two.

confidence is the matcher's score between 0 and 1; match_signals records which fields agreed and how strongly, which is what a reviewer reads to see why it was proposed. status is one of proposed, needs_review, confirmed, rejected, superseded. proposed_by says where the proposal came from — import_job, match_job (the nightly batch matcher), person or staff — and proposed_at when. reviewed_by, reviewed_at and review_note are the human part, and a hypothesis may not reach confirmed or rejected without a reviewed_at. At most one live hypothesis exists per pair — live means proposed, needs_review or confirmed.

docs.title: Lifecycle
docs.text:
matcher proposes ──> proposed ──┬── staff confirms ──> confirmed ──> [merge executed]
                                  ├── staff rejects  ──> rejected (the pair becomes
                                  │                       proposable again — see §4)
                                  └── person asserts ──> needs_review → staff confirms/rejects

Three entry points:

  1. Import or background matching proposes hypotheses automatically at low confidence.
  2. A registering person asserts their own history — "I was a member 1990–2010" — which creates a hypothesis against the candidate rows, usually with proposed_by = 'person'.
  3. A sign-up that strong-matches a person who already exists raises one by itself, without anyone asserting anything, and that hypothesis holds the new account out of active (§4, D-089). The queue is the same queue and the review is the same review; what a person at a registration form adds is the ability to put a row in it.

A person's own assertion is evidence, not proof. It must still be reviewed, because claiming someone else's history is the obvious attack on an import-based system — and the prize is that person's data. Never auto-confirm a self-asserted link.

docs.title: 4. Match signals
docs.text:
The matcher scores candidate pairs on independent signals. Recorded in match_signals so a reviewer sees why the system proposed a match:

Signal Strength Notes Exact legacy member number decisive The corpus carries these (D-056). Same number, same person — matched, not scored. Exact birth date + exact normalised name strong Still not automatic — twins with similar names exist. Birth date within ±1 day or year-only match + name moderate Common with hand-written records. Name match after normalisation (diacritics, case, spacing) moderate Necessary but weak alone; "Jan Novák" is not unique. Same postal address at the same time moderate Strong if the address is distinctive. Read from person_contact history — there is no household table (D-057). Guardian name match weak Useful for minors in old records. Name-only fuzzy match weak — never sufficient alone

The decisive row changes the matcher's job. With a number on the record, the question is not "are these two the same person?" but "does this number already point somewhere?" — a lookup. The scored signals below are then for the rows the number cannot resolve: legacy records predating the numbering, records where the number is illegible, and people who were never issued one. At thousands of rows (D-056) this split is what makes D-004 affordable: the numbered rows are the trustworthy set and the rest is a work queue.

docs.title: Normalisation
docs.text:
Applied before comparison, and the normalised form is stored so matching is reproducible:

  • Unicode NFKD, strip diacritics, casefold, collapse whitespace.
  • Common nickname/legal-name equivalences (configurable per locale — Jan/Jano, Josef/Josip).
  • Typo distance (Levenshtein/Jaro-Winkler) above a threshold counts as a partial match, never a full one.

docs.title: Thresholds
docs.text:
• confidence < 0.60 — not surfaced. Stored only for diagnostics.
  • 0.60 ≤ confidence < 0.90 — proposed, queued for human review.
  • confidence ≥ 0.90 — still requires human confirmation, but flagged as high priority. There is no auto-merge threshold.

No automatic merging at all, even for a near-certain match (D-004), and the rule does not need the premise that a merge cannot be undone — it can (§6). It rests on what the reversal cannot reach: the merged window stays one row's history, and the union of permissions is exercised from the moment the merge commits, whatever is discovered afterwards. A privacy incident from a bad merge is worse than any amount of manual review. The volume of the corpus — thousands of rows in two exports (D-092), most people rows carrying a number that makes the match a lookup rather than a judgement — is known, so no auto-merge tier is needed and none is reserved.

docs.title: The same signals at sign-up, split at the top of the band
docs.text:
A registration form collides with these signals too. A sign-up that strong-matches an existing person raises an identity_hypothesis and is then held out of active by it — an account may not reach active while an unresolved hypothesis names its person (D-089). The sign-up's own rows are created exactly as any sign-up creates them and stay pending_verification; what "creates nothing" rules out is the outcome — nothing is merged, nothing is linked, nothing is activated. The address the person typed stays on the pending account as the credential it was offered as, which matters because the reviewer's other answer is "this is a different person", and that answer should leave the applicant finishing the sign-up they started rather than starting it again (01-identity.md §4, 02-actors.md §3). Confirming the hypothesis merges the two rows under §5 and the pending account goes with the row that was absorbed; rejecting it lifts the gate and the account activates.

Here the threshold is not a tuning parameter, it is the entire answer. The band is split at its top, and only the top reaches the gate:

Signal at sign-up Raises a blocking hypothesis? Exact legacy member number yes Exact birth date and exact normalised name yes Birth date ±1 day, or year-only + name no Name-only fuzzy match, shared address, guardian name no

The soft band raises nothing at sign-up; the nightly matcher may still propose the pair for review, at a confidence that queues it rather than blocking anybody. The tempting rule, "raise one whenever the score is high", produces the failure this design would most deserve: a stranger's registration blocked by a fuzzy score. The cost of the version chosen is bounded and self-correcting (a true duplicate slips through, is matched nightly, and is reviewed); the cost of the tempting version is a child who cannot sign up for a camp on the day the form closes, which is not self-correcting at all.

Two obligations come with the gate, and neither is a queue-management nicety:

  • A hypothesis that is blocking an account gets an age check, and it alerts. Its victim is a specific person who cannot log in and whose only remaining channel is to telephone someone. The check is shaped like field_conflict's thirty days (01-identity.md §10); the alerting is the point.
  • The holding message confirms nothing. It says the request was received and will be checked. It says nothing about whether the name, the birth date or the number matched anything, because a sign-up form that can answer "yes, that person exists" is an existence oracle, and this system's roster is children.

"I have a new e-mail address" is not this case and must not be routed through it: account_credential holds many credentials for one account, so a new address is an addition to the login a person already has. The collision case is narrower than signing up twice — it is a person arriving through a door the system did not know they had. Resolving the claim is confirming or rejecting a hypothesis, so it is person.merge, held by identity_reviewer (../appendix/permission-catalog.md §2); there is deliberately no account.link code, because an automatic link would be D-004 under another name.

docs.title: 5. The merge operation
docs.text:
Merging is a soft merge: the absorbed row survives as a tombstone.

person (surviving, id=100)          person (absorbed, id=847, tombstoned)
        ▲                                     │
        │                                     ▼
        └────────── person_merge ────► merged_into_person_id = 100
                 (id, surviving_person_id, merged_person_id,
                  merged_at, merged_by, hypothesis_id, reason)

docs.title: What moves
docs.text: Table Action person_contact Reassigned to survivor. Conflicts (two is_primary of the same type) resolved by review, not by rule. person_identifier Reassigned. Duplicate scheme+value collapses to one. person_attribute Reassigned. Two current values for one code is a review item, never a choice made by rule — this table holds one value per person and code with no validity period to keep both, so unlike two past addresses a merge cannot leave the pair standing: the pair is raised as a field_conflict and a human decides, exactly as two is_primary contacts of one type are decided. Where the definition allows several values (allow_multiple), the two rows simply coexist and nothing is decided (../data-model/09-attributes.md §3). person_name Reassigned, keeping validity periods — this is how a maiden name survives. account Reassigned to survivor. If the survivor already has an account, the absorbed account is closed, not deleted. membership Reassigned. Overlapping periods flagged for review — with one type (D-037) and a person-level no-overlap rule, an overlap here means a bad merge. An imported period can produce one too: the source states its own periods and nothing in the file knows that one human appears on two rows. Two imported periods covering the same date are outside the exclusion constraint — it watches the live statuses only — so the merge review is where they surface, and the honest reading of a pair is "the source said this", not "somebody decided this". person_group_member Reassigned, with the same overlap check. Two rows for one person in one group over overlapping dates is a review item and not a dedupe: two people who turn out to be one may genuinely have been put in the group twice, on different evidence, and the honest repair is one row whose dates a person chose. role_holder Reassigned. An office held twice by one person over overlapping periods is the same review case, with the same refusal to guess silently — and it is read out loud rather than filed quietly, because this table's rows are exactly what ROLE(x) reaches, so a duplicate holder row is a duplicate audience member. guardianship (as dependent) Reassigned. guardianship (as guardian) Reassigned. access_grant Reassigned. Union of permissions results — this is the security-critical step. Merging two people silently merges two sets of authority, and since D-099 that union is literally the rows both people leave behind: no rank resolves a collision, so a deny on the absorbed row survives alongside the survivor's allows rather than being deduplicated away, which is the outcome to read out loud at review. audience_operand, where selector_kind is PERSON Repointed, not reassigned. Every hand-named person in the system is a selector_arg_id — a column with deliberately no foreign key (D-011), which is why this row is a requirement on the merge and not something the database notices (D-105). The failure is asymmetric and it is the loud one: a leaf that resolves to nobody is the empty set, so a grant reading EVERYONE - PERSON(x) where x was merged away stops subtracting anybody and denies everybody. An orphan scan is the backstop; the merge is the mechanism. The same walk covers the other four argument kinds — an absorbed person_group, a deleted role, an event, a nested audience — because none of them has a key either person_merge Row inserted here. field_conflict Populated for anything that could not be resolved automatically.

docs.title: What does not happen
docs.text:
• Nothing is deleted. The absorbed person row keeps its id and gains merged_into_person_id. All historical foreign keys pointing at it still resolve, so a question about who belonged to something in 1998 keeps working.
  • Overlapping memberships are never silently deduplicated. Two overlapping memberships after a merge is suspicious — it may mean the merge was wrong. It becomes a review item.

docs.title: The cycle is refused here, not at the read
docs.text:
Chains are permanent (§6): merged_into_person_id is never rewritten forward, so A→B→C stays a chain and resolve_person() walks it. A chain that loops would make that walk never end, so a merge is refused when the person chosen as survivor resolves — by walking the chain — to the person being absorbed (D-087). That subsumes the case already ruled out, nobody merges into themselves, and catches the one that actually happens: absorbing B into A when A has already been absorbed into B.

Checking on the way in is the whole guard, and a read-side step limit is not an acceptable substitute. A hop bound does not prevent the cycle; its only achievement is deciding which of two wrong answers to return, and the wrong answer it returns is a tombstoned id — the exact failure resolve_person() exists to prevent.

The other half of the same rule is softer and needs a net under it. "Every place that accepts a person id from outside must call resolve_person()" is a rule application code can forget, and the schema carries no way to catch it (D-072). What catches it is a report of live rows that reference a tombstoned person, which is the only form of this failure that is visible after the fact (../data-model/01-identity.md §10).

docs.title: The security rule that must not be skipped
docs.text:
Merging unions the two people's permissions. If a bad merge is performed, the survivor gains the absorbed person's access. Therefore:

  1. A merge is always performed by a human with person.merge permission.
  2. The merged result's effective permissions are re-displayed for confirmation before the merge commits.
  3. A merge can be undone (§6). The merged period cannot: access_grant rows created during it cannot be attributed to either human. Hence rule 2 — an unmerge repairs the record afterwards and does not repair this.
  4. Nothing is invalidated by a merge, because nothing is stored that a merge could invalidate: no row maps a person to an answer (D-114), and a merge is not a write that bumps the ruleset version. What the merge does to an answer is what the next check computes, from the survivor's grant rows and the PERSON(x) leaves the merge repointed. That is the same fact that makes rule 2 load-bearing rather than courteous: with nothing stored, the re-displayed effective permissions are the only place the merged answer is computed before the merge commits. See 06-authorization-model.md §8.

docs.title: 6. Reversing a merge
docs.text:
Unmerge is a required operation, not a courtesy for mistakes an organization hopes it will not make (D-087). It is also why merge chains exist: over a chain a reversal is a replay of pointers, while over a flattened pointer it would be a reconstruction of facts nobody recorded. Flattening is therefore closed off, not merely slower — it is a trade against a named feature, not against tidiness.

A permanent chain needs two rules, and neither is enforced on the read:

  • No cycle, checked at the merge (§5). Resolution deliberately has no hop limit.
  • Chain length is a signal, not an error. Resolution is unbounded; a chain longer than three hops is reported. Four merges in a row on one line of people does not mean the row is odd — it means the matcher is producing duplicates faster than a human can settle them, which is a statement about the queue and not about the row. A survivor that has itself been absorbed is normal; only the length means anything (../data-model/01-identity.md §10).

The reversal is four steps, and they restore the row split:

  1. Clear person.merged_into_person_id on the absorbed row. The tombstone comes off.
  2. Reassign rows created before merged_at back to the absorbed person.
  3. Flag rows created after merged_at for human review. Those are the ambiguous ones, and they are reviewed rather than split by a rule.
  4. Record the unmerge on the person_merge row as reversed_at, reversed_by and reversal_note. person_merge is append-only, so an unmerge records that a merge was undone rather than erasing the record of the mistake.

The access_grant rows are the specific hazard. Any grant created during the merged window might belong to either human. Flag every one of them; do not guess.

The asymmetry, stated plainly: the merge is reversible and the merged window is not. Steps 1, 2 and 4 repair the record. Step 3 is an admission. Whatever those two humans did while they were one row stays one row's history, because the grants exercised in that window were really exercised by somebody the record can no longer separate — which is precisely why the confirmation-before-commit rule in §5 is not made redundant by the existence of a reversal.

Unmerge needs no permission code of its own. Undoing an identity correction is the same act as making one, performed by a named human, so it is person.merge (../appendix/permission-catalog.md §2). A person.unmerge code would grade undoing a mistake as safer than making one. Like the merge, the reversal splits a person's permissions back in two, and there is nothing to invalidate: the split is simply visible on the next check.

docs.title: 7. Legacy import pipeline
docs.text:
Staged, reviewed, idempotent. Never a direct write into live tables.

What is arriving is two exports, and neither is a roster (D-092). A roster is evidence of presence in a unit, which is not what the source says. The source says two things:

Half What a row says What the batch writes The membership export a name, a birth date, and when that person was a member of the organization a person, and a bounded membership — both ends dated, data_confidence = 'low', batch id on it (D-093) The attendance export an event, and who came to it an event, and one event_registration per attendee at attending / was_present = true (D-094)

Neither names a sub-unit, and nothing is assigned to one. The parser keeps its parsed unit code — an export that surprises whoever runs it with a unit column is exactly what that field and its unit_not_found warning are for, and keeping them costs nothing — but nothing reads them, no org_unit is created by any batch, and no sub-unit participation row is ever imported. Two halves also means two shapes of batch on one import_batch: a people batch and an events batch, each carrying the field map and the checks that fit its half, rather than one batch holding two mappers that can never both apply.

Say where it hurts, because somebody will ask this question. The historical record this import leaves behind contains no sub-units. "Who was in Pack 12 in 2011?" has no answer at go-live — not a wrong one, none — and the first answer anyone reads will be a roster somebody typed in by hand. Nothing in the model is missing: it is what the source can say, and it is written here so that the first person to ask finds the sentence rather than the absence.

  source file(s)
       │
       ▼
  [1] staging_import          ── raw rows, verbatim, with the source file + line ref
       │
       ▼
  [2] staging_import_row      ── parsed: normalised name, parsed birth date,
       │                          detected unit, parse warnings
       ▼
  [3] matching                ── for each row, find candidate person rows and score them
       │
       ▼
  [4] review queue            ── human confirms: link to existing | create new | discard
       │
       ▼
  [5] apply                   ── a people batch writes person + bounded membership; an events
       │                          batch writes event + event_registration. Never an org_unit,
       │                          never a sub-unit participation row, never an open-ended
       │                          membership
       │
       ▼
  [6] import_log              ── what was applied, by whom, when; reversal instructions

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Idempotent. Re-running the same import must not duplicate people. Each staged row carries a deterministic source_row_hash; re-import matches on it.
  • Reversible per batch. import_log records every row created or modified in a batch, so a bad batch can be rolled back without touching other data.
  • Never overwrites self-registered data. If a legacy row matches a self_registered person, the import may add what the export evidences — a bounded historical membership period, a registration on an imported event — but never alters names, contacts, identifiers, or descriptive values the person maintains themselves. An added closed period contradicts nothing the person typed: it is a dated claim about the past, sitting beside their live row rather than over it. An open-ended period would be a different thing entirely, which is why the surviving ban is exactly that one.
  • Preserves provenance. Every imported row records import_batch_id and source_reference (file + line), so any value can be traced back to the paper it came from. When someone disputes a historical record, you can show them where it came from.
  • Records uncertainty rather than guessing. A row that cannot be parsed cleanly goes to the review queue with the raw value intact — it does not get a best-effort guess written as if it were fact.

docs.title: Raw columns become codes
docs.text:
Old rosters carry columns about the person — a remarks column, a "medical" column, a list of shirt sizes — and each of those arrives at step [5] as a value against a code, not as a blob beside the record (D-084). Those columns are in the membership export; the attendance export brings nothing that maps to an attribute code (D-090). The map therefore belongs to the people batch and a code-to-registration map to the events batch: one batch, one map. That makes the first import the single largest event in the life of this vocabulary — several hundred codes out of one file. The rest of the rules live in staging (../data-model/09-attributes.md §7); three consequences follow from arriving all at once.

  • The map is authored and read before the batch applies, not after. The mapping is recorded on the batch as one object rather than per staged row because it is one artefact a person reads once, top to bottom, and the reading is what makes the codes it names trustworthy. Reading it afterwards would put the live vocabulary at the mercy of whatever the batch had already written. Changing an applied map is curation with an audit entry, not a migration.
  • A raw column that maps to no code stops the batch, unless someone maps it or marks it discarded with a reason. An unmapped column is a decade of something the organization used to collect vanishing quietly.
  • A column nobody recognises becomes a code named from the column, never a guess at an existing code: an import-time merge is invisible and unreviewable, and the review queue above is for people, not for vocabulary. The codes the map names arrive live. A curator has just read every name in the map, which is exactly the endorsement proposed withholds. proposed keeps its meaning of improvised later by a person at a desk — a fact with no code yet — and not "whatever the import did not understand". Several hundred codes landing proposed on day one would open the curation queue full, make its age signal meaningless before it had ever meant anything, and teach the organization that the attribute layer's warning queue is noise. Who holds attribute.define day to day, and how long a runtime proposal may sit, stays open (AT-2).

docs.title: What each source row lands on
docs.text:
What the source says It becomes Why "Jan Novák, born 1962, member 1990–1995" a person with record_origin = 'legacy_import', and one membership per period the source states — valid_from and valid_to set, data_confidence = 'low', import_batch_id set, the renewal chain left to whoever reconstructs it A stated period is evidence of membership and infers nothing; a closed period cannot gate anything (D-093) the same, with the year repeated in the file a second membership only if the source states a second period; consecutive stated years stretch to one row, a gap in the source opens another One row per stated period keeps one row per membership, and a lapse stays visible in the one table that means it an event, and who came to it an event with no owner column at all, one event_registration per attendee at attending with was_present = true, and the per-event instantiation of the seeded answers-view grant Nothing owns an event: its people are named by selectors that bind to it (D-102) a person who might have come and did not nothing An export lists who came. Writing not_attending from silence puts words in a source that said nothing (D-059) a sub-unit nothing, ever — and there is now nothing that could be one The corpus names none (§7) and there is no structure to attach a name to. The row stays because it is the one a reader holding a 1998 spreadsheet will ask, and the answer has to be written down rather than inferred from absence money nothing — and no fee_obligation The corpus has no money in it (D-090)

The ban is one sentence, and it is the whole point: never an open-ended membership, and never one inferred from an attendance row. is_current_member() and the permission gate (D-039) both read membership, so a row running to no valid_to hands whoever signs up under that name authority in the present. The ban is sized for what it now guards: one reviewed batch whose map is read before it applies, on a corpus that will never arrive twice.

The line the whole design turns on is evidence against inference. A row that says member 1990–1995 is evidence of a membership; a row that says in Pack 12 in 1998 is evidence of presence and nothing more. Generating a membership for every historical row because the old data model implied it, and then marking it inferred, is the refusal that stands. A related observation worth keeping in front of anybody implementing this: a conditional with one live arm is not a safe default — wording of the form "X unless there is payment evidence", on a corpus that carries no payment data at all, leaves an arm with an empty set to fire on while still inviting somebody to build it.

Four consequences that arrive with the memberships.

  • No obligation, no payment, no balance. An imported membership creates no fee_obligation, and that has to be a rule rather than an accident: an obligation per historical year would land as unpaid and turn a decade of members into a wall of debt with a 1999 due_date for the lapse sweep to choke on. Related, and load-bearing rather than incidental: outstanding_balance is null on these rows — a zero would be a claim of settled that no export supports.
  • The person-level no-overlap rule is in the import's path. One row per period the source states, not one per calendar year, is a rule with a consequence: two stated periods covering one date violate it and reach the review queue (§5).
  • These rows are the oldest layer of the skeleton D-088 keeps forever (D-088): thousands of named people with birth dates who were never asked and never used the system, held on an unverified legal basis. Same judgement as for live rows, much larger population.
  • Every cross-decade member count is a mixture of an export and a register, distinguished only by data_confidence and import_batch_id. A membership-rate chart spanning the import boundary compares a source that states membership with a system that records it, and nothing in the query knows the difference.

A historical membership is also obtainable as a human act. Where the organization has a period the export does not state — a ledger found later, a written confirmation, a person who was a member in a year the file lost — the period is entered by hand under membership.backdate (../appendix/permission-catalog.md §4). The pipeline carries the stated ones; this is the route for the unstated: deliberate, attributed, outside the batch.

End dates are still often unknown, and this is the sharpest case of it. A period the export leaves open — someone last seen in a 2003 row with no end stated — cannot be written open: that is the one shape refused outright, and an unbounded historical record is the same hazard wearing a different name. Convention: end it at the end of the school/organizational year of the last row they appear in, marked as inferred. That is the only date the import infers — the periods themselves are stated — and it is precisely what the organizational year boundary is needed for, which is still open (A-4). With attendance and no money in the corpus, it is the sharpest remaining import question. Document the rule you choose; it will be questioned.

docs.title: 8. The returning-member case
docs.text:
The scenario member 1990–2010, returns 2024, should be the smooth path, because it is a common and important one (returning alumni become adult leaders and donors).

Flow:

  1. Person registers in 2024, self-asserting past membership.
  2. The system matches them against legacy rows and proposes hypotheses.
  3. A registrar reviews and confirms.
  4. The historical membership (1990–2010) and the current membership (2024–present) now sit under one person row, as two membership rows.
  5. Their profile shows their full history; the gap is explicit data.
  6. Any seniority or "years of service" calculation reads across both.

A 1990–2010 membership appears only where the source states the period or somebody records it by hand on evidence (membership.backdate, §7). The smooth path restores a person's member history without a human typing it, and what makes that safe is that the source states the period rather than the import guessing one.

Steps 2–3 can be streamlined when the match is strong (exact old membership number), but the confirmation step remains, for the reason in §3.

What the activation gate costs this path. The gate does not distinguish why a hypothesis exists: an account may not reach active while an unresolved hypothesis names its person, and a self-asserted claim names that person exactly as a collision does. So the smooth path has a human between registration and login, where the review could otherwise happen after the person was already using the system. The mitigation is the age check that alerts (§4), plus the fact that with a legacy number in hand step 2 is a lookup a registrar settles in seconds. What is not settled is whether a hypothesis the person raised about themselves should hold their account out of active at all, as against a hypothesis the system raised about a stranger who happened to match. Recorded in §9.

docs.title: Self-service without weakening the guarantee
docs.text: Rather than auto-linking, give the person a claim flow: they assert a past membership, staff confirm. Record the assertion on the hypothesis row, so that if the claim later proves false, you can see it was self-asserted rather than discovered.

docs.title: 9. Open issues
docs.text:
Still open, and tracked in ../open-questions.md:

  • Whether twins/siblings with similar names and the same birth date need a documented disambiguation procedure (recommend: yes, and never merge them automatically). The sign-up gate in §4 sharpens this: same birth date plus a normalised name is exactly the collision pair, and a collision now stops a registration instead of merely queueing a card.
  • Whether a hypothesis a person raised about themselves should hold their account out of active, as against one the system raised because a stranger's sign-up strong-matched them (§8).
  • The organizational year boundary that historical end dates get inferred from (A-4). With stated membership periods, attendance, and no money (§7) it is load-bearing by itself, and the inferred date closes a membership row, so the number of rows it touches is large.
  • Whether indefinite retention of named membership and fee rows has a legal basis. The design keeps that skeleton indefinitely as the organization's own history while audit payloads are emptied after 24 months (D-088); a decision log cannot grant the basis, so it is recorded as an assumption awaiting review.

Decisions behind this page: D-004, D-011, D-037, D-038, D-039, D-056, D-057, D-059, D-072, D-084, D-085, D-087, D-088, D-089, D-090, D-092, D-093, D-094, D-097, D-099, D-102, D-105, D-114.

docs.title: Groups
docs.text:
One organization, and the named sets of people inside it.

The vocabulary, first, because everything here leans on it.

Word Means Stored as unit the organization itself. There is exactly one. It is a scope, never a row nothing — a code in grant_scope_type group a named set of people with explicitly dated members and a lifetime. A set, not a body person_group + person_group_member role an office: a small, visible set of holders — leaders, finance, IT role + role_holder audience an expression over named sets, which a grant is aimed at audience selector one operand of that expression: MEMBERS, GROUP(x), ROLE(x), … selector_type, audience_operand

Roles and audiences belong to the authorization model (06-authorization-model.md, ../data-model/05-authorization.md) and are not re-specified here. This page owns the unit and the group.

docs.title: 1. The organization is one unit, and the unit is a scope
docs.text:
There is one unit and it is the organization. It has no parent, no children, no type, no code, no path, no depth, and no row. It is the non-item scope that grant_scope_type already carries — code unit, is_item_scoped = false — and a grant written at it has no scope_id. Nothing in the schema represents it, because there is nothing to represent: a second unit cannot appear, for the same reason a second answer to a question cannot appear in a field that does not exist.

Membership is unchanged and is not a group. One membership per person, at the unit, paid for yearly:

  • "everyone in the organization" is one query against membership;
  • "everyone in the Thursday group" is one query against person_group_member.

Two shapes, and neither one borrows the other's table. Renewal opens a new membership row rather than extending the old one (D-016).

A grant at the unit reaches everything — every item of every type — because nothing stands between the unit and an item and there is no ownership relation to test. That is a sentence about the permission system; it is stated here only because it is what "scope" means now that "row" does not.

Why the design carries no hierarchy: the legacy corpus names no units at all — two exports, people with their membership period and events with attendance, no unit column anywhere (D-092) — and a structure that describes nothing imported and restricts nothing carries no information (D-097).

docs.title: What that costs, said once
docs.text:
These are properties the hierarchy was carrying, listed here rather than distributed through the page. They are not argued away.

  1. The unit is not a locus of accountability for a child's records. This is the one that matters. Nothing in the model reproduces "access to a body's children was granted by that body" — by the people who know them, who recruited its leader, and who can be asked. With one unit there is no "outside it" to be stopped from, so the rule has no subject rather than a weaker form. A permission held at the unit reaches every member, and person.view is the widest read permission in the system (D-083, D-086). What stands between a child and a stranger's read is a permission held by a named adult, an audit trail whose payloads expire after two years (D-088), and a report of who holds the write.
  2. There is no subtree question. "Who was in the Thursday group in 2011?" stays answerable, because group member rows are dated (§5). "And everything nested under it" has no subject: a set of people has no sub-sets stored inside it.
  3. Restructuring is not a recorded event. A group that splits is an old group that ended and two that began, with no edge between them — and no table where such an edge could go (§4).
  4. Unit-scoped reports have nothing to report on. "A pack's roster", "a pack's events", "which units exist" are not hard questions, they are questions with no subject. The organizational-year reports that matter — membership and fees — live at the unit and are untouched.

One invariant class now has no instance at all: shape 4 of F-10, a column that may not change once set, whose violation leaves every row individually valid.

It is not a two-way door. This is the deletion of a dimension, not a flag. Adding structure back is a decision with a reason attached — most plausibly "the organization has outgrown one center's visibility" — and it would have to argue the accountability rule from its own premises, because the mechanism that made it work — a scope written by the body it covered — does not exist.

docs.title: 2. What a group is, and everything a group is not
docs.text:
A group is a person_group: a name, a description, its own lifetime, and explicitly dated members. It is a set of people, not a body. Somebody names it, somebody puts people in it, somebody ends it, and the record of who was in it when is the roster's own (§5). A weekly meeting group, a project crew, a trainers' pool, schuzka2026-1 — all the same kind of thing, and the system has no opinion about which ones deserve to exist. A person may be on several rosters at once; none of them is marked as the one to show first.

Everything a body would have had, a group does not have.

A group has Because no parent and no children there are no sub-units, and groups do not nest no type, and no vocabulary of types a group needs no word for what kind of set it is no code, no path, no depth a label carries no identity (§4); a set has no position to sit at no nesting rules there is nothing to nest no rename history the name is a column, and the old name is not kept (§4) no split, merger or succession edge restructuring is not an event (§1, cost 3) no leadership of its own see §6 no roles an office is a role and a role is held at the unit; a group has none of its own, and no leadership column will be added to make one look derivable no fee membership is at the unit and is the only thing that costs money no permissions over its members see immediately below

Membership of a group confers nothing, and tidier storage does not quietly change that. A member of a group cannot do anything: participation is not authority, and it stays not-authority when it moves into a table with better columns. Authority arrives only through a grant that names the group, which is §4 of ../data-model/02-organization.md.

Where the line against an audience is drawn — the two are one row apart in shape and a mile apart in meaning: a group states its members, a selector picks them. A group's members are a list of people that is true whether or not any permission points at it. A leaf in an audience — a PERSON(y) row (D-105) — is an addition to an expression, meaningful only inside the expression it completes. A group exists to be talked about; a selector exists to be aimed at something. Merging them would make the permission table the system's roster.

Where the line against a role is drawn, in one sentence, because it decides who may edit the list. A role is an office with a small, visible set of holders and is written by the most sensitive code family in the catalog (role.*, 🔒🔒); a group is company, and its roster is written by person_group.member.manage (⚠). One table with a kind column would give a single permission that both adds a child to the Thursday group and puts the holder among the administrators (D-100). GROUP(x) and ROLE(x) stay distinct in the grant text so the distinction is visible to whoever reads the grant.

docs.title: 3. Joining a group is somebody else's act
docs.text:
Nobody writes themselves onto a roster. The gate is person_group.member.manage, held at the unit — which reaches every group, because nothing stands between a unit-scope grant and an item — or granted on one group as an item, which is how "these two people may work this roster" is said without inventing a scope (D-098, D-099). There is no self-scoped variant and none will be added.

Who enforces "do not place a child where nobody is responsible for them": whoever may write the member row in person_group_member, audited and naming who wrote it. A permission refuses every write by the wrong person regardless of the child's age (D-081).

What that costs. The system cannot say which groups are for children. Nothing on a person_group answers that question and, consistent with "no special features", nothing will: no allows_minors, no is_children, no type to hang it on. Combined with no recorded background checks (D-043) and with cost 1 above, the safeguarding story of this module is a permission held by named adults, an audit trail that forgets values after two years, and a report. If that turns out to be too little — after an incident, or an insurer's question — the route back is a rule about who may be placed where, argued once as a decision with its enforcement layer named in D-081's terms, and not a resurrected column whose name implies it enforces something.

A membership request is a request for membership of the unit, and carries no group. There is no requested_unit_id on a request: which group a new member lands in is a write on the group, not a preference on the request. The request flow in 05-membership-lifecycle.md ends at the unit; a roster is somebody else's decision afterwards.

docs.title: 4. A name carries no identity
docs.text:
A group name is a label, and a label is not the group: a group name that comes back after a decade is a new group, unless somebody records that it is not.

Why the default matters: continuity is not a property of a label, it is a claim about the world, and only a human knows whether the crew refounded in 2026 is the crew of 2016. Left unstated, the question is answered anyway — by whoever writes the matching screen, who will match on name and let a thirty-year gap sit inside one group's life. So the default points at a new person_group row. A rename is an edit to one column and the previous name is not kept (§2).

The continuity claim has nowhere to live. Groups keep no group-to-group edges — no split, no merger, no succession — so an assertion of continuity has no field to hold it (D-098). What the method guarantees is therefore the direction of the default, which is the half that was ever enforceable: a returning name is a new group, and two groups that are really one look like two unless a person writes that down somewhere. Where that sentence goes is not decided. The cheapest true answer available today is a note on the second group's member rows and on the group's description, which nothing reads and nothing links; the honest alternative is to accept that the organization's memory of its own continuity is prose. Status: assumption — this page does not choose, and the question is recorded in ../open-questions.md.

Names are one namespace with roles and audiences. Because ROLE(x) and GROUP(x) do not have to disambiguate, a bare COUNSELORS resolves against roles and groups together, so names are unique across the tables, case/whitespace/separators are folded on write, and every selector_type.code is a reserved name — a group called MEMBERS is refused at the save rather than silently rewriting every expression in the system (D-101). audience.code is in the namespace too (D-103), and the pair of rules is worth holding apart: a bare name never resolves to an audience — the arm must be written AUDIENCE(veterans) — yet a group still may not borrow an audience's code, because a name that resolves two ways is a silent grant whatever the resolution rules say. No single constraint spans the three tables, so the write path carries the rule and an integrity check asserts that it does. What a grant stores is kind + id, never a name, so renaming a group never rewrites a grant. Mechanics: ../data-model/02-organization.md §1.

docs.title: 5. A roster is history
docs.text:
Member rows are dated, and that is what makes the roster answerable. person_group_member carries valid_from and valid_to per person, so joining, leaving and coming back are all periods on the same pair, and the roster has a history of its own instead of borrowing the audit trail's. "Who was in schuzka2026-1 on 14 March 2026?" is a point-in-time read over those rows. It survives the audit trail's 24-month payload expiry (D-088) because it does not depend on the trail — which is the entire reason the rows are dated rather than a live flag, and the reason a naming habit like schuzka2026-1 is a habit an organization may or may not keep rather than the mechanism history rests on.

This is where a group is ahead of the operand that looks most like it. An audience named as an operand evaluates live, so its past shape survives only in the audit trail and stops surviving when the payloads expire; a group's set is its dated rows, so it keeps a past the audit trail cannot take away. "Who could see this child's data in 2024?" is answerable when the grant pointed at a group and is not answerable when it pointed at a nested audience (D-103). That asymmetry is a fact about which of the two is a roster, and it is the strongest reason the pair stays two tables.

Two facts, both kept, and not to be conflated. The group's valid_from/valid_to says the group existed over that span; the member rows' periods say who was in it. An open group with dated members answers the historical question perfectly well, and an ended group's rows are not tidied up. Ending the group is not an edit anyone makes on their own: setting that end date is refused while a live grant, or a live audience reachable from one, names the group, because an empty set inside a subtraction widens a deny that the person ending the group did not write and would not look at again (the write path and the checks that watch it are ../data-model/02-organization.md §3).

A person who left in 2020 and came back in 2024 is two rows, never one row edited in place, because the edit destroys the answer to "was she in the group in 2019?" (D-016, D-002).

Moving from one group to another closes one row and opens another: never rewrite a member row to point at a different group. Rewriting destroys "where was this child in 2003?", and unlike most tempting edits this one leaves no evidence that anything happened. Mechanics: ../data-model/02-organization.md §4.

No member row is ever inferred. The corpus names no groups any more than it names units (D-092), so the one-off import owes no group rows and no member rows at all: every person_group_member row in this system is typed by a person, which is also the only way one could be true.

docs.title: 6. Appointments
docs.text:
An appointment is a role_holder row: a role, a person, a period, who granted it, a note. Written by role.assign and removed by role.unassign, always held at the unit, because there is one scope and nowhere else to hold an office. It confers nothing by itself: the codes an office carries are the live grants whose expression names ROLE(x) (../data-model/05-authorization.md §3–§4). "That these two may manage the counselors roster" is a grant on the role, the same move a group gets. There is no position, no slot, no max_holders, and no is_leadership flag: nothing in the system records a seat that exists unfilled.

This module holds no eligibility rule of any kind. There is no requires_membership and no min_age on an office, and no gate in the resolver: membership is an operand, written into the grant.

The expression that says each thing, in the form D-101's canonical rendering stores it — every compound operand bracketed, a leaf left bare:

The rule to express The expression the office applies only to current members (MEMBERS * ROLE(x)) the office applies whether or not the holder is a member ROLE(x), written without MEMBERS one named person is exempt from the membership requirement (MEMBERS * ROLE(x)) + PERSON(y)

PERSON(y) is the only way to name a human being in an expression. A set of named people is written PERSON(a) + PERSON(b), and there is no second spelling of it (D-105). A person who must be excepted is subtracted as themselves, and the exemption belongs + PERSON(y) inside the very grant that carries the rule, so the exception is read next to the thing it exempts. The registry of named operands lives in one table — the selector registry — and this page does not recite its row count.

The posture is opt-in per grant, so a grant written as ROLE(TREASURERS) with no MEMBERS authorizes a lapsed member silently and forever. The controls are a standing report of live grants that name a ROLE(...) operand without MEMBERS, seeded grants that carry MEMBERS, and an import count — not the resolver. Nothing forces a holder row to end either; the report is the control (D-071). All of that belongs to the authorization model and is named here only because these were this module's workflows: 06-authorization-model.md.

Three consequences, stated plainly.

  • "The leader of the Thursday group" has no referent. A group has no leadership and no roles (§2), so the sentence means a person on that roster who also holds some office, and nothing links the two. The office is ROLE(leaders) and means what its name says.
  • Elected versus appointed is not stored data. It survives only as roles the organization invents (elected_council beside appointed_it) — or not at all.
  • A vacancy is not a reportable state. "This seat has been empty since March" needs a slot that exists unfilled. An empty office is the absence of rows in role_holder, and absence has no start date on the office. A rule-filled role stays refused: F-12's answer is no, role_holder names one person, because an office record that cannot answer "who was treasurer in 2023" is not an office record (F-12).

docs.title: 7. The module and the permission system, in one table
docs.text:
Stated once here so that nothing below the line is re-specified in this page's voice. Full detail: 06-authorization-model.md and ../data-model/05-authorization.md.

Question Answer Owner Where is authority held? at the unit, or on exactly one item — nothing in between D-097, D-099 What is a group to the resolver? an item in grant_scope_type, and a GROUP(x) leaf in an expression D-098, D-101 Does being in a group grant anything? no. A set is not a grant D-005, D-098, D-102 for ORGANIZERS What may a role do? read the live grants whose expression names ROLE(x) — a role confers nothing D-100 How is precedence decided? allowed iff some live allow applies and no live deny applies. There is no level and no locality D-099 Does a unit-scope grant reach an item? yes, every item of every type. A grant on one item reaches that item only D-099, D-102 Is there a membership gate in the resolver? no. MEMBERS is an operand, evaluated live on the checked date D-100 Can the center be locked out of a body's data? the question has no subject: there is one body and its people are the only people there are D-097

There is no ancestor walk, because there is no tree: no unit_ancestors(), no unit_descendants(), no path-consistency check. The permission check matches scope exactly — the unit, or the item.

docs.title: 8. Open issues
docs.text:
Open, and tracked in ../open-questions.md:

  • Where a claimed group continuity is recorded. The method says continuity is asserted, never matched (§4); no table accepts the assertion. Until somebody rules, the default is the whole rule: a returning name is a new group.
  • Whether a group's previous name should be kept at all. It is not, deliberately, as part of "no special features". If the organization turns out to rename groups often, the answer is a decision and not a column someone adds quietly.
  • Whether an ended group should be hidden from pickers. A person_group with valid_to set has no stated behaviour either way yet.
  • F-10, which layer writes the no-overlap invariant on member rows. It is named in ../data-model/02-organization.md §2 and remains unanswered.

Decisions behind this page: D-002, D-005, D-016, D-043, D-081, D-083, D-086, D-088, D-092, D-096, D-097, D-098, D-099, D-100, D-101, D-102, D-103, D-105, D-071.

docs.title: Membership Lifecycle
docs.text: Register → request → accept → pay → member. Plus the parts that are usually forgotten: gaps, returns, multiple periods, and renewal.

docs.title: 1. The flow you described
docs.text:
"The people can register on their own to get access to the system, however they become member only if they request a membership, they get accepted and pay a yearly fee."

Four distinct stages, each a separate record, because each can independently fail, stall, or be reversed:

Stage Record Can be reversed? What it means 1. Register person + account account can be closed "This person can log in." 2. Request membership_request yes — reject/withdraw "This person applied." 3. Accept membership_request.status = 'approved' yes — revoke before activation "The organization said yes." 4. Pay fee_obligation + payment refund "The obligation is met." 5. Activate membership opened yes — lapse/terminate "This person is a member."

Why stage 5 is separate from stage 3. Approval and activation are distinct because payment sits between them. A person can be approved and never pay; the organization needs to see that state ("approved, awaiting payment") to chase it, and it must not appear as a member.

Decided: membership activates on payment (D-040). membership opens at stage 5, and pending_payment is a real membership status so that "approved, awaiting payment" is a visible worklist rather than an invisible backlog.

docs.title: Two doors, one gate each
docs.text:
The flow above is one of two ways a person ends up in the organization's records, and for eight rounds this document wrote as if it were the only one. There are two entry paths and each has exactly one gate, with no third control anywhere (D-095, whose reasoning D-098 transfers to groups intact — joining one is still somebody else's act):

Membership of the unit A group How you get in You pay. Stages 1–5 above are this door, and it is the only self-service entry in the system — it opens a membership and nothing beside it Somebody else writes a person_group_member row What stops you The fee person_group.member.manage, held at the unit — which reaches every group — or granted on one group as an item Money The yearly fee Nothing

Nobody writes themselves into a group. The people who run a group add people to it; that is the whole of the rule, and it is carried by a permission rather than by a workflow. person_group.member.manage has no self-scoped variant and none will be added — a grant is always "over this group's roster", never "over my own", so the shape of request that would let a person place themselves is not refused by a check, it is not expressible. The same holds for offices: nobody appoints themselves, and the catalog holds no code that could say otherwise (../appendix/permission-catalog.md §5).

No fee below the membership, and no model wants one. The fee is the organization's; joining a group carries no money — "into the sub-units, there is no fee, it is entirely managed by the organization, including adding more members." That was said about units and it transfers unchanged, a group being among the things listed as having no fee (D-098). Putting a fee on a member row would immediately ask who sets the amount, who chases it, and what happens to a child whose family cannot pay a group's arrears, and none of those questions exist in the corpus or in any answer given. That is a refused model, not an unasked one.

What the asymmetry costs. The group door has no membership check behind it — a counselor may add somebody who is not a member, and nothing in the write stops them, because D-095 refuses a third gate as firmly as it refuses the first two. What keeps that person from reading anything is MEMBERS in the grants that matter — the test D-039 was, now carried in the grant text rather than the resolver (D-100) — which is what that test was always for. A group membership is a fact about belonging, not a credential: a member of a group can do nothing by being one, and the tidier table does not quietly promote it (D-098). The other cost is directional and appears in the other direction at import: the membership door is the only place a person's own initiative can produce a record, which is why the legacy corpus could be matched against people and never against groups (domain/03 §7).

And one cost is new, named where D-097 names it. Under the deleted hierarchy, access to a body's children had to be granted by that body, by people who recruited its leader and can be asked. A group's roster write is the same shape of permission and may be held at the unit, where it reaches every group in the organization, so what is left of the safeguarding story is a permission held by a named adult, an audit trail whose recorded values expire after two years (D-088), and a report of who holds the write — minus the part where the named adult was somebody the body chose. Nothing in the remaining model reproduces that property, and this document says so rather than letting the reader infer it.

docs.title: 2. Membership request
docs.text:
A request records the person it is for and the membership type asked for, and nothing else. status is one of draft, submitted, under_review, approved, rejected, withdrawn, expired, and submitted_at says when it went in. The review is carried on the same row: who took it up, when they decided, and on a rejection a rejection_reason_code with a free-text rejection_note beside it. An approved request points at the membership it produced; the link is not optional once the approval exists.

A request asks for membership of the unit, and it names no group. requested_unit_id is deleted, along with the index over it (D-098). ~~The unit named on a request is a preference, not a door: a request opens the root and produces a root participation row, and the pack the applicant wrote down is a sentence addressed to whoever reviews it.~~ Withdrawn by D-098, which also deleted the table the column pointed at (D-097). The want behind the field is genuine — a reviewer would like to know where the applicant hopes to turn up — and it is served by the notes the row already carries, which is what the field always was in effect: a sentence, carrying no authority. Which group a new member lands in is a write on the group, not a preference on the request: one person_group_member row, written by somebody holding person_group.member.manage (§1), in a separate act with its own permission and its own audit entry. An approved request that produced no group row is a complete, ordinary outcome.

docs.title: Why a request is not a membership with a status
docs.text:
Tempting to collapse them, but:

  • A request can be rejected, producing no membership at all. A membership row with status rejected would pollute every "list members" query forever.
  • A person may submit several requests over time (rejected in 2024, approved in 2025). One table for both would need a request-version column and every query would need to filter it.
  • Requests carry review data (who reviewed, why, what was checked) that has no meaning on a membership.
  • Requests have different permissions: submitting is self-service; reviewing is a staff capability.

docs.title: There are no request requirements
docs.text:
Removed entirely (D-044). A request is accepted on identity and payment alone: no blocking checklist, no evidence collection, no waiver workflow, no requirement_code and no membership_request_requirement table.

Your answer, asked what a request must contain to be accepted: "Just identity and the fee — nothing to verify." The option to keep the mechanism as empty infrastructure for later was offered and not taken, which is the right call — a checklist that is always empty is a checklist nobody maintains, and it would have implied a gate that does not exist.

What this does not weaken. Two things that look like requirements are unaffected, because neither was a membership requirement to begin with:

  • Guardian consent for a minor's account is a fact about the guardianship relation, held in guardianship_permission, not a box ticked during an application (data-model/04).
  • Who may hold an office — a scoutmaster must be an adult — was never a property of membership, and after D-100 it is not a stored property of the office either: position.min_age is deleted with positions and role carries no age column, so what remains is is_minor() in a report (§7). Membership is ageless (D-038).

And background checks do not exist in this system at all (D-043). If the organization introduces them, the home is a dated record with an expiry, and it belongs with the office rather than the membership gate — a lapsed check is a reason someone may not hold a role, not a reason they stop being a member. Which layer would hold it is unresolved, since the layer that used to hold eligibility went out with positions (D-100; §7 and §9).

docs.title: 3. Membership
docs.text: A membership row belongs to one person and one membership type, and carries a status of pending_payment, active, lapsed, terminated, completed or suspended — always chosen deliberately, never defaulted. The period is valid_from and valid_to, and an absent valid_to means the period is still open: it is the current membership, not a row someone forgot to close. joined_via_request_id records the request it came out of, termination_reason_code the reason it was ended, data_confidence is high, medium or low, and import_batch_id is set on imported rows and on nothing else. **For one round these two For one round these two columns were dead on this table — the corpus carried no payment evidence, so the batch wrote person rows and left membership to the live register, and this paragraph said a membership row is never imported D-093 reversed that, because it turned out the source states a membership period directly rather than only attendance: the import now writes membership rows for the periods the export states, data_confidence = 'low' and import_batch_id set on every one of them, both ends of the period dated (domain/03 §7). What did not come back is the open-ended row: an imported membership never runs to today and none is inferred from an attendance row, which is the half of the old rule that was doing the protecting. So data_confidence on this table has two live sources again and they mean different things: on a backdated row it is a human's judgement (membership.backdate, attributed to whoever typed it), on an imported row it is the batch speaking for itself.

docs.title: Overlap rules — the invariant that matters
docs.text:
A person must not hold two open memberships at the same time, and the rule is enforced by the database rather than by application code. Its precise statement is in data-model/03-membership.md §3; what it says, in words:

  • Two membership periods of one person may not cover the same date while either of them is pending_payment, active or suspended. Those three statuses are the whole of the rule's reach — a lapsed row, a terminated one and a completed one are outside it, which is why an ending period and a later beginning one sit beside each other without complaint.
  • Periods are half-open, so a membership ending on 30 June and another opening on 30 June do not collide.

The constraint used to be scoped to membership_type_id, because a person might legitimately be an honorary and an adult member at once. With one membership type (D-037) that escape hatch is gone, and the constraint becomes the clean person-level invariant: one person, one open membership, ever. The type column was what made "am I a paid-up member?" a hard question; now it is one row, one status, one date. (This sentence cited D-041 until round 10; that decision was about belonging to a sub-unit, its table is deleted (D-097), and nothing about this invariant ever depended on it.)

This is the invariant the import now writes against. For one round the sentence could be written the other way — with no imported membership, there is nothing for it to violate — and D-093 removed the premise, not the rule (domain/03 §7). Say exactly what fires, because the rule's reach is narrow: it watches the three live statuses, so what the exclusion constraint refuses at apply time is an imported period colliding with a live membership — an export period that runs into or past the person's current one, which an open-ended imported row would produce for thousands of people in one transaction. What it does not refuse is an overlap between two closed imported periods: the statuses are outside its reach by design, so a source file that double-books somebody across 1993 lands quietly, marked only as data_confidence = 'low'. That is the honest cost of the same decision that keeps a returning member's old period from gating anything today, and it is why the batch is reviewed before it applies rather than after.

Assumption: btree_gist is available (PostgreSQL), because a temporal overlap is the one rule that can only be refused during the write that would create it. If the target database cannot express exclusion constraints, the fallback is a check inside the writing transaction plus the nightly consistency report — one of the strongest guarantees in the model degrading into the weakest class (data-model/00 §6a, open question F-10 shape 1): an application-level count is wrong exactly when two writers run at once, which is when an overlap is actually created, and the report finds it a day later in a form nobody can attribute. So it is not merely "weaker" and must be recorded as an accepted risk, chosen deliberately, rather than discovered in a migration tool's limitations.

docs.title: There is one membership type, and membership is ageless
docs.text:
A type row is a code and a name, four calendar values, and a sort_order. The calendar values start at twelve months' duration, expiry_month 1 and expiry_day 1 — the fee expires on 1 January (D-047) — and renewal_grace_days 60, which is the renewal window and not a status (D-048).

Seeded with exactly one row, member (D-037). Everything the old type carried — category, min_age, max_age, requires_background_check, requires_guardian_consent, fee_schedule_id — is gone, and what is left is the two parameters a period needs: how long it lasts, and how long after it the person may renew without re-applying. The fee itself is not a property of the type at all: it is a flat per-person amount that lives on fee_schedule and is snapshotted onto each obligation, so "what did we charge in 1998?" is answered from the obligation, not the type.

Membership is ageless (D-038). No age floor, no age ceiling, no age-out, no child→adult transition. Age survives as a fact about a person (person.birth_date) and matters where the law makes it matter: guardianship and safeguarding (§7 was the age-transition section — there is no longer a §7). Being a counselor or a leader is a role, never a membership type (D-100).

docs.title: 4. Multiple memberships over a lifetime
docs.text:
This is your 1990–2010 / 2024–present case. It is not an edge case; it is the normal shape of a long-lived organization's data.

person 100 — Jan Novák
  ├── membership #1   member   1990-09-01 → 2010-06-30   terminated  (left)
  │     └── (nothing here: the corpus names no groups, so nobody's data says where he was)
  ├── (gap 2010 → 2024 — 14 years, no membership rows)
  └── membership #2   member   2024-10-01 → NULL          active
        └── person_group_member  Thursday group  2024-10-01 → NULL
        └── role_holder          counselors      2025-01-01 → NULL

Note what the two membership rows now share: the same type. They differ only in their period and their end reason. In the original framing this person was a child member and then an adult member; in this one they were a member, twice, and were a child and then an adult the whole time. The second framing is the true one, and it is why the memorable case still works: the person never changed, and neither did the type — only the period did.

Half of this picture is reachable without a human, and the other half is not. Membership #1 and its dates are exactly what the membership export states, so the one-off import writes them — bounded, data_confidence = 'low', batch id set (D-093). The group row is the other half: the corpus names no groups either, so a 1990s roster exists only because somebody who remembers typed it, and the import owes no belonging rows of any kind (D-097, D-098). What the diagram used to draw beside each membership — a root-unit participation row mirroring the very same period — is gone with the table, and the picture is now about the two periods, which is the most the import can actually say. The 1990s belonging the deleted rows might once have held was never in the corpus either (D-092), so what is lost is a place it could have been written down, not a fact that was stored and then thrown away.

One row of the new diagram is thinner than the row it replaced, and the difference is a fact about roles. position_assignment could name the body a person led; role_holder cannot, because D-097 left exactly one scope and there is no body to hold an office of — a role is always held at the unit. So "he was scoutmaster of that group" is no longer a stored pair: the office and the group are two rows about the same person, and the link between them is somebody's reading of them. D-100 records the neighbouring loss in the same register — the elected-versus-appointed distinction survives only as a role the organization invents — and neither is a hole this module can fill.

Everything the system needs follows from this:

  • "Is this person a member?" → is there a membership with valid_to IS NULL (or covering today) and status = 'active'?
  • "How long have they been a member?" → sum of membership period lengths, not today − first join date. The gap must not count.
  • "How old were they when they joined?" → membership #2.valid_from − person.birth_date.
  • "Are they an adult?" → is_minor(person_id), computed from person.birth_date. In 2005 the same query said yes. The membership row is identical either way; only the person's birth date and today's date moved.

Never store is_member, member_since, member_type, or is_child on person. Every one of those is derivable, and every one of them will be wrong the moment history is corrected or a person returns.

docs.title: 5. Transitions and who can perform them
docs.text:
From To Trigger Permission required — draft person starts an application own draft submitted person submits membership.request.create (own, or the guardianship channel at write for a guardian — D-074) submitted under_review reviewer picks it up membership.request.review under_review approved reviewer approves membership.request.approve under_review rejected reviewer rejects membership.request.approve any withdrawn applicant withdraws own, or guardian with permission approved membership pending_payment approval processed system pending_payment active payment confirmed system (or fee.record for manual) active lapsed fee unpaid past the organization's expiry date membership.lapse or the yearly sweep active terminated disciplinary / cause membership.terminate — separate, more restricted permission active suspended temporary hold membership.suspend

There is no completed row any more. It existed only for ageing out, and ageing out no longer exists (D-038).

Termination must not be the same permission as lapsing. A lapse is administrative (nobody paid). A termination is a decision about a person's standing in a youth organization, often with safeguarding implications. Conflating them means every volunteer who chases unpaid fees can also expel a member.

A lapse has two faces, and only one of them is a human decision. A lapse triggered by non-payment is the yearly sweep doing its job — nobody decided anything, and "why did I lose access?" has a date for an answer rather than a person. A lapse triggered by a staff decision is a deliberate act with a permission behind it. Both land in the same status; access_log is what distinguishes them, which is another reason the lapse is recorded as an event and not just a column change.

docs.title: 6. Renewal and the yearly fee
docs.text: The fee is flat, per person, yearly, and it expires on a fixed date — typically January (D-040). The membership-relevant part, in full:

docs.title: Renewal opens a new period, not an extended one
docs.text: Shape A, decided (D-016). The previous row closes and a new one opens, linked by membership.renewed_from_membership_id. Extending valid_to in place would be fewer rows and would silently lose the most commonly asked question about renewals — did they renew every year, or skip one and come back?

docs.title: The renewal window replaces the grace status
docs.text:
The old design had a grace status: during it the person was still a member. That is gone. What replaces it is a window tracked as dates, not as a status (D-040):

When What is true On 1 January The membership lapses. They are not a member, and member permissions stop. Inside the window (60 days after expiry) Still not a member — but they may renew without re-applying, and a payment now opens the new period at the expiry date, so the record shows no gap. After 2 March A payment opens a new membership at the payment date. The gap is real. Still no new application required.

The 1 January date has a consequence that reaches past the membership table. The yearly sweep is the only bulk event in a system carefully built to have none: on a single day, every membership in the organization lapses at once. That makes it the day every MEMBERS-gated answer in the organization moves at once, and the day renewal traffic peaks. It is no longer also the day the permission cache is invalidated for everyone: D-114 deleted the stored answer, so the period ending and the lapsed status are the whole of the change, and each member's next check sees it. And it used to be, on the same day, the day the system administrator lost access to the system they administer, which is the hazard D-051 existed to close.

That mechanism is deleted (D-100): there is no system.gate_exempt, no person_holds_gate_exempt, and no resolver clause left to hold a door open. The answer now sits in grant text. A grant written MEMBERS * ROLE(it) stops applying to its holder at the sweep; a grant written ROLE(it) does not, because MEMBERS is simply not in it — which is exactly how D-100 says a whole office is made exempt, and the same sentence that makes the administrator survivable is the one that makes a lapsed treasurer dangerous. Assumption: which offices are written without MEMBERS, and who decides, is not settled by D-100 — the standing report of live grants naming a ROLE(...) operand without MEMBERS is what makes each choice visible to a human (data-model/03 §6), and §9 lists the undecided half as a question.

All four calendar values are columns — duration_months, expiry_month, expiry_day, renewal_grace_days — and that is a requirement rather than a convenience. The organizational year runs with the calendar, and 60 days was chosen for the window on the explicit condition that it stays easy to change (D-048): "Make it 60 days, but it should not be hard to modify."
