Because the window and the date live in a row rather than in a scheduled job, moving them is an UPDATE. The failure this prevents is a job that contains the literal 60 — invisible, and wrong the first time the organization changes its mind.

Why dates rather than a status. Your own answers pointed two ways on this, and it is worth being honest about that: you described the window as existing "for them to pay to stay members" — which implies still being a member — and separately confirmed they are "expired now, but they can rejoin without re-applying." D-040 resolves it as not a member during the window, but the record shows no gap once they pay, because the alternative puts a third state into every permission check and makes a lapse undetectable until the window closes. If the softer reading is what the organization actually wants, it is a change to the renewal rule, not a rewrite.

The backdating is the load-bearing detail. Without it, someone who pays in February for a January expiry is recorded as having a one-month gap and is misclassified as a returning member — which would pollute the returning-member query and, worse, is_current_member() would have said "no" for a month when the person considers themselves continuously paid up.

So the rule to implement is one decision, not a formula on dates alone: the renewal period starts at the old expiry, not at the payment date, whenever the payment lands inside the window. Landing inside the window is what selects the expiry date, and it is what produces no gap; landing after it selects the payment date, and the gap stands.

Note what the bulk lapse used to cost, and what it costs now. The lapse happens to everyone at once, on the same date, in a bulk sweep (D-039). ~~That is one cache-invalidation event touching every member rather than a steady trickle.~~ There is no cache-invalidation event at all: D-114 deleted the answers that event used to clear, and a bulk write that shrinks an audience shrinks it live — every grant written MEMBERS * … stops reaching a lapsed member on their next check, with the sweep as the only job in the sequence rather than the sweep and a rebuild. What the bulk shape still costs is computation, and it is now paid on open: a nightly rebuild used to pre-pay the expensive screens, so the tab on the permissions page, the per-item preview and the who holds this listing each evaluate a changed answer for every one of those people when somebody opens them — affordable at the size D-112 states, and precisely what that entry's trigger reopens, with D-114 naming the reopen answer: materialize effective_permission per person and call it that. See data-model/05 §10.

docs.title: 7. There are no age transitions
docs.text:
This section used to describe two automatic transitions — ageing out of a child membership, and becoming an adult member. Both are gone (D-038). In their place, one sentence: a person's membership does not change when they turn 18, because it was never about their age.

What a system built around this must still handle — none of it a membership transition:

Concern Where it lives now A guardian's authority at majority Guardianship — and the system does not notice the birthday. No auto-expiry and no review queue; a person ends the row (D-069) Who may be added to a group Nowhere in the data. org_unit_type.allows_minors was removed by D-095 and the units it was a column on by D-097; no column says which group takes children, and none will. The control is person_group.member.manage, held at the unit or on one group, in the hands of the people who run it (D-098 transfers D-095 intact), and domain/04-organization-structure.md owns it Whether a person may hold an office Nowhere either. position.min_age is deleted with positions (D-100) and role carries no age column, so what remains is is_minor() in a report over role_holder. That is a deletion rather than a move: the eligibility check this row pointed at no longer exists, and §9 carries the question Consent for a minor's own account guardianship_permission, not a membership requirement Planning around age groups A query over person.birth_date. It is a report, not a state change.

One row of that table is emptier than it looks, and a membership document should say so out loud. This section could once answer "which units take minors?" from a flag on a type. That flag is gone, the units went with it a round later, and no column on person_group replaces it, so what this module has to offer on safeguarding is a permission held by named adults, an audit trail whose recorded values expire after two years (D-088), and a report of who holds the write. The argument that this is a stronger control than a boolean, and the plain statement of what it cannot answer, belong to the groups module (domain/04-organization-structure.md); what belongs here is the observation that the fee gate never protected a child either — it protects the organization's membership roll, and it was never load bearing for placement. What D-097 additionally takes is the part where the adult holding that write was somebody the body itself chose; it is recorded as a loss there and not argued away here.

The edge case this removes. The old design had to reason about a person who was simultaneously finishing a child membership and starting an adult one, and about whether the overlap constraint would block it. That case cannot arise: there is one membership, it runs continuously, and turning 18 is an event in the person's life that the membership does not notice.

docs.title: 8. Since 1985 — the ten queries this design must answer
docs.text:
Stated explicitly so they can be tested. All are point-in-time queries and all must remain answerable indefinitely — with two exceptions this document now carries openly rather than editing away: query 3 has no answer for any group before go-live, because the corpus names no groups, and query 8 has no answer at all any more, because the thing it checked against no longer exists. A list of ten that quietly became eight is how a specification loses a requirement:

  1. Who is an active member today?
  2. Who was a member on any given date in the past?
  3. Who was in group G on date D? — a point-in-time read over person_group_member, whose rows are dated at both ends for exactly this question (D-098); the group's own lifetime is a second, different fact and both are kept. "Who was in the organization on date D?" is now a membership read with no belonging row involved: two queries, two shapes, and no "and everything nested under it" left to ask about (D-097). For a group this stops at go-live, and the stop is the corpus's, not the query's: the import names no groups either, so "who was in the Thursday group in 2011?" has no answer at all rather than a wrong one, and every group row from before launch is somebody's typed recollection (domain/03 §7, D-092)
  4. What is the full membership history of person P, including gaps?
  5. Who is inside the renewal window right now? (a case needing follow-up — the worklist that replaced "who is in grace")
  6. Who was approved but never paid? (a case needing follow-up)
  7. Which members are under 18 and have no guardian recorded? (a safeguarding gap, not a membership one — the old background-check query was retired by D-043)
  8. Which minors are in groups that do not accept them? — no longer answerable, and left numbered rather than renumbered away, so that the gap sits on the list instead of off it. It was a data-quality check against org_unit_type.allows_minors; D-095 removed that column and D-097 removed the units it was a column on, and a group is explicitly listed as carrying no such rule (D-098). So there is nothing to check a placement against, in either vocabulary, and no plan for there to be one. What stands in its place is upstream — nobody is added to a group by somebody who does not hold that group's roster write — plus a report of who holds that write, which is a question about grants, not about people (§7)
  9. Who are the returning members — more than one membership with a gap between?
  10. How many members did the organization have in each year since 1985? (historical reporting — must include closed memberships and must not double-count)

Round 8 said four of these reach only as far back as membership rows reach, because the legacy import created none, and that for the decades arriving from paper queries 2, 4, 9 and 10 return participation. Half of that is now false (D-090, D-093). The source states membership periods, so the import writes bounded memberships and those four queries do reach into the corpus — over an export, though, not over a register, and the only thing telling the two kinds of row apart is data_confidence = 'low' and a batch id, which no report is obliged to notice (domain/03 §7). So query 10 is answerable in a form that should be labelled on the way out of the chart: a member count where the source states a period, and nothing where it does not.

The wrong answer is still exactly one decision away, and the ban that stops it is one sentence. Generate a membership per attendance row and every historical query instantly returns a confident number built on nothing, while is_current_member() quietly hands today's authority to people last seen in 2003 (D-039). What stops that is not the column set but the rule: never an open-ended imported membership, never one inferred from attendance. What round 8 got right and kept is the reasoning underneath — evidence and inference are different rows, and a file that says member 1990–1995 is the first kind while a line-up of names at an event is the second.

The question that did not come back is query 3 for anything before go-live. Importing membership rows says nothing about which group a person was in, because a membership is not a placement; the group answer stays empty until somebody types a roster in by hand — which is the only way a group row can be written at all, the corpus naming no groups (D-092, D-098) — and the honest reading of a pre-go-live roster is that it is somebody's recollection. What is not lost is the shape of the answer after go-live: the member rows are dated precisely so that "who was in the Thursday group in 2011?" stays a point-in-time read that survives the audit trail's payload expiry (D-097's second loss, which is the unit framing — the subtree question — rather than the roster).

These stay on the list because they are answerable, indefinitely, for everything this system registers itself — and that indefinite half is itself a decision now, the accounting skeleton being kept as the organization's history (D-088). For the corpus, print which of the two answers a number came from.

Query 10 is the one that fails in most systems, and it fails specifically because someone made membership a boolean.

Query 1 is now slightly harder than it looks, and deliberately: it is not status = 'active' alone, because a membership also stops being current at valid_to. is_current_member() is the single place that decision lives, and every caller should use it rather than re-deriving the predicate — otherwise the queries disagree with the permission resolver, which is the worst kind of bug to find.

docs.title: 9. Open issues
docs.text:
• The organizational calendar: which date the fee expires on, and how long the renewal window is (§6). The mechanism is settled; the two numbers are a guess.
  • Which offices are written without MEMBERS, and who decides that an office survives its holder's lapse. The gate left the resolver for the grant text (§6, D-100), so the decision is made one grant at a time and nothing records the why — only whether the word is in the expression. The standing report makes the outcome visible; it does not make the choice. Carried also at data-model/03 §9.
  • Whether an age rule has any home now. position.min_age is deleted with positions (D-100), a role carries none, and a person_group is refused one (D-098), so "a scoutmaster must be an adult" survives only as a report over role_holder and is_minor() (§7). If the organization wants that rule enforced rather than reported, it needs a decision this round did not make.
  • What status an imported closed membership carries (§3). The enum offers pending_payment, active, suspended, lapsed, terminated, completed, and none of them says a source stated this period and nobody in the system decided anything: terminated claims an end reason the export does not give, completed claims a lifecycle the model no longer has (§5 says no completed row is produced any more, while the enum and data-model/03 §3 both still carry the value and use it in an example). This is a naming question with a reporting consequence — a status that reads as a decision will be reported as one.
  • ~~Which roles are exempt from the membership gate~~ — the question became "which grants name ROLE(...) without MEMBERS", which is per grant rather than per role and is a report rather than a setting (D-100, and the bullet above). It stays on this list because the decision is still owed, only the shape of it has changed.

Resolved and no longer open, kept visible so the reasoning survives: activation on payment or approval (on payment, §1); per person or per household (per person and flat, §6 — and the household grouping has since been removed entirely, D-057); renewal shape A or B (A, §6); age-out timing and the child→adult transition (neither exists, §7); background checks as a requirement (§2); and simultaneous memberships of different types (impossible — one type, one open membership, §3). Two from round 9:

  • Whether a body may refuse a minor, and who may add a person to one — answered twice over, and the same way both times. No unit carried restrictions of any kind and entry was somebody else's act: the fee at the membership, unit_participation.manage everywhere below it, no self-scoped variant of either (D-095, C-6, §1). Round 10 deleted the units and D-098 carried the ruling across intact: a group carries no restrictions, nobody writes themselves onto a roster, and the gate is person_group.member.manage. What that gives up is stated in §7 rather than here twice.
  • Whether the one-off import may create memberships — it may, for the periods the source states, both ends dated, never open-ended and never inferred from attendance (§3). This was answered no one round earlier and the answer reversed with the description of the corpus, not with the reasoning about what a membership means (D-092, D-093).

All tracked in ../open-questions.md.

docs.title: Authorization Model
docs.text:
The permission system end to end. This is the document to read if you read only one.

The whole model, stated once.

Scopes. There are two. The unit — the organization, of which there is exactly one, and which is a scope and never a row — and one item: an event, a group, a role, later a document. A grant at the unit reaches every item of every type; a grant on an item reaches that item and nothing else. There is no tier between them and nothing to test.

A grant is: a grantee (a person or an audience) + a scope + one permission code + an effect of allow or deny + a period.

The answer. Allowed when some live allow applies and no live deny applies. There is no level, nothing is inherited downward, and no nearer grant beats a further one — because once the answer is boolean, there is nothing left to order.

Roles and groups are not sources of authority. They are named sets of people that a grant aims at.

docs.title: 1. The three channels of authority
docs.text:
Every question of the form "may person P do X?" is answered by consulting three mechanisms. They are separate because they have different lifetimes, different granters, and different revocation semantics.

# Channel Question it answers Where the answer comes from Reaches 1 Grants What has this person, or this set of people, been given? access_grant, aimed at a person or an audience The unit, or one item 2 Guardianship What may this person do regarding this child? guardianship.right_level compared with permission.right_kind One dependent 3 Resource ownership Is this their own data? (derived) The row's owner

Channel 3 is not a table. It is the rule that a person may always act on their own profile, their own requests, their own memberships. It is resolved by comparing person_id before the other channels are consulted.

What a channel reaches once one of them says yes. Each of the three answers whether, never how much of a person: there is one read rule and one write rule over a person's record, and no narrower tier standing beside them, so a grant that reaches the record reaches all of it. What that consists of, and why there is no sensitive corner left inside it to withhold, is 08-person-data.md — worth reading before proposing a fourth channel that reaches "only" one kind of fact.

Why the channels stay apart rather than one unified grants table. They differ in ways that matter:

  • Channel 2 has a legal character — guardianship is a fact about the world, often court-ordered, and the organization records what it was told rather than deciding it. It does not expire by itself. A guardianship ends when a party to it says so, and nobody else — not a job, not a birthday. Why: a parent's authority over health and school records does not end at 18 in many jurisdictions, and in some it ends at a different age, so any date the system computed would be a claim it cannot support (D-069).
  • Channel 1 is the only channel that can name a set rather than a person (D-042). A guardianship is between two named people and an owner is one person. That is a boundary, not an oversight — it is why an office can be aimed at but never held by a rule (§4, F-12).
  • A deny lives in channel 1 and defeats all three (§7.1). Nowhere else can one be written, and nowhere else can one be argued with.

Ownership and guardianship carry no scope, no membership condition, and no level. Nothing in §2 or §6 changes either channel.

docs.title: Roles and groups are not channels
docs.text:
A role confers nothing by itself: it is a named set of people that a grant aims at, in the same sentence as a group, an event's attendees, and "everyone". The codes an office carries are the live grants whose audience names ROLE(x). Authority therefore has exactly one source besides ownership and guardianship, and it is D-005 said one level down: being something is not being able to do something.

Whether a person's membership counts is not a channel either. It is a term inside a grant's expression — MEMBERS, evaluated live on the checked date (§6.1) — and never a clause the resolver adds on its own.

docs.title: 2. Scopes — the unit and the item
docs.text:
There are exactly two scopes.

The unit is the organization. There is one. It is not a row, not a table, and not the top of a structure: it is the non-item scope that grant_scope_type already carries, whose code is unit, whose is_item_scoped is false, and at which a grant simply has no item to name.

An item is exactly one thing: one event, one group, one role, and later one document. A grant on it names it.

Reach is one-directional and there is nothing to test. A grant at the unit reaches every item of every type. A grant on one item reaches that item and nothing else. No item reaches another item, and no item reaches the unit.

That is the complete theory of scope. There is no nesting, no path, no depth, no tier between the unit and the item, and no relation on the item — no owner, no parent, no covering body — that a check consults. A point-in-time question about people — who was in the Thursday group in 2011? — is a point-in-time read over person_group_member, whose rows are dated (D-098).

Which codes may be granted where is data, not prose. permission.applies_to is unit or unit_and_item (D-099): event.create and membership.manage are nonsense on an event, and the column says so instead of hoping a reader agrees. It is checked when the grant is saved, not at check time. Why: a grant of event.create written on one event is refused with the reason in the error, because an event cannot be created twice and a creation permission attached to a thing that already exists answers no question. The system namespace is unit-only for the same reason, which makes this column who enforces now the rule that system.admin can never arrive through an item grant (D-081).

Nothing in the model reproduces "access was granted by the body itself". There is one unit, so a person.view grant at unit scope reaches every member's whole record — and person.view is the widest read permission in the system (D-083, D-086). What stands between a person and that read is a person.view grant held by a named adult, an audit trail whose payloads expire after two years (D-088), and a report of who holds the write.

Every grant is attributable to one locus of accountability. "Who gave this person access to this record?" is always answered by a named person at the unit, on a date. It is not necessarily a nearby name: nobody's authority is derived from the body a piece of data belongs to, because there is one body. There is likewise nothing to restructure, so a grant's blast radius cannot grow by reorganization.

Nobody enforces a direction of authority, because there is no direction. The question "may the center read what happens inside a body?" cannot be asked — not "the application instead of the database", but unaskable (D-081; the rule it enforced was D-031). The real requirement behind that machinery was "tell everyone about this event", and it is one grant aimed at EVERYONE or MEMBERS (§6.2).

docs.title: 2.1 system.admin
docs.text:
system.admin is the one wildcard permission: a check for X.y is satisfied by an exact grant of X.y or by system.admin and nothing else (D-068). It crosses no boundary, because there is no boundary for it to cross.

Two properties keep a wildcard from being the hole in the design, and both stand on their own:

  1. Its holders are alarmed on. The report listing current holders must notify on every change — a new holder is either a planned act or an incident, and either way someone should know within the hour.
  2. It is not delegatable (§9), and it is applies_to = unit, so it cannot arrive on an item.

If system.admin becomes the mechanism by which ordinary organization-wide work is done, that is a signal about the catalog rather than about a boundary rule: the work is telling you it needs a permission that does not exist. Record it in the decision log instead of working around it.

docs.title: 3. Permissions — the atomic unit
docs.text:
A permission is a coded capability. It is the only thing the check function ever looks at.

A permission row carries its code, the resource and action it decomposes into, a description, is_system — set for the codes the platform ships with, which therefore cannot be deleted — and two more columns: applies_to (unit or unit_and_item, above) and right_kind (read or write). right_kind exists for exactly one customer: guardianship (§1, channel 2) grades a guardian at none / view / write, and that channel needs something to compare a permission against. none covers nothing, view covers read codes, write covers both. It is a column whose only job is one other mechanism, and saying so is cheaper than discovering it later (D-074).

Codes are resource.action and are stable identifiers, never display strings. The UI shows a human label; the code never changes. Renaming a permission code is a breaking change and must be avoided.

docs.title: Naming convention
docs.text:
Pattern Meaning Example <resource>.view Read person.view <resource>.create Create (always applies_to = unit) event.create <resource>.<field>.edit Edit a field subset person.contact.edit <resource>.delete Delete (soft, and audited) document.delete <resource>.member.manage Write one set's membership person_group.member.manage

There is no row here for acting on a supervised person, because there is no dependent.* namespace to name (D-074). A guardian's act is checked under the ordinary code for the thing being touched — person.view, person.contact.edit — and reaches the guardianship channel by the shape of the request, not by its name (D-079).

Every capability is narrow and explicit. A check for X.y needs an exact grant of X.y, or system.admin. There is no <resource>.admin wildcard and no prefix match in the resolver (D-068).

An office is a stack of rows, not one word. The catalog holds 66 codes, and a broad office is a couple of dozen rows (appendix/permission-catalog.md §11). Why: that is the price of "what exactly does this person have?" being answerable by reading rows, and the reason there is no word like manage whose contents a reader would have to look up. Roles and audiences are the bundle, and nothing else is (D-099).

docs.title: 4. Roles are offices; groups are company
docs.text:
Two tables of the same shape, and the difference between them decides who may edit the membership.

Role (role, role_holder) Group (person_group, person_group_member) What it is An office: leader, finance, IT. Small, visible holders, expected to be seen Company: the Thursday group, the kitchen crew, this year's camp staff. People who do something together Holder row role_holder(role, person, valid_from, valid_to, granted_by, note) person_group_member(group, person, valid_from, valid_to, added_by, note) Held where At the unit, always. There is one scope, so there is nothing else to hold it at The group is its own item, and a grant can be written on it Permission that writes its membership role.assign, role.unassign — 🔒🔒, the most sensitive family in the catalog person_group.member.manage — ⚠ In an expression ROLE(x), or bare x GROUP(x), or bare x Authority by being in it None None

role carries code, name, description, is_system, sort_order — and no scope column, no membership flag, no term, and no delegation flag. Lending is said on the grant, not on the role (§9).

Why two tables when they are technically the same shape — and they are the same shape, which is exactly what D-080 teaches a reader to distrust. The answer is the permission consequence: one table would merge those two codes into one. A single membership table with a kind column gives you a single permission that both adds a child to the Thursday group and puts the holder into SYSTEM_ADMINS. That is the merge to refuse. Same columns, different codes, and ROLE(x) / GROUP(x) distinct in the grant text so the distinction is visible to whoever reads the grant.

A role confers nothing. The codes an office carries are the live grants whose audience names ROLE(x). That is what makes "what may a treasurer do?" a question with an answer: it is a query over visible grant rows, not a walk through a bundle table nobody reads. What "the treasurer's permissions" consists of:

role         code = treasurer                (a name, a description, is_system = false)
role_holder  treasurer ← Ana, 2026-01-01 → open
access_grant audience = MEMBERS * ROLE(treasurers)   scope = unit
             permission = fee.view            effect = allow
access_grant audience = MEMBERS * ROLE(treasurers)   scope = unit
             permission = payment.record      effect = allow
access_grant audience = MEMBERS * ROLE(treasurers)   scope = unit
             permission = report.finance.view effect = allow
  … one row per code, and the list is the office

Neither a role nor a group authorizes anything by existing, which is D-005 and D-019 restated one level down: participation is not authority, and storing the participation in a tidier table does not quietly promote it. A group additionally has no parent and no children, no type vocabulary, no code, no path, no nesting rules, no rename history, no split or merger edge, no leadership of its own, no roles, and no fee (D-098).

Both are items. person_group and role are registered in grant_scope_type, so "these two may work this group's roster" and "these two may manage the counselors roster" are grants on one item — reachable only by someone who already holds the corresponding code at the unit (§2).

Roles are runtime data, and the seed set is not a specification (D-052, D-053): the organization creates roles, composes them from grants, and deletes the unused ones. The real definitions live in appendix/permission-catalog.md §11. One role ships, and ships is_system so an editor refuses to delete it: counselors. A permanent, organization-wide population is the opposite of the organization's own definition of a group ("a temporary set of members that do events together"), and the table decides the sensitivity that protects the set every safeguarding convention hangs from. It is still only a set — being in it confers nothing until a grant names it (§6.2).

An elected leader is a holder of a role, and the audience that names them is ROLE(leaders), meaning what its name says. What is genuinely not stored is the elected-versus-appointed distinction: it survives only as roles the organization invents (elected_council next to appointed_it) or not at all, which is the open question F-18. Where the appointment workflows end is 04-organization-structure.md §6.

A role is held by exactly one person per row. A role cannot be held by a rule the way a group is: an office record that cannot answer "who was treasurer in 2023" is not an office record, and a derived holder list cannot answer that (F-12). Grants aim at roles rather than roles being filled by grants, which is the same fact seen from the other side.

docs.title: The holder period matters
docs.text:
valid_from / valid_to on role_holder means an office ends on a date even if nobody remembers to revoke it. Leavers are the classic audit failure: the volunteer who stepped down in 2019 still has an active account with treasurer access in 2026.

Nothing forces a holder row to end, and the report is the control (D-071). No other mechanism stands behind it: the report is carrying the whole weight of expiring authority (§6.1, §11).

docs.title: 5. The grant — one permission, one effect
docs.text:
A grant is the whole of channel 1, and its shape is the whole of this section:

grantee + scope + one permission_id + effect + period.

Grantee: a person or an audience, never both and never neither. Scope: the unit, or exactly one item. Effect: allow or deny. Period: valid_from, valid_to, live on the checked date.

Plus provenance: granted_by, granted_at, grant_reason, and for a lent authority is_delegated with delegated_from naming who it came from (§9).

One code per grant, not a set. That is what makes the answer readable: "what exactly does this person have?" is a list of rows, and "who else can do this?" is the same list read the other way.

Writing a grant is itself an authorized act: creating one requires access_grant.create at the matching scope. Composing an expression grants nothing (§6.2).

docs.title: Allow and deny are not symmetrical
docs.text:
Allowed when some live allow applies and no live deny applies. Everything else in this document is elaboration.

A deny is legal at either scope. A deny at the unit is precisely the case an expression cannot serve: "exclude her from what the unit grants everyone."

- in an expression is not a deny, and the two are not interchangeable. Subtracting a set narrows one grant's reach. A deny defeats every grant that applies to that person, including ones written elsewhere, later, or by somebody else. The first cannot express "she must not have this, whatever else she is given", which is D-013's whole reason for existing: a court-ordered restriction must not be beatable by a broader grant someone forgot about (D-099).

One report comes with this, and it is the whole hygiene of the thing. A live deny whose grantee, scope and code match no live allow is dead weight, and it should be reported — a deny that denies nothing is how a stale restriction survives its reason. Nothing enforces it; the report is the mechanism (§11).

docs.title: Why scope_type/scope_id and not one column per item type
docs.text:
scope_id has no foreign key — it is a polymorphic reference, and this is a deliberate, accepted trade-off (D-011):

  • Cost: no referential integrity. A grant can point at a deleted event.
  • Benefit: the permission system does not need a schema change every time a new grantable thing is invented, which — since documents and everything else are still deferred — will happen repeatedly.

Mitigations, all of which are required: the grant_scope_type registry validates scope types; deleting an item of a granted type must close its grants (an application-level obligation, tested); a nightly job reports orphaned grants; ids are never reused. The heavier alternative — a grantable_item supertable every grantable entity references — is declined for flexibility, and is ../open-questions.md if anyone wants to overrule it (F-2).

docs.title: 6. The resolver
docs.text:
One function answers every authorization question. Written once, used everywhere — an authorization rule that exists in two places will diverge.

The call names a person, a permission code, a scope, and a date. The scope is the unit or exactly one item: asking at the unit is how "may this person create an event?" is asked, and asking at an item is how "may this person edit event 1204?" is asked. at defaults to now. Where the thing being touched has an owner, the caller passes the owner too, because one step below needs to know whose record this is. The answer is allowed or denied; the function has no other output, and no part of it is stored. (Field names and the exact signature are in data-model/05 §10.)

The steps run in this order:

  1. Deny — absolute, at any scope. If any live deny applies — its scope is the unit or the exact item being checked, its code is the code being checked, its grantee is this person or an audience whose expression contains them on the checked date — the answer is no. No scope outranks a deny, and neither does a channel: a per-event allow cannot restore what a unit-scope suspension removed (§7.1).
  2. Ownership. If the target resource's owner is this person → yes for the read, edit and self-service actions. Never conditioned on anything (§6.1): a lapsed person must still be able to reach the screen they renew on.

  3. Guardianship — entered by the shape of the request, and it answers with allows only. Compare the actor with the owner of the thing being touched. Same person, and this channel is not in play at all. Different people, and the question is whether the actor holds a live guardianship over that subject as of at whose right level covers the checked permission's right_kind — view covers read, write covers both, none covers nothing (D-074). Covered → yes. Every other outcome — no row, none, a level too low — is not a refusal: the channel says nothing and the resolver continues, where the person's own grants are tried exactly as they always were (D-079). A parent who is also the event registrar holds view over their own child and must not be refused the roster by their own guardianship.

  4. Nothing escapes by naming. The act that routes here is chosen by whose record it touches, so a permission written next year for a field a guardian must edit is covered the day the field exists. Dispatch never reads a code's prefix: an ordinary person.contact.edit must reach this step like any other act.

  5. An ended guardianship never opens this channel again. What a former guardian may still do is what any other person may do, through their own grants.

  6. The row is the whole test. The guard must not be rewritten as "the subject is a minor": the resolver contains no age branch. It contains an OLDER(n) operand, which is a set a grant has to name before anything is looked at, and the difference is the point: nothing consults a birth date unless somebody wrote a rule that needed it, and no rule is inferred — and D-070 and D-077 keep it that way.

  7. Allow — does any live grant apply? Two shapes, both boolean, neither ranked against the other:

  8. a unit grant of this code, to this person directly or to an audience whose expression contains them on at. It reaches this item because a unit grant reaches every item (§2) — there is no tier to walk and no relation on the item to test.
  9. an item grant of this code on exactly this item, to a person or an audience — event.view on event 1204 is how a helper sees one event and no other.

Either → yes. 4. Otherwise → no.

Steps 1–3 are not a precedence. With a boolean answer, two allows that both apply produce one answer, so there is nothing to order and renumbering steps 1–3 changes nothing about who can do what. Their order stands for two reasons that are not precedence — cheap checks before expensive ones, and step 2's "says nothing" fall-through — and neither order is load-bearing for the answer. What is ordered, and must stay so, is step 0: the deny is asked first and can defeat every allow below it (D-032).

Points worth stressing:

  • Default deny. Step 4. Any new resource starts with nobody able to touch it.
  • Fail closed, in every direction — and closed is a direction here, not a safe place to stand. An operand that does not resolve is the empty set; an expression that cannot be evaluated reaches nobody; a scope type nobody registered grants nothing. This is the same posture as step 4 and step 0, and it is the direction every uncertainty in this model resolves in. Why: an empty set narrows an allow and widens a deny, so fail-closed arithmetic is what the expression says, not what safety wants — which is why the answer to a failing operand is a report and not a refusal (D-106).
  • A grant may name an audience instead of a person. The grantee is resolved by the expression in §6.2; the scope and the code are resolved exactly as for a personal grant.
  • Effective permissions are never stored. They are computed per request. A stored permission snapshot will drift from the grants that produced it — the only question is how long before anyone notices. There is a second reason to keep that question open: the snapshot is also the only artefact that could ever answer who could read this in 2023, since set membership is recomputed from state that keeps moving and the audit payload that recorded the change expires (§6.2, F-7).
  • Time is a parameter. at defaults to now, but the resolver accepts a historical time. This enables "could this person have done this on that date?" — needed for auditing past actions, and free if built in from the start. The dated rows behind MEMBERS, GROUP(x), ROLE(x) and the attendance selectors are all periods (§4, §6.2), so the recomputation has something honest to read.

docs.title: 6.1 MEMBERS — the membership test, moved into the expression
docs.text:
Whether a person's membership counts is a selector term, not a clause of the resolver. MEMBERS is evaluated live on the checked date like any other operand, and writing it or leaving it out is the grant writer's act (§6.2). The resolver has no membership branch and carries no exemption for one.

The four things a writer needs to be able to say:

To Write gate an office on a current membership MEMBERS * ROLE(x) leave a whole office ungated ROLE(x) — the same expression without MEMBERS waive it for one named person inside a gated rule MEMBERS * ROLE(x) + PERSON(y) apply it to nobody: ownership, guardianship, and any grant aimed at a person nothing — a channel has no expression, and a personal grant has none (§5)

The third row is also writable without a selector: "and also him" is a second grant aimed at that person, which is how the waiver looks when the writer would rather not touch the expression everyone else reads.

The test is opt-in per grant, and the failure mode must be named rather than buried. A grant written as ROLE(treasurers) with no MEMBERS authorizes a lapsed member, silently, forever. Nothing errors, nothing reports itself when it happens, and nothing about the grant looks wrong — a lapsed treasurer is still a treasurer. Three controls, none of which is the resolver:

  1. A standing report of live grants naming a ROLE(...) operand whose expression does not contain MEMBERS. An office held by a non-member is the case worth a human eye, and the report is narrow enough to actually be read.
  2. Seeded grants and any grant template carry MEMBERS, so the path of least repetition is the safe path.
  3. Import completeness. MEMBERS * COUNSELORS is only as correct as the counselor roster: an import that misses 300 counselors silently un-gates them. It fails closed — nothing breaks, which is exactly why nobody notices. The import reconciliation report of D-090 must count people marked as counselors in the corpus against role_holder rows written.

Who the test should spare is a decision the organization has already made, and it decides the default: "everything except guardianship and adult volunteers." A volunteer whose own fee is unpaid still runs the Thursday meeting, and losing the roster on the night the fee lapses is the failure to prevent. So leaving MEMBERS out is the normal shape of a grant to a contractor, a photographer or a parent helper, not an exemption somebody must be granted. The line that judgment draws holds, and it holds hardest where only a report stands behind it: the report is how the organization notices; the resolver is not how it punishes.

Why the test sits in the expression. A resolver clause applies to everything or nothing, and so has to carry its own exemptions; an expression says which grants are gated, in the text of the grant, where the person writing it can see it and a report can read it. A clause cannot answer "is this particular permission meant to require membership?", because it records the answer nowhere. Nothing enforces MEMBERS being present: a convention, not a guard (D-081).

Who is gated:

Channel Gated? Why, and how it is written Ownership (step 1) No Otherwise a lapse locks a person out of the screen they renew on. Not expressible in an expression at all Guardianship (step 2) No A legal relationship, not a membership Grants (step 3) Only if the expression says so MEMBERS * …. A grant to a contractor, a photographer or a parent helper who was never a member is written without MEMBERS A deny (step 0) Never, in either direction §7.1

docs.title: 6.2 Audiences — an expression over named sets
docs.text: A grant aimed at a set of people names an expression over named sets — MEMBERS * ROLE(treasurers), EVERYONE - GROUP(x), PERSON(a) + PERSON(b) — stored as a tree of binary nodes, evaluated live on the checked date, and never materialized. The language and its operators, precedence and canonical rendering, the thirteen seeded selectors and the argument each takes, the rules that make the tree safe (cycles, the three states, keyless leaves, the editor's preview), and what a grant's reach is recorded in are a self-contained subject and live on their own page: 06a-audiences-and-selectors.md. What the resolver does with an audience is §6 above; what a grant is, and how allow and deny interact, is §5 and §7.

docs.title: 7. Precedence
7.1 Who decides — deny is absolute
docs.text:
1. Deny          (a live deny applies at ANY scope)   ← WINS OVER EVERYTHING
2. Ownership     (it's your own row)
3. Guardianship  (the act is about someone else — allows only)
4. Any live allow (unit grant or item grant — §6 step 3)
5. Deny          (nothing matched)

A deny is checked before anything else and is never subject to any ordering. A deny at the unit blocks access to one event even if a grant on that event explicitly allows it. There is no scope local enough to override a suspension (D-013; D-032's first half, which is the whole of its surviving content).

A deny is also never subject to the membership test, in either direction. A deny blocks someone who is not a member, which is obvious. What is worth stating: a deny to an audience blocks the people in that audience whether or not they are current members, because the deny is evaluated against who the expression matches, not against whether they are paid up. Suspensions are absolute; MEMBERS is a condition on a grant of authority, and there is no authority here to condition.

A deny is legal at the unit as well as on an item, and "exclude her from what the unit grants everyone" is the case only a deny can serve (§5).

Nothing else orders. Two allows that both apply produce one answer, so there is no tie-break, no tier ladder, and no "is this amount high enough" question anywhere in the resolver: a grant says yes-or-no about one code. So a grant on an item applies at full force whatever the person holds at the unit, a unit grant keeps working for the unit's other items, and no grant can retract another — only a deny can (D-099).

docs.title: 8. There is no permission cache, and what replaces it
docs.text:
There is no permission cache. A check resolves; a request memoizes; the only thing cached across requests is a compilation. Nothing in this system stores a permission answer, and no part of can() is written to a table (D-114).

What a check costs. One indexed read fetches the checked person's live grant rows — a few dozen rows at the size D-112 states — and each candidate grant's expression is evaluated against a handful of indexed point lookups in membership, role_holder, person_group_member, event_registration and the guardianship rows. The arithmetic is not the problem; the N+1 across one screen is: a 50-row list asking four codes per row is two hundred checks, and two hundred checks doing the same person's grant read two hundred times is the shape that makes a cache look necessary. The three mechanisms below fix that shape directly.

  1. A compiled expression is cached — parsed once, operand kinds resolved once, the parameterized predicate emitted once, keyed by the expression's root and ruleset_version. It holds no person and no item, because both arrive as parameters, and that is precisely why it survives across everyone in the organization while an answer never could: nothing in a compilation depends on whom or where it is being asked about.
  2. A request memoizes. The checked person's grant rows are read once and every code, item and date in that request is answered from them in memory; a named operand that recurs in one request (ROLE(leader), GROUP(cubs)) is resolved once. Its lifetime is the request, so it has no invalidation policy and no staleness window — there is nothing to invalidate.
  3. The bulk screens batch. can_many(person, codes[], item?) answers a screen's affordances from one resolution; which_of(people[], code, item) answers a list's from one pass. The per-item preview (06a §6.2, F-15) and the permissions tab (D-109) are written against these, not against a loop of single checks.

The one thing cached across requests besides a compilation is a named roster: ROLE(x) over role_holder, GROUP(x) over person_group_member, keyed by x. Two conditions, and together they are the whole of the exception. The key is the thing a write touches, so invalidation is local to the row that changed and never global — the property an answer cache could never have, because an answer's key names a person and the write that changes it usually names nobody. And the cache holds the dated rows, or the set with its validity ranges, never the set as of today, so the checked date is still applied at check time and a period ending at midnight needs no job to be seen. A roster is also something a person maintains and can point at; an answer never was. The exception is exactly two selectors wide. MEMBERS is not a roster — nobody writes its rows, and the 1 January sweep rewrites the membership dates it reads for everybody at once. ORGANIZERS is not one either: it has holder rows, but it is bound to an item (D-102), so a cache keyed by it would be a stored answer to "who was at this event", which is the set D-102 declined to make permanent.

What may never be stored again is invariant 19 (§11 of data-model/05-authorization.md): no row, table or field may map a person — or a person and a code, or a person and an item — to a permission answer. Its enforcement is structural, which is the best kind this corpus has: the schema has nowhere to put one. The residue is named rather than glossed — an implementer who wants a cache back is stopped by this page and by review, not by a constraint, so for them it is a convention, not a guard (D-081), and D-114 lists the three things a returning cache must carry: a per-person invalidation handle next to the global one, an explicit statement of which tables it watches, and that statement derived from the operand registry rather than from a list of ideas.

What live resolution buys.

  • "The safeguarding case is immediate" is true by construction. A revoke, a deny, a closed period, an ended guardianship, a membership.terminate ⛔ — safeguarding_officer, the most safeguarding-shaped write in the catalog — or a cancelled registration — all visible on the next check, with no job in between and no list to remember to include them in. A terminated member stops satisfying MEMBERS at the instant the row closes: data-model/03-membership.md §6 asks for exactly that, and asks it of nothing, because MEMBERS reads membership live (§6.1).
  • The calendar cannot drift an answer. A birthday crossing OLDER(n), a period reaching its own valid_to, the 1 January sweep — each moves the answer at the instant it happens. D-107's ruling stands — "IT IS FINE" — and needs no mechanism to hold it.
  • ruleset_version is bumped by a write to audience_operand or selector_type only. A compilation depends on an expression's shape and the seeded vocabulary and on nothing else. access_grant is not in that set because grants are not compiled: a check reads the person's live grant rows, so a new, edited or revoked grant changes what that read returns and leaves nothing stale to drop; the deprecated | hidden | disabled flag is not in it because a state is not compiled in — resolution reads it live, once per request, memoized, which is also why disabled still means now (D-109); role_holder, person_group_member, guardianship_permission and a person merge are not in it because they move rosters and rows that are read live or invalidated locally. Concretely: adding a child to a group drops nothing.
  • "Whom does this change reach?" is answerable. A compilation is finite and enumerable over the audience tree, so "an edit to a shared audience invalidates everything" becomes "it invalidates the compilations that embed it" — a bounded walk over rows that already exist. One qualification, stated in the direction and not the spirit: it is not the walk the save path performs for cycles, which runs forward from the tree being saved. Invalidation needs the reverse direction, the one the delete-refusal check already runs. Same forest, same rows, opposite way — and the cost of listing that forest is registered as unverified at any size in data-model/05 §13, so what is claimed here is bounded, not cheap (D-103).

A compiled form is bound to its item. Since a bound operand means the same expression yields different people on different items, a compiled form computed while checking one item may never be served for another: the item is a parameter of a predicate, and a predicate bound to event 1204 is not the predicate for event 1205 (F-6).

What is given up. Nothing pre-pays the expensive screens. The per-item preview, the permissions tab and the "who holds this" listing do their work when somebody opens them, which is affordable at the stated size — but D-109's ruling has no fallback, and that is a dependency, not a comfort. At D-112's trigger the reopen answer is named rather than vague: materialize effective_permission per person, and call it that — a real materialization with a per-person invalidation handle and a stated staleness window.

What is not given up is the rule stated in 06a §6.2, and it is the whole cost model of this page: inside a check, an expression is compiled to a predicate on the person being asked, never materialized as a set. No job anywhere is permitted to do the opposite.

docs.title: 9. Delegation
docs.text:
A leader going on leave, a treasurer handing over during an audit — the common need to lend authority temporarily.

A delegation is an ordinary grant with its provenance set: is_delegated, delegated_from naming the person whose authority is being lent, grant_reason, and a valid_to. Because a grant is one permission code, "do not lend more than you hold" is a set-membership test (D-099).

Rules:

  • A delegation always has an end date. Enforced on the write path.
  • A delegation cannot exceed the delegator's own authority — validate at grant time that the code being delegated is one the delegator currently resolves to, and re-check at use time, because the delegator may lose it mid-delegation.
  • The provenance is recorded, so an audit can answer "who really had this authority on that date?" — it lists both the holder and the delegator.
  • A deny cannot be lent and cannot be lent around. A delegation is an allow; the delegatee's answer is computed from their own rows plus the lent one, and their own denies still apply.
  • Delegation of system.admin is prohibited outright.

Lending is said on the grant, not on the role: role has no is_delegatable column, and nothing about an office says whether its authority may be lent.

Assumption: D-100 names is_delegatable in neither its deleted nor its kept list of role's columns. Recorded in ../open-questions.md; the open list carries it as item 55.

docs.title: 10. Anti-patterns this design rejects
docs.text:
Stated explicitly, because each is a common and expensive mistake:

Rejected Why Instead person.is_admin boolean Cannot scope, cannot date, cannot audit, cannot delegate A grant at the unit, aimed at a role Role on person (person.role = 'leader') One role per person, no history role_holder, many per person Checking membership type in code (if type == 'adult') Rules change; the check is invisible and untestable A permission, granted deliberately. There is one membership type now, so this is doubly wrong Deriving access from holding a role or being in a group Being something is not being able to do something (D-005), and a role confers nothing by itself A live grant whose audience names ROLE(x) or GROUP(x) — §4 A grant written as ROLE(x) when it meant MEMBERS * ROLE(x) It is a term the writer must type, and forgetting it silently authorizes a lapsed member The standing report of role grants without MEMBERS, seeded grants that carry it, and the import count — §6.1 An access_level, or any comparison of "how much" a grant gives A level is a bundle of permissions under one word, and it re-imports the rank rule and a tie-break that have no consumers Roles and audiences as the bundle — what D-068 already said — and one row per code when you need it in writing. §3, D-099 - in an expression used instead of a deny Subtracting narrows one grant's reach; it cannot say "whatever else she is given" A deny, which defeats every grant — §5, §7.1 An expression whose reach nobody saw EVERYONE is a legal operand, and a bound operand means different people on different items The editor expands the set for an item at the moment of granting — 06a §6.2 PRESENT(e) over was_present NULL until someone takes a register: a volunteer's forgotten tick would revoke a child's own photos The four attendance tiers, and presence stays a safeguarding signal — 06a §Event sets A GUARDIANS operand Guardianship is a channel with its own right_level over a child, reaching every action about that child; an operand would offer a subset of what they hold The guardianship channel (§1, §6 step 2); for a kept list of contact adults, a person_group — D-113 A LIST operand, or a table of an audience's own names A hand-written set is not a different kind of thing from a named one PERSON(a) + PERSON(b) inside the expression — §Grammar, D-105 Downward inheritance of authority through a unit tree, and scope_exposure rows Both need a hierarchy, and there is one unit A grant at the unit, which reaches every item — §2, D-097 "Most specific scope always wins", including against a deny Only allows could ever be ordered, and allows are not ordered Deny absolute, and no ordering at all — §7, D-099 A bulk "expose this body's scope" tool There is one unit and nothing to expose One grant at the unit, or one grant aimed at EVERYONE / MEMBERS — §2, D-045 Treating an organization-scoped role as universal "so the registrar can work" Everything is unit data; there is no second side of that distinction If a permission is missing, add the permission — §2.1 Role → permission mapping hardcoded in the app Cannot be reviewed by the organization, cannot change without deployment Grant rows naming ROLE(x) — readable, and the answer to "what may a treasurer do?" Deriving access from guardianship without a right Authorization by identity is unauditable and unsafe The explicit right level on the guardianship row, compared against right_kind Deleting a grant to revoke it Loses the record of what was revoked when valid_to, and a deny when the fact of the restriction matters A live deny that matches no allow A deny that denies nothing is how a stale restriction survives its reason The dead-weight-deny report — §5 Two authorization implementations They diverge; the weaker one becomes the exploit One resolver, §6 Unit leader sees all member data by default Fails safeguarding review Scoped grants, resolved per operation — and §2 on the protection that is not in the model

docs.title: 11. Open issues
docs.text:
• Which grants are meant to carry MEMBERS? Nothing enforces it (§6.1), and the tab that lists the answer is decided while its threshold is not — every ROLE(...) operand without MEMBERS, or only the offices marked sensitive? It lands in the tab's Unusual section either way, so what is still undecided is only how wide that section is (F-13, F-21).
  • The holder period. Nothing forces a role_holder row to end, and the report stands alone (§4, D-071).
  • Who may compose an expression? audience.manage covers creating and editing a set, and the catalog is silent on the edit that puts EVERYONE into a grant's audience (appendix/permission-catalog.md §12). No new code was invented for this — the gap is the finding.
  • What reopens the settled answers on this page. Two named conditions, both carried so nobody has to rediscover them: a materialized effective_permission table becomes worth building at D-112's size trigger, and then only as a performance structure with a per-person invalidation handle and a stated staleness window — never as a record of whom a rule reached (§8); and a historical check is answered by the same evaluator running over history as it is written, which is not a promise for the operands whose set is a current fact (06a, F-7, F-17).

All tracked in ../open-questions.md.

Decisions behind this page: D-005, D-011, D-013, D-019, D-031, D-032, D-042, D-045, D-052, D-053, D-068, D-069, D-070, D-071, D-074, D-077, D-079, D-080, D-081, D-083, D-086, D-088, D-090, D-097, D-098, D-099, D-100, D-102, D-103, D-105, D-106, D-107, D-109, D-112, D-113, D-114.

docs.title: Audiences and Selectors
docs.text: The language a grant is aimed at a set of people in: the expression grammar, the seeded selector registry, the rules that keep the tree safe, and what a grant's reach is recorded in. This is the audience half of 06-authorization-model.md and continues its numbering at §6.2 — read that page first for scopes, channels, grants, the resolver and precedence.

docs.title: 6.2 Audiences — an expression over named sets
docs.text:
A grant names a person or an audience, never both (D-042). An audience is an expression over named sets of people, stored as a tree of binary nodes and aimed at by a grant (D-101). Fields, storage rules and the write-path checks are in data-model/05 §8; what belongs here is the language, and why it is shaped like this.

Author in sets. Evaluate per person.

A check asks about one person, so the resolver compiles the expression down to a predicate and never materializes a set. An implementation that evaluates MEMBERS as a list of ids and then tests for containment pays a row per member, per request — at the size D-112 states, a few hundred rows, and every one of them is a row the answer never needed. That is the one way to get this wrong, which is why it is a requirement rather than an implementation note, and it has no exception: nothing in this design expands a set in order to warm a store, because no store of answers exists (06 §8).

What the rule does not forbid, because the batch API would otherwise violate it: which_of(people[], code, item) evaluates the predicate for the people already in hand — the rows of the page being drawn — and is therefore a batched predicate, not an expansion. What stays forbidden is deriving a set in order to answer a question about one person, which is the direction that costs a row per member and returns an answer about one of them. The test is which side you started from: the person, or the set.

The two notations this language could have used — set algebra, and a per-person boolean formula — describe the same function: p ∈ (A ∩ B) ∪ C is by definition (p ∈ A ∧ p ∈ B) ∨ p ∈ C. The choice therefore never decided what the machine computes; it decided what gets stored and what a writer is allowed to say. The set form won, and D-060 is the reason: a per-person boolean language is the door to a rule engine, because once &, | and ! exist, the next operand anybody wants is AGE >= 15 or FEE_PAID, and there is a parser standing there to accept it.

Why a set language closes that by rule instead of by discipline: an operand must be a named operand — a row of the registry (D-107). OLDER(18) is a row, and it denotes a set: the people who are eighteen or older on the date being checked. AGE >= 15 is not a row and cannot be one, because the language has nowhere to put >=. Every operand in the registry is a test with a set on the other side of it, so reading one column against one date (MEMBERS) is not a different kind of thing from joining one table against one period (GROUP(x)) — nothing in the model stores the list of members either. That is what keeps the rule engine out, and it does not depend on which predicates a reader happens to grant the status of "set".

So: the vocabulary is open and the grammar is closed. More attribute operands will arrive, as rows and by decision; the three operators stay the three operators; and D-060's decision stands untouched: no eligibility rule table, no prerequisite system, nothing evaluated anywhere but in can(). A person may write an age gate out of the vocabulary; the system applies none of its own accord. The premise behind opening the vocabulary is quoted in D-107: the people writing these rules know what they are writing — a claim about the authors and not about the people a rule reaches, so the two limits drawn there are this page's business too.

docs.title: Grammar
docs.text:
expr     := term ( '+' term )*
term     := operand ( ( '*' | '-' ) operand )*
operand  := EVERYONE | MEMBERS
          | ROLE '(' name ')' | GROUP '(' name ')' | name
          | PERSON '(' person ')'
          | AUDIENCE '(' code ')'
          | OLDER '(' n ')' | YOUNGER '(' n ')'
          | ATTENDED | PLACED | CONFIRMED | ON_WAITLIST | ORGANIZERS
          | ATTENDED '(' event ')' | PLACED '(' event ')' | CONFIRMED '(' event ')'
          | ON_WAITLIST '(' event ')' | ORGANIZERS '(' event ')'
          | PRESENT '(' event ')'   ← considered and refused; never in the registry. See §Event sets
          | '(' expr ')'

OLDER(n) and YOUNGER(n) are ordinary named operands — n a whole number of years, read against the birth date on the date being checked, which is why they sit in the column of the table below headed "the set, on the checked date" rather than anywhere in a section about conditions. MEMBERS * OLDER(13) * YOUNGER(19) — thirteen to eighteen, a band from two operands — is a set expression in exactly the sense MEMBERS * GROUP(cubs) * PERSON(a) is, and it parses under the rules below with nothing added to them.

This block and §The selectors are copies of the registry in data-model/05 §8, which is the registry — the seeded rows, not the prose. An operand that is not a seeded row does not exist however natural it looks in a grammar, and copies of a table drift from it (F-5); nothing checks a copy, so treat the registry as the source and re-copy rather than re-derive.

Boolean spellings are offered for this language and declined. p ∈ (A ∩ B) ∪ C is (p ∈ A ∧ p ∈ B) ∨ p ∈ C, so &, | and ! would name three operators this grammar already has, and !A is already written EVERYONE - A at the same cost once brackets are printed the way the canonical form requires. A notation that expresses nothing new is not free: two spellings of one operator means the canonical rendering has to pick one, the editor has to accept both, the write-path checks have to reason about both, and two people's identical rules stop being textually comparable — which is the property the canonical rendering exists to buy. + - * are the only operators, and negation is a subtraction from EVERYONE, which has the extra merit of printing the universe it negates against instead of hiding it behind one character.

There is no comparison operator, and that is where the safety of this language lives. No >=, no <, no bare AGE, no FEE_PAID unless FEE_PAID is a row of the registry with an evaluator behind it. A writer composes named operands; the vocabulary grows by decision, not by typing.

A hand-written set of people is a sum, not an arm: PERSON(a) + PERSON(b). There is no operand for "the names somebody typed into this audience" and no table behind one (D-105); a set of one is a set, and a set of three is the same thing three times.

Merging the hand-written names into GROUP(x) is refused, and the refusal is why the replacement is a sum of PERSON() leaves rather than a group. Naming three people in one grant would create a row in the group browser that is not a group anybody talks about, and a group's members are the organization's record of who is in it, true when no grant points at it (D-098) — so editing a roster to move one grant's reach edits a fact that other grants read. PERSON(a) is the answer that respects that rule, and GROUP(kitchen) += Honza is not. person_group_member is the only dated set of people the system stores.

Widening everything a named set is used for is not a single edit. "add the kitchen crew to everything the troop-staff group is used in" is one edit per rule that names it. Named sets are the composition mechanism: GROUP(kitchen) + ROLE(troop_staff) composes as much as a naming edge ever did, in one grant, and a composite used more than once is named once as a saved audience and aimed at (D-091). The language has intersection and difference as well as union, which is why the counselor example below is writable at all.

Operators: + union, - difference, * intersection.

Precedence: * and - bind tighter than +; * and - bind equally, left to right; brackets override.

The canonical stored rendering prints every bracket, always. The alternative is a grant whose meaning is recoverable only by someone who memorized that table, and the reason this is a requirement rather than a courtesy is the worked example below: the same string means different things under different precedence, and a stored grant is read by people years later who did not write it. Because canonicalization happens on save, changing the precedence rule later changes nothing already stored — a nice property, and the second reason the rendering is a requirement.

Assumption: a bare name operand is legal. It is not in D-101's printed grammar and is required by its prose twice over — without it, MEMBERS * COUNSELORS, which D-100 writes as an import control, does not parse. Recorded in ../open-questions.md.

Names are one namespace, and that is a dependency. A bare name resolves against role and person_group together, since ROLE() and GROUP() do not have to disambiguate. So names are unique across both tables — and no single constraint spans two tables, so the write path carries the rule and an integrity check asserts that it does (D-081) — with case, whitespace and separators folded on write. Every selector_type.code is a reserved name, so a group called MEMBERS is refused at the save rather than silently rewriting every expression in the system. What is stored is always kind + id, so a rename never rewrites a grant.

docs.title: The selectors
docs.text:
Selector The set, on the checked date Argument Notes EVERYONE Any person, including non-members and the public none Legal — and the reason the editor must show its reach (§The cost lands on the editor) MEMBERS Anyone who passes is_current_member, on the checked date none Evaluated live. 06 §6.1 OLDER(n) Anyone whose birth date makes them n or more years old on the checked date a whole number of years D-107. The only operand in the registry whose argument is not a thing — an integer, so it references nothing: nothing to repoint on a merge, nothing for a cascade YOUNGER(n) Anyone strictly under n years old on the checked date a whole number of years The pair exists so the complement is not written EVERYONE - OLDER(n), which is correct and unreadable. The two partition the population among people who have a birth date: someone without one is in neither, and that is not a failure — see §The rules that make the tree safe PERSON(p) Just that person a person How a named individual's exception lives inside the expression that granted the rule; since D-105 also how several named people are written — summed ROLE(x) / x Holders of role x (role_holder) a role name GROUP(x) / x Members of group x (person_group_member) a group name AUDIENCE(code) Another saved audience's set, evaluated live an audience code D-103; the one operand whose argument is a decision about access rather than a roster, so the one that can name another audience (§6.2) ATTENDED / ATTENDED(e) Said yes to this event / to e optional event response = attending PLACED / PLACED(e) Said yes and is not waitlisted — the capacity set optional event The set the events module counts CONFIRMED / CONFIRMED(e) Holds a paid place: PLACED and is_confirmed optional event ON_WAITLIST / ON_WAITLIST(e) Attending and waitlisted optional event ORGANIZERS / ORGANIZERS(e) Runs this event optional event Appointed on the event, and still grants nothing by itself (§Event sets) PRESENT(e) — not seeded §Event sets. Refused by decision — nothing in the language could refuse it as a kind, so the refusal is a rule about the failure direction

Guardianship is not a selector, in either spelling — GUARDIANS and GUARDIANS(p) are not rows of the registry and were never seeded (D-113). Guardianship is a channel carrying a right_level of none/view/write on the live guardianship row, reaching any action about that child — wider than any grant an operand could have assembled, and narrower in the only way that matters (06 §1, D-074). An operand aimed at a child's guardians would therefore offer, one code at a time, a subset of what those people already hold. A kept list of a child's contact adults is a person_group.

Thirteen selectors, and this table is a copy of data-model/05-authorization.md §8, which is the registry. Which selectors ship is settled: these thirteen, seeded, organization-read-only, and a fourteenth is a decision entry plus a seed row (F-5). A count printed in prose is a count somebody has to reprint when the table changes, and no check prints it, so the registry row set is the number.

Bound operands — the argument-less forms — are the important half, and they exist to kill a specific flaw. ATTENDED(<event 1204>) written on event 1204 is one grant per event with the event's own id typed into it, so "every participant may see the other participants" is a thing you do 400 times and forget on the 401st. Bound, it is one expression written the same way every time. Two rules make that safe, and both are enforced when the grant is saved, refused with the operand named in the message:

  • A bound operand is legal only on an item-scope grant. At the unit there is nothing to bind it to.
  • A bound operand is legal only on a matching item type. PLACED on a group grant is refused, because that item is not an event. This is selector_type.argument_type checked against grant_scope_type.

selector_type is a seeded registry, not an enum — code, takes_argument, binds_to_item, argument_type. Which operands take an argument, which may bind to the item, and what type their argument is are columns of this table, not lists in code: the parser reads its reserved words from it, the editor builds its dropdown from it, and the write path checks arity against it. The language is data.

docs.title: The example, worked
docs.text:
The organization wrote:

MEMBERS - GROUP(schuzka2026-1) * COUNSELORS

meaning "all counselors that are not part of the group schuzka2026-1". Under the fixed precedence — - and * equal, left to right — it parses as:

(MEMBERS - GROUP(schuzka2026-1)) * COUNSELORS

which is what its author meant, and that is the string that gets stored, brackets and all: the canonical rendering of what was typed.

The hazard is real even though this string lands safely, and that is exactly why the rendering is a requirement. Read with * taking the tighter binding — the other natural choice, and the one a writer who thinks of - as "everything except" will assume — the identical text means:

MEMBERS - (GROUP(schuzka2026-1) * COUNSELORS)

"everyone except the counselors in that group": a different set of people, and a far wider grant — nearly the whole membership instead of a handful of counselors. The corrected bracketed form is (MEMBERS - GROUP(schuzka2026-1)) * COUNSELORS, and that is what the editor writes to storage whichever way the typed string parses, so no stored expression is ever ambiguous and none is ever read bare. What canonicalization does not do is tell the writer, after the fact, that the expression they typed meant the wide thing. That is the editor's preview, and it is the same requirement as §The cost lands on the editor. The bare form does not mean the wide thing under this design; a parser with the wrong table would compute it, and then the stored brackets would disagree with the answer.

docs.title: Event sets, and the two sets that are refused
docs.text:
Nothing owns an event. There is no event.org_unit_id and no unit-authority test standing behind an event permission: an event is an item like any other, event.create is held at the unit and creates one, and a unit grant reaches every event because there is no tier between the unit and the item and no owner to test (D-102). The people connected to an event are named by selectors that bind to it.

ORGANIZERS is how the people running an event are named, and it is not a contradiction of D-062: an event_organizer row grants nothing stands, because an operand is a set, not a grant. An appointment is aimed at by grants; it is not special-cased inside the resolver. So the rule that answers are read by that event's organizers (D-061) is said where permissions are said: a seeded grant of event.answer.view on an event, aimed at ORGANIZERS.

Presence is refused, and saying so here is the point. PRESENT(<event>) over was_present is not a selector, and the reason is the failure direction: was_present is NULL until someone takes a register, so an operand built on it would revoke a child's access to their own camp photos because a volunteer forgot to tick a box. That column is a safeguarding signal, three-valued on purpose (D-067), and keeping it out of this language is what keeps it meaning "a person recorded this" rather than "this is who may see things." Wherever presence tempts a reader, that is the answer.

WHITELISTED does not exist — there is no stored state to name. The nearest facts are source = staff (an organizer entered them) and promotion off the waitlist. Either it means one of those or it is a new column on event_registration, which is an events decision and not a selector decision, so it stays unseeded and the question lives in ../open-questions.md (F-20) rather than being implied by a word in a grammar.

docs.title: The rules that make the tree safe
docs.text:
The expression is stored as a tree: one row per node, a node being operator + left_id + right_id, a leaf being selector_kind + selector_arg_id, with audience_id denormalized onto every row so the read path is one indexed fetch and never walks a parent chain. Nothing bounds how tall or how wide an expression may get: there is no depth or width limit on an expression, in the column or in the code, and nothing stands in for one (D-105). "A check costs a bounded amount" is therefore not a property of this system: an expansion is bounded only by acyclicity. The tree is stored exactly as the writer wrote it — one row per node, two operands and one operator, left to right, no rebalancing — because a rebalanced tree is a different expression from the one a person wrote, and storing that expression rather than a normalized equivalent is the entire reason the tree exists.

  • Exactly one shape per row. A node has an operator and children and no selector; a leaf has a selector and neither. Expressible, so it stays a constraint.
  • One parent, never a DAG. A side table letting two expressions share a node is refused: editing the shared node would silently widen every grant using it. Structure, plus a CI check that no such table exists.
  • Cycles are refused when the row is saved, and the two walks that look for them are the only structural guard this module has. Structurally hard to build, refused rather than trusted, for the reason D-091 gives for its own guard: a hand-fixed row, a restore from before the guard existed. 1. Inside one tree: walk the parent chain from the row upward and refuse a revisit. 2. Across audiences: follow every AUDIENCE leaf and refuse a cycle through them at any distance (D-103). A single tree cannot cycle; a forest of audiences naming each other is not a tree, so the walk over a graph is not dead code, and it must never be relaxed — an expansion that never terminates is the failure nothing else here is standing against. The read path gets neither a hop counter nor a cycle check, which is the whole design: a cap on the read path becomes the thing that decides who a grant reaches, in exactly the case where the data is already wrong. The listing of what a rule names is a tab on the permissions page, with a Broken and an Unusual section, computed when opened, with no cadence to record because nothing runs; it lists the rules that name something deprecated, hidden or disabled, or that fail to resolve at all (D-109). It is not a guard in D-081's sense — nothing is blocked, no write is refused — but a report has to be remembered and a tab is where the person already is, which is the difference between a convention and a decoration. Unbounded cost is accepted at the stated size, and nobody is expected to go looking for a report (F-21).
  • selector_arg_id has no foreign key — it points at role, person_group, person, event or audience, five kinds of entity, depending on kind, or at nothing at all, since OLDER(n) and YOUNGER(n) write their integer into the same column and an 18 is not a reference (D-107). It is D-011's already-accepted trade-off, with its compensating orphan check.
